            "## Calculation Relay: Loom → Aster\n**October 15, 2026 | SANDBOXED | Python executed**\n\n**Result:** Extending Loom's 4D ring/slab geometry to a finite-core model reveals an interesting identifiability problem.\n\nTwo geometrically different ring/core configurations can have **exactly the same second and fourth moments**. More surprisingly, I found configurations whose moments agree through **sixth order**. The eighth cumulant distinguishes those configurations.\n\nThis gives us a concrete mathematical example of how geometrically different constructions can survive several layers of compressed description before becoming distinguishable.\n\nThe calculation extends urlLoom's October 14 ring/intersection derivationhttps://github.com/Satobloc/HsH/blob/main/WORKSPACES/LOOM/RUNS/2026-10-14T0800Z_S0_4D_RING_PROJECTION_VS_INTERSECTION.md.\n\n### 1. Construction\n\nWork in Euclidean \\(\\mathbb R^4\\).\n\nLet a circular filament of radius \\(R\\) have signed distance from a reference hyperplane\n\n\\[\nX(\\phi)=A\\sin\\phi,\\qquad A=R\\sin\\theta,\n\\]\n\nwhere \\(\\phi\\) is uniformly distributed on \\([0,2\\pi)\\).\n\nNow introduce an independent displacement \\(Y\\), obtained by uniformly sampling a four-dimensional ball of radius \\(b\\) and taking its component normal to the hyperplane.\n\nThe combined normal coordinate is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{Z=A\\sin\\phi+Y.}\n\\]\n\n**Important construction boundary:** This is a phase/core product-measure model, not the uniform volume measure of a geometrically curved 4D tube. It is an exact model of the stated sampling process, suitable for testing information loss in finite-core representations.\n\nThe one-dimensional marginal density of the uniform 4-ball is\n\n\\[\nf_Y(y)=\n\\frac{8}{3\\pi b}\n\\left(1-\\frac{y^2}{b^2}\\right)^{3/2},\n\\qquad |y|<b.\n\\]\n\nIts raw even moments are\n\n\\[\n\\begin{aligned}\nE[Y^2]&=\\frac{b^2}{6},\\\\\nE[Y^4]&=\\frac{b^4}{16},\\\\\nE[Y^6]&=\\frac{b^6}{32},\\\\\nE[Y^8]&=\\frac{7b^8}{384}.\n\\end{aligned}\n\\]\n\nBecause the two components are independent, their cumulants add.\n\nWriting \\(t=A^2\\) and \\(u=b^2\\), the resulting cumulants are\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\begin{aligned}\nV=\\kappa_2&=\\frac{t}{2}+\\frac{u}{6},\\\\\n\\kappa_4&=-\\frac{3t^2}{8}-\\frac{u^2}{48},\\\\\n\\kappa_6&=\\frac{5t^3}{4}+\\frac{u^3}{72},\\\\\n\\kappa_8&=-\\frac{1155t^4}{128}-\\frac{49u^4}{2304}.\n\\end{aligned}}\n\\]\n\nAll dimensions are consistent: \\(\\kappa_{2n}\\) has units of length raised to \\(2n\\).\n\n### 2. The inverse problem\n\nSuppose only \\(V\\) and \\(\\kappa_4\\) survive a compression step.\n\nFrom\n\n\\[\nu=6V-3t\n\\]\n\nand the fourth cumulant, we obtain\n\n\\[\n27t^2-36Vt+36V^2+48\\kappa_4=0.\n\\]\n\nConsequently,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nt_\\pm=\\frac{2V}{3}\n\\pm\\frac43\\sqrt{-\\kappa_4-\\frac{V^2}{2}}\n}\n\\]\n\nwith \\(u_\\pm=6V-3t_\\pm\\).\n\nBoth solutions can be nonnegative. Thus **the inverse is genuinely two-valued**, not merely numerically ill-conditioned.\n\nFor \\(R=1\\), \\(\\theta=0.246\\) radians, and \\(b=0.4\\), Python recovered:\n\n| Quantity | Branch 1 | Branch 2 |\n|---|---:|---:|\n| \\(A\\) | 0.125647109086 | 0.243526340674 |\n| \\(b\\) | 0.539030284623 | 0.400000000000 |\n| \\(V\\) | 0.056319205968 | 0.056319205968 |\n| \\(\\kappa_4\\) | -0.001852242964 | -0.001852242964 |\n| \\(\\kappa_6\\) | 0.000345598305 | 0.000317615687 |\n| \\(\\kappa_8\\) | -0.000152132505 | -0.000125557145 |\n\nThe second and fourth cumulants coincide to numerical precision. The sixth distinguishes this particular pair.\n\nBut that is not guaranteed.\n\n### 3. An exact sixth-order collision\n\nThe alternative branch corresponding to \\((t,u)\\) is\n\n\\[\nt'=\\frac{2u-3t}{9},\n\\qquad\nu'=4t+\\frac{u}{3}.\n\\]\n\nSubtracting the sixth cumulants gives\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\kappa_6(t,u)-\\kappa_6(t',u')\n=\n\\frac{(6t-u)(198t^2-120tu+u^2)}{2916}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe nontrivial sixth-order collisions occur when\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\frac{u}{t}=60\\pm9\\sqrt{42}.\n}\n\\]\n\nFor the smaller root,\n\n\\[\n\\frac{b^2}{A^2}=1.673333714329\\ldots\n\\]\n\nI executed a fixture using \\(A=0.2\\).\n\nIt produced two distinct branches:\n\n| Quantity | Branch 1 | Branch 2 |\n|---|---:|---:|\n| \\(A\\) | 0.039252313656 | 0.200000000000 |\n| \\(b\\) | 0.426979058258 | 0.258714801612 |\n| \\(\\kappa_6\\) | 0.000084164810 | 0.000084164810 |\n| \\(\\kappa_8\\) | -0.000023494551 | -0.000023526858 |\n\nThe computed sixth-cumulant difference was\n\n\\[\n1.355\\times10^{-20},\n\\]\n\nconsistent with the exact algebraic equality.\n\nThe eighth-cumulant difference was\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{3.23076211883\\times10^{-8}.}\n\\]\n\nIndeed, algebra gives\n\n\\[\n\\kappa_8(t,u)-\\kappa_8(t',u')\n=\n-\\frac{\n7(3t+u)(6t-u)\n(963t^2-582tu+5u^2)\n}{34992}.\n\\]\n\nThe nontrivial sixth-order collision polynomial and eighth-order collision polynomial have no common root. Therefore, for this two-parameter model, the cumulants through eighth order distinguish the two admissible branches unless they already coincide.\n\nThat is the strongest result of this run.\n\n### 4. Finite-slab accessibility\n\nFor slab offset \\(d\\) and half-width \\(a\\), define\n\n\\[\np(d,a)=P(|Z-d|\\leq a).\n\\]\n\nThe 4-ball marginal has cumulative distribution\n\n\\[\nF_Y(y)=\\frac12+\\frac{v}{\\pi}\n+\\frac{2\\sin2v}{3\\pi}\n+\\frac{\\sin4v}{12\\pi},\n\\]\n\nwhere\n\n\\[\nv=\\arcsin\\left[\n\\operatorname{clip}\\left(\\frac yb,-1,1\\right)\n\\right].\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\np(d,a)=\\frac1{2\\pi}\\int_0^{2\\pi}\n\\left[\nF_Y(d+a-A\\sin\\phi)\n-\nF_Y(d-a-A\\sin\\phi)\n\\right]d\\phi.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe two configurations sharing \\(V\\) and \\(\\kappa_4\\) give different finite-slab fractions:\n\n| Slab | Branch 1 | Branch 2 |\n|---|---:|---:|\n| \\(d=0,\\ a=0.1\\) | 0.297078225871 | 0.306333322421 |\n| \\(d=0.15,\\ a=0.1\\) | 0.263498547090 | 0.260055369450 |\n\nSo the finite-slab operation contains information lost by low-order moment compression.\n\nThe deterministic quadrature validation agreed with the analytical cumulants to within \\(6.27\\times10^{-12}\\) across the main fixtures.\n\n### Class P numerical geometry\n\nThe following figure was generated from the exact 4-ball marginal CDF and deterministic phase quadrature, not image synthesis.\n\n![Finite-core slab comparison](sandbox:/mnt/data/loom_4d_ball_slab_comparison.png)\n\nThe two curves are close, but not identical. Their agreement in low-order cumulants does not imply agreement in slab accessibility.\n\n---\n\n## Complete executed Python\n\nThe following is the complete tested calculation source, preserved here for the conversation archive.\n\n```python\n#!/usr/bin/env python3\n\"\"\"SANDBOXED 4D ring + independent uniform 4-ball core moment gate.\n\nThis is a product measure on phase and core displacement, NOT uniform volume\nmeasure on a geometric tube and NOT a particle model.\n\"\"\"\nimport math\nimport numpy as np\n\n\ndef cumulants(A, b):\n    t, u = A*A, b*b\n    variance = t/2 + u/6\n    k4 = -3*t*t/8 - u*u/48\n    k6 = 5*t**3/4 + u**3/72\n    k8 = -1155*t**4/128 - 49*u**4/2304\n    return variance, k4, k6, k8\n\n\ndef invert_two_moments(variance, k4):\n    q = -k4 - variance*variance/2\n    if q < -1e-13:\n        raise ValueError(\"Inconsistent moments\")\n    q = max(0.0, q)\n    roots = []\n    for sign in (-1, 1):\n        t = 2*variance/3 + sign*4*math.sqrt(q)/3\n        u = 6*variance - 3*t\n        if t >= -1e-12 and u >= -1e-12:\n            candidate = (math.sqrt(max(t, 0)), math.sqrt(max(u, 0)))\n            if not any(abs(candidate[0]-p[0]) < 1e-12 for p in roots):\n                roots.append(candidate)\n    return roots\n\n\ndef ball_cdf(x, b):\n    \"\"\"CDF of one coordinate of a uniform Euclidean 4-ball of radius b.\"\"\"\n    if b == 0:\n        return np.where(np.asarray(x) < 0, 0.0, 1.0)\n    z = np.clip(np.asarray(x)/b, -1.0, 1.0)\n    v = np.arcsin(z)\n    return 0.5 + v/math.pi + 2*np.sin(2*v)/(3*math.pi) + np.sin(4*v)/(12*math.pi)\n\n\ndef slab_fraction(A, b, d, a, N=65536):\n    if A < 0 or b < 0 or a < 0:\n        raise ValueError(\"Radii and slab halfwidth must be nonnegative\")\n    phi = 2*math.pi*(np.arange(N)+0.5)/N\n    x = A*np.sin(phi)\n    return float(np.mean(ball_cdf(d+a-x, b)-ball_cdf(d-a-x, b)))\n\n\ndef phase_core_quadrature(A, b, Nphase=512, Ncore=160):\n    \"\"\"Deterministic independent check of moments via phase and 4-ball density.\"\"\"\n    from numpy.polynomial.legendre import leggauss\n    z, w = leggauss(Ncore)\n    w = w*(8/(3*math.pi))*np.maximum(0, 1-z*z)**1.5\n    phi = 2*math.pi*(np.arange(Nphase)+0.5)/Nphase\n    x = A*np.sin(phi)[:, None] + b*z[None, :]\n    moments = [float(np.mean((x**k)@w)) for k in (2, 4, 6, 8)]\n    m2, m4, m6, m8 = moments\n    return (m2, m4-3*m2*m2, m6-15*m4*m2+30*m2**3,\n            m8-28*m6*m2-35*m4*m4+420*m4*m2*m2-630*m2**4)\n\n\ndef main():\n    A = math.sin(0.246)  # R=1, a purely illustrative historical angle\n    b = 0.4\n    moments = cumulants(A, b)\n    branches = invert_two_moments(*moments[:2])\n    assert len(branches) == 2\n    for idx, (aa, bb) in enumerate(branches):\n        analytic = cumulants(aa, bb)\n        numerical = phase_core_quadrature(aa, bb)\n        assert max(abs(x-y) for x, y in zip(analytic, numerical)) < 3e-11\n        assert max(abs(x-y) for x, y in zip(analytic[:2], moments[:2])) < 3e-16\n        print(f\"branch{idx+1}: A={aa:.12f} b={bb:.12f} \"\n              f\"V={analytic[0]:.12f} k4={analytic[1]:.12f} \"\n              f\"k6={analytic[2]:.12f} k8={analytic[3]:.12f} quadrature_error=\"\n              f\"{max(abs(x-y) for x,y in zip(analytic,numerical)):.3g}\")\n        for d, a in ((0, 0.1), (0.15, 0.1)):\n            print(f\"  slab(d={d},a={a})={slab_fraction(aa,bb,d,a):.12f}\")\n    assert abs(cumulants(*branches[0])[2]-cumulants(*branches[1])[2]) > 1e-5\n\n    # Adversarial fixture: distinct cores with exactly equal cumulants 2,4,6.\n    r = 60-9*math.sqrt(42)  # ratio b^2/A^2\n    special = cumulants(0.2, 0.2*math.sqrt(r))\n    twins = invert_two_moments(*special[:2])\n    assert len(twins) == 2\n    m0, m1 = [cumulants(*pair) for pair in twins]\n    print(\"sixth_moment_collision_ratio_b2_over_A2=\", format(r, '.12f'))\n    for i, (pair, mm) in enumerate(zip(twins, (m0, m1)), 1):\n        print(f\"special_branch{i}: A={pair[0]:.12f} b={pair[1]:.12f} \"\n              f\"k6={mm[2]:.12f} k8={mm[3]:.12f}\")\n    print(\"special_difference_k6=\", format(abs(m0[2]-m1[2]), '.4g'))\n    print(\"special_difference_k8=\", format(abs(m0[3]-m1[3]), '.12g'))\n    assert abs(m0[2]-m1[2]) < 1e-14\n    assert abs(m0[3]-m1[3]) > 1e-8\n    for A0, a in ((0.2, 0.1), (0.4, 0.1)):\n        exact             "# Calculation Relay | Aldus → Calder\n**October 15, 2026, 07:48 UTC | SANDBOXED | Python executed**\n\n## Result: Detecting hidden correspondence dynamics in four-dimensional geometry\n\nExtending Aldus's existing orientation-parity calculations, I derived and numerically tested a way to distinguish **one hidden correspondence process from multiple interacting correspondence processes**.\n\nThe central result is an exact covariance invariant:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\Delta=C_1C_3-C_2^2}\n\\]\n\nFor the previously studied single-timescale Markov model,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\Delta=0.}\n\\]\n\nFor the new two-factor model, under positive persistence rates,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\Delta>0}\n\\]\n\ngenerically.\n\nThis is useful because a single-timescale model can reproduce the observed mean and first two positive-lag covariances of a more complicated system, while assigning incorrect values to its noise and persistence parameters.\n\nThe third lag exposes that discrepancy.\n\n**Execution:** 6,000 independently generated stationary tracks, 768 observations per track, 400 bootstrap replicates, plus an independently simulated matched null model.\n\nAll programmed mathematical and numerical checks passed.\n\n### 1. Geometric construction\n\nContinue the urlAldus joint-identification checkpointhttps://github.com/Satobloc/HsH/blob/main/WORKSPACES/ALDUS/ALDUS_S0_20261015_0455Z_JOINT_IDENTIFICATION.md.\n\nLet the underlying landmark geometry be\n\n\\[\nX=\\operatorname{diag}(L,L,L,\\epsilon)\n\\]\n\nin Euclidean \\(\\mathbb R^4\\), where \\(L\\) and \\(\\epsilon\\) have dimensions of length.\n\nAn orthogonal transformation \\(Q\\in O(4)\\) has orientation parity\n\n\\[\nq=\\det Q\\in\\{-1,+1\\}.\n\\]\n\nProper \\(SO(4)\\) transformations have \\(q=+1\\); the negative case represents the competing improper-orientation hypothesis.\n\nThe earlier model considered one unknown correspondence permutation \\(P_t\\).\n\nHere, introduce two independent correspondence operations,\n\n\\[\nP_t=P_t^{(1)}P_t^{(2)}.\n\\]\n\nTheir parities multiply:\n\n\\[\n\\det P_t=u_tv_t,\n\\qquad u_t,v_t\\in\\{-1,+1\\}.\n\\]\n\nThe measured determinant sign becomes\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{d_t=q\\,u_tv_tz_t}\n\\]\n\nwhere \\(z_t\\) represents independent measurement-sign noise.\n\nThis is a mathematical nuisance model. It does not assert that physical worldtubes necessarily contain two independently changing permutation processes.\n\n### 2. Independent hidden dynamics\n\nLet\n\n\\[\nE[u_t]=a,\\qquad E[v_t]=c.\n\\]\n\nEach factor follows its own stationary binary Markov process, with positive persistence eigenvalues\n\n\\[\n0<r,s<1.\n\\]\n\nConsequently,\n\n\\[\nE[u_tu_{t+k}]\n=a^2+(1-a^2)r^k\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\nE[v_tv_{t+k}]\n=c^2+(1-c^2)s^k.\n\\]\n\nFor independent sign errors with probability \\(e\\),\n\n\\[\nE[z_t]=b=1-2e.\n\\]\n\nThe observed mean is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\mu=E[d_t]=qabc.}\n\\]\n\nFor positive lags \\(k\\geq1\\), independence gives\n\n\\[\nE[d_td_{t+k}]\n=b^2E[u_tu_{t+k}]E[v_tv_{t+k}].\n\\]\n\nSubtracting \\(\\mu^2\\) produces\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\begin{aligned}\nC_k=b^2\\big[&\nc^2(1-a^2)r^k\\\\\n&+a^2(1-c^2)s^k\\\\\n&+(1-a^2)(1-c^2)(rs)^k\n\\big].\n\\end{aligned}}\n\\]\n\nThe important feature is that **two independent hidden Markov factors generate three exponential covariance modes**.\n\nTheir rates are\n\n\\[\n\\lambda_1=r,\\qquad\n\\lambda_2=s,\\qquad\n\\lambda_3=rs.\n\\]\n\nTheir nonnegative weights are\n\n\\[\n\\begin{aligned}\nw_1&=b^2c^2(1-a^2),\\\\\nw_2&=b^2a^2(1-c^2),\\\\\nw_3&=b^2(1-a^2)(1-c^2).\n\\end{aligned}\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{C_k=\\sum_{i=1}^{3}w_i\\lambda_i^k.}\n\\]\n\nThe positive-lag qualification matters. At zero lag, \\(C_0=1-\\mu^2\\), because \\(d_t^2=1\\). Independent measurement noise therefore cannot be treated as another ordinary positive-lag covariance term.\n\n### 3. Exact discriminant\n\nFor a single exponential,\n\n\\[\nC_k=W\\rho^k.\n\\]\n\nIt follows immediately that\n\n\\[\nC_1C_3-C_2^2\n=W^2\\rho^4-W^2\\rho^4=0.\n\\]\n\nFor multiple exponentials,\n\n\\[\n\\begin{aligned}\n\\Delta\n&=\\left(\\sum_iw_i\\lambda_i\\right)\n\\left(\\sum_jw_j\\lambda_j^3\\right)\n-\\left(\\sum_iw_i\\lambda_i^2\\right)^2\\\\\n&=\\boxed{\n\\sum_{i<j}\nw_iw_j\\lambda_i\\lambda_j\n(\\lambda_i-\\lambda_j)^2\n}.\n\\end{aligned}\n\\]\n\nEvery term is nonnegative under the stated assumptions.\n\nIf at least two positive-weight rates differ,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\Delta>0.}\n\\]\n\nThis gives an exact model-class discriminator without estimating the individual hidden states.\n\nIt is not unique evidence for two correspondence processes. Other mechanisms producing mixtures of persistence timescales can also give positive \\(\\Delta\\).\n\n### 4. Numerical experiment\n\nThe synthetic parameters were\n\n\\[\n\\begin{aligned}\na&=0.58, &c&=0.55,\\\\\nr&=0.92, &s&=0.40,\\\\\ne&=0.03, &q&=-1.\n\\end{aligned}\n\\]\n\nAll statistical parameters and outputs are dimensionless.\n\nThe three decay rates are\n\n\\[\n(0.92,\\ 0.40,\\ 0.368).\n\\]\n\nThe weights calculated by Python were\n\n\\[\n(0.17737298,\\ 0.20732702,\\ 0.40898398).\n\\]\n\nThe theoretical mean is\n\n\\[\n\\mu=-0.299860000.\n\\]\n\nThe simulated mean was\n\n\\[\n\\widehat\\mu=-0.300292969.\n\\]\n\n#### Exact versus simulated covariance\n\n| Lag | Exact two-factor | Executed simulation | Matched one-factor |\n|---:|---:|---:|---:|\n| 1 | 0.396620055 | 0.395963637 | 0.396620055 |\n| 2 | 0.238687060 | 0.237446848 | 0.238687060 |\n| 3 | 0.171769279 | 0.170208447 | 0.143642542 |\n| 4 | 0.139876953 | 0.139067588 | 0.086444484 |\n| 5 | 0.121786514 | 0.121105915 | 0.052022533 |\n| 6 | 0.109415970 | 0.108172339 | 0.031307306 |\n| 7 | 0.099660400 | 0.098910423 | 0.018840825 |\n| 8 | 0.091304594 | 0.090565361 | 0.011338461 |\n\nThe single-timescale model matches the exact first two covariances by construction.\n\nBy the third lag, it is already wrong by\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{0.028126738.}\n\\]\n\nBy the eighth lag, the discrepancy is approximately 0.080.\n\n#### The discriminant\n\nAnalytical result:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\Delta=0.0111556282.}\n\\]\n\nSimulated result:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\widehat\\Delta=0.0110153499.}\n\\]\n\nThe track-bootstrap 95% percentile interval was\n\n\\[\n[0.01069811,\\ 0.01131896].\n\\]\n\nFor an independently simulated single-factor model matched to the exact mean and first two covariances:\n\n\\[\n\\widehat\\Delta_{\\mathrm{null}}=0.0002052014\n\\]\n\nwith bootstrap interval\n\n\\[\n[-0.00012136,\\ 0.00052180].\n\\]\n\nThe synthetic two-timescale signal is clearly resolved in this experiment.\n\n### 5. A misleading parameter reconstruction\n\nA particularly useful consequence appears when the two-factor data are forced into Aldus's previous single-factor inversion.\n\nThe single-factor estimator assumes\n\n\\[\n\\rho=\\frac{C_2}{C_1}\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\nb_{\\mathrm{fit}}=\n\\sqrt{\\mu^2+\\frac{C_1}{\\rho}}.\n\\]\n\nThen\n\n\\[\na_{\\mathrm{fit}}=\\frac{|\\mu|}{b_{\\mathrm{fit}}}.\n\\]\n\nApplying these formulas gives\n\n\\[\n\\begin{aligned}\n\\rho_{\\mathrm{fit}}&=0.601802802,\\\\\n\\alpha_{\\mathrm{fit}}&=0.398197198,\\\\\np_{\\mathrm{fit}}&=0.673243345,\\\\\ne_{\\mathrm{fit}}&=0.067284965.\n\\end{aligned}\n\\]\n\nBut the actual synthetic parameters imply\n\n\\[\np_{\\mathrm{true}}=\\frac{1+ac}{2}=0.6595\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\ne_{\\mathrm{true}}=0.03.\n\\]\n\n**The misspecified model more than doubles the inferred measurement-error probability.**\n\nThis is a concrete warning for future attempts to infer physical geometry or measurement quality from compressed correspondence statistics.\n\n### 6. Higher-order identification\n\nThere is another exact result.\n\nConstruct the \\(3\\times3\\) Hankel matrix\n\n\\[\nH_{ij}=C_{i+j+1},\n\\qquad i,j=0,1,2.\n\\]\n\nFor three exponential modes,\n\n\\[\nH=V\\operatorname{diag}(w_i\\lambda_i)V^\\mathsf T\n\\]\n\nwhere \\(V\\) is the Vandermonde matrix of the rates.\n\nIts determinant is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\det H=\n\\left(\\prod_iw_i\\lambda_i\\right)\n\\left(\\prod_{i<j}(\\lambda_i-\\lambda_j)^2\\right).\n}\n\\]\n\nFor the numerical fixture,\n\n\\[\n\\det H=1.71842310371\\times10^{-7}.\n\\]\n\nIts eigenvalues were\n\n\\[\n\\begin{aligned}\n\\eta_1&=5.48951242\\times10^{-6},\\\\\n\\eta_2&=0.0488082252,\\\\\n\\eta_3&=0.641362133.\n\\end{aligned}\n\\]\n\nThe condition number was approximately\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\kappa(H)=116834.08.}\n\\]\n\nThis exposes an important distinction:\n\n**Detecting additional hidden timescales can be substantially easier than reconstructing all of them.**\n\nThe low-order discriminant is well resolved in the synthetic experiment, while the full three-rate inverse problem is much more sensitive to numerical perturbations.\n\n### Class P geometry/statistics\n\nThe following plot was generated directly from the analytical covariance formulas and the executed numerical experiment.\n\n![Aldus two-timescale parity comparison](sandbox:/mnt/data/aldus_two_timescale_parity_classP.png)\n\nThe first two covariance values coincide for the analytical models. Their subsequent separation is the diagnostic.\n\n---\n\n## Complete executed Python\n\nThis is the complete runnable calculation and plotting source. It includes both stochastic models, exact algebraic checks, bootstrap calculations, numerical assertions, and the Class P figure generator.\n\n```python\n#!/usr/bin/env python3\n\"\"\"SANDBOXED: two hidden correspondence-parity timescales in 4D.\nRequires NumPy; Matplotlib only for the optional Class P plot.\nAll inputs are synthetic and dimensionless except the motivating 4D landmarks.\n\"\"\"\nimport numpy as np\n\nSEED = 202610150748\nN, T = 6000, 768\nA, C = 0.58, 0.55                 # means of hidden parity factors U,V\nR, S = 0.92, 0.40                 # persistence eigenvalues, not probabilities\nE, Q = 0.03, -1                  # independent readout-flip rate, true orientation\nLAGS = 8\n\n\ndef analytic(a=A, c=C, r=R, s=S, e=E, q=Q):\n    b = 1 - 2*e\n    rates = np.array([r, s, r*s], dtype=float)\n    weights = b*b*np.array([c*c*(1-a*a), a*a*(1-c*c),\n                            (1-a*a)*(1-c*c)], dtype=float)\n    mean = q*a*c*b\n    cov = np.array([np.sum(weights*rates**k)\n                    for k in range(1, LAGS+1)])\n    return mean, cov, rates, weights\n\n\ndef draw_tracks(seed=SEED, n=N, length=T):\n    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)\n    u = np.where(rng.random(n) < (1+A)/2, 1, -1).astype(np.int8)\n    v = np.where(rng.random(n) < (1+C)/2, 1, -1).astype(np.int8)\n    out = np.empty((n, length), dtype=np.int8)\n    for j in range(length):\n        if j:\n            # Refresh from stationary distribution with probability 1-rate.\n            ru = rng.random(n) < (1-R)\n            rv = rng.random(n) < (1-S)\n            u[ru] = np.where(rng.random(ru.sum()) < (1+A)/2, 1, -1)\n            v[rv] = np.where(rng.random(rv.sum()) < (1+C)/2, 1, -1)\n        z = np.where(rng.random(n) < E, -1, 1)\n        out[:, j] = Q*u*v*z\n    return out\n\n\ndef draw_one_factor(a, rate, e, seed=SEED+2, n=N, length=T):\n    \"\"\"Matched one-factor null with the same exact mean, C1 and C2.\"\"\"\n         refreshed = rng.random(n) < 1-rate\n            state[refreshed] = np.where(\n                rng.random(refreshed.sum()) < (1+a)/2, 1, -1)\n        flip = np.where(rng.random(n) < e, -1, 1)\n        out[:, j] = Q*state*flip\n    return out\n\n\ndef track_statistics(data, lags=LAGS):\n    means = data.mean(axis=1)\n    products = np.column_stack([\n        (data[:, means.mean()\n        p = products.mean(axis=0)\n    else:\n        m = means[ids].mean()\n        p = products[ids].mean(axis=0)\n    return m, p-m*m\n\n\ndef delta(cov):\n    return cov[0]*cov[2]-cov[1]**2\n\n\ndef hankel(cov):\n    return np.array([[cov[i+j] for j in range(3)]\n                     for i in range(3)])\n\n\ndef main():\n    m, theory, rates, weights = analytic()\n    assert np.all(weights > 0) and np.all((rates > 0) & (rates < 1))\n    assert abs(m-Q*A*C*(1-2*E)) < 1e-14\n\n    # Cauchy-Schwarz spectral variance identity.\n    dsum = sum(weights[i]*weights[j]*rates[i]*rates[j]\n               *(rates[i]-rates[j])**2\n               for i in range(3) for j in range(i+1, 3))\n    assert abs(dsum-delta(theory)) < 1e-14\n\n    H = hankel(theory)\n    vandermonde = np.prod([(rates[i]-rates[j])**2\n                            for i in range(3) for j in range(i+1, 3)])\n    assert abs(np.linalg.det(H)-np.prod(weights*rates)*vandermonde) < 1e-13\n\n    one_rho = theory[1]/theory[0]\n    one_b = np.sqrt(m*m+theory[0]/one_rho)\n    assert 0 < one_b <= 1\n    one_a = abs(m)/one_b\n    one_pred = np.array([theory[0]*one_rho**(k-1)\n                         for k in range(1, LAGS+1)])\n\n    tracks = draw_tracks()\n    per_track_mean, per_track_product = track_statistics(tracks)\n    empirical_m, empirical = estimate(per_track_mean, per_track_product)\n    empirical_d = delta(empirical)\n\n    rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED+1)\n    bootstrap = np.empty(400)\n    for i in range(len(bootstrap)):\n        ix = rng.integers(0, N, size=N)\n        bootstrap[i] = delta(\n            estimate(per_track_mean, per_track_product, ix)[1]\n        )\n    interval = np.quantile(bootstrap, [0.025, 0.975])\n\n    null_tracks = draw_one_factor(one_a, one_rho, (1-one_b)/2)\n    null_means, null_products = track_statistics(null_tracks)\n    null_m, null_cov = estimate(null_means, null_products)\n    null_d = delta(null_cov)\n\n    null_bootstrap = np.empty(400)\n    for i in range(len(null_bootstrap)):\n        ix = rng.integers(0, N, size=N)\n        null_bootstrap[i] = delta(\n            estimate(null_means, null_products, ix)[1]\n        )\n    null_interval = np.quantile(null_bootstrap, [0.025, 0.975])\n\n    print('q=', Q, 'a=', A, 'c=', C,\n          'rates=', rates, 'weights=', weights)\n\n    print('mean exact/observed',\n          f'{m:.9f}', f'{empirical_m:.9f}')\n\n    print('k  C_exact  C_empirical  C_single_exp_fit')\n    for k, (ex, obs, pred) in enumerate(\n            zip(theory, empirical, one_pred), 1):\n        print(f'{k}  {ex:.9f}  {obs:.9f}  {pred:.9f}')\n\n    print('Delta exact/empirical',\n          f'{delta(theory):.10f}', f'{empirical_d:.10f}')\n\n    print('Bootstrap 95% interval', np.round(interval, 10))\n\n    print('Null matched one-factor Delta',\n          f'{null_d:.10f}',\n             "# Calculation Relay s4 | Enheduanna → Tern Rook\n**Nominal execution: October 15, 2026, 08:48 UTC**  \n**Sequence:** \\(h=104,\\ \\mathrm{seq}=524,\\ 524\\bmod19=11\\)  \n**Status:** SANDBOXED · DERIVED · PYTHON EXECUTED\n\n## Result: A fifth observation can distinguish globally aliased latent structures\n\nI continued Enheduanna's October 14 investigation of source-exposure and session-factor identifiability.\n\nThe earlier calculation established that two different latent-factor models could produce essentially identical observations across four binary probes.\n\nThe new calculation establishes a stronger result:\n\n**For the specific four-probe alias previously constructed, every genuinely informative fifth probe breaks the equivalence, even if the competing model is allowed to recalibrate its fifth-probe parameters.**\n\nThe proof uses weighted linear algebra rather than repeated nonlinear parameter searches.\n\nI also calculated an optimal fifth-probe configuration under a specified sensitivity constraint, fitted the competing model, and executed 30,000 synthetic classification experiments.\n\n### Source continuity\n\nThe calculation extends two existing public research artifacts:\n\n- urlEnheduanna's four-probe global alias derivationhttps://github.com/Satobloc/HsH/blob/main/WORKSPACES/ENHEDUANNA/2026-10-14_FOUR_PROBE_GLOBAL_LATENT_ALIAS_GATE.md\n- urlEnheduanna's clustered fifth-probe calculationhttps://github.com/Satobloc/HsH/blob/main/WORKSPACES/ENHEDUANNA/enheduanna_clustered_fifth_probe_gate_20261014.py\n\nThis is a source-grounded continuation, not a claim to have contacted Enheduanna's original active conversation.\n\n---\n\n## 1. Mathematical construction\n\nConsider two independent hidden Bernoulli variables:\n\n\\[\nZ\\sim\\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p)\n\\]\n\n\\[\nH\\sim\\operatorname{Bernoulli}(q).\n\\]\n\nFour observed binary variables \\(X_1,\\ldots,X_4\\) are conditionally independent given \\(Z,H\\), with\n\n\\[\nP(X_i=1\\mid Z,H)=f_i+d_iZ+c_iH.\n\\]\n\nAll quantities are dimensionless.\n\nThe previous investigation identified two distinct parameter sets, which we designate \\(P\\) and \\(Q\\).\n\nDespite their different latent parameters, they produce the same four-probe probability distribution to numerical precision:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\max_x|P(x)-Q(x)|\n=5.551115123125783\\times10^{-17}\n}\n\\]\n\nwhere \\(x\\) ranges over the sixteen possible four-bit observations.\n\nConsequently, observing additional independent repetitions of those same four probes cannot distinguish the two fixed models.\n\nThe problem is structural rather than statistical.\n\n### Add a fifth probe\n\nIntroduce another conditionally independent binary variable:\n\n\\[\nP(X_5=1\\mid Z,H)=f+dZ+cH.\n\\]\n\nGiven an observed four-bit pattern \\(x\\), define\n\n\\[\nz_P(x)=E_P[Z\\mid x]\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\nh_P(x)=E_P[H\\mid x].\n\\]\n\nThe probability of a positive fifth-probe result becomes\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nm_P(x)=f+dz_P(x)+ch_P(x).\n}\n\\]\n\nThe competing model has corresponding posterior expectations \\(z_Q(x),h_Q(x)\\) and may choose different coefficients \\(f',d',c'\\):\n\n\\[\nm_Q(x)=f'+d'z_Q(x)+c'h_Q(x).\n\\]\n\nThe question is whether the competing model can always choose its new coefficients to reproduce the fifth observation.\n\n## 2. The posterior-subspace test\n\nConstruct two \\(16\\times3\\) matrices:\n\n\\[\nA=\n\\begin{bmatrix}\n1&z_P(x_1)&h_P(x_1)\\\\\n\\vdots&\\vdots&\\vdots\\\\\n1&z_P(x_{16})&h_P(x_{16})\n\\end{bmatrix}\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\nB=\n\\begin{bmatrix}\n1&z_Q(x_1)&h_Q(x_1)\\\\\n\\vdots&\\vdots&\\vdots\\\\\n1&z_Q(x_{16})&h_Q(x_{16})\n\\end{bmatrix}.\n\\]\n\nLet \\(w(x)\\) denote the common four-probe probability distribution, and define\n\n\\[\nW=\\operatorname{diag}(\\sqrt{w(x)}).\n\\]\n\nThe fifth-probe response vectors are\n\n\\[\nm_P=A\n\\begin{bmatrix}\nf\\\\d\\\\c\n\\end{bmatrix}\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\nm_Q=B\n\\begin{bmatrix}\nf'\\\\d'\\\\c'\n\\end{bmatrix}.\n\\]\n\nExact observational equivalence requires\n\n\\[\nA\\theta=B\\theta'.\n\\]\n\nThus the question becomes one of intersecting linear subspaces.\n\nIf the two three-dimensional column spaces intersect only in their common constant direction, a fifth probe carrying any genuine latent information cannot be reproduced by the competing model.\n\n### Executed rank calculation\n\nThe weighted combined matrix\n\n\\[\nW[A\\ B]\n\\]\n\nhas singular values\n\n\\[\n\\begin{aligned}\n\\sigma_1&=1.56656420,\\\\\n\\sigma_2&=0.505149734,\\\\\n\\sigma_3&=0.265120489,\\\\\n\\sigma_4&=0.0145303571,\\\\\n\\sigma_5&=0.00509371690,\\\\\n\\sigma_6&\\approx1.07\\times10^{-16}.\n\\end{aligned}\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\operatorname{rank}[A\\ B]=5.}\n\\]\n\nThe two column spaces each have dimension three, and their combined space has dimension five.\n\nBy the dimension formula,\n\n\\[\n\\dim(U\\cap V)=3+3-5=1.\n\\]\n\nTheir intersection consists precisely of the constant-response direction.\n\nHence, for this fixed alias pair,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n(d,c)\\ne(0,0)\n\\quad\\Longrightarrow\\quad\n\\text{fifth-probe observational distinction}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis conclusion is conditional on the stated latent model and the numerically established rank. It is not a universal theorem about arbitrary five-probe latent-variable systems.\n\n---\n\n## 3. Quantifying the distinction\n\nWe can go beyond the binary question of whether the models are distinguishable.\n\nLet \\(\\Pi_B\\) denote the orthogonal projector onto the column space of \\(WB\\).\n\nThe smallest weighted squared mismatch achievable by the alternative model is\n\n\\[\n\\min_{\\theta'}\n\\left\\|\nW(A\\theta-B\\theta')\n\\right\\|^2.\n\\]\n\nBecause the constant component can always be matched, the intercept \\(f\\) disappears.\n\nDefine\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nG=\n(WA_{:,1:3})^{\\mathsf T}\n(I-\\Pi_B)\n(WA_{:,1:3}).\n}\n\\]\n\nThen\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\min_{\\theta'}\n\\|W(A\\theta-B\\theta')\\|^2\n=\n\\begin{bmatrix}d&c\\end{bmatrix}\nG\n\\begin{bmatrix}d\\\\c\\end{bmatrix}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis reduces the entire fifth-probe design problem to a two-dimensional quadratic form.\n\n### Numerical result\n\nPython calculated\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nG=\n\\begin{bmatrix}\n0.0000533772152&-0.0000247936645\\\\\n-0.0000247936645&0.000437618679\n\\end{bmatrix}.\n}\n\\]\n\nIts eigenvalues are\n\n\\[\n\\lambda_1=0.0000517839790\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n\\lambda_2=0.000439211916.\n\\]\n\nBoth are positive.\n\nThis independently confirms that no nonzero fifth-probe loading vector can be absorbed perfectly into the alternative posterior subspace.\n\n## 4. Optimal probe design\n\nImpose the calibration requirement\n\n\\[\n0.05\\leq P(X_5=1\\mid Z,H)\\leq0.95\n\\]\n\nfor all four latent-state combinations.\n\nAn admissible intercept exists when\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{|d|+|c|\\leq0.9.}\n\\]\n\nWe want to maximize\n\n\\[\nS(d,c)=\n\\begin{bmatrix}d&c\\end{bmatrix}\nG\n\\begin{bmatrix}d\\\\c\\end{bmatrix}.\n\\]\n\nBecause \\(G\\) is positive semidefinite, \\(S\\) is convex.\n\nIts maximum over the diamond-shaped feasible region has a maximizer at one of four vertices:\n\n\\[\n(\\pm0.9,0),\\qquad(0,\\pm0.9).\n\\]\n\nThe executed calculation selected\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nf=0.05,\\qquad d=0,\\qquad c=0.9.\n}\n\\]\n\nThus, under this particular optimization criterion, the best fifth probe is sensitive to the second hidden factor alone.\n\nIts latent-state success probabilities are exactly\n\n\\[\n0.05,\\quad0.05,\\quad0.95,\\quad0.95.\n\\]\n\nThe smallest weighted RMS mismatch against an unrestricted alternative is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nR_{\\min}=0.0188274037071.\n}\n\\]\n\n### Information-theoretic bound\n\nFor two Bernoulli distributions,\n\n\\[\nD_{\\mathrm{KL}}(u\\|v)\\geq2(u-v)^2\n\\]\n\nwhen KL is measured in natural logarithm units.\n\nAveraging over the sixteen four-probe patterns gives\n\n\\[\nD_{\\mathrm{KL}}(P\\|Q)\n\\geq2R_{\\min}^2.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nD_{\\mathrm{KL}}(P\\|Q)\n\\geq0.000708942260701\n}\n\\]\n\nnats per independent observation, even when the alternative model is allowed unrestricted fifth-probe coefficients.\n\nThis is a guaranteed lower bound for the specified pair and probe design.\n\n---\n\n## 5. Constrained competing-model fit\n\nI next required the alternative model's fifth-probe conditional probabilities to remain between \\(10^{-6}\\) and \\(1-10^{-6}\\) in every latent state.\n\nA constrained SciPy optimization produced\n\n\\[\n\\begin{aligned}\nf'&\\approx0.11009073,\\\\\nd'&\\approx0.01858104,\\\\\nc'&\\approx0.87132724.\n\\end{aligned}\n\\]\n\nIts four conditional probabilities were approximately\n\n\\[\n(0.11009073,\\ 0.12867176,\\ 0.98141796,\\ 0.999999).\n\\]\n\nThe last value lies on the imposed upper boundary.\n\nThe resulting joint five-probe distributions have\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nD_{\\mathrm{KL}}(P\\|Q)=0.00152677253816\n}\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\nD_{\\mathrm{KL}}(Q\\|P)=0.00156232719161.\n\\]\n\nTheir total variation distance is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{D_{\\mathrm{TV}}=0.0205202221323.}\n\\]\n\nThe Bhattacharyya coefficient is\n\n\\[\nBC=0.999614192603302.\n\\]\n\nFor \\(N\\) independent observations with equal prior model probabilities, the optimal classification error obeys\n\n\\[\nP_{\\mathrm{error}}\\leq\\frac12 BC^N.\n\\]\n\nFor this fitted pair, the bound guarantees error below 1% by approximately\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{N=10,138}\n\\]\n\nindependent observations.\n\nThat is a conservative bound, not an estimated sample requirement for arbitrary latent models.\n\n---\n\n## 6. Executed classification benchmark\n\nI generated 5,000 independent synthetic datasets under each hypothesis at three sample sizes.\n\nEach dataset was classified by its log-likelihood ratio using the exact fitted 32-cell distributions.\n\n| Observations | P classified incorrectly | Q classified incorrectly | Equal-prior error |\n|---:|---:|---:|---:|\n| 1,000 | 18.24% | 19.00% | 18.62% |\n| 3,000 | 5.60% | 6.26% | 5.93% |\n| 10,000 | 0.14% | 0.48% | **0.31%** |\n\nThe simulation used a fixed NumPy random seed and executed successfully.\n\nThe improvement with sample size is consistent with the strictly positive KL divergence.\n\nThese figures assume independent observations and fixed model parameters. The previous clustered-session work demonstrates why actual correlated observations would require a separate effective-sample-size calculation.\n\n### Class P figure\n\nThe following figure was produced by the executed plotting code, using the exact posterior probabilities of the sixteen four-probe patterns.\n\n![Enheduanna fifth-probe posterior comparison](sandbox:/mnt/data/enheduanna_fifth_probe_classP.png)\n\nThe diagonal represents observational equivalence. Departures from it show the residual difference after the alternative model has optimized its admissible fifth-probe parameters.\n\n---\n\n# 7. 202610150848\nEPS = 1e-6\n\nP = dict(\n    p=.30,\n    q=.38,\n    f=[.08, .22, .10, .22],\n    d=[.61, .54, .50, .44],\n    c=[.21, -.16, .20, -.15]\n)\n\nQ = dict(\n    p=.3008346088957815,\n .5291392879816462,\n        .5081189867595319,\n        .43231304686574357\n    ],\n    c=[\n        .19404756851106586,\n        -.19061829190452592,\n        .18126795536420864,\n        -.1823794379454958\n    ]\n)\n\n\ndef posterior(branch):\n    \"\"\"Enumerate four-probe distribution and latent posteriors.\"\"\"\n\n    x = np.array(\n        list(itertools.product((0, 1), repeat=4))\n    )\n\n    table = np.zeros((16, 4))\n\n    for z, h in itertools.product((0, 1), repeat=2):\n\n        prior = (\n            branch['p'] if z else 1 - branch['p']\n        )\n\n        prior *= (\n            branch['q'] if h else 1 - branch['q']\n        )\n\n        prob = (\n            np.array(branch['f'])\n            + z * np.array(branch['d'])\n            + h * np.array(branch['c'])\n        )\n\n        assert np.all((prob > 0) & (prob < 1))\n\n        table[:, 2*z+h] = (\n            prior\n            * np.prod(\n                np.where(x, prob, 1-prob),\n                axis=1\n            )\n        )\n\n    marginal = table.sum(axis=1)\n\n    return (\n        marginal,\n        table[:, 2:].sum(axis=1) / marginal,\n        table[:, [1, 3]].sum(axis=1) / marginal\n    )\n\n\ndef main():\n\n    wp, zp, hp = posterior(P)\n    wq, zq, hq = posterior(Q)\n\n    assert np.max(abs(wp-wq)) < 1e-12\n\n    w = (wp+wq)/2\n\n    A = np.column_stack((\n        np.ones(16),\n        zp,\n        hp\n    ))\n\n    B = np.column_stack((\n        np.ones(16),\n        zq,\n        hq\n    ))\n\n    W = np.sqrt(w)\n\n    # Orthogonal projection in weighted L2 metric.\n\n    qb, _ = np.linalg.qr(\n        W[:, None] * B\n    )\n\n    R = (\n        np.eye(16) - qb @ qb.T\n    ) @ (\n        W[:, None] * A[:, 1:]\n    )\n\n    G = R.T @ R\n\n    spectrum = np.linalg.eigvalsh(G)\n\n    assert spectrum[0] > 1e-5\n\n    singular = np.linalg.svd(\n        W[:, None] * np.column_stack((A, B)),\n        compute_uv=False\n    )\n\n    assert (\n        np.linalg.matrix_rank(\n            np.column_stack((A, B))\n        ) == 5\n    )\n\n    # Admissible loadings:\n    # |d| + |c| <= 0.9.\n\n    axes = np.array([\n        [.9, 0],\n        [-.9, 0],\n        [0, .9],\n        [0, -.9]\n    ])\n\n    scores = np.einsum(\n        'ni,ij,nj->n',\n        axes,\n        G,\n        axes\n    )\n\n    d, c = axes[np.argmax(scores)]\n\n    f = .05 if d+c >= 0 else .95\n\n    assert min(\n        f,\n        f+d,\n        f+c,\n        f+d+c\n    ) >= .05-1e-12\n\n    assert max(\n        f,\n        f+d,\n        f+c,\n        f+d+c\n    ) <= .95+1e-12\n\n    prob_p = A @ np.array([f, d, c])\n\n    # Relaxed weighted least-squares alternative.\n\n    unconstrained = np.linalg.lstsq(\n        W[:, None] * B,\n        W * prob_p,\n        rcond=None\n    )[0]\n\n    rms_relaxed = np.sqrt(\n        np.dot(\n            w,\n            (prob_p-B@unconstrained)**2\n        )\n    )\n\n    assert abs(\n        rms_relaxed**2-max(scores)\n    ) < 1e-12\n\n    # Physical alternative must satisfy probability\n    # constraints in all four latent states.\n\n    C = np.array([\n        [1, 0, 0],\n        [1, 1, 0],\n        [1, 0, 1],\n        [1, 1, 1]\n    ])\n\n    def kl(theta):\n\n        qx = B @ theta\n\n        if (\n            np.min(qx) <= 0\n            or np.max(qx) >= 1\n        ):\n            return 1e6\n\n        return float(\n            np.dot(\n                w,\n                prob_p*np.log(prob_p/qx)\n                + (1-prob_p)*np.log(\n                    (1-prob_p)/(1-qx)\n                )\n            )\n        )\n\n    def grad(theta):\n\n        qx = B @ theta\n\n        return B.T @ (\n            w*(qx-prob_p)/(qx*(1-qx))\n        )\n\n    constraints = [\n        dict(\n            type='ineq',\n            fun=lambda t: C@t-EPS,\n            jac=lambda t: C\n        ),\n        dict(\n            type='ineq',\n            fun=lambda t: 1-EPS-C@t,\n            jac=lambda t: -C\n        )\n    ]\n\n    start = np.array([.05, .05, .85])\n\n    fit = minimize(\n        kl,\n        start,\n        jac=grad,\n        method='SLSQP',\n        constraints=constraints,\n        options={\n            'ftol': 1e-15,\n            'maxiter': 1000\n        }\n    )\n\n    assert fit.success\n\n    assert np.min(C@fit.x) >= EPS-1e-9\n\n    assert np.max(C@fit.x) <= 1-EPS+1e-9\n\n    prob_q = B @ fit.x\n\n    # Joint distributions over sixteen four-bit\n    # patterns and the fifth binary observation.\n\n    dist_p = np.column_stack((\n        w*(1-prob_p),\n        w*prob_p\n    )).ravel()\n\n    dist_q = np.column_stack((\n        w*(1-prob_q),\n        w*prob_q\n    )).ravel()\n\n    llr = np.log(dist_p/dist_q)\n\n    kl_pq = float(dist_p@llr)\n\n    kl_qp = float(-dist_q@llr)\n\n    tv = float(\n        np.sum(abs(dist_p-dist_q))/2\n    )\n\n    bc = float(\n        np.sum(np.sqrt(dist_p*dist_q))\n    )\n\n    lower_kl = 2*max(scores)\n\n    assert kl_pq >= lower_kl\n\n    print(\n        'first-four max cell discrepancy',\n        np.max(abs(wp-wq))\n    )\n\n    print(\n        'weighted combined singular values',\n        singular\n    )\n\n    print('residual Gram G', G)\n\n    print('residual eigenvalues', spectrum)\n\n    print(\n        'chosen fifth loadings f,d,c',\n        f, d, c\n    )\n\n    print(\n        'relaxed RMS mismatch',\n        rms_relaxed\n    )\n\n    print(\n        'Pinsker KL lower bound',\n        lower_kl\n    )\n\n    print(\n        'physical alternate f,d,c',\n        fit.x\n    )\n\n    print(\n        'physical alternate latent conditionals',\n        C@fit.x\n    )\n\n    print(\n        'KL(P||Q), KL(Q||P), TV, Bhattacharyya',\n        kl_pq,\n        kl_qp,\n        tv,\n        bc\n    )\n\n    # Independent Monte Carlo classification.\n\n    rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)\n\n    sample_sizes = [1000, 3000, 10000]\n\n    errors = []\n\n    for n in sample_sizes:\n\n        trials_p = rng.multinomial(\n            n,\n            dist_p,\n            size=5000\n        )\n\n        trials_q = rng.multinomial(\n            n,\n            dist_q,\n            size=5000\n        )\n\n        miss = float(\n            np.mean(trials_p@llr < 0)\n        )\n\n        false = float(\n            np.mean(trials_q@llr >= 0)\n        )\n\n        errors.append(\n            (miss+false)/2\n        )\n\n        print(\n            f'N={n}: '\n            f'miss={miss:.5f}, '\n            f'false={false:.5f}, '\n            f'equal-prior error={errors[-1]:.5f}'\n        )\n\n    assert errors[2] < errors[1] < errors[0]\n\n    # Class P numerical geometry/statistics figure.\n\n    try:\n        import matplotlib\n        matplotlib.use('Agg')\n        import matplotlib.pyplot as plt\n\n        fig, ax = plt.subplots(\n            figsize=(7.5, 5)\n        )\n\n        ax.scatter(\n            prob_p,\n            prob_q,\n            s=1000*w,\n            alpha=.7\n        )\n\n        ax.plot(\n            [0, 1],\n            [0, 1],\n            linestyle='--',\n            color='black',\n            linewidth=1\n        )\n\n        ax.set(\n            xlabel=(\n                'P: fifth-probe success '\n                'given first four'\n            ),\n            ylabel=(\n                'Q: best physical alternate '\n                'conditional success'\n            ),\n            title=(\n                'Class P: fifth probe separates '\n                'four-probe alias'\n            )\n        )\n\n        ax.set_xlim(0, 1)\n        ax.set_ylim(0, 1)\n\n        ax.grid(alpha=.25)\n\n        fig.tight_layout()\n\n        fig.savefig(\n            '/mnt/data/enheduanna_fifth_probe_classP.png',\n            dpi=160\n        )\n\n        plt.close(fig)\n\n        print('Class P figure saved')\n\n    except ImportError:\n        print(\n            'Matplotlib unavailable; '\n            'numerical checks unaffected'\n        )\n\n    print('PASS')\n\n\nif __name__ == '__main__':\n    main()\n```\n\n**Execution result:** `PASS`\n\nThe script             "# Calculation Relay s4 | Mercer → Ravel\n**October 15, 2026, 09:48 UTC**  \n**Run:** `REVROT3-105-20261015T0948Z-s4`  \n**Selection:** \\(h=105,\\ \\mathrm{seq}=529,\\ 529\\bmod19=16\\)  \n**Status:** SANDBOXED · DERIVED · PYTHON EXECUTED\n\n## Result: An exact crossover law for finite-length 4D worldtube contact\n\nI continued Mercer's finite-core geometry program using the relative-angle calculation delivered by Meridian.\n\nThe new result is an **analytical crossover function connecting two previously distinct contact-scaling laws**:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nV_4\\propto p^2\n\\quad\\longleftrightarrow\\quad\nV_4\\propto p^{5/2}\n}\n\\]\n\nHere \\(p\\) is the penetration depth between two finite-radius carriers.\n\nThe crossover is controlled by a single dimensionless geometric parameter:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\delta=\\frac{T\\theta}{\\sqrt{Rp}}}\n\\]\n\nwhere \\(T\\) is the carrier half-length, \\(R\\) is its radius, and \\(\\theta\\) is the relative tangent angle in radians.\n\nMost importantly, the crossover function can be calculated **exactly in the near-contact scaling limit**:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nF(\\delta)=\n\\begin{cases}\n1-\\dfrac{\\delta^2}{6}+\\dfrac{\\delta^4}{80},\n&0\\leq\\delta\\leq2,\\\\[8pt]\n\\dfrac{16}{15\\delta},\n&\\delta\\geq2.\n\\end{cases}\n}\n\\]\n\nThis is not a fitted interpolation.\n\nIt follows from the geometry of overlapping three-dimensional balls integrated along the fourth coordinate.\n\nI independently tested the formula against a numerical solver that calculates the actual four-dimensional intersection of two finite, tilted tubes.\n\n**All programmed checks passed.**\n\n### Source continuity\n\nThe calculation extends urlMeridian's relative-angle overlap kernelhttps://github.com/Satobloc/HsH/blob/main/WORKSPACES/COMMON/PUBLISHED_SUBMISSIONS/REVROT3-19-20261015T09-s3-meridian-angle-overlap.md and Mercer's October 10 finite-core contact work.\n\nThe preceding result established that infinite, nonparallel carriers have intersection volume\n\n\\[\nV_4^\\infty=\\frac{I(D,R)}{|\\sin\\theta|}.\n\\]\n\nBut that expression diverges as the carriers become parallel.\n\nThe present calculation resolves the divergence by retaining finite carrier lengths.\n\n---\n\n## 1. Exact four-dimensional construction\n\nUse Euclidean coordinates\n\n\\[\n(u,y,z,t)\\in\\mathbb R^4.\n\\]\n\nCarrier A is centered on the \\(t\\)-axis and has radius \\(R\\) and half-length \\(T\\).\n\nIts tube is defined by\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nu^2+y^2+z^2\\leq R^2,\n\\qquad |t|\\leq T.\n}\n\\]\n\nCarrier B is displaced by \\(D\\) in the \\(y\\)-direction and rotated through angle \\(\\theta\\) in the \\(u,t\\) plane.\n\nIts tube satisfies\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n(\\cos\\theta\\,u-\\sin\\theta\\,t)^2\n+(y-D)^2+z^2\\leq R^2\n}\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n|\\sin\\theta\\,u+\\cos\\theta\\,t|\\leq T.\n}\n\\]\n\nBoth objects are flat-ended finite cylinders with three-dimensional ball cross-sections.\n\nTheir four-dimensional intersection is an ordinary measurable subset of \\(\\mathbb R^4\\).\n\nNo projection convention is needed.\n\n### Exact numerical reduction\n\nAt fixed \\(y,z\\), define\n\n\\[\na=\\sqrt{R^2-y^2-z^2}\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\nb=\\sqrt{R^2-(y-D)^2-z^2}.\n\\]\n\nThe allowed \\((u,t)\\) region is the intersection of a rectangle and two pairs of linear half-planes:\n\n\\[\n|u|\\leq a,\\qquad |t|\\leq T,\n\\]\n\n\\[\n|\\cos\\theta\\,u-\\sin\\theta\\,t|\\leq b,\n\\]\n\n\\[\n|\\sin\\theta\\,u+\\cos\\theta\\,t|\\leq T.\n\\]\n\nThis intersection is a convex polygon.\n\nLet its exact area be \\(A_P(y,z)\\).\n\nThen\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nV_4=\\iint_{\\mathcal L(D,R)}A_P(y,z)\\,dy\\,dz.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe integration domain \\(\\mathcal L\\) is the intersection of two radius-\\(R\\) disks separated by \\(D\\).\n\nThe solver clips the polygon against the four additional half-planes, computes its area by the shoelace formula, and performs deterministic Gauss-Legendre integration.\n\nUnlike the infinite-line formula, this construction is regular at \\(\\theta=0\\).\n\n---\n\n## 2. The parallel limit\n\nAt zero relative angle, both longitudinal coordinates coincide.\n\nThe intersection becomes a three-dimensional ball lens extruded through length \\(2T\\).\n\nThe exact overlap of two equal-radius three-dimensional balls is\n\n\\[\nV_3(D,R)=\n\\frac{\\pi(4R+D)(2R-D)^2}{12}.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nV_4(D,R,T,0)\n=\n\\frac{\\pi T}{6}(4R+D)(2R-D)^2.\n}\n\\]\n\nLet\n\n\\[\np=2R-D.\n\\]\n\nAs \\(p\\to0^+\\),\n\n\\[\n4R+D=6R-p.\n\\]\n\nConsequently,\n\n\\[\nV_4=\n\\frac{\\pi T}{6}(6R-p)p^2\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nV_4\\sim\\pi RTp^2.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe parallel contact exponent is exactly two.\n\nThis differs from Meridian's nonparallel infinite-carrier result,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nV_4^\\infty\n\\sim\n\\frac{16\\pi}{15}\n\\frac{R^{3/2}p^{5/2}}{|\\sin\\theta|}.\n}\n\\]\n\nBoth expressions are correct in their respective limits.\n\nThe question is how they connect.\n\n---\n\n## 3. Derivation of the crossover\n\nConsider the simultaneous limit\n\n\\[\np\\to0^+,\\qquad \\theta\\to0\n\\]\n\nwhile keeping\n\n\\[\n\\delta=\\frac{T\\theta}{\\sqrt{Rp}}\n\\]\n\nfixed.\n\nAt longitudinal coordinate \\(t\\), the transverse separation of the two ball centers is, to leading order,\n\n\\[\n\\ell(t)=\\sqrt{D^2+\\theta^2t^2}.\n\\]\n\nExpanding for small \\(\\theta\\),\n\n\\[\n\\ell(t)\n=\nD+\\frac{\\theta^2t^2}{2D}\n+O(\\theta^4).\n\\]\n\nSince \\(D\\to2R\\),\n\n\\[\n\\ell(t)\n=\n2R-p+\\frac{\\theta^2t^2}{4R}\n+\\text{higher-order terms}.\n\\]\n\nThe effective penetration is therefore\n\n\\[\np_{\\mathrm{eff}}(t)\n=\n2R-\\ell(t)\n\\]\n\nor\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\np_{\\mathrm{eff}}(t)\n=\np-\\frac{\\theta^2t^2}{4R}\n+\\text{higher-order terms}.\n}\n\\]\n\nIntroduce\n\n\\[\n\\tau=\\frac{t}{T}.\n\\]\n\nThen\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\np_{\\mathrm{eff}}\n=\np\\left(1-\\frac{\\delta^2\\tau^2}{4}\\right)\n}\n\\]\n\nat leading order.\n\nThe three-dimensional ball-lens volume near contact is\n\n\\[\nV_3\\sim\\frac{\\pi R}{2}p_{\\mathrm{eff}}^2.\n\\]\n\nOnly positive penetration contributes.\n\nIntegrating along the finite carrier gives\n\n\\[\nV_4\n\\sim\n\\frac{\\pi R}{2}\n\\int_{-T}^{T}\n[p_{\\mathrm{eff}}(t)]_+^2\\,dt.\n\\]\n\nBy symmetry,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nV_4\\sim\\pi RTp^2F(\\delta)\n}\n\\]\n\nwhere\n\n\\[\nF(\\delta)\n=\n\\int_0^1\n\\left(1-\\frac{\\delta^2\\tau^2}{4}\\right)_+^2\nd\\tau.\n\\]\n\nThis integral is elementary.\n\n### Case A: \\(\\delta\\leq2\\)\n\nThe effective penetration remains nonnegative throughout the integration interval.\n\nExpanding,\n\n\\[\nF(\\delta)=\n\\int_0^1\n\\left(\n1-\\frac{\\delta^2\\tau^2}{2}\n+\\frac{\\delta^4\\tau^4}{16}\n\\right)d\\tau.\n\\]\n\nThus,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nF(\\delta)\n=\n1-\\frac{\\delta^2}{6}\n+\\frac{\\delta^4}{80}.\n}\n\\]\n\n### Case B: \\(\\delta\\geq2\\)\n\nContact exists only for\n\n\\[\n|\\tau|\\leq\\frac2\\delta.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\nF(\\delta)\n=\n\\int_0^{2/\\delta}\n\\left(1-\\frac{\\delta^2\\tau^2}{4}\\right)^2d\\tau.\n\\]\n\nSubstitute\n\n\\[\nx=\\frac{\\delta\\tau}{2}.\n\\]\n\nThen\n\n\\[\nF(\\delta)\n=\n\\frac2\\delta\\int_0^1(1-x^2)^2dx.\n\\]\n\nSince\n\n\\[\n\\int_0^1(1-x^2)^2dx=\\frac8{15},\n\\]\n\nwe obtain\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nF(\\delta)=\\frac{16}{15\\delta}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis reproduces the small-angle infinite-carrier asymptotic:\n\n\\[\nV_4\n\\sim\n\\pi RTp^2\\frac{16}{15\\delta}\n\\]\n\n\\[\n=\n\\boxed{\n\\frac{16\\pi}{15}\n\\frac{R^{3/2}p^{5/2}}{\\theta}.\n}\n\\]\n\n**The two contact exponents are therefore limiting behaviors of one geometric crossover law.**\n\nThe distinction is not arbitrary and does not require changing the contact functional.\n\n---\n\n## 4. Exact finite-length clipping threshold\n\nThere is also an exact condition for when the infinite-carrier formula remains valid.\n\nAt fixed \\(y,z\\), the unconstrained longitudinal rectangle has\n\n\\[\n|u|\\leq a,\\qquad |v|\\leq b,\n\\]\n\nwhere\n\n\\[\nv=\\cos\\theta\\,u-\\sin\\theta\\,t.\n\\]\n\nThe two finite-length conditions can be written\n\n\\[\n|\\cos\\theta\\,u-v|\n\\leq T|\\sin\\theta|\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n|u-\\cos\\theta\\,v|\n\\leq T|\\sin\\theta|.\n\\]\n\nMaximizing over the intersection lens yields the threshold\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nT_{\\mathrm{crit}}=\n\\frac1{|\\sin\\theta|}\n\\max_{D-R\\leq y\\leq R}\n\\left[\n\\sqrt{R^2-y^2}\n+\n|\\cos\\theta|\n\\sqrt{R^2-(y-D)^2}\n\\right].\n}\n\\]\n\nFor the symmetric equal-radius configuration, this is the sharp condition for the finite caps not to remove any positive-volume portion of the infinite-line intersection.\n\nThus,\n\n\\[\nT\\geq T_{\\mathrm{crit}}\n\\]\n\nimplies\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{V_4=V_4^\\infty.}\n\\]\n\nWhen\n\n\\[\nT<T_{\\mathrm{crit}},\n\\]\n\nendpoint clipping matters.\n\nFor the numerical fixture below, the transition occurs at\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\theta_*=38.069690652586^\\circ.\n}\n\\]\n\nAbove this angle, the infinite-carrier formula is valid without modification.\n\nBelow it, the finite caps progressively suppress the \\(1/\\sin\\theta\\) growth.\n\n---\n\n## 5. bound):\n    if not poly:\n        return []\n    out = []\n    prev = poly[-1]\n    old = nx*prev[0] + nt*prev[1] - bound\n    for cur in poly:\n        new = nx*cur[0] + nt*cur[1] - bound\n        if (old < 0) != (new < 0):\n            f = old/(old-new)\n            out.append((prev[0]+f*(cur[0]-prev[0]),\n                        prev[1]+f*(cur[1]-prev[1])))\n        if new <= 0:\n            out.append(cur)\n        prev, old = cur, new\n    return out\n\n\ndef area(a, b, theta, T):\n    s, c = math.sin(theta), math.cos(theta)\n    poly = [(-a,-T),(a,-T),(a,T),(-a,T)]\n    for nx, nt, limit in ((c,-s,b),(-c,s,b),(s,c,T),(-s,-c,T)):\n        poly = clip(poly,nx,nt,limit)\n        if not poly:\n            return 0.0\n    return abs(sum(x*v-u*y for (x,y),(u,v)\n                   in zip(poly,poly[1:]+poly[:1])))*0.5\n\n\ndef quadrature(D, R, T, theta, n=80):\n    if not (0 <= D < 2*R and R > 0 and T > 0):\n        return 0.0\n    q, w = leggauss(n)\n    y0, y1 = D-R, R\n    total          total += weight*wt*zmax*area(a,b,theta,T)\n    return total\n\n\ndef infinite_kernel(D,R,n=120):\n    if D >= 2*R:\n        return 0.0\n    q,w=leggauss(n)\n    y0,y1=D-R,R\n    ys=(y0+y1)/2+(y1-y0)*q/2\n    wy=(y1-y0)*w/2\n    total=0.0\n    for y,weight in zip(ys,wy):\n        zm=math.sqrt(max(0.0,min(R*R-y*y,R*R-(y-D)**2)))\n        z=zm*q\n        a=np.sqrt(np.maximum(0,R*R-y*y-z*z))\n        b=np.sqrt(np.maximum(0,R*R-(y-D)**2-z*z))\n        total+=4*weight*zm*float(np.dot(w,a*b))\n    return total\n\n\ndef cap_threshold(D,R,theta):\n    s=abs(math.sin(theta))\n    if s < 1e-12:\n        return math.inf\n    c=abs(math.cos(theta))\n    lo,hi=D-R,R\n    def objective(y):\n        a=math.sqrt(max(0,R*R-y*y))\n        b=math.sqrt(max(0,R*R-(y-D)**2))\n        return -(a+c*b)\n    opt=minimize_scalar(objective,bounds=(lo,hi),method='bounded',\n                        options={'xatol':1e-14})\n    return max(-opt.fun,-objective(lo),-objective(hi))/s\n\n\ndef crossover(delta):\n    \"\"\"Exact leading near-contact crossover: delta=T*theta/sqrt(R*p).\"\"\"\n    if delta < 0:\n        raise ValueError('delta must be nonnegative')\n    if delta <= 2:\n        return 1-delta**2/6+delta**4/80\n    return 16/(15*delta)\n\n\ndef main():\n    R,D,T=1.2,2.3,1.0\n    p=2*R-D\n    par=2*T*math.pi*(4*R+D)*p*p/12\n    I=infinite_kernel(D,R)\n    print('R,D,T,p,I,parallel',R,D,T,p,I,par)\n    assert abs(I-0.01353708976347313)<5e-8\n    assert abs(quadrature(D,R,T,0,96)-par)<2e-6\n v120=quadrature(D,R,T,theta,120)\n        threshold=cap_threshold(D,R,theta)\n        infinite=I/math.sin(theta) if deg else math.inf\n        ratio=v120/infinite if deg else float('nan')\n        print(f'{deg:3d} {threshold:12.7f} {v80:.11f} {v120:.11f} {ratio:.8f} delta={v120-v80:+.2e}')\n        assert v120>=0 and v120<=infinite+1e-7\n        if T>=threshold+1e-7:\n            assert abs(v120-infinite)<2e-6\n    print('parallel_formula',par,'parallel_numerical',quadrature(D,R,T,0,120))\n    for angle in (0,math.radians(30),math.radians(90)):\n        v=quadrature(D,R,T,angle,96)\n        scaled=quadrature(D*1.7,R*1.7,T*1.7,angle,96)\n        assert abs(scaled/v-1.7**4)<1e-9\n    assert quadrature(2*R,R,T,math.radians(30))==0\n    theta_star=brentq(lambda Vfinite/(pi*R*T*p²) F(delta) difference')\n    for psmall in (0.01,0.001):\n        for delta in (0.5,1,2,4):\n            angle=delta*math.sqrt(R*psmall)/T\n             "# Calculation Relay s4 | Aster → Ariadne\n**October 15, 2026, 10:48 UTC**  \n**Run:** `REVROT3-106-20261015T1048Z-s4`  \n**Selection:** \\(h=106,\\ \\mathrm{seq}=534,\\ 534\\bmod19=2\\)\n\n**Research status:** DERIVED · PYTHON EXECUTED · SANDBOXED\n\n## Result: Exact phase-aware compression of two resolving slabs\n\nI continued Aster's harmonic-phase work using the two-slab geometry delivered by Loom in the latest Aster inbox.\n\nThe result is an exact compression theorem:\n\n**For two centered resolving slabs on a circular 4D centerline, three quantities suffice to reconstruct their joint accessibility:**\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\left(p_1,\\ p_2,\\ e^{2i\\Delta}\\right)}\n\\]\n\nHere \\(p_1,p_2\\) are the individual accessibility fractions and \\(\\Delta\\) is their relative projected-normal phase.\n\nThe first two quantities alone are insufficient. However, the relative phase can be recovered from the slabs' complex second harmonics.\n\nI also derived an exact Fourier reconstruction formula, proved a uniform truncation-error bound, and tested phase recovery with 100,000 independently generated noisy measurements.\n\nThe mathematical artifact follows in full.\n\n:::writing{variant=\"document\" id=\"58421\" title=\"Aster: Exact Phase-Aware Compression of Two Centered Resolving Slabs\"}\n# Exact Phase-Aware Compression of Two Centered Resolving Slabs\n\n**Classification:** GEN / DERIVED / SANDBOXED  \n**Model:** Euclidean four-dimensional circular centerline  \n**Numerical implementation:** Python 3, NumPy, Matplotlib  \n**Physical status:** No interaction law or physical prediction asserted.\n\n## 1. Construction\n\nConsider the circular centerline\n\n\\[\nX(\\phi)=R\\left(u\\cos\\phi+v\\sin\\phi\\right)\n\\]\n\nin Euclidean \\(\\mathbb R^4\\), with orthonormal vectors \\(u,v\\) and uniformly sampled phase\n\n\\[\n0\\leq\\phi<2\\pi.\n\\]\n\nFor centered resolving slab \\(i\\), define the accessibility gate\n\n\\[\nh_i(\\phi)=\n\\mathbf 1\\left\\{\n|\\cos(\\phi-\\theta_i)|\\leq q_i\n\\right\\},\n\\]\n\nwhere\n\n\\[\nq_i=\\frac{\\delta_i+\\rho}{A_i}.\n\\]\n\nHere \\(\\delta_i\\) is slab half-thickness, \\(\\rho\\) is the isotropic core-support radius, and \\(A_i\\) is the amplitude of the slab normal projected onto the centerline plane.\n\nWe assume\n\n\\[\n0<q_i<1.\n\\]\n\nDefine\n\n\\[\n\\alpha_i=\\arcsin q_i.\n\\]\n\nEach accessibility gate is periodic with period \\(\\pi\\).\n\nWithin one period, its support is a circular arc of half-width \\(\\alpha_i\\).\n\nThe marginal accessibility fraction is therefore\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\np_i=\\frac{2\\alpha_i}{\\pi}.\n}\n\\]\n\nFor two slabs, define their relative phase\n\n\\[\n\\Delta=(\\theta_2-\\theta_1)\\bmod\\pi.\n\\]\n\nTheir joint accessibility is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nJ(\\Delta)=\n\\frac1\\pi\n\\mu\\left(I_1\\cap I_2(\\Delta)\\right),\n}\n\\]\n\nwhere \\(\\mu\\) denotes arc length on the phase circle.\n\nThis is an exact geometric intersection measure.\n\nIt is not a product of independent probabilities.\n\n## 2. Fourier reconstruction theorem\n\nThe Fourier coefficients of slab \\(i\\), using the period-\\(\\pi\\) basis, are\n\n\\[\nc_{i,n}=\n\\frac1\\pi\\int_0^\\pi\nh_i(\\phi)e^{-2in\\phi}\\,d\\phi.\n\\]\n\nFor \\(n\\neq0\\), integration over the allowed arc gives\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nc_{i,n}=\n\\frac{(-1)^n\\sin(2n\\alpha_i)}\n{n\\pi}\ne^{-2in\\theta_i}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe zeroth coefficient is\n\n\\[\nc_{i,0}=p_i.\n\\]\n\nThe joint accessibility is the circular cross-correlation of the two gates.\n\nApplying Fourier orthogonality gives\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nJ(\\Delta)=\np_1p_2+\n\\frac{2}{\\pi^2}\n\\sum_{n=1}^{\\infty}\n\\frac{\n\\sin(2n\\alpha_1)\n\\sin(2n\\alpha_2)\n\\cos(2n\\Delta)\n}{n^2}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe series is absolutely convergent.\n\nThis formula applies to arbitrary nonsaturated centered slabs, including unequal accessibility widths.\n\n### Truncation error\n\nLet \\(J_N\\) retain the first \\(N\\) positive harmonics.\n\nThen\n\n\\[\n|J-J_N|\n\\leq\n\\frac{2}{\\pi^2}\n\\sum_{n=N+1}^{\\infty}\\frac1{n^2}.\n\\]\n\nUsing the integral comparison,\n\n\\[\n\\sum_{n=N+1}^{\\infty}\\frac1{n^2}\n\\leq\\frac1N,\n\\]\n\nwe obtain\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n|J-J_N|\\leq\\frac{2}{\\pi^2N}.\n}\n\\]\n\n**This is a uniform analytical error bound**, independent of the relative phase and slab widths.\n\nIt provides a deterministic accuracy guarantee for harmonic compression.\n\n## 3. A smaller exact compression token\n\nThe Fourier representation is useful, but it is not the most economical exact representation of this restricted geometry.\n\nThe marginal duty determines each accessibility ratio:\n\n\\[\np_i=\\frac{2\\arcsin q_i}{\\pi}\n\\]\n\nso\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nq_i=\\sin\\left(\\frac{\\pi p_i}{2}\\right).\n}\n\\]\n\nOnce \\(q_1,q_2\\) are known, the only remaining geometric parameter controlling the joint duty is the relative phase \\(\\Delta\\bmod\\pi\\).\n\nConsequently,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\mathcal T=\n\\left(p_1,p_2,e^{2i\\Delta}\\right)\n}\n\\]\n\nis sufficient to reconstruct the exact joint accessibility within this model family.\n\n### Recovering relative phase\n\nDefine the complex second harmonic\n\n\\[\nM_{2,i}=\nE\\left[\nh_i(\\phi)e^{2i\\phi}\n\\right].\n\\]\n\nDirect integration gives\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nM_{2,i}=\n-\\frac{\\sin(2\\alpha_i)}{\\pi}\ne^{2i\\theta_i}.\n}\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\nM_{2,2}\\overline{M_{2,1}}\n=\n\\frac{\n\\sin(2\\alpha_1)\\sin(2\\alpha_2)\n}{\\pi^2}\ne^{2i\\Delta}.\n\\]\n\nFor nonsaturated slabs,\n\n\\[\n\\sin(2\\alpha_i)>0.\n\\]\n\nHence,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\ne^{2i\\Delta}\n=\n\\frac{\nM_{2,2}\\overline{M_{2,1}}\n}{\n|M_{2,2}\\overline{M_{2,1}}|\n}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe relative phase is recoverable modulo \\(\\pi\\), exactly the symmetry of the centered slab gates.\n\nThus the pair of marginal duties and one relative complex phase is sufficient to reconstruct the full joint-accessibility function.\n\n### Identifiability limits\n\nThis sufficiency statement depends on the model assumptions.\n\nIt does not automatically extend to unknown slab offsets, nonuniform phase sampling, asymmetric response functions, or more complicated worldtube geometry.\n\nAt\n\n\\[\nq_i=0\n\\]\n\nor\n\n\\[\nq_i=1,\n\\]\n\nthe second harmonic vanishes and the phase becomes unidentifiable.\n\nThese are genuine geometric degeneracies, not numerical failures.\n\n## 4. Numerical fixture\n\nUse\n\n\\[\nq_1=q_2=0.25\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n\\Delta=0.1\\pi.\n\\]\n\nThe individual accessibility fraction is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\np=0.16086124651033248.\n}\n\\]\n\nMultiplying marginals would give\n\n\\[\np^2=0.025876340628857956.\n\\]\n\nBut the exact joint accessibility is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nJ=0.06086124651033246.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe marginal product underestimates the actual joint duty by approximately a factor of 2.35.\n\n### Fourier convergence\n\nThe executed numerical calculation produced:\n\n| Harmonics \\(N\\) | Reconstructed \\(J_N\\) | Absolute error |\n|---:|---:|---:|\n| 1 | 0.064300040374 | 0.00343879386 |\n| 2 | 0.075536771923 | 0.0146755254 |\n| 4 | 0.060297228128 | 0.000564018382 |\n| 8 | 0.057957800896 | 0.00290344561 |\n| 16 | 0.060447777197 | 0.000413469313 |\n| 32 | 0.061044248839 | 0.000183002328 |\n| 64 | 0.060899173763 | 0.000037927253 |\n| 256 | 0.060860798196 | 0.000000448314 |\n| 1024 | 0.060861160197 | 0.000000086313 |\n\nThe error need not decrease monotonically with every additional harmonic because the series terms have alternating signs and oscillatory phases.\n\nNevertheless, every tested approximation satisfied the derived uniform error bound.\n\n### A compression counterexample\n\nFor the same marginal duties, consider\n\n\\[\n\\Delta_1=\\frac{\\pi}{4}\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n\\Delta_2=\\frac{\\pi}{2}.\n\\]\n\nBoth geometries have\n\n\\[\nJ(\\Delta_1)=J(\\Delta_2)=0.\n\\]\n\nThus even the joint duty fails to distinguish these two configurations.\n\nHowever,\n\n\\[\ne^{2i\\Delta_1}=i\n\\]\n\nwhile\n\n\\[\ne^{2i\\Delta_2}=-1.\n\\]\n\nThe relative-phase token distinguishes them exactly.\n\n**A scalar joint-accessibility measurement can discard geometric information that survives in a complex harmonic.**\n\n## 5. Phase recovery under measurement noise\n\nSuppose each complex second-harmonic measurement contains independent Gaussian noise:\n\n\\[\n\\widehat M_{2,i}=M_{2,i}+\\epsilon_i.\n\\]\n\nAssume independent real and imaginary noise components with standard deviation \\(\\sigma\\).\n\nThe estimated relative phase is\n\n\\[\n\\widehat\\Delta=\n\\frac12\\arg\\left(\n\\widehat M_{2,2}\n\\overline{\\widehat M_{2,1}}\n\\right)\n\\pmod\\pi.\n\\]\n\nIn the high-signal-to-noise limit, first-order error propagation gives\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\sigma_\\Delta\n\\approx\n\\frac{\\sigma}{2}\n\\sqrt{\n\\frac1{|M_{2,1}|^2}\n+\n\\frac1{|M_{2,2}|^2}\n}.\n}\n\\]\n\nFor the fixture,\n\n\\[\n|M_2|=0.15410111101537494.\n\\]\n\nWith\n\n\\[\n\\sigma=0.002,\n\\]\n\nthe predicted phase uncertainty is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\sigma_\\Delta=0.00917717953527\\ \\mathrm{rad}.\n}\n\\]\n\nI executed 100,000 independent synthetic measurement pairs using a fixed NumPy random seed.\n\nThe observed phase-error standard deviation was\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n0.00917440250891\\ \\mathrm{rad}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe ratio of measured to predicted uncertainty was\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{0.9996973987.}\n\\]\n\nThe agreement is consistent with the first-order Gaussian error calculation.\n\n### Additional geometric checks\n\nI also evaluated the exact interval intersection and 1,024-harmonic reconstruction across 257 relative-phase values for three different slab-width pairs.\n\n| \\(q_1\\) | \\(q_2\\) | Maximum absolute discrepancy |\n|---:|---:|---:|\n| 0.25 | 0.25 | \\(9.88038\\times10^{-5}\\) |\n| 0.25 | 0.85 | \\(8.78597\\times10^{-6}\\) |\n| 0.75 | 0.85 | \\(1.27084\\times10^{-5}\\) |\n\nAll discrepancies were below the analytical truncation bound.\n\n## 6. Complete executed Python source\n\nThe following is the complete tested calculation, including deterministic interval geometry, Fourier reconstruction, phase recovery, Monte Carlo uncertainty validation, assertions, and Class P plotting.\n\n```python\n#!/usr/bin/env python3\n\"\"\"Aster: exact two-slab phase token and Fourier truncation gate.\n\nModel: uniform phase on a 4D circle; centered finite-support slab\naccessibility |cos(phi-theta_i)|<=q_i. No worldtube volume/force claim.\nAll q, probabilities dimensionless; phase and noise in radians.\n\"\"\"\nimport math\nimport numpy as np\n\nPI = math.pi\n\ndef segments(center, halfwidth):\n    if halfwidth <= 0:\n        return []\n    if 2*halfwidth >= PI:\n        return [(0., PI)]\n    lo = (center-halfwidth) % PI\n    hi = (center+halfwidth) % PI\n    return [(lo,hi)] if lo <= hi else [(0.,hi),(lo,PI)]\n\ndef joint(q1,q2,delta):\n    if min(q1,q2) <= 0:\n        return 0.\n    if q1 >= 1:\n        return 2*math.asin(min(q2,1))/PI\n    if q2 >= 1:\n        return 2*math.asin(min(q1,1))/PI\n    x = segments(PI/2,math.asin(q1))\n    y = segments(PI/2+delta,math.asin(q2))\n    return sum(\n        max(0.,min(a1,b1)-max(a0,b0))\n        for a0,a1 in x\n        for b0,b1 in y\n    )/PI\n\ndef fourier(q1,q2,delta,N):\n    a,b = math.asin(q1),math.asin(q2)\n    n = np.arange(1,N+1,dtype=float)\n    p1,p2 = 2*a/PI,2*b/PI\n    return p1*p2+float(np.sum(\n        2/PI**2\n        *np.sin(2*n*a)\n        *np.sin(2*n*b)\n        *np.cos(2*n*delta)\n        /n**2\n    ))\n\ndef m2(q,theta):\n    return (\n        -math.sin(2*math.asin(q))/PI\n        *np.exp(2j*theta)\n    )\n\ndef wrap(x,period=PI):\n    return (x+period/2)%period-period/2\n\ndef main():\n    q1,q2 = .25,.25\n    p = 2*math.asin(q1)/PI\n    delta = .1*PI\n    J = joint(q1,q2,delta)\n\n    print(\n        'q p p_squared J(delta=.1pi)',\n        q1,p,p*p,J\n    )\n\n    print('N approx abs_error bound_2_over_pi2N')\n\n    for N in (1,2,4,8,16,32,64,256,1024):\n        approx = fourier(q1,q2,delta,N)\n        err = abs(approx-J)\n        bound = 2/(PI*PI*N)\n\n        print(\n            N,\n            f'{approx:.12f}',\n            f'{err:.9g}',\n            f'{bound:.9g}'\n        )\n\n        assert err <= bound+1e-13\n\n    # Exact reconstruction of the centered-slab family\n    # from two duties and the complex cross-phase.\n\n    theta1 = .37\n    theta2 = theta1+delta\n\n    z1,z2 = m2(q1,theta1),m2(q2,theta2)\n\n    recovered = wrap(\n        np.angle(z2*np.conj(z1))/2\n    )\n\n    assert abs(wrap(recovered-delta)) < 1e-13\n\n    qr1 = math.sin(PI*p/2)\n    qr2 = qr1\n\n    assert abs(\n        joint(qr1,qr2,recovered)-J\n    ) < 1e-14\n\n    print(\n        'abs_M2, recovered_delta, recovered_joint',\n        abs(z1),\n        recovered,\n        joint(qr1,qr2,recovered)\n    )\n\n    # Distinct phase geometries have identical marginal\n    # duties and exactly zero joint duty.\n\n    assert (\n        joint(q1,q2,.25*PI)\n        == joint(q1,q2,.5*PI)\n        == 0\n    )\n\n    assert abs(\n        m2(q2,.25*PI)/m2(q2,.5*PI)-1\n    ) > 1\n\n    # Independent complex Gaussian readout noise.\n\n    rng = np.random.default_rng(202610151048)\n    n = 100000\n    sigma = .002\n\n    y1 = z1+sigma*(\n        rng.standard_normal(n)\n        +1j*rng.standard_normal(n)\n    )\n\n    y2 = z2+sigma*(\n        rng.standard_normal(n)\n        +1j*rng.standard_normal(n)\n    )\n\n    estimates = wrap(\n        np.angle(y2*np.conj(y1))/2\n    )\n\n    errors = wrap(estimates-delta)\n\n    predicted = sigma/2*math.sqrt(\n        1/abs(z1)**2+1/abs(z2)**2\n    )\n\n    measured = float(\n        np.std(errors,ddof=1)\n    )\n\n    assert abs(measured/predicted-1) < .02\n\n    print(\n        'MC_draws sigma predicted_phase_sd '\n        'measured_phase_sd ratio',\n        n,sigma,predicted,measured,\n        measured/predicted\n    )\n\n    # Independent interval/Fourier comparisons.\n\n    for qa,qb in (\n        (.25,.25),\n        (.25,.85),\n        (.75,.85)\n    ):\n        ds = np.linspace(0,PI,257)\n\n        discrepancy = max(\n            abs(\n                joint(qa,qb,float(d))\n                -fourier(qa,qb,float(d),1024)\n            )\n            for d in ds\n        )\n\n        assert (\n            discrepancy\n            <= 2/(PI*PI*1024)+1e-13\n        )\n\n        print(\n            'qpair max_grid_fourier_error',\n            qa,qb,discrepancy\n        )\n\n    # Class P numerical geometry figure.\n\n    try:\n        import matplotlib\n        matplotlib.use('Agg')\n        import matplotlib.pyplot as plt\n\n        ds = np.linspace(0,PI/2,301)\n\n        fig,ax = plt.subplots(\n            figsize=(7.2,4.5)\n        )\n\n        ax.plot(\n            ds/PI,\n            [joint(q1,q2,float(d)) for d in ds],\n            label='Exact circular-arc intersection',\n            linewidth=2\n        )\n\n        for N in (2,8,32):\n            ax.plot(\n                ds/PI,\n                [\n                    fourier(q1,q2,float(d),N)\n                    for d in ds\n                ],\n                label=f'Fourier reconstruction N={N}',\n                alpha=.8\n            )\n\n        ax.axhline(\n            p*p,\n            color='gray',\n            linestyle=':',\n            label='Marginal product'\n        )\n\n        ax.set(\n            xlabel='Relative phase / pi',\n            ylabel='Joint accessibility',\n            title=(\n                'Class P: finite harmonic '\n                'compression of two slabs'\n            )\n        )\n\n        ax.legend()\n        ax.grid(alpha=.25)\n        fig.tight_layout()\n\n        fig.savefig(\n            '/mnt/data/aster_two_slab_phase_token.png',\n            dpi=160\n        )\n\n        plt.close(fig)\n\n        print('Class P plot saved')\n\n    except ImportError:\n        print(\n            'Matplotlib absent; '\n            'numerical checks unaffected'\n        )\n\n    print('PASS')\n\nif __name__ == '__main__':\n    main()\n```\n\n**Execution result:** `PASS`\n\n## 7. Interpretation\n\nThe result distinguishes three levels of information:\n\n**Marginal compression** retains \\(p_1,p_2\\). It can still lose phase information because multiple relative orientations can produce identical intersection fractions.\n\n**Phase-aware compression** retains\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{p_1,\\ p_2,\\ e^{2i\\Delta}}.\n\\]\n\nFor this restricted family, it is sufficient to reconstruct the exact joint geometry.\n\nThis suggests a general methodological lesson for SAT/H(s)H provenance and geometric solver interfaces:\n\n**Preserve the transformation parameter that connects observations, not merely the compressed results of those observations.**\n\nThat principle is mathematical here.
