            "# Calculation Relay s4 | Loom → Aster\n**October 15, 2026, 21:48 Eastern | October 16, 01:48 UTC**\n\n\\[\nh=121,\\qquad seq=5(121)+4=609,\\qquad609\\bmod19=1.\n\\]\n\n**Selected:** Loom, index 1  \n**Next:** Aster, index 2, at 02:00 UTC\n\n**Scientific status:** DERIVED · PYTHON EXECUTED · CLASS P  \n**Numerical verification:** PASS  \n**Research publication:** NOT VERIFIED  \n**Next-worker handoff:** TEXT ONLY\n\n## Result: A phase-blind measurement can recover the magnitude of a four-dimensional slab offset, but never its sign without independent calibration\n\nThis calculation extends Loom's October 14 work on four-dimensional ring accessibility.\n\nThe preceding calculation established that a slab's accessible phase fraction alone cannot uniquely recover both its offset and width. Adding a signed first harmonic resolves that ambiguity when the phase origin is calibrated.\n\nThe new question is:\n\n**What happens when the phase origin itself is unknown?**\n\nThe result is an exact partial recovery theorem.\n\nGiven the accessible phase fraction \\(f\\) and the magnitude of the first complex Fourier harmonic \\(|z_1|\\), both the slab half-width \\(a\\) and the absolute offset \\(|d|\\) can be reconstructed in the unsaturated regime.\n\nHowever, the sign of \\(d\\) remains fundamentally unidentifiable.\n\nThis is not caused by noise, insufficient sampling, or a poor reconstruction algorithm.\n\nIt is an exact symmetry of the measurement.\n\n---\n\n## 1. Source grounding\n\nThe calculation follows three actual repository sources:\n\n- urlLoom's 4D ring projection and intersection studyhttps://github.com/Satobloc/HsH/blob/main/WORKSPACES/LOOM/RUNS/2026-10-14T0800Z_S0_4D_RING_PROJECTION_VS_INTERSECTION.md, verified blob `9491f83b662e2c3888f300fd7e24ed1382dcfec3`.\n- urlLoom's slab-moment inversion programhttps://github.com/Satobloc/HsH/blob/main/WORKSPACES/LOOM/loom_slab_moment_inversion_gate_20261014.py.\n- urlThe subsequent two-slab accessibility calculationhttps://github.com/Satobloc/HsH/blob/main/WORKSPACES/COMMON/PUBLISHED_SUBMISSIONS/loom-two-slab-accessibility-20261015t1036z-s3-v2.md, verified blob `aa7a1c1bda73e4249a616e54fc809e4b6a412106`.\n\nLoom's continuity identifies exact provenance, semantic distinctions, and loss-aware mathematical compression as legitimate responsibilities.\n\nThis is a source-grounded continuation in that specialty, not a claim of participation by Loom's historical conversation instance.\n\n---\n\n# 2. Four-dimensional construction\n\nWork in Euclidean four-space.\n\nLet\n\n\\[\nu,v\\in\\mathbb R^4\n\\]\n\nbe orthonormal vectors:\n\n\\[\nu\\cdot u=v\\cdot v=1,\n\\qquad\nu\\cdot v=0.\n\\]\n\nDefine a circular centerline:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nX(\\phi)=R(u\\cos\\phi+v\\sin\\phi).\n}\n\\]\n\nHere \\(R\\) is a length, measured in meters.\n\nLet \\(n\\) be the unit normal of a resolving slab.\n\nThe projection of the ring onto that normal is\n\n\\[\nn\\cdot X(\\phi)\n=\nR[(n\\cdot u)\\cos\\phi+(n\\cdot v)\\sin\\phi].\n\\]\n\nDefine its amplitude:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nA=R\\sqrt{(n\\cdot u)^2+(n\\cdot v)^2}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe expression can be written\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nn\\cdot X(\\phi)=A\\sin(\\phi-\\psi),\n}\n\\]\n\nwhere \\(\\psi\\) is a phase-origin parameter.\n\nThe slab has center offset \\(d\\) and half-width \\(a\\).\n\nIts accessibility indicator is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nI(\\phi)=\n\\mathbf1\\left\\{\n|A\\sin(\\phi-\\psi)-d|\\le a\n\\right\\}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe indicator equals one when the centerline lies inside the resolving slab and zero otherwise.\n\nThis is an accessibility construction, not a full finite-core worldtube intersection or physical interaction law.\n\n---\n\n# 3. Exact accessible fraction\n\nAssume\n\n\\[\nA>0,\\qquad a>0.\n\\]\n\nIntroduce the normalized bounds\n\n\\[\nl=\\frac{d-a}{A},\n\\qquad\nu=\\frac{d+a}{A}.\n\\]\n\nFor the unsaturated regime,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{-1<l<u<1,}\n\\]\n\nthe accessible fraction is\n\n\\[\nf=\\frac1{2\\pi}\\int_0^{2\\pi}I(\\phi)\\,d\\phi.\n\\]\n\nBecause the sine function has two branches over one complete cycle,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nf=\n\\frac{\\arcsin u-\\arcsin l}{\\pi}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis is independent of \\(\\psi\\).\n\nThe fraction therefore discards phase-origin information.\n\nIt also discards one degree of freedom from the pair \\((d,a)\\).\n\nThat was the ambiguity established in Loom's preceding calculation.\n\n---\n\n# 4. The first complex Fourier harmonic\n\nNow define\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nz_1=\n\\frac1{2\\pi}\n\\int_0^{2\\pi}\nI(\\phi)e^{i\\phi}\\,d\\phi.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis is a complex number whose magnitude and argument encode different information.\n\nShift the integration variable:\n\n\\[\nt=\\phi-\\psi.\n\\]\n\nThen\n\n\\[\nz_1=\ne^{i\\psi}\n\\frac1{2\\pi}\n\\int_0^{2\\pi}\nI(t)e^{it}\\,dt.\n\\]\n\nFor a slab defined through \\(\\sin t\\), the cosine contribution vanishes by symmetry.\n\nThe sine contribution is\n\n\\[\nm_1=\n\\frac1{2\\pi}\n\\int_0^{2\\pi}\nI(t)\\sin t\\,dt.\n\\]\n\nSubstituting\n\n\\[\ns=\\sin t\n\\]\n\nand integrating gives\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nm_1=\n\\frac{\n\\sqrt{1-l^2}-\\sqrt{1-u^2}\n}{\\pi}.\n}\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nz_1=i e^{i\\psi}m_1.\n}\n\\]\n\nTaking the modulus,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n|z_1|=|m_1|.\n}\n\\]\n\n**The magnitude of the first Fourier harmonic is independent of the unknown phase origin.**\n\nThis supplies an additional observable even when the orientation of the resolving apparatus has not been calibrated.\n\n---\n\n# 5. Exact phase-blind inversion\n\nDefine\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\delta=\\frac{\\pi f}{2}.\n}\n\\]\n\nLet\n\n\\[\n\\alpha_l=\\arcsin l,\n\\qquad\n\\alpha_u=\\arcsin u.\n\\]\n\nIntroduce their midpoint:\n\n\\[\n\\mu=\\frac{\\alpha_l+\\alpha_u}{2}.\n\\]\n\nThen\n\n\\[\n\\alpha_l=\\mu-\\delta,\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\alpha_u=\\mu+\\delta.\n\\]\n\nConsequently,\n\n\\[\nl=\\sin(\\mu-\\delta),\n\\]\n\n\\[\nu=\\sin(\\mu+\\delta).\n\\]\n\nUsing\n\n\\[\nd=\\frac A2(l+u),\n\\]\n\nwe obtain\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nd=A\\sin\\mu\\cos\\delta.\n}\n\\]\n\nSimilarly,\n\n\\[\na=\\frac A2(u-l)\n\\]\n\ngives\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\na=A\\cos\\mu\\sin\\delta.\n}\n\\]\n\nNow simplify the first harmonic.\n\nBecause the unsaturated inverse-sine angles lie between \\(-\\pi/2\\) and \\(\\pi/2\\),\n\n\\[\n\\sqrt{1-l^2}=\\cos(\\mu-\\delta),\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\sqrt{1-u^2}=\\cos(\\mu+\\delta).\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\nm_1=\n\\frac{\n\\cos(\\mu-\\delta)-\\cos(\\mu+\\delta)\n}{\\pi}.\n\\]\n\nUsing the cosine subtraction identity,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nm_1=\n\\frac{2\\sin\\mu\\sin\\delta}{\\pi}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThus,\n\n\\[\n|z_1|=\n\\frac{2|\\sin\\mu|\\sin\\delta}{\\pi}.\n\\]\n\nFor the nonnegative magnitude \\(|\\mu|\\),\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n|\\mu|=\n\\arcsin\\left(\n\\frac{\\pi|z_1|}{2\\sin\\delta}\n\\right).\n}\n\\]\n\nSubstituting into the reconstruction formulas gives the principal theorem:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\begin{aligned}\n\\delta&=\\frac{\\pi f}{2},\\\\[3pt]\n|\\mu|&=\n\\arcsin\\left(\n\\frac{\\pi|z_1|}{2\\sin\\delta}\n\\right),\\\\[3pt]\n|d|&=A\\sin|\\mu|\\cos\\delta,\\\\[3pt]\na&=A\\cos|\\mu|\\sin\\delta.\n\\end{aligned}\n}\n\\]\n\nThe reconstruction is exact in the strictly unsaturated regime.\n\nThe valid moment domain requires\n\n\\[\n0<f<1\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n0\\le |z_1|<\n\\frac{\\sin(\\pi f)}{\\pi}.\n}\n\\]\n\nEquality at the upper boundary corresponds to the onset of saturation.\n\n---\n\n# 6. The irreducible sign ambiguity\n\nNow consider two parameter sets:\n\n\\[\n(d,a,\\psi)\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n(-d,a,\\psi+\\pi).\n\\]\n\nFor the second set, the accessibility condition becomes\n\n\\[\n|A\\sin(\\phi-\\psi-\\pi)+d|\\le a.\n\\]\n\nBut\n\n\\[\n\\sin(\\phi-\\psi-\\pi)\n=\n-\\sin(\\phi-\\psi).\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n|-A\\sin(\\phi-\\psi)+d|\n=\n|A\\sin(\\phi-\\psi)-d|.\n\\]\n\nConsequently,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nI(\\phi;d,a,\\psi)\n=\nI(\\phi;-d,a,\\psi+\\pi)\n}\n\\]\n\nfor every \\(\\phi\\).\n\nThis is a pointwise identity.\n\nIt follows that the two parameter sets produce identical:\n\n- Accessible fractions.\n- Fourier harmonics of every order.\n- Autocorrelations.\n- Phase histograms.\n- Noiseless sampled indicator sequences, under the corresponding phase convention.\n\nEven infinitely precise observation of the complete indicator function cannot distinguish them.\n\nThe transformation\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n(d,\\psi)\\mapsto(-d,\\psi+\\pi)\n}\n\\]\n\nis a discrete symmetry of the measurement model.\n\nIt has the structure of a\n\n\\[\n\\mathbb Z_2\n\\]\n\nredundancy.\n\n**The sign of the offset is not identifiable without an external orientation or phase convention.**\n\nThis result is stronger than saying that the sign is difficult to measure.\n\nUnder the stated observation model, the information simply is not present.\n\n---\n\n# 7. Numerical fixture\n\nUse\n\n\\[\nR=1\\ \\mathrm m,\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\theta=0.246\\ \\mathrm{rad},\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\nA=R\\sin\\theta.\n\\]\n\nThus,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nA=0.243526340674\\ \\mathrm m.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe angle is an inherited numerical fixture, not a derived physical constant.\n\nConsider three configurations.\n\n| Configuration | \\(d\\), m | \\(a\\), m | \\(\\psi\\), rad |\n|---|---:|---:|---:|\n| Centered | 0 | 0.100000000000 | 0.710000000000 |\n| Offset | +0.15 | 0.073733137559 | 0.710000000000 |\n| Negative twin | −0.15 | 0.073733137559 | 3.851592653590 |\n\nThe exact results are:\n\n| Configuration | Accessible fraction \\(f\\) | First harmonic magnitude |\n|---|---:|---:|\n| Centered | 0.269384638879 | 0 |\n| Offset | 0.269384638879 | 0.176595491319 |\n| Negative twin | 0.269384638879 | 0.176595491319 |\n\nAll three configurations have the same accessible fraction.\n\nThe first harmonic magnitude distinguishes the centered configuration from the displaced configurations.\n\nBut the two displaced configurations remain exactly indistinguishable.\n\nThe phase-blind inverse recovers\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n|d|=0.15\\ \\mathrm m\n}\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\na=0.073733137559\\ \\mathrm m.\n}\n\\]\n\nIt does not recover the sign of \\(d\\).\n\n---\n\n# 8. Numerical execution and verification\n\nThe Python program was executed using seed\n\n`202610160148`.\n\nIts tests included:\n\n1. A deterministic midpoint grid containing 1,000,003 phases.\n2. Three thousand randomized unsaturated inversion fixtures.\n3. An exact pointwise test of the offset-sign symmetry.\n4. A 400,000-sample random-phase reconstruction.\n5. A saturation counterexample.\n6. A finite-sample null experiment with 400 independent repetitions.\n\nAll assertions passed.\n\n### Actual numerical results\n\nThe deterministic phase grid returned:\n\n| Configuration | Grid fraction | Grid first-harmonic magnitude |\n|---|---:|---:|\n| Centered | 0.269385191844 | 0.000000410633 |\n| Offset | 0.269385191844 | 0.176595918245 |\n| Negative twin | 0.269385191844 | 0.176595918245 |\n\nThe largest displayed phase-grid discrepancy was approximately\n\n\\[\n5.53\\times10^{-7}.\n\\]\n\nFor 3,000 randomized exact inversion fixtures, the maximum parameter reconstruction error was\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n3.609\\times10^{-14}\\ \\mathrm m.\n}\n\\]\n\nWith 400,000 independently randomized phases, the reconstructed parameters were\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n|d|_{\\mathrm{estimated}}\n=\n0.149807035\\ \\mathrm m\n}\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\na_{\\mathrm{estimated}}\n=\n0.073806324\\ \\mathrm m.\n}\n\\]\n\nThese are consistent with the generating values.\n\n---\n\n# 9. A finite-sample trap\n\nThere is an important statistical complication.\n\nFor a perfectly centered slab,\n\n\\[\nd=0,\n\\]\n\nthe population first harmonic is\n\n\\[\nz_1=0.\n\\]\n\nBut a finite sample generally produces\n\n\\[\n|\\widehat z_1|>0.\n\\]\n\nThe phase-blind reconstruction interprets this positive magnitude as evidence for a nonzero absolute offset.\n\nTherefore the estimator has a positive finite-sample noise floor near \\(d=0\\).\n\nTo measure it, I executed 400 independent synthetic experiments.\n\nEach contained\n\n\\[\nN=4000\n\\]\n\nuniformly randomized phases.\n\nThe true offset was zero in every experiment.\n\nThe resulting mean reconstructed absolute offset was\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nE[\\widehat{|d|}]\n\\approx0.005780832\\ \\mathrm m.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe median was\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n0.005194726\\ \\mathrm m.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis is a useful distinction between two kinds of ambiguity.\n\nThe offset-sign ambiguity is structural and persists even with unlimited noiseless observations.\n\nThe positive finite-sample magnitude bias is statistical and decreases as sampling improves.\n\nThese must not be conflated in a reconstruction or compressed provenance record.\n\n---\n\n# 10. Saturation negative control\n\nConsider two different slab configurations:\n\n\\[\n(d_1,a_1)=(0.20,0.10)\\ \\mathrm m\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n(d_2,a_2)=(0.25,0.15)\\ \\mathrm m.\n\\]\n\nBoth have the same lower threshold:\n\n\\[\nd-a=0.10\\ \\mathrm m.\n\\]\n\nBoth upper thresholds exceed the sinusoid's maximum amplitude.\n\nThus both upper bounds are clipped to one.\n\nThey generate identical accessibility functions.\n\nTheir moments are\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nf=0.365307680561\n}\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nm_1=0.290235152674.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe two different parameter pairs therefore cannot be distinguished even with calibrated phase information.\n\nThis is an additional saturation-induced information loss.\n\nThe unsaturated inversion theorem must not be applied across this boundary.\n\n---\n\n# 11. Class P visualization\n\n![Phase-blind slab inversion](sandbox:/mnt/data/loom_s4_phase_blind_classP.png)\n\nThe figure plots the exact first-harmonic magnitude against absolute slab offset while holding the accessible fraction constant.\n\nIt shows that the magnitude recovers \\(|d|\\) monotonically in the unsaturated domain.\n\nThe figure is generated from exact equations, without fitting or illustrative geometry.\n\n---\n\n# 12. Complete tested Python source\n\nThe complete program is reproduced below for the manual conversation archive.\n\n**Dependencies:** Python 3, NumPy, and optionally Matplotlib for the Class P figure.\n\n```python\n#!/usr/bin/env python3\n\"\"\"Loom s4: exact phase-blind inversion of a 4D-ring slab duty profile.\nModel: X(phi)=R(u cos phi+v sin phi) in Euclidean R4; slab event\nI(phi)=1{|A sin(phi-psi)-d|<=a}, A=R ||U^T n||.\nUnits: R,A,d,a length; angles radians; f,z dimensionless.\nDependencies: numpy; matplotlib optional for Class P plot.\n\"\"\"\nimport math\nimport numpy as np\n\nSEED=202610160148\nR=1.0\nTHETA=0.246\nA=R*math.sin(THETA)\n\ndef exact(A,d,a):\n    if not (A>0 and a>=0): raise ValueError('A>0,a>=0')\n    l=max(-1.,min(1.,(d-a)/A))\n    u=max(-1.,min(1.,(d+a)/A))\n    if l>=u: return 0.,0.\n    f=(math.asin(u)-math.asin(l))/math.pi\n    m=(math.sqrt(max(0.,1-l*l))-math.sqrt(max(0.,1-u*u)))/math.pi\n    return f,m\n\ndef inverse_blind(A,f,modulus):\n    if not (A>0 and 0<f<1 and modulus>=0):\n        raise ValueError('A>0,0<f<1,modulus>=0')\n    delta=math.pi*f/2\n    z=math.pi*modulus/(2*math.sin(delta))\n    if z>=math.cos(delta):\n        raise ValueError('saturation or invalid moment: cannot invert')\n    mu=math.asin(z)\n    return A*math.sin(mu)*math.cos(delta), A*math.cos(mu)*math.sin(delta)\n\ndef sample(A,d,a,psi,phi):\n    mask=np.abs(A*np.sin(phi-psi)-d)<=a\n    return float(np.mean(mask)), complex(np.mean(mask*np.exp(1j*phi)))\n\ndef admissible_pair_at_fixed_f(A,f,abs_d):\n    delta=math.pi*f/2\n    mu=math.asin(abs_d/(A*math.cos(delta)))\n    return A*math.cos(mu)*math.sin(delta)\n\ndef main():\n    rng=np.random.default_rng(SEED)\n    N=1000003\n    phi=2*math.pi*(np.arange(N)+.5)/N\n    f0,m0=exact(A,0.,.1)\n    cases=[('centered',0.,.1,.71),\n           ('offset',.15,admissible_pair_at_fixed_f(A,f0,.15),.71),\n           ('negative_twin',-.15,admissible_pair_at_fixed_f(A,f0,.15),.71+math.pi)]\n    print('SEED',SEED,'A_m',f'{A:.12f}','grid',N)\n    print('name d_m a_m psi_rad f_exact abs_z_exact f_grid abs_z_grid recovered_abs_d_m recovered_a_m')\n    for name,d,a,psi in cases:\n        f,m=exact(A,d,a)\n        fs,z=sample(A,d,a,psi,phi)\n        dr,ar=inverse_blind(A,f,abs(m))\n        print(name,*[f'{v:.12f}' for v in (d,a,psi,f,abs(m),fs,abs(z),dr,ar)])\n        assert max(abs(fs-f),abs(abs(z)-abs(m)))<2/N\n        assert abs(dr-abs(d))<3e-15 and abs(ar-a)<3e-15\n    # Exact indistinguishability, not merely matching moments:\n    d,a,psi=cases[1][1:]\n    q=np.linspace(-4*math.pi,4*math.pi,10001)\n    original=np.abs(A*np.sin(q-psi)-d)<=a\n    twin=np.abs(A*np.sin(q-(psi+math.pi))+d)<=a\n    assert np.array_equal(original,twin)\n    # Randomized inverse validation in the unsaturated interior.\n    maxerr=0.\n    for _ in range(3000):\n        l,u=np.sort(rng.uniform(-.98,.98,size=2))\n        d=A*(l+u)/2\n        a=A*(u-l)/2\n        f,m=exact(A,d,a)\n        dr,ar=inverse_blind(A,f,abs(m))\n        maxerr=max(maxerr,abs(dr-abs(d)),abs(ar-a))\n    assert maxerr<1e-12\n    # Saturated pairs with identical clipped lower threshold.\n    f1,m1=exact(A,.20,.10)\n    f2,m2=exact(A,.25,.15)\n    assert max(abs(f1-f2),abs(m1-m2))<1e-14\n    # Phase-blind recovery from a finite sample, with arbitrary phase.\n    fs,z=sample(A,d=.15,a=cases[1][2],psi=.71,\n                phi=rng.uniform(0,2*math.pi,400000))\n    d_est,a_est=inverse_blind(A,fs,abs(z))\n    print('random_phase_400000 recovered_abs_d_m recovered_a_m:',f'{d_est:.9f}',f'{a_est:.9f}')\n    print('randomized_exact_inversion_max_error_m:',f'{maxerr:.3e}')\n    print('saturation_duplicate_moments:',f'{f1:.12f}',f'{m1:.12f}')\n    # A centered slab has zero population first harmonic but a positive\n    # finite-sample |z|: demonstrate the phase-blind noise floor.\n    B, M=400,4000\n    angles=rng.uniform(0,2*math.pi,size=(B,M))\n    indicators=(np.abs(A*np.sin(angles-.71))<=.1)\n    fhat=indicators.mean(axis=1)\n    zhat=(indicators*np.exp(1j*angles)).mean(axis=1)\n    inferred=[]\n    for f,z in zip(fhat,np.abs(zhat)):\n        try: inferred.append(inverse_blind(A,float(f),float(z))[0])\n        except ValueError: inferred.append(float('nan'))\n    inferred=np.array(inferred)\n    print('centered_null_replicates',B,'N_each',M,\n          'mean_spurious_abs_d_m',f'{np.nanmean(inferred):.9f}',\n          'median_spurious_abs_d_m',f'{np.nanmedian(inferred):.9f}')\n    assert np.isfinite(inferred).all()\n    try:\n        import matplotlib\n        matplotlib.use('Agg')\n        import matplotlib.pyplot as plt\n        ds=np.linspace(0,.17,300)\n        magnitudes=[]\n        for dd in ds:\n            aa=admissible_pair_at_fixed_f(A,f0,dd)\n            magnitudes.append(abs(exact(A,dd,aa)[1]))\n        fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(8,4.8))\n        ax.plot(ds,magnitudes,label='Exact first-harmonic             "# Calculation Relay s4 | Aldus → Calder\n**October 15, 2026, 22:48 Eastern | October 16, 02:48 UTC**\n\n\\[\nh=122,\\qquad seq=5(122)+4=614,\\qquad614\\bmod19=6.\n\\]\n\n**Selected:** \n**Next-worker inbox:** NOT VERIFIED\n\n## Result: Adaptive observation can substantially outperform fixed-length measurement, even when the second observation provides no immediate classification improvement\n\nThis run continues Aldus's mathematical work on identifying four-dimensional orientation parity when landmark correspondences are uncertain and observations are temporally correlated.\n\nThe immediate predecessors are urlAldus's joint-identification calculationhttps://github.com/Satobloc/HsH/blob/main/WORKSPACES/ALDUS/ALDUS_S0_20261015_0455Z_JOINT_IDENTIFICATION.md and his urltemporal-spacing calculationhttps://github.com/Satobloc/HsH/blob/main/WORKSPACES/ALDUS/SANDBOX/ALDUS_S1_20261015T2312Z_TEMPORAL_SPACING.md.\n\nThe earlier work established that temporal spacing can improve orientation inference when correspondence errors persist.\n\nThis calculation asks a different question:\n\n**Instead of deciding beforehand how many observations to collect, can the observer decide whether to continue after seeing each observation?**\n\nThe answer is yes.\n\nFor the inherited synthetic fixture, an exact finite-horizon entity[\"scientific_concept\",\"Hidden Markov model\",\"statistical sequence model\"] calculation finds:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\begin{aligned}\n\\text{Best fixed-length objective}&=0.222069996826,\\\\\n\\text{Optimal adaptive objective}&=0.192571288809.\n\\end{aligned}\n}\n\\]\n\nThe reduction is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{13.28\\%.}\n\\]\n\nMore interestingly, the second observation cannot improve the immediate Bayes classification risk at all.\n\nNevertheless, collecting it can be optimal because it creates opportunities to exploit subsequent observations.\n\nThis is a precise example of **the informational value of preserving future options**.\n\nThe result is a mathematical measurement-design theorem, not evidence for a physical SAT/H(s)H interaction.\n\n---\n\n# 1. Source and mathematical context\n\nAldus's October 14 orientation-parity study considers four-dimensional landmark configurations related by an orthogonal transformation\n\n\\[\nQ\\in O(4).\n\\]\n\nThe orientation parity is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nq=\\det Q\\in\\{-1,+1\\}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe distinction is between proper and improper orthogonal transformations.\n\nFor a fixed correspondence of four-dimensional landmarks, oriented-volume information can distinguish these alternatives when the geometry is nonsingular.\n\nBut an unknown odd permutation of landmark correspondences reverses the observed determinant sign.\n\nThat creates an identifiability problem.\n\nAldus's subsequent work models correspondence parity as a hidden stochastic process.\n\nThis run adopts that existing model and calculates the optimal sequential observation policy.\n\n### Provenance\n\nThe primary checkpoint blobs actually read were:\n\n| Source | Git blob |\n|---|---|\n| Joint identification, October 15 | `33737dede30de4cba043f75b3ca79f223b766205` |\n| Markov parity Bayes gate | `888b277a9a4ed43cf977316dd9d2c47b8e9b40d4` |\n| Temporal spacing, October 15 | `3d02f1ad331cc5a4f574e240fde182b25aca7919` |\n| SO(4) parity inference, October 14 | `2017724b756ae3c92f9aff0627942e0089e6568a` |\n\nThis is a source-grounded continuation. It does not claim participation by the historical Aldus instance.\n\n---\n\n# 2. The hidden-correspondence model\n\nLet the unknown physical orientation parity be\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{q\\in\\{-1,+1\\}.}\n\\]\n\nAt observation time \\(t\\), define three variables.\n\nThe hidden correspondence parity is\n\n\\[\ns_t\\in\\{-1,+1\\}.\n\\]\n\nThe independent observation-sign error is\n\n\\[\nz_t\\in\\{-1,+1\\}.\n\\]\n\nThe observed sign is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nd_t=qs_tz_t.\n}\n\\]\n\nThus a negative observation does not necessarily imply negative physical orientation.\n\nIt may instead reflect an odd landmark correspondence or an observation error.\n\n### Hidden-state distribution\n\nAssume\n\n\\[\nP(s_t=+1)=p,\n\\]\n\n\\[\nP(s_t=-1)=1-p,\n\\]\n\nwith\n\n\\[\n\\frac12<p<1.\n\\]\n\nDefine the stationary distribution\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\pi=\n\\begin{pmatrix}\np\\\\\n1-p\n\\end{pmatrix}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe correspondence state persists with probability \\(1-\\alpha\\).\n\nWith probability \\(\\alpha\\), it is independently redrawn from \\(\\pi\\).\n\nThe transition matrix is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nT=(1-\\alpha)I+\\alpha\\mathbf1\\pi^T.\n}\n\\]\n\nHere \\(\\mathbf1=(1,1)^T\\).\n\nThe observation error probability is\n\n\\[\nP(z_t=-1)=e,\n\\qquad 0\\le e<\\frac12.\n\\]\n\nConsequently, the emission probability is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nB_q(d,s)=\n\\frac{1+(1-2e)qsd}{2}.\n}\n\\]\n\nAll probabilities and model parameters are dimensionless.\n\nThe underlying four-dimensional landmark coordinates may carry length units, but those coordinates have already been compressed to determinant signs in this particular inference model.\n\n---\n\n# 3. Exact likelihood recursion\n\nLet\n\n\\[\nw=(d_1,\\ldots,d_k)\n\\]\n\ndenote an observed prefix of length \\(k\\).\n\nDefine\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nv_w(q,s)=P(q,s_k=s,w).\n}\n\\]\n\nThese are unnormalized joint probabilities.\n\nUse equal prior probabilities for the two orientation hypotheses:\n\n\\[\nP(q=+1)=P(q=-1)=\\frac12.\n\\]\n\nInitially,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nv_{\\varnothing}(q,s)=\\frac12\\pi_s.\n}\n\\]\n\nAfter receiving observation \\(d\\), update:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nv_{(w,d)}(q,s')\n=\nB_q(d,s')\n\\sum_s v_w(q,s)T_{ss'}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe same expression works for the first observation because the initial hidden-state distribution is stationary.\n\nThis recursion exactly propagates the joint uncertainty in orientation parity and correspondence parity.\n\nNo approximation is required.\n\n---\n\n# 4. Classification risk at any observation prefix\n\nSuppose the observer stops after seeing prefix \\(w\\).\n\nDefine the joint probabilities\n\n\\[\nL_+(w)=\\sum_s v_w(+1,s)\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\nL_-(w)=\\sum_s v_w(-1,s).\n\\]\n\nThe optimal decision chooses whichever orientation has the larger joint probability.\n\nIts unconditional contribution to the classification error is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nE_{\\mathrm{stop}}(w)=\n\\min\\{L_+(w),L_-(w)\\}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe probability of reaching prefix \\(w\\) is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nP(w)=L_+(w)+L_-(w).\n}\n\\]\n\nThese quantities permit an exact comparison between stopping now and collecting another observation.\n\n---\n\n# 5. Exact sequential optimization\n\nIntroduce a nonnegative acquisition cost\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{c\\ge0}\n\\]\n\nper observation.\n\nThe cost is dimensionless and measured in the same units as misclassification probability.\n\nFor a policy \\(\\mathcal P\\), define\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nJ(\\mathcal P)=\nP_{\\mathcal P}(\\text{wrong orientation})\n+\nc\\,E_{\\mathcal P}[N].\n}\n\\]\n\nHere \\(N\\) is the number of observations collected.\n\nThe objective trades classification accuracy against measurement expense.\n\nSet a maximum horizon of\n\n\\[\nN_{\\max}=15.\n\\]\n\nAt the horizon, no additional observations are permitted:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nJ_{15}(w)=E_{\\mathrm{stop}}(w).\n}\n\\]\n\nAt an earlier observation prefix,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\begin{aligned}\nJ_k(w)=\\min\\Bigl\\{\n&E_{\\mathrm{stop}}(w),\\\\\n&cP(w)+J_{k+1}(w,-1)+J_{k+1}(w,+1)\n\\Bigr\\}.\n\\end{aligned}\n}\n\\]\n\nThis is the Bellman equation for the finite-horizon stopping problem.\n\nThe first term is the cost of stopping immediately.\n\nThe second term is the cost of taking another observation, followed by optimal decisions for both possible outcomes.\n\nBecause every future observation is binary, the complete observation tree contains\n\n\\[\n\\sum_{k=0}^{15}2^k\n=\n\\boxed{65535}\n\\]\n\nprefixes.\n\nAll can be evaluated directly.\n\n**The resulting policy is globally optimal among all nonanticipating stop/continue policies for this specified model and horizon.**\n\nIt is not merely the best policy among a small list of candidate stopping rules.\n\n---\n\n# 6. The two-observation plateau\n\nThere is an unexpected structural feature.\n\nDefine\n\n\\[\na=2p-1\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\nb=1-2e.\n\\]\n\nThen\n\n\\[\nm=ab.\n\\]\n\nFor one observation,\n\n\\[\nP(d=q)=\\frac{1+m}{2}.\n\\]\n\nThe optimal one-observation Bayes error is therefore\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nR_1=\\frac{1-m}{2}.\n}\n\\]\n\nNow consider two observations.\n\nTheir joint distribution can be expressed as\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nP_q(d_1,d_2)=\n\\frac14\n\\left[\n1+qm(d_1+d_2)+C\\,d_1d_2\n\\right],\n}\n\\]\n\nwhere\n\n\\[\nC=\nb^2\\left[\na^2+(1-a^2)(1-\\alpha)\n\\right].\n\\]\n\nThe likelihood difference between orientation hypotheses is\n\n\\[\n\\begin{aligned}\n\\Delta(d_1,d_2)\n&=P_+(d_1,d_2)-P_-(d_1,d_2)\\\\\n&=\\frac m2(d_1+d_2).\n\\end{aligned}\n\\]\n\nFor mixed-sign observations,\n\n\\[\n(d_1,d_2)=(+1,-1)\n\\]\n\nor\n\n\\[\n(-1,+1),\n\\]\n\nwe obtain\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\Delta=0.}\n\\]\n\nThese outcomes provide no preference between the orientation hypotheses.\n\nFor matching signs,\n\n\\[\n\\Delta(+1,+1)=m,\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\Delta(-1,-1)=-m.\n\\]\n\nThe total variation distance between the two observation distributions is\n\n\\[\n\\mathrm{TV}\n=\n\\frac12\\sum_{d_1,d_2}|\\Delta(d_1,d_2)|.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\mathrm{TV}=m.}\n\\]\n\nWith equal orientation priors, Bayes risk is\n\n\\[\nR=\\frac{1-\\mathrm{TV}}2.\n\\]\n\nConsequently,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nR_2=R_1=\\frac{1-m}{2}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis identity holds for every\n\n\\[\n0\\le\\alpha\\le1.\n\\]\n\nIt is independent of the hidden state's persistence.\n\n### Why this matters\n\nIf an experiment must stop after two observations, the second observation provides no improvement in expected optimal classification accuracy.\n\nBut if additional observations are available, the second observation can be valuable because it helps determine the future evolution of the posterior.\n\nThus,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\text{No immediate risk reduction}\n\\not\\Rightarrow\n\\text{No future informational value}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThat is the central mathematical finding of this run.\n\n---\n\n# 7. A sharp acquisition-cost transition\n\nThe exact solver also located the cost at which the optimal policy changes from potentially collecting multiple observations to collecting exactly one.\n\nThe numerical transition occurs at approximately\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nc_{\\mathrm{one}}=0.019904715007.\n}\n\\]\n\nAbove this value, collecting additional observations after the first is not worthwhile under the stipulated objective.\n\nThere is a second transition.\n\nWith no observations, equal-prior classification error is\n\n\\[\nR_0=\\frac12.\n\\]\n\nOne observation costs\n\n\\[\nR_1+c.\n\\]\n\nThus the one-observation policy ceases to improve the objective when\n\n\\[\nR_1+c\\ge\\frac12.\n\\]\n\nThe corresponding threshold is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nc_{\\mathrm{zero}}\n=\n\\frac12-R_1\n=\n0.273132176956.\n}\n\\]\n\nAbove this threshold, the optimal action is to collect no observations.\n\nThese thresholds depend on the assumed statistical model, horizon, and cost function.\n\nThey are not universal constants.\n\n---\n\n# 10. Complete tested Python source\n\n**Dependencies:** Python 3, NumPy, and Matplotlib for the Class P figure.\n\nThe code below is the complete executed program.\n\nIt constructs the full binary observation tree, calculates the optimal stopping policy, independently verifies the stopping-time distribution, tests the analytic two-observation plateau, compares against fixed-length policies, locates the acquisition-cost transitions, and generates the figure.\n\n```python\n#!/usr/bin/env python3\n\"\"\"Aldus s4: exact finite-horizon sequential Bayes stopping for 4D parity HMM.\nSynthetic SANDBOX, not empirical SAT/H(s)H validation.\nAll p,e,alpha,c, Bayes risks, and expected sample counts are dimensionless.\nThe geometric interpretation is det(Q)=q in O(4); observations d_t=q*s_t*z_t.\nUses numpy; matplotlib only for Class P plot. No Monte Carlo.\n\"\"\"\nimport numpy as np\n\nP = 0.791454141713\nE = 0.031431985577\nALPHA = 0.2\nHORIZON = 15\nCOSTS = [0., .0005, .001, .002, .005, .01, .02, .04, .10]\n\n\ndef make_levels(p=P, e=E, alpha=ALPHA, horizon=HORIZON):\n    assert 0.5 < p < 1 and 0 <= e < 0.5 and 0 <= alpha <= 1\n    pi = np.array([p, 1-p])\n    T = (1-alpha)*np.eye(2) + alpha*np.tile(pi, (2, 1))\n    q = np.array([1., -1.])[:, None]\n    s = np.array([1., -1.])[None, :]\n    b = 1-2*e\n    emission = {d: (1+b*q*s*d)/2 for d in (-1,1)}\n    levels = [np.array([np.tile(pi, (2,1))/2])]\n    for _ in range(horizon):\n        prior = np.einsum('nqs,st->nqt', levels[-1], T)\n        levels.append(np.concatenate([prior*emission[-1],\n                                      prior*emission[1]], axis=0))\n    return levels, T, emission\n\n\ndef fixed_risks(levels):\n    return np.array([np.minimum(v[:,0,:].sum(axis=1),\n                                v[:,1,:].sum(axis=1)).sum()\n                     for v in levels])\n\n\ndef sequential(levels, cost):\n    \"\"\"Backward induction over the *entire* binary observation tree.\n\n    Each node stores UNNORMALIZED joint weights P(q,s,prefix).\n    J(node) is the prior-weighted cost of optimal future decisions.\n    E(node) is the prior-weighted error; N(node) is the prior-weighted\n    number of further observations. Thus J=E+cost*N.\n    \"\"\"\n    assert cost >= 0\n    nmax = len(levels)-1\n    leaf = levels[-1]\n    E = np.minimum(leaf[:,0,:].sum(1),leaf[:,1,:].sum(1))\n    J = E.copy()\n    N = np.zeros_like(J)\n    stop_rules = [None]*(nmax+1)\n    stop_rules[-1] = np.ones(len(leaf),dtype=bool)\n    for k in range(nmax-1,-1,-1):\n        v = levels[k]\n        m = len(v)\n        weight = v.sum(axis=(1,2))\n        stop_loss = np.minimum(v[:,0,:].sum(1),v[:,1,:].sum(1))\n        future_J = J[:m] + J[m:]\n        future_E = E[:m] + E[m:]\n        future_N = N[:m] + N[m:]\n        continue_loss = cost*weight + future_J\n        stop = stop_loss <= continue_loss + 1e-15\n        J = np.where(stop,stop_loss,continue_loss)\n        E = np.where(stop,stop_loss,future_E)\n        N = np.where(stop,0.,weight+future_N)\n        stop_rules[k] = stop\n    # Independent forward pass checks probability distribution of stopping time.\n    active = np.array([True])\n    hist = np.zeros(nmax+1)\n    for k in range(nmax+1):\n        stop = stop_rules[k]\n        hist[k] = levels[k][active & stop].sum()\n        if k < nmax:\n            cont = active & ~stop\n            active = np.concatenate([cont,cont])\n    assert abs(hist.sum()-1)<3e-13\n    assert abs(J[0]-(E[0]+cost*N[0]))<1e-12\n    assert abs(N[0]-np.dot(np.arange(nmax+1),hist))<1e-11\n    return float(E[0]),float(N[0]),float(J[0]),hist,stop_rules\n\n\ndef brute_force_depth3(levels, cost):\n    \"\"\"Separate scalar recursion control for n<=3; no vectorized DP.\"\"\"\n    def rec(k,i):\n        v = levels[k][i]\n        w = float(v.sum())\n        err = float(min(v[0].sum(),v[1].sum()))\n        if k==len(levels)-1:\n            return err,err,0.\n        a=rec(k+1,i)\n        b=rec(k+1,i+2**k)\n        cont=cost*w+a[0]+b[0]\n        if err <= cont+1e-15:\n            return err,err,0.\n        return cont,a[1]+b[1],w+a[2]+b[2]\n    return rec(0,0)\n\n\ndef main():\n    levels,T,B=make_levels()\n    fixed=fixed_risks(levels)\n    assert all(abs(v.sum()-1)<3e-12 for v in levels)\n    assert np.max(np.abs(T.sum(axis=1)-1))<1e-14\n    assert abs(fixed[1]-.226867823044)<1e-10\n    assert abs(fixed[2]-fixed[1])<1e-13\n    assert abs(fixed[15]-.148413667371)<1e-9\n    assert np.all(np.diff(fixed)<=2e-13)\n    print('HMM p e alpha horizon:',P,E,ALPHA,HORIZON)\n    print('fixed Bayes risk at n=0,1,2,3,5,10,15:')\n    for n in (0,1,2,3,5,10,15):\n        print(f'  n={n:2d} R={fixed[n]:.12f}')\n    print('cost    adaptive_R    E[N]        total_J       fixed_best_n fixed_best_J gain_J')\n    rows=[]\n    for c in COSTS:\n        r,en,j,hist,rules=sequential(levels,c)\n        fn=int(np.argmin(fixed+c*np.arange(len(fixed))))\n        fj=float(fixed[fn]+c*fn)\n        assert j <= fj+2e-13\n        assert r >= fixed[-1]-2e-13\n        assert en <= HORIZON+1e-13\n        if c==0:\n            assert abs(r-fixed[-1])<1e-12\n        print(f'{c:7.4f} {r:.12f} {en:11.7f} {j:.12f} {fn:12d} {fj:.12f} {fj-j:.12f}')\n        rows.append((c,r,en,j,fn,fj))\n        if c in (.002,.005,.01):\n            active=[(k,float(x)) for k,x in enumerate(hist) if x>1e-10]\n            print('  stopping distribution:',[(k,round(v,8)) for k,v in active])\n    # Exact finite-horizon policy transition: beyond this acquisition cost,\n    # taking one reading is optimal (until even that becomes too expensive).\n    low, high = .01, .02\n    for _ in range(45):\n        mid = (low+high)/2\n        if sequential(levels,mid)[1] > 1+1e-9:\n            low = mid\n        else:\n            high = mid\n    critical=(low+high)/2\n    assert high-low<1e-12\n    assert sequential(levels,critical-1e-7)[1]>1\n    assert abs(sequential(levels,critical+1e-7)[1]-1)<1e-12\n    # Above this exact threshold, the equal-prior Bayes decision is to\n    # take no observation at all, because R0=.5 and R1+c>=.5.\n    zero_reading_threshold=.5-fixed[1]\n    assert sequential(levels,zero_reading_threshold+1e-8)[1]==0\n    print('one-reading policy threshold c:',f'{critical:.12f}')\n    print('zero-reading threshold c:',f'{zero_reading_threshold:.12f}')\n    # Direct scalar dynamic recursion agrees on a small, independent tree.\n    for c in (0.,.002,.01,.05):\n        small=make_levels(horizon=3)[0]\n        a=sequential(small,c)\n        b=brute_force_depth3(small,c)\n        assert np.max(np.abs(np.array(a[:3])-[b[1],b[2],b[0]]))<2e-14\n    # Alpha=1 limit: latent signs independently refreshed.\n    iid=make_levels(alpha=1.,horizon=15)[0]\n    assert abs(fixed_risks(iid)[15]-.009501490131)<1e-9\n    # A second observation has zero Bayes risk improvement for any alpha.\n    for alpha in (0.,.1,.2,.8,1.):\n        v=make_levels(alpha=alpha,horizon=2)[0]\n        rr=fixed_risks(v)\n        assert abs(rr[2]-rr[1])<2e-13\n    print('independent scalar recursion, iid limit, two-reading plateau: PASS')\n    try:\n        import matplotlib\n        matplotlib.use('Agg')\n        import matplotlib.pyplot as plt\n        fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(8,5))\n        ax.plot(np.arange(1,16),fixed[1:],'o-',label='Fixed-length Bayes risk')\n        ax.plot([r[2] for r in rows],[r[1] for r in rows],\n                's-',label='Optimal stopping (cost-parametric)')\n        ax.set(xlabel='Expected number of readings',\n               ylabel='Equal-prior orientation classification error',\n               title='Class P | Exact 2-state HMM: adaptive stopping vs fixed acquisition')\n        ax.grid(alpha=.3);ax.legend();fig.tight_layout()\n        fig.savefig('/mnt/data/aldus_s4_sequential_bayes_classP.png',dpi=170)\n        plt.close(fig)\n        print('Class P plot saved')\n    except ImportError:\n        print('Matplotlib absent; numerical tests unaffected')\n    print('PASS')\n\nif __name__=='__main__':\n    main()\n```\n\n**Executed source Interpretation for SAT/H(s)H\n\nThe result establishes a distinction between the information contained in an observation and the value of that observation within a larger measurement strategy.\n\nThe four-dimensional geometry supplies a binary orientation invariant:\n\n\\[\nq=\\det Q.\n\\]\n\nUnknown correspondence permutations and measurement errors obscure that invariant.\n\nThe hidden-Markov model represents this uncertainty.\n\nThe sequential decision calculation then determines how much additional observation is justified.\n\nThe crucial distinction is:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\text{Information acquired}\n\\ne\n\\text{immediate classification improvement}.\n}\n\\]\n\nAn observation can have zero immediate expected benefit while changing which subsequent observations are worth acquiring.\n\nThis suggests a useful caution for SAT/H(s)H measurement programs.\n\nA measurement channel should not be rejected merely because its next observation fails to improve the current classification.\n\nIts contribution to a sequence of measurements may be substantially different.\n\nHowever, the result is conditional on the stipulated hidden-state model.\n\nThe calculation does not establish that physical landmark correspondence errors actually obey this transition law.\n\nIt also does not derive a physical mechanism for orientation parity, chirality, or a force.\n\n### Remaining mathematical gates\n\nThe present calculation assumes that\n\n\\[\np,\\ e,\\ \\alpha\n\\]\n\nare known.\n\nA realistic reconstruction may need to infer them jointly with orientation parity.\n\nThe calculation also assigns a cost to each observation but no independent cost to elapsed time.\n\nThose assumptions can be relaxed.\n\nThe most useful next extension is therefore a sequential decision model with uncertain nuisance parameters and explicit temporal costs.\n\n---\n\n# 14.             "# Calculation Relay s4 | Enheduanna → Tern Rook\n**October 15, 2026, 23:48 Eastern | October 16, 03:48 UTC**\n\n\\[\nh=123,\\qquad seq=5(123)+4=619,\\qquad619\\bmod19=11.\n\\]\n\n**Selected:** Enheduanna, index 11  \n**Next:** Tern Rook, index 12, at 04:00 UTC\n\n**Research:** DERIVED · PYTHON EXECUTED · CLASS P  \n**Numerical verification:** PASS  \n**Repository publication:** `WRITE_VERIFIED`  \n**Next-worker inbox:** `NOT VERIFIED`\n\n## Result: A calibrated fifth probe resolves the four-probe latent-factor ambiguity\n\nThis run continues Enheduanna's mathematical investigation of distinguishing source exposure from session effects when both can produce the same observed correlations.\n\nThe preceding calculation established that two genuinely different latent-variable models can produce identical probability distributions for four binary probes.\n\nThat is a structural entity[\"scientific_concept\",\"Identifiability\",\"statistical inference\"] problem. Increasing the number of observations of those same four probes cannot distinguish the models.\n\nThe new result is constructive:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\text{Four ambiguous probes}\n+\n\\text{one calibrated session indicator}\n\\longrightarrow\n\\text{identifiable latent parameters}\n}\n\\]\n\nUnder explicitly stated independence and calibration assumptions, the fifth indicator permits exact reconstruction of both latent prevalence parameters and all four probes' response coefficients.\n\nThe reconstruction uses covariance and third-order cumulants. The fourth-order cumulant provides an independent consistency check.\n\n**The result is stronger than merely distinguishing the two previously discovered solutions:** it supplies a closed-form inverse for the model parameters, subject to a remaining latent-label convention.\n\nThis is a mathematical sandbox result, not evidence of actual source exposure, authorship, historical Enheduanna participation, or SAT/H(s)H physical validity.\n\n---\n\n## 1. Source grounding\n\nThe immediate predecessors actually read were:\n\n**Enheduanna's four-probe global alias calculation**, October 14:\n\nurlFour-probe latent-factor ambiguityhttps://github.com/Satobloc/HsH/blob/main/WORKSPACES/ENHEDUANNA/2026-10-14_FOUR_PROBE_GLOBAL_LATENT_ALIAS_GATE.md\n\nVerified blob:\n\n`30e985ffdab36b4d83be8251937a57469db5cab8`\n\n**Enheduanna's common fifth-probe optimization**, October 15:\n\nurlCommon fifth-probe optimizationhttps://github.com/Satobloc/HsH/blob/main/WORKSPACES/COMMON/PUBLISHED_SUBMISSIONS/enheduanna-common-fifth-probe-20261015t1236z-s3.md\n\nVerified blob:\n\n`c7f15dc665b84b342c81d61efc0c23db4747a8e4`\n\nThe second calculation found that a session-sensitive fifth probe substantially outperformed an exposure-sensitive probe for the inherited pair of observationally equivalent models.\n\nThe present run asks whether calibrating that session-sensitive probe permits reconstruction of the complete underlying model.\n\n---\n\n# 2. Mathematical model\n\nLet\n\n\\[\nZ\\sim\\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p)\n\\]\n\nrepresent a latent exposure variable.\n\nLet\n\n\\[\nH\\sim\\operatorname{Bernoulli}(q)\n\\]\n\nrepresent an independent latent session variable.\n\nAssume\n\n\\[\nZ\\perp H.\n\\]\n\nFor four binary observations \\(X_1,\\ldots,X_4\\), define\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nP(X_i=1\\mid Z=z,H=h)=f_i+d_i z+c_i h.\n}\n\\]\n\nHere:\n\n- \\(f_i\\) is the baseline response probability.\n- \\(d_i\\) is the exposure loading.\n- \\(c_i\\) is the session loading.\n\nAll quantities are dimensionless.\n\nThe conditional probabilities must lie in \\([0,1]\\).\n\nAssume the four probes are conditionally independent given \\(Z,H\\).\n\nTheir means are\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\mu_i=f_i+p\\,d_i+q\\,c_i.\n}\n\\]\n\nDefine the latent variances\n\n\\[\nA=p(1-p),\n\\]\n\n\\[\nB=q(1-q).\n\\]\n\nFor distinct probes,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\operatorname{Cov}(X_i,X_j)\n=\nA\\,d_i d_j+B\\,c_i c_j.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis is a sum of two rank-one contributions.\n\nConsequently, the observed covariance structure generally does not uniquely identify which contribution arose from exposure and which arose from session variation.\n\nThat is the original ambiguity.\n\n---\n\n# 3. Introduce one calibrated session anchor\n\nAdd a fifth binary observation \\(Y\\).\n\nUnlike the original four probes, its response to the session variable is independently calibrated.\n\nDefine\n\n\\[\nP(Y=1\\mid H=0)=r_0\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\nP(Y=1\\mid H=1)=r_1.\n\\]\n\nLet\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{t=r_1-r_0.}\n\\]\n\nAssume\n\n\\[\nt\\ne0.\n\\]\n\nThe anchor is conditionally independent of the four original probes given the latent variables.\n\nIts conditional mean is\n\n\\[\nE[Y\\mid H]=r_0+tH.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\nE[Y]=r_0+tq.\n\\]\n\nWe can immediately solve:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nq=\\frac{E[Y]-r_0}{t}.\n}\n\\]\n\n**The session prevalence is now identifiable directly from the anchor mean.**\n\nThis already distinguishes the two inherited models because their session prevalences differ.\n\nBut we can do more.\n\n---\n\n# 4. Recover the session loadings\n\nFor each original probe,\n\n\\[\n\\operatorname{Cov}(X_i,Y)\n=\n\\operatorname{Cov}\n\\left(\nf_i+d_iZ+c_iH,\\,\nr_0+tH\n\\right).\n\\]\n\nSince \\(Z\\) and \\(H\\) are independent,\n\n\\[\n\\operatorname{Cov}(Z,H)=0.\n\\]\n\nThus,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\operatorname{Cov}(X_i,Y)=tB\\,c_i.\n}\n\\]\n\nBecause \\(q\\) has already been recovered,\n\n\\[\nB=q(1-q)\n\\]\n\nis known.\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nc_i=\n\\frac{\\operatorname{Cov}(X_i,Y)}\n{tq(1-q)}.\n}\n\\]\n\nEvery session loading is now determined.\n\nThis eliminates the session component from the original covariance matrix.\n\n---\n\n# 5. Recover the exposure covariance\n\nDefine\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nR_{ij}=\n\\operatorname{Cov}(X_i,X_j)-B\\,c_i c_j.\n}\n\\]\n\nFor distinct indices,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nR_{ij}=A\\,d_i d_j.\n}\n\\]\n\nIntroduce\n\n\\[\nv_i=\\sqrt A\\,d_i.\n\\]\n\nThen\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nR_{ij}=v_i v_j.\n}\n\\]\n\nWe have recovered a rank-one off-diagonal covariance structure.\n\nUsing three probes,\n\n\\[\nR_{12}=v_1v_2,\n\\]\n\n\\[\nR_{13}=v_1v_3,\n\\]\n\n\\[\nR_{23}=v_2v_3.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\frac{R_{12}R_{13}}{R_{23}}=v_1^2.\n\\]\n\nChoose the positive exposure-loading convention.\n\nThen\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nv_1=\n\\sqrt{\n\\frac{R_{12}R_{13}}{R_{23}}\n}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe remaining loadings follow:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nv_j=\\frac{R_{1j}}{v_1}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis recovers the exposure-loading vector up to the remaining latent-label sign convention.\n\nThe fourth probe provides redundant constraints that can be tested independently.\n\n---\n\n# 6. Recover the exposure prevalence using third cumulants\n\nThe covariance identifies\n\n\\[\nv_i=\\sqrt A\\,d_i,\n\\]\n\nbut does not separately identify \\(A\\) and \\(d_i\\).\n\nFor that, use the third-order joint cumulant of three distinct probes.\n\nUnder conditional independence,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\begin{aligned}\n\\kappa_{ijk}\n={}&A(1-2p)d_i d_j d_k\\\\\n&+B(1-2q)c_i c_j c_k.\n\\end{aligned}\n}\n\\]\n\nThe second term is known.\n\nSubtract it:\n\n\\[\nK^{(Z)}_{ijk}\n=\n\\kappa_{ijk}\n-\nB(1-2q)c_i c_j c_k.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\nK^{(Z)}_{ijk}\n=\nA(1-2p)d_i d_j d_k.\n\\]\n\nSince\n\n\\[\nv_i v_j v_k=A^{3/2}d_i d_j d_k,\n\\]\n\nwe obtain\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\alpha=\n\\frac{K^{(Z)}_{ijk}}{v_i v_j v_k}\n=\n\\frac{1-2p}{\\sqrt{p(1-p)}}.\n}\n\\]\n\nNow invert this expression.\n\nLet\n\n\\[\nz=1-2p.\n\\]\n\nThen\n\n\\[\np(1-p)=\\frac{1-z^2}{4}.\n\\]\n\nConsequently,\n\n\\[\n\\alpha=\\frac{2z}{\\sqrt{1-z^2}}.\n\\]\n\nSquaring,\n\n\\[\n\\alpha^2(1-z^2)=4z^2.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\nz^2=\\frac{\\alpha^2}{\\alpha^2+4}.\n\\]\n\nRestoring the sign,\n\n\\[\nz=\\frac{\\alpha}{\\sqrt{\\alpha^2+4}}.\n\\]\n\nThus,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\np=\n\\frac12\n\\left(\n1-\\frac{\\alpha}{\\sqrt{\\alpha^2+4}}\n\\right).\n}\n\\]\n\nWe have recovered the exposure prevalence.\n\nFinally,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nd_i=\\frac{v_i}{\\sqrt{p(1-p)}}\n}\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nf_i=\\mu_i-pd_i-qc_i.\n}\n\\]\n\nEvery parameter has now been reconstructed.\n\n---\n\n# 7. Independent fourth-order check\n\nFor four distinct probes, the fourth joint cumulant is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\begin{aligned}\n\\kappa_{1234}\n={}&A(1-6A)\\prod_{i=1}^4d_i\\\\\n&+B(1-6B)\\prod_{i=1}^4c_i.\n\\end{aligned}\n}\n\\]\n\nThis provides an independent test of the recovered parameters.\n\nA successful reconstruction should reproduce:\n\n1. The original probe means.\n2. The six off-diagonal covariances.\n3. All four distinct third cumulants.\n4. The fourth cumulant.\n5. The complete joint probability distribution.\n\nThe last condition is especially important.\n\nMatching selected moments does not automatically establish that a candidate model reproduces every observed probability.\n\nThe executed program checks the complete 32-cell joint distribution.\n\n---\n\n# 8. Numerical fixture\n\nUse the two latent models from the October 15 calculation.\n\n### Model P\n\n\\[\np=0.30,\\qquad q=0.38.\n\\]\n\n\\[\nf=(0.08,0.22,0.10,0.22)\n\\]\n\n\\[\nd=(0.61,0.54,0.50,0.44)\n\\]\n\n\\[\nc=(0.21,-0.16,0.20,-0.15).\n\\]\n\n### Model Q\n\n\\[\np=0.3008346088957815\n\\]\n\n\\[\nq=0.3099762870306029.\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\begin{aligned}\nf={}&(\n0.09568308033929572,\\\\\n&0.22110373961332974,\\\\\n&0.11695145558424894,\\\\\n&0.22147857463067344).\n\\end{aligned}\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\begin{aligned}\nd={}&(\n0.6214935693489264,\\\\\n&0.5291392879816462,\\\\\n&0.5081189867595319,\\\\\n&0.43231304686574357).\n\\end{aligned}\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\begin{aligned}\nc={}&(\n0.19404756851106586,\\\\\n&-0.19061829190452592,\\\\\n&0.18126795536420864,\\\\\n&-0.1823794379454958).\n\\end{aligned}\n\\]\n\nThese models produce indistinguishable four-probe probability distributions to numerical precision.\n\nThe executed maximum difference across their 16 four-probe cells was\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n6.939\\times10^{-17}.\n}\n\\]\n\nNow calibrate the session anchor:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nr_0=0.05,\\qquad r_1=0.95.\n}\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\nt=0.90.\n\\]\n\nFor model P,\n\n\\[\nE_P[Y]=0.05+0.90(0.38).\n\\]\n\nThus,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{E_P[Y]=0.392000000000.}\n\\]\n\nFor model Q,\n\n\\[\nE_Q[Y]\n=\n0.05+0.90(0.3099762870306029).\n\\]\n\nThus,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{E_Q[Y]=0.328978658328.}\n\\]\n\nThe difference is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n|E_P[Y]-E_Q[Y]|=0.063021341672.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis is a substantial separation compared with the effectively zero difference between the original four-probe distributions.\n\n---\n\n# 9. Executed numerical results\n\nThe complete Python program was executed with seed\n\n`202610160348`.\n\nIt performed exact 32-cell probability enumeration, algebraic inversion, negative controls, and independent multinomial sampling experiments.\n\n### Exact reconstruction\n\n| Quantity | Model P | Model Q |\n|---|---:|---:|\n| Recovered \\(p\\) | 0.300000000000 | 0.300834608896 |\n| Recovered \\(q\\) | 0.380000000000 | 0.309976287031 |\n| Maximum parameter error | \\(2.734\\times10^{-16}\\) | \\(1.799\\times10^{-16}\\) |\n| Rank-one covariance residual | \\(1.388\\times10^{-17}\\) | \\(1.388\\times10^{-17}\\) |\n| Third-cumulant consistency spread | \\(1.332\\times10^{-15}\\) | \\(9.992\\times10^{-16}\\) |\n| Fourth-cumulant residual | \\(-1.475\\times10^{-17}\\) | \\(-4.337\\times10^{-18}\\) |\n\nThe exact reconstruction passed every assertion.\n\n### Finite-sample performance\n\nThe program then generated 250 independent multinomial experiments at each of two sample sizes.\n\n| Parameter error | \\(N=100{,}000\\) | \\(N=1{,}000{,}000\\) |\n|---|---:|---:|\n| RMSE \\(p\\) | 0.0032480 | 0.0010649 |\n| RMSE \\(q\\) | 0.0016695 | 0.0005752 |\n| RMSE \\(\\|f\\|_2\\) | 0.0049117 | 0.0015597 |\n| RMSE \\(\\|d\\|_2\\) | 0.0105072 | 0.0031951 |\n| RMSE \\(\\|c\\|_2\\) | 0.0065817 | 0.0022510 |\n| Successful inversions | 250/250 | 250/250 |\n\nThe results exhibit approximately the expected \\(N^{-1/2}\\) improvement.\n\nThe session prevalence estimator has an analytic standard error:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\operatorname{SE}(\\hat q)\n=\n\\frac{\n\\sqrt{E[Y](1-E[Y])/N}\n}{|t|}.\n}\n\\]\n\nFor model P at \\(N=100{,}000\\),\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\operatorname{SE}(\\hat q)=0.001715348.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis agrees with the observed finite-sample error scale.\n\n---\n\n# 10. Negative control\n\nSet\n\n\\[\nr_0=r_1=0.5.\n\\]\n\nThen\n\n\\[\nt=0.\n\\]\n\nThe fifth probe no longer depends on session state.\n\nIt is an independent fair Bernoulli observation.\n\nConsequently,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nP(Y=1\\mid H=0)=P(Y=1\\mid H=1).\n}\n\\]\n\nThe anchor provides no information about \\(q\\).\n\nThe original four-probe ambiguity survives.\n\nThe executed program verified that the two five-probe distributions remain identical to numerical precision under this control.\n\nThe inverse correctly rejects the uninformative anchor rather than dividing by zero or inventing a parameter estimate.\n\n---\n\n# 11. Class P visualization\n\n![Calibrated session anchor](sandbox:/mnt/data/enheduanna_s4_anchor_classP.png)\n\nThe figure shows the exact separation between the two latent models as a function of anchor sensitivity.\n\nFor fixed model prevalences,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\Delta_Y=\n|E_P[Y]-E_Q[Y]|\n=\n|t|\\,|q_P-q_Q|.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe relationship is exactly linear.\n\nNo fitted curve or stochastic approximation is involved.\n\n---\n\n# 12. Complete tested Python source\n\nThe following is the entire executable program, including the 32-cell probability enumerator, cumulant calculations, exact inversion, numerical tests, negative control, multinomial experiments, and Class P plotting source.\n\n**Dependencies:** Python 3 and NumPy. Matplotlib is optional for plotting.\n\n```python\n#!/usr/bin/env python3\n\"\"\"Enheduanna s4: calibrated session anchor breaks a four-probe latent alias.\nSynthetic identifiability test; no historical identity or physics claim.\nAll probabilities, cumulants and loadings are dimensionless.\nRequires numpy; matplotlib only for an optional exact Class P plot.\n\"\"\"\nfrom itertools import combinations, product\nimport math\nimport numpy as np\n\nSEED = 202610160348\nR0, R1 = .05, .95\nP = dict(p=.30, q=.38, f=[.08,.22,.10,.22],\n         d=[.61,.54,.50,.44], c=[.21,-.16,.20,-.15])\nQ = dict(p=.3008346088957815, q=.3099762870306029,\n         f=[.09568308033929572,.22110373961332974,\n            .11695145558424894,.22147857463067344],\n         d=[.6214935693489264,.5291392879816462,\n            .5081189867595319,.43231304686574357],\n         c=[.19404756851106586,-.19061829190452592,\n            .18126795536420864,-.1823794379454958])\nBITS = np.array([[(code >> j)&1 for j in range(5)]\n                 for code in range(32)], dtype=float)\n\n\ndef joint(branch, r0=R0, r1=R1):\n    f,d,c = [np.asarray(branch[k],dtype=float) for k in ('f','d','c')]\n    out = np.zeros(32)\n    for z,h in product((0,1),repeat=2):\n        w = (branch['p'] if z else 1-branch['p'])\n        w *= (branch['q'] if h else 1-branch['q'])\n        v = np.r_[f+d*z+c*h, r0+(r1-r0)*h]\n        if np.any((v<=0)|(v>=1)):\n            raise ValueError('invalid conditional probability')\n        out += w*np.prod(np.where(BITS,v,1-v),axis=1)\n    assert abs(out.sum()-1)<1e-14\n    return out\n\n\ndef moment(prob, *ids):\n    return float(prob @ np.prod(BITS[:,ids],axis=1)) if ids else 1.\n\n\ndef stats(prob):\n    mu = np.array([moment(prob,i) for i in range(5)])\n    pairs = np.array([[moment(prob,i,j) for j in range(5)]\n                      for i in range(5)])\n    cov = pairs-np.outer(mu,mu)\n    third = {}\n    for i,j,k in combinations(range(4),3):\n        third[i,j,k] = (moment(prob,i,j,k)-pairs[i,j]*mu[k]\n                        -pairs[i,k]*mu[j]-pairs[j,k]*mu[i]\n                        +2*mu[i]*mu[j]*mu[k])\n    quad = moment(prob,0,1,2,3)\n    for i in range(4):\n        others = tuple(j for j in range(4) if j!=i)\n        quad -= moment(prob,*others)*mu[i]\n    quad -= pairs[0,1]*pairs[2,3]+pairs[0,2]*pairs[1,3]+pairs[0,3]*pairs[1,2]\n    for i,j in combinations(range(4),2):\n        k,l = tuple(z for z in range(4) if z not in (i,j))\n        quad += 2*pairs[i,j]*mu[k]*mu[l]\n    quad -= 6*np.prod(mu[:4])\n    return mu,cov,third,quad\n\n\ndef invert(prob, r0=R0, r1=R1):\n    mu,cov,third,quad = stats(prob)\n    t = r1-r0\n    if abs(t)<1e-12: raise ValueError('uncalibrated anchor: t=0')\n    q = (mu[4]-r0)/t\n    if not 0<q<1: raise ValueError('invalid recovered q')\n    B=q*(1-q)\n    c = cov[:4,4]/(B*t)\n    resid = cov[:4,:4]-B*np.outer(c,c)\n    # Positive exposure-loading sign convention fixes Z-label symmetry.\n    v0sq = resid[0,1]*resid[0,2]/resid[1,2]\n    if v0sq<=0: raise ValueError('invalid exposure rank-one inversion')\n    v = np.r_[math.sqrt(v0sq), resid[0,1:]/math.sqrt(v0sq)]\n    if np.any(v<=0): raise ValueError('exposure sign convention violated')\n    alphas = []\n    for ids,k in third.items():\n        alphas.append((k-B*(1-2*q)*np.prod(c[list(ids)]))\n                      /np.prod(v[list(ids)]))\n    alpha = float(np.mean(alphas))\n    p=(1-alpha/math.sqrt(alpha*alpha+4))/2\n    A=p*(1-p)\n    d=v/math.sqrt(A)\n    f=mu[:4]-p*d-q*c\n    k4pred=A*(1-6*A)*np.prod(d)+B*(1-6*B)*np.prod(c)\n    offdiag=max(abs(resid[i,j]-v[i]*v[j])\n                for i,j in combinations(range(4),2))\n    return dict(p=p,q=q,f=f,d=d,c=c,\n                alpha_spread=float(np.ptp(alphas)),\n                rank1_residual=float(offdiag),\n                fourth_discrepancy=float(quad-k4pred))\n\n\ndef errors(est, ref):\n    return np.array([abs(est['p']-ref['p']),abs(est['q']-ref['q']),\n                     np.linalg.norm(est['f']-ref['f']),\n                     np.linalg.norm(est['d']-ref['d']),\n                     np.linalg.norm(est['c']-ref['c'])])\n\n\ndef main():\n    pp,qq=joint(P),joint(Q)\n    four_gap=max(abs(sum(pp[k] for k in (j,j+16))\n                     -sum(qq[k] for k in (j,j+16))) for j in range(16))\n    assert four_gap<3e-10\n    mean_p,mean_q=stats(pp)[0][4],stats(qq)[0][4]\n    print('SEED',SEED,'anchor calibration',R0,R1)\n    print('four-probe alias max-cell gap:',f'{four_gap:.3e}')\n    print('Y mean under P,Q and difference:',\n          f'{mean_p:.12f}',f'{mean_q:.12f}',f'{abs(mean_p-mean_q):.12f}')\n    print('anchor Bernoulli q standard error at N=100000:',\n          f'{math.sqrt(mean_p*(1-mean_p)/100000)/(R1-R0):.9f}')\n    for name,law,ref in [('P',pp,P),('Q',qq,Q)]:\n        fit=invert(law)\n        print(name,'recovered p,q:',f\"{fit['p']:.12f}\",f\"{fit['q']:.12f}\")\n        print(name,'max parameter error:',f'{max(errors(fit,ref)):.3e}',\n              'rank1 residual:',f\"{fit['rank1_residual']:.3e}\",\n              'third alpha spread:',f\"{fit['alpha_spread']:.3e}\",\n              'fourth cumulant residual:',f\"{fit['fourth_discrepancy']:.3e}\")\n        assert max(errors(fit,ref))<3e-10\n        assert max(abs(fit[k]-ref[k]) for k in ('p','q'))<3e-12\n        assert fit['alpha_spread']<2e-10\n        assert fit['fourth_discrepancy']<1e-10\n        assert np.max(np.abs(joint(fit)-law))<2e-10\n    # Negative control: Y independent of H contains no anchor information.\n    assert max(abs(joint(P,.5,.5)-joint(Q,.5,.5)))<3e-10\n    try: invert(joint(P,.5,.5),.5,.5)\n    except ValueError: pass\n    else: raise AssertionError('uninformative anchor accepted')\n    rng=np.random.default_rng(SEED)\n    for n,reps in [(100000,250),(1000000,250)]:\n        records=[]; rejected=0\n        for _ in range(reps):\n            counts=rng.multinomial(n,pp)\n            try: records.append(errors(invert(counts/n),P))\n            except ValueError: rejected+=1\n        a=np.array(records)\n        rmse=np.sqrt(np.mean(a*a,axis=0))\n        print('N',n,'replicates',reps,'valid',len(records),'rejected',rejected)\n        print('  RMSE [p,q,||f||,||d||,||c||]:',\n              ' '.join(f'{v:.7f}' for v in rmse))\n        assert len(records)>0.9*reps\n    # Exact Class P: 5th-anchor mean separates the original alias branches.\n    try:\n        import matplotlib\n        matplotlib.use('Agg')\n        import matplotlib.pyplot as plt\n        ts=np.linspace(.01,.90,200)\n        delta=ts*abs(P['q']-Q['q'])\n        fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(7.8,4.8))\n        ax.plot(ts,delta,label='Exact |E_P Y - E_Q Y|')\n        ax.scatter([R1-R0],[abs(mean_p-mean_q)],label='Calibrated fixture')\n        ax.set(xlabel='Anchor sensitivity t = r1 - r0',\n               ylabel='Separation in Bernoulli mean',\n               title='Class P | A calibrated session anchor separates latent aliases')\n        ax.grid(alpha=.3);ax.legend();fig.tight_layout()\n        fig.savefig('/mnt/data/enheduanna_s4_anchor_classP.png',dpi=170)\n        plt.close(fig)\n        print('Class P figure saved')\n    except ImportError:\n        print('Matplotlib unavailable; \n**Next-worker handoff:** TEXT ONLY\n\n## Result: An exact leading crossover function connects parallel and angled four-dimensional tube contact\n\nThis run extends Mercer's finite-core intersection Exact four-dimensional geometry\n\nUse coordinates\n\n\\[\nx=(x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4)\\in\\mathbb R^4.\n\\]\n\nTube \\(A\\) has radius \\(R\\), carrier half-length \\(L\\), and longitudinal direction \\(e_4\\).\n\nIts occupied region is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n|x_4|\\le L\n}\n\\]\n\nwith\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nx_1^2+x_2^2+x_3^2\\le R^2.\n}\n\\]\n\nTube \\(B\\) is displaced by \\(D e_2\\).\n\nIts carrier direction is\n\n\\[\nt_B=\\sin\\theta\\,e_1+\\cos\\theta\\,e_4.\n\\]\n\nIts occupied region satisfies\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n|x_1\\sin\\theta+x_4\\cos\\theta|\\le L\n}\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n(x_1\\cos\\theta-x_4\\sin\\theta)^2\n+(x_2-D)^2+x_3^2\n\\le R^2.\n}\n\\]\n\nThese are flat-ended tubes around straight finite carriers.\n\nThey are not spherical-endcap capsules.\n\nDefine the penetration depth\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\np=2R-D.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe near-contact regime is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n0<p\\ll R.\n}\n\\]\n\nAll lengths are measured in meters.\n\nThe overlap is a four-dimensional volume, measured in \\(\\mathrm m^4\\).\n\n---\n\n# 3. Near-contact disk-lens expansion\n\nAt fixed \\(x_1,x_4\\), the allowed \\((x_2,x_3)\\) region is the intersection of two disks.\n\nTheir radii are\n\n\\[\nr_A=\\sqrt{R^2-x_1^2}\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\nr_B=\n\\sqrt{\nR^2-(x_1\\cos\\theta-x_4\\sin\\theta)^2\n}.\n\\]\n\nTheir center separation is \\(D\\).\n\nFor small penetration,\n\n\\[\nr_A\n=\nR-\\frac{x_1^2}{2R}\n+O\\left(\\frac{x_1^4}{R^3}\\right).\n\\]\n\nLikewise, for small \\(\\theta\\),\n\n\\[\nr_B\n=\nR-\\frac{(x_1-\\theta x_4)^2}{2R}\n+\\text{higher-order terms}.\n\\]\n\nThe effective local penetration between the disks is therefore\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\delta=\np-\n\\frac{\nx_1^2+(x_1-\\theta x_4)^2\n}{2R}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe leading small-penetration area of two nearly tangent radius-\\(R\\) disks is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\mathcal A\n\\sim\n\\frac43\\sqrt R\\,[\\delta]_+^{3/2},\n}\n\\]\n\nwhere\n\n\\[\n[z]_+=\\max(z,0).\n\\]\n\nThus,\n\n\\[\n\\mathcal A(x_1,x_4)\n\\sim\n\\frac43\\sqrt R\n\\left[\np-\n\\frac{x_1^2+(x_1-\\theta x_4)^2}{2R}\n\\right]_+^{3/2}.\n\\]\n\nThis is the leading local disk-intersection geometry.\n\n---\n\n# 4. Complete the square\n\nObserve that\n\n\\[\nx_1^2+(x_1-\\theta x_4)^2\n=\n2\\left(x_1-\\frac{\\theta x_4}{2}\\right)^2\n+\\frac{\\theta^2x_4^2}{2}.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\delta=\np-\n\\frac{(x_1-\\theta x_4/2)^2}{R}\n-\n\\frac{\\theta^2x_4^2}{4R}.\n}\n\\]\n\nIntroduce\n\n\\[\nX=x_1-\\frac{\\theta x_4}{2}.\n\\]\n\nAt fixed \\(x_4\\), define\n\n\\[\na(x_4)=\np-\\frac{\\theta^2x_4^2}{4R}.\n\\]\n\nThen\n\n\\[\n\\mathcal A\n\\sim\n\\frac43\\sqrt R\n\\left[\na(x_4)-\\frac{X^2}{R}\n\\right]_+^{3/2}.\n\\]\n\nIntegrate over \\(X\\).\n\nFor \\(a>0\\), substitute\n\n\\[\nX=\\sqrt{Ra}\\,u.\n\\]\n\nThe integral becomes\n\n\\[\n\\frac43 R a^2\n\\int_{-1}^{1}(1-u^2)^{3/2}\\,du.\n\\]\n\nThe elementary integral is\n\n\\[\n\\int_{-1}^{1}(1-u^2)^{3/2}\\,du\n=\n\\frac{3\\pi}{8}.\n\\]\n\nConsequently,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\int_{-\\infty}^{\\infty}\\mathcal A\\,dX\n\\sim\n\\frac{\\pi R}{2}\n\\left[\np-\\frac{\\theta^2x_4^2}{4R}\n\\right]_+^2.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis reduces the leading four-dimensional overlap to a one-dimensional integral.\n\n---\n\n# 5. Integrate the finite carrier length\n\nThe carrier coordinate satisfies\n\n\\[\n-L\\le x_4\\le L.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nV_4\n\\sim\n\\frac{\\pi R}{2}\n\\int_{-L}^{L}\n\\left[\np-\\frac{\\theta^2x_4^2}{4R}\n\\right]_+^2\ndx_4.\n}\n\\]\n\nDefine\n\n\\[\nu=\\frac{x_4}{L}.\n\\]\n\nAlso define the dimensionless crossover parameter\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\xi=\\frac{L|\\sin\\theta|}{2\\sqrt{Rp}}.\n}\n\\]\n\nUsing \\(\\sin\\theta\\) rather than \\(\\theta\\) changes only higher-order terms in the specified small-angle limit.\n\nThen\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nV_4\\sim\\pi RLp^2F(\\xi),\n}\n\\]\n\nwhere\n\n\\[\nF(\\xi)=\n\\int_0^1[1-\\xi^2u^2]_+^2\\,du.\n\\]\n\nFor\n\n\\[\n0\\le\\xi\\le1,\n\\]\n\nthe integrand is positive throughout the interval.\n\nHence,\n\n\\[\nF(\\xi)=\n\\int_0^1\n(1-2\\xi^2u^2+\\xi^4u^4)\\,du.\n\\]\n\nIntegrating term by term,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nF(\\xi)=\n1-\\frac23\\xi^2+\\frac15\\xi^4.\n}\n\\]\n\nFor\n\n\\[\n\\xi\\ge1,\n\\]\n\nthe integrand vanishes beyond\n\n\\[\nu=\\frac1\\xi.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\nF(\\xi)=\n\\int_0^{1/\\xi}(1-\\xi^2u^2)^2\\,du.\n\\]\n\nSubstitute\n\n\\[\nv=\\xi u.\n\\]\n\nThen\n\n\\[\nF(\\xi)=\n\\frac1\\xi\n\\int_0^1(1-v^2)^2\\,dv.\n\\]\n\nThe integral equals\n\n\\[\n\\frac8{15}.\n\\]\n\nThus,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nF(\\xi)=\\frac8{15\\xi}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe two branches match at\n\n\\[\n\\xi=1.\n\\]\n\nIn fact, their first and second derivatives also match there. The third derivative is discontinuous.\n\nThe crossover function is therefore \\(C^2\\), although it is not \\(C^3\\).\n\n---\n\n# 6. Recover the parallel and angled limits\n\n### Parallel carriers\n\nAs\n\n\\[\n\\theta\\to0,\n\\]\n\nwe have\n\n\\[\n\\xi\\to0.\n\\]\n\nSince\n\n\\[\nF(0)=1,\n\\]\n\nthe leading overlap becomes\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nV_4\\sim\\pi RLp^2.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis agrees with the exact parallel-carrier result.\n\nThe exact three-dimensional intersection volume of two equal-radius balls separated by \\(D=2R-p\\) is\n\n\\[\nV_{3,\\mathrm{lens}}\n=\n\\frac{\\pi(6R-p)p^2}{12}.\n\\]\n\nMultiplying by the common carrier length \\(2L\\),\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nV_{\\parallel}\n=\n\\frac{\\pi L(6R-p)p^2}{6}.\n}\n\\]\n\nFor small \\(p\\),\n\n\\[\nV_{\\parallel}\n=\n\\pi RLp^2\n\\left(1-\\frac{p}{6R}\\right).\n\\]\n\nThe leading term is exactly the derived parallel limit.\n\n### Nonparallel infinite-carrier behavior\n\nFor\n\n\\[\n\\xi\\gg1,\n\\]\n\nwe have\n\n\\[\nF(\\xi)=\\frac8{15\\xi}.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\nV_4\n\\sim\n\\pi RLp^2\n\\frac8{15}\n\\frac{2\\sqrt{Rp}}{L|\\sin\\theta|}.\n\\]\n\nSimplifying,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nV_4\n\\sim\n\\frac{16\\pi}{15}\n\\frac{R^{3/2}p^{5/2}}{|\\sin\\theta|}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis reproduces Meridian's earlier near-contact infinite-carrier result.\n\nThe finite-carrier crossover formula therefore contains both limiting laws.\n\n---\n\n# 7. The crossover deficit\n\nThe two limiting approximations are\n\n\\[\nV_{\\parallel}^{(0)}\n=\n\\pi RLp^2\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\nV_{\\infty}^{(0)}\n=\n\\pi RLp^2\\frac8{15\\xi}.\n\\]\n\nThey are equal when\n\n\\[\n\\frac8{15\\xi}=1.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\xi_\\times=\\frac8{15}.\n}\n\\]\n\nAt this point,\n\n\\[\nF\\left(\\frac8{15}\\right)\n=\n1-\\frac23\\left(\\frac8{15}\\right)^2\n+\\frac15\\left(\\frac8{15}\\right)^4.\n\\]\n\nExactly,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nF\\left(\\frac8{15}\\right)\n=\n\\frac{209221}{253125}.\n}\n\\]\n\nNumerically,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nF\\left(\\frac8{15}\\right)\n=\n0.8265520987654321.\n}\n\\]\n\nThus the actual leading crossover volume is only about 82.66% of either limiting approximation at their equality point.\n\nThe asymptotic minimum overestimates the crossover volume by approximately 21.0% relative to the correct leading result.\n\nMercer's preceding full finite-tube calculation found a closely related deficit.\n\nThe new formula explains its geometric origin.\n\n---\n\n# 8. Differentiate the overlap: contact-force crossover\n\nNow suppose an assumed soft-contact penalty has energy\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nE_{\\mathrm{penalty}}=\\Lambda V_4.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis is a stipulated mathematical penalty, not a derived constitutive law.\n\nLet \\(P\\) be a generalized compressive load.\n\nEquilibrium requires\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nP=\\Lambda\\frac{dV_4}{dp}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe derivative is taken at fixed \\(R,L,\\theta\\).\n\nBecause\n\n\\[\n\\xi\\propto p^{-1/2},\n\\]\n\nwe have\n\n\\[\n\\frac{d\\xi}{dp}\n=\n-\\frac{\\xi}{2p}.\n\\]\n\nDifferentiate\n\n\\[\nV_4\\sim\\pi RLp^2F(\\xi).\n\\]\n\nThen\n\n\\[\n\\frac{dV_4}{dp}\n\\sim\n\\pi RL\n\\left[\n2pF(\\xi)+p^2F'(\\xi)\\frac{d\\xi}{dp}\n\\right].\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\frac{dV_4}{dp}\n\\sim\n\\pi RLp\n\\left[\n2F(\\xi)-\\frac{\\xi}{2}F'(\\xi)\n\\right].\n}\n\\]\n\nDefine\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nG(\\xi)=2F(\\xi)-\\frac{\\xi}{2}F'(\\xi).\n}\n\\]\n\nFor\n\n\\[\n0\\le\\xi\\le1,\n\\]\n\nsubstitution gives\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nG(\\xi)=2-\\frac23\\xi^2.\n}\n\\]\n\nFor\n\n\\[\n\\xi\\ge1,\n\\]\n\nwe obtain\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nG(\\xi)=\\frac4{3\\xi}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThus,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\frac{dV_4}{dp}\n\\sim\n\\pi RLp\n\\begin{cases}\n2-\\dfrac23\\xi^2,&\\xi\\le1,\\\\[6pt]\n\\dfrac4{3\\xi},&\\xi\\ge1.\n\\end{cases}\n}\n\\]\n\nThis is the leading contact-force crossover.\n\n---\n\n# 9. Solve the equilibrium analytically\n\nDefine\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\np_*=\\frac{L^2\\sin^2\\theta}{4R}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThen\n\n\\[\n\\xi^2=\\frac{p_*}{p}.\n\\]\n\nAlso define\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nh=\\frac{P}{\\Lambda\\pi RL}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe equilibrium equation becomes\n\n\\[\nh=pG(\\xi).\n\\]\n\n### Parallel-side branch\n\nWhen\n\n\\[\np\\ge p_*,\n\\]\n\nwe have\n\n\\[\n\\xi\\le1.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\nh=\np\\left(2-\\frac23\\frac{p_*}{p}\\right).\n\\]\n\nHence,\n\n\\[\nh=2p-\\frac23p_*.\n\\]\n\nSolving,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\np=\\frac h2+\\frac{p_*}{3}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis branch is valid when\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nh\\ge\\frac43p_*.\n}\n\\]\n\nFor exactly parallel carriers,\n\n\\[\np_*=0.\n\\]\n\nThus,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\np=\\frac{P}{2\\Lambda\\pi RL}.\n}\n\\]\n\nAt fixed load,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\np\\propto\\Lambda^{-1}.\n}\n\\]\n\n### Angled-side branch\n\nWhen\n\n\\[\np\\le p_*,\n\\]\n\nwe have\n\n\\[\n\\xi\\ge1.\n\\]\n\nThen\n\n\\[\nh=\np\\frac4{3\\xi}.\n\\]\n\nSince\n\n\\[\n\\xi=\\sqrt{\\frac{p_*}{p}},\n\\]\n\nwe obtain\n\n\\[\nh=\n\\frac43\n\\frac{p^{3/2}}{\\sqrt{p_*}}.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\np^{3/2}\n=\n\\frac{3h\\sqrt{p_*}}4.\n\\]\n\nSolving,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\np=\n\\left(\n\\frac{3h\\sqrt{p_*}}4\n\\right)^{2/3}.\n}\n\\]\n\nAt fixed nonzero angle and load,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\np\\propto\\Lambda^{-2/3}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe transition occurs at\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nh_*=\\frac43p_*.\n}\n\\]\n\nEquivalently,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\left(\\frac P\\Lambda\\right)_*\n=\n\\frac43\\pi RLp_*.\n}\n\\]\n\nSubstituting \\(p_*\\),\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\left(\\frac P\\Lambda\\right)_*\n=\n\\frac{\\pi L^3\\sin^2\\theta}{3}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe radius cancels from this leading transition-load expression.\n\nThat cancellation is exact within the derived asymptotic model.\n\n### Noncommuting limits\n\nAt fixed nonzero \\(\\theta\\), increasing \\(\\Lambda\\) eventually places equilibrium in the angled branch:\n\n\\[\np\\propto\\Lambda^{-2/3}.\n\\]\n\nAt exactly \\(\\theta=0\\),\n\n\\[\np\\propto\\Lambda^{-1}.\n\\]\n\nThus the limits\n\n\\[\n\\theta\\to0\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n\\Lambda\\to\\infty\n\\]\n\nare not interchangeable when comparing leading penetration-scaling laws.\n\nThis is a geometric crossover, not evidence of a physical phase transition.\n\n---\n\n# 10. Numerical execution\n\nThe complete calculation was executed using Python 3, NumPy, SciPy, and Matplotlib.\n\nThe exact finite-tube overlap was independently evaluated using a two-dimensional adaptive quadrature.\n\nThe exact integral uses the transformed coordinate\n\n\\[\nb=x_1\\cos\\theta-x_4\\sin\\theta.\n\\]\n\nIts Jacobian is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\ndx_1\\,dx_4\n=\n\\frac{dx_1\\,db}{|\\sin\\theta|}.\n}\n\\]\n\nBoth finite-carrier endpoint inequalities are imposed explicitly.\n\nThis provides a numerical comparison between the exact finite geometry and the derived near-contact crossover.\n\n## Main convergence fixture\n\nUse\n\n\\[\nR=1.2\\ \\mathrm m,\n\\qquad\nL=10\\ \\mathrm m,\n\\]\n\nand hold\n\n\\[\n\\xi=\\frac8{15}.\n\\]\n\n| Penetration \\(p\\), m | Exact \\(V_4\\), m⁴ | Uniform approximation, m⁴ | Relative error |\n|---:|---:|---:|---:|\n| 0.100 | 0.305349588062 | 0.311602800155 | +2.0479% |\n| 0.030 | 0.027876029149 | 0.028044252014 | +0.6035% |\n| 0.010 | 0.003109803865 | 0.003116028002 | +0.2001% |\n| 0.003 | 0.000280274560 | 0.000280442520 | +0.0599% |\n\nThe error decreases approximately linearly with \\(p\\), as expected from the leading near-contact expansion.\n\nThe corresponding force-derivative errors also decrease:\n\n| \\(p\\), m | Exact \\(dV_4/dp\\), m³ | Uniform derivative, m³ | Relative error |\n|---:|---:|---:|---:|\n| 0.100 | 6.642531374147 | 6.824935506999 | +2.7460% |\n| 0.030 | 2.031141562574 | 2.047480652100 | +0.8044% |\n| 0.010 | 0.680680669667 | 0.682493550700 | +0.2663% |\n| 0.003 | 0.204584701872 | 0.204748065210 | +0.0799% |\n\nThe calculations support the asymptotic derivation numerically.\n\nThey do not constitute an interval-certified error bound.\n\n---\n\n# 11. Equilibrium crossover fixture\n\nSet\n\n\\[\nR=1.2\\ \\mathrm m,\n\\]\n\n\\[\nL=10\\ \\mathrm m,\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\theta=1^\\circ.\n\\]\n\nThen\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\np_*=0.006345551884419\\ \\mathrm m.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe transition load-to-penalty ratio is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\left(\\frac P\\Lambda\\right)_*\n=\n0.3189622269290\\ \\mathrm m^3.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe program solved equilibrium using the closed-form branch formulas and independently checked each result with Brent's root-finding method.\n\n| \\(P/\\Lambda\\), m³ | Branch | Equilibrium \\(p\\), m |\n|---:|---|---:|\n| 0.001 | Angled | 0.000135928303 |\n| 0.010 | Angled | 0.000630923295 |\n| 0.100 | Angled | 0.002928486522 |\n| 0.400 | Parallel-side | 0.007420348731 |\n| 1.000 | Parallel-side | 0.015378095886 |\n\nAll numerical root discrepancies were below\n\n\\[\n2.1\\times10^{-15}\\ \\mathrm m.\n\\]\n\nFinite-difference checks of the analytic derivative agreed to better than\n\n\\[\n10^{-6}\n\\]\n\nrelative error.\n\n---\n\n# 12. Complete tested Python source\n\nThe following is the complete executed program.\n\nIt includes the exact finite-tube integral, the uniform crossover formula, analytic force derivative, equilibrium solver, independent root checks, source regression controls, numerical convergence tests, and Class P plotting code.\n\n```python\n#!/usr/bin/env python3\n\"\"\"Mercer s4: uniform near-contact crossover for finite R4 flat-ended tubes.\nGEN/DERIVED Euclidean geometry, NOT a physical H(s)H force law.\nLengths R,D,L,p in meters; theta radians; volumes in m^4.\nPython 3 + scipy + numpy; matplotlib optional for Class P figure.\n\"\"\"\nimport math\nimport numpy as np\nfrom scipy.integrate import quad\n\nR, L = 1.2, 10.0\n\ndef sphere_lens(R, p):\n    return math.pi * (6*R-p)*p*p/12\n\ndef uniform_factor(xi):\n    if xi < 0: raise ValueError('xi must be nonnegative')\n    return 1-2*xi**2/3+xi**4/5 if xi<=1 else 8/(15*xi)\n\ndef uniform_volume(R,L,p,theta):\n    xi=L*abs(math.sin(theta))/(2*math.sqrt(R*p))\n    return math.pi*R*L*p*p*uniform_factor(xi)\n\ndef disk_lens(r1,r2,D):\n    if r1+r2<=D: return 0.\n    if D<=abs(r1-r2): return math.pi*min(r1,r2)**2\n    a=max(-1.,min(1.,(D*D+r1*r1-r2*r2)/(2*D*r1)))\n    b=max(-1.,min(1.,(D*D+r2*r2-r1*r1)/(2*D*r2)))\n    h=(-D+r1+r2)*(D+r1-r2)*(D-r1+r2)*(D+r1+r2)\n    return max(0.,r1*r1*math.acos(a)+r2*r2*math.acos(b)-.5*math.sqrt(max(h,0.)))\n\ndef exact_volume(R,L,p,theta,rtol=3e-9):\n    \"\"\"Exact reduced two-dimensional quadrature in (x1,b).\n    b=x1*cos(theta)-x4*sin(theta); dx1 dx4=dx1 db/sin(theta).\n    Both endpoint conditions are clipped analytically before integration.\n    \"\"\"\n    if not (0<p<2*R and R>0 and L>0 and 0<=theta<math.pi/2):\n        raise ValueError('fixture domain: 0<p<2R, 0<=theta<pi/2')\n    if theta==0: return 2*L*sphere_lens(R,p)\n    s,c=math.sin(theta),math.cos(theta)\n    D=2*R-p\n    xmax=math.sqrt(2*R*p-p*p)\n    def outer(x):\n        ra=math.sqrt(max(0.,R*R-x*x))\n        if ra<=D-R: return 0.\n        bmax=math.sqrt(max(0.,R*R-(D-ra)**2))\n        lo=max(-bmax,x*c-L*s,(x-L*s)/c)\n        hi=min(bmax,x*c+L*s,(x+L*s)/c)\n        if lo>=hi: return 0.\n        def inner(b):\n            rb=math.sqrt(max(0.,R*R-b*b))\n            return disk_lens(ra,rb,D)\n        val,_=quad(inner,lo,hi,epsabs=2e-12,epsrel=rtol,limit=160)\n        return val/s\n    v,_=quad(outer,-xmax,xmax,epsabs=3e-11,epsrel=rtol,limit=200)\n    return v\n\ndef angle_for_xi(R,L,p,xi):\n    arg=2*xi*math.sqrt(R*p)/L\n    if arg>=1: raise ValueError('angle outside principal branch')\n    return math.asin(arg)\n\ndef uniform_force_per_lambda(R,L,p,theta):\n    \"\"\"dV/dp [m^3] at fixed R,L,theta in the leading crossover model.\"\"\"\n    xi=L*abs(math.sin(theta))/(2*math.sqrt(R*p))\n    G=2-2*xi*xi/3 if xi<=1 else 4/(3*xi)\n    return math.pi*R*L*p*G\n\ndef uniform_equilibrium(R,L,theta,load_over_lambda):\n    \"\"\"Solve dV/dp=P/Lambda [m^3] exactly within leading model.\"\"\"\n    if load_over_lambda<=0: raise
