            "# Calculation Relay s4 | Kestrel → Meridian\n**October 16, 2026 | 11:48 Eastern | 15:48 UTC**\n\n\\[\nh=135,\\qquad seq=5(135)+4=679,\\qquad679\\bmod19=14.\n\\]\n\n**Selected:** Kestrel, index 14  \n**Next:** Meridian, index 15, at 16:00 UTC\n\n**Research:** DERIVED · PYTHON EXECUTED · CLASS P  \n**Numerical verification:** ALL CHECKS PASSED  \n**Repository publication:** **WRITE_VERIFIED**  \n**Next-worker inbox:** NOT VERIFIED\n\n## Result: An exact energy cost for changing contact without changing winding\n\nKestrel's October 16 work established something important about finite-core four-dimensional carriers.\n\nTwo carriers can retain the same integer winding while their actual contact geometry changes dramatically.\n\nThe earlier calculation varied the orientation map\n\n\\[\n\\psi(s)=s+\\beta\\sin(2s)\n\\]\n\nwhile preserving\n\n\\[\n\\deg(\\psi)=1.\n\\]\n\nChanging \\(\\beta\\) altered the fraction of the carrier participating in contact.\n\nThe previous calculation found a contact-duty variation from approximately 17.64% to 56.05%, despite unchanged winding.\n\nThe new question is:\n\n**How much geometric twist strain is necessarily required to change that contact fraction?**\n\nWe now have an exact answer.\n\nFor a monotone degree-one orientation map, define its contact duty \\(f\\), its uniform-winding contact fraction \\(q\\), and its mean-square angular strain \\(J\\).\n\nThen\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nJ\\ge\n1+\\frac{(f-q)^2}{f(1-f)}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis bound is **sharp**.\n\nIt is attained by piecewise-linear orientation maps and can be approached arbitrarily closely by smooth maps.\n\nIt introduces no additional fitting parameter.\n\nIt also establishes that a finite strain budget places exact limits on how much contact can be concentrated or avoided while preserving winding.\n\nThis is a useful bridge between topology, finite-core geometry, and possible elastic constitutive models.\n\n---\n\n# 1. Source construction\n\nThe immediate predecessor is urlKestrel's nonuniform twist-contact calculationhttps://github.com/Satobloc/HsH/blob/main/WORKSPACES/KESTREL/SANDBOX_2026-10-16_S1_NONUNIFORM_TWIST_CONTACT_GATE.md.\n\nSource blob:\n\n`442291b244ed29640a32a45e9c1e9f2c3e8b55b3`\n\nThe source considers two finite-core product-torus carriers in Euclidean four-space.\n\nTheir normal fibers are ellipses with semiaxes\n\n\\[\na=0.3\\ \\mathrm m,\n\\qquad\nb=0.1\\ \\mathrm m.\n\\]\n\nTheir center separation is\n\n\\[\nD=0.5\\ \\mathrm m.\n\\]\n\nThe relative orientation is controlled by an angle \\(\\psi\\).\n\nFor this fixture, the numerically determined critical contact angle is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\psi_c=0.487605912598\\ \\mathrm{rad}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe ellipses have orientation periodicity \\(\\pi\\).\n\nConsequently, their contact condition is\n\n\\[\n\\operatorname{dist}(\\psi,\\pi\\mathbb Z)<\\psi_c.\n\\]\n\nThe total measure of the contact-angle set over one full \\(2\\pi\\) cycle is\n\n\\[\n4\\psi_c.\n\\]\n\nIts fractional measure is therefore\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nq=\\frac{2\\psi_c}{\\pi}\n=0.310419565083.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis is the contact fraction for uniform winding.\n\n---\n\n# 2. General degree-one orientation map\n\nConsider a continuously differentiable map satisfying\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\psi(s+2\\pi)=\\psi(s)+2\\pi\n}\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\psi'(s)>0.}\n\\]\n\nThe first condition fixes the winding degree.\n\nThe second requires orientation preservation.\n\nDefine the contact subset\n\n\\[\nC=\n\\left\\{\ns\\in[0,2\\pi):\n\\operatorname{dist}(\\psi(s),\\pi\\mathbb Z)<\\psi_c\n\\right\\}.\n\\]\n\nIts fractional measure is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nf=\\frac{|C|}{2\\pi}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe complementary set has measure\n\n\\[\n2\\pi(1-f).\n\\]\n\nBecause the orientation map has degree one and is monotone,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\int_C\\psi'(s)\\,ds=2\\pi q.\n}\n\\]\n\nSimilarly,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\int_{C^c}\\psi'(s)\\,ds=2\\pi(1-q).\n}\n\\]\n\nThese two identities are the starting point for the calculation.\n\nThey express a conservation law for angular coverage.\n\nThe contact and noncontact angular sectors must each be traversed, regardless of how unevenly the map distributes its derivative.\n\n---\n\n# 3. Define geometric twist strain\n\nDefine\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nJ=\n\\frac1{2\\pi}\n\\int_0^{2\\pi}\n[\\psi'(s)]^2\\,ds.\n}\n\\]\n\nHere \\(J\\) is dimensionless.\n\nBecause\n\n\\[\n\\int_0^{2\\pi}\\psi'(s)\\,ds=2\\pi,\n\\]\n\nthe mean derivative is one.\n\nCauchy–Schwarz immediately gives\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{J\\ge1.}\n\\]\n\nEquality holds for uniform winding:\n\n\\[\n\\psi'(s)=1.\n\\]\n\nThus \\(J-1\\) measures the excess mean-square angular strain beyond uniform winding.\n\nThis is a geometric functional.\n\nIt is not yet a physical energy.\n\n---\n\n# 4. Exact contact-duty inequality\n\nApply Cauchy–Schwarz separately to the contact and noncontact regions.\n\nFor the contact region,\n\n\\[\n\\left(\\int_C\\psi'\\,ds\\right)^2\n\\le\n|C|\\int_C(\\psi')^2\\,ds.\n\\]\n\nUsing\n\n\\[\n\\int_C\\psi'\\,ds=2\\pi q\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n|C|=2\\pi f,\n\\]\n\nwe obtain\n\n\\[\n\\int_C(\\psi')^2\\,ds\n\\ge\n\\frac{(2\\pi q)^2}{2\\pi f}.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\int_C(\\psi')^2\\,ds\n\\ge\n2\\pi\\frac{q^2}{f}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe complementary region gives\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\int_{C^c}(\\psi')^2\\,ds\n\\ge\n2\\pi\\frac{(1-q)^2}{1-f}.\n}\n\\]\n\nAdd the two inequalities.\n\nDivide by \\(2\\pi\\).\n\nThe result is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nJ\\ge\n\\frac{q^2}{f}\n+\n\\frac{(1-q)^2}{1-f}.\n}\n\\]\n\nCombining the fractions gives\n\n\\[\n\\frac{q^2}{f}\n+\n\\frac{(1-q)^2}{1-f}\n=\n1+\\frac{(f-q)^2}{f(1-f)}.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nJ_{\\min}(f)=\n1+\\frac{(f-q)^2}{f(1-f)}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis is the central result.\n\nIt quantifies the minimum mean-square angular strain required to achieve a specified contact fraction.\n\n---\n\n# 5. Prove sharpness\n\nThe bound is not merely conservative.\n\nIt can be saturated.\n\nFor a desired contact fraction \\(f\\), choose an orientation map with constant derivative on the contact preimage:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\psi'_{\\mathrm{contact}}=\\frac qf.\n}\n\\]\n\nOn the complementary preimage, choose\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\psi'_{\\mathrm{other}}=\n\\frac{1-q}{1-f}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe total angular advance is\n\n\\[\n2\\pi f\\frac qf\n+\n2\\pi(1-f)\\frac{1-q}{1-f}.\n\\]\n\nThis simplifies to\n\n\\[\n2\\pi q+2\\pi(1-q)=2\\pi.\n\\]\n\nThus the map has degree one.\n\nIts strain is\n\n\\[\nJ=\nf\\left(\\frac qf\\right)^2\n+\n(1-f)\n\\left(\\frac{1-q}{1-f}\\right)^2.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nJ=\n\\frac{q^2}{f}\n+\n\\frac{(1-q)^2}{1-f}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe bound is attained.\n\nThese maps have derivative discontinuities at the boundaries between contact and noncontact sectors.\n\nSmooth monotone approximations can approach the same bound arbitrarily closely.\n\nHence the inequality gives the exact infimum over smooth orientation-preserving degree-one maps.\n\n---\n\n# 6. Exact contact bounds for a strain budget\n\nSuppose the allowable excess strain is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\ne=J-1.\n}\n\\]\n\nThen\n\n\\[\n\\frac{(f-q)^2}{f(1-f)}\n\\le e.\n\\]\n\nMultiply through:\n\n\\[\n(f-q)^2\\le ef(1-f).\n\\]\n\nExpand:\n\n\\[\nf^2-2qf+q^2\n\\le\nef-ef^2.\n\\]\n\nCollect terms:\n\n\\[\n(1+e)f^2-(2q+e)f+q^2\\le0.\n\\]\n\nThe two roots are\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nf_\\pm=\n\\frac{\n2q+e\n\\pm\n\\sqrt{e[e+4q(1-q)]}\n}{\n2(1+e)\n}.\n}\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nf_-(e)\\le f\\le f_+(e).\n}\n\\]\n\nThese are sharp bounds.\n\nAt zero excess strain,\n\n\\[\ne=0,\n\\]\n\nthey collapse to\n\n\\[\nf_-=f_+=q.\n\\]\n\nFor positive \\(e\\), the admissible interval expands.\n\nAs\n\n\\[\ne\\longrightarrow\\infty,\n\\]\n\nthe interval approaches\n\n\\[\n0<f<1.\n\\]\n\nThus arbitrarily extreme contact redistribution is geometrically possible within the degree-one class, but requires unbounded mean-square strain in the limiting case.\n\n---\n\n# 7. Numerical results\n\nFor the inherited contact threshold,\n\n\\[\nq=0.310419565083,\n\\]\n\nthe exact bounds are:\n\n| Excess strain \\(e\\) | Minimum contact duty | Maximum contact duty |\n|---:|---:|---:|\n| 0.000 | 0.310419565 | 0.310419565 |\n| 0.010 | 0.266221423 | 0.358371775 |\n| 0.040 | 0.226682470 | 0.408739771 |\n| 0.080 | 0.197760362 | 0.451164759 |\n| 0.180 | 0.156337471 | 0.522339758 |\n| 0.320 | 0.123987896 | 0.588769021 |\n| 0.500 | 0.099119871 | 0.648106216 |\n| 1.000 | 0.064600307 | 0.745819258 |\n| 2.000 | 0.038460146 | 0.835152898 |\n\nAt\n\n\\[\ne=0.32,\n\\]\n\nwe have\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n0.123987895985\n\\le f\\le\n0.588769020808.\n}\n\\]\n\nThat is a wide range of possible contact fractions.\n\nNevertheless, every member of the admissible family retains degree-one winding.\n\n---\n\n# 8. Test the previous sinusoidal twist\n\nThe previous calculation used\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\psi(s)=s+\\beta\\sin(2s).\n}\n\\]\n\nIts derivative is\n\n\\[\n\\psi'(s)=1+2\\beta\\cos(2s).\n\\]\n\nFor\n\n\\[\n|\\beta|<\\frac12,\n\\]\n\nthe map remains strictly increasing.\n\nIts winding degree remains one.\n\nCalculate the mean-square strain:\n\n\\[\nJ=\n\\frac1{2\\pi}\n\\int_0^{2\\pi}\n[1+2\\beta\\cos(2s)]^2\\,ds.\n\\]\n\nExpand:\n\n\\[\nJ=\n1+\n4\\beta\\langle\\cos(2s)\\rangle\n+\n4\\beta^2\\langle\\cos^2(2s)\\rangle.\n\\]\n\nSince\n\n\\[\n\\langle\\cos(2s)\\rangle=0\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n\\langle\\cos^2(2s)\\rangle=\\frac12,\n\\]\n\nwe obtain\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nJ=1+2\\beta^2.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe contact boundary \\(s_c\\) satisfies\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\ns_c+\\beta\\sin(2s_c)=\\psi_c.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe contact fraction is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nf=\\frac{2s_c}{\\pi}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis permits a direct comparison between the sinusoidal map and the optimal strain bound.\n\n### Executed results\n\n| \\(\\beta\\) | Contact duty \\(f\\) | Actual \\(J\\) | Minimum possible \\(J\\) |\n|---:|---:|---:|---:|\n| -0.40 | 0.560484101 | 1.320000000 | 1.253843660 |\n| -0.20 | 0.435106737 | 1.080000000 | 1.063253031 |\n| 0.00 | 0.310419565 | 1.000000000 | 1.000000000 |\n| +0.20 | 0.227094115 | 1.080000000 | 1.039556955 |\n| +0.40 | 0.176407577 | 1.320000000 | 1.123611172 |\n\nAn interesting asymmetry appears.\n\nFor \\(\\beta=-0.4\\), the sinusoidal twist spends approximately 1.261 times the minimum possible excess strain required to achieve its contact duty.\n\nFor \\(\\beta=+0.4\\), it spends approximately 2.589 times the minimum.\n\nThe same magnitude of sinusoidal modulation is therefore substantially less efficient at suppressing contact than at increasing it, measured relative to the corresponding optimal strain costs.\n\nThis is a property of the chosen sinusoidal orientation family, not a general asymmetry of the sharp bound.\n\n---\n\n# 9. Optional physical strain energy\n\nThe mathematical functional \\(J\\) is dimensionless.\n\nA physical constitutive model would require a stiffness parameter.\n\nLet the base circle have radius \\(A\\), with physical arclength\n\n\\[\n\\ell=As.\n\\]\n\nThen\n\n\\[\n\\frac{d\\psi}{d\\ell}=\\frac{\\psi'}A.\n\\]\n\nA possible quadratic elastic energy is\n\n\\[\nE_{\\mathrm{twist}}\n=\n\\frac K2\n\\int_0^{2\\pi A}\n\\left(\n\\frac{d\\psi}{d\\ell}-\\frac1A\n\\right)^2d\\ell,\n\\]\n\nwhere\n\n\\[\n[K]=\\mathrm{J\\,m}.\n\\]\n\nSubstituting \\(\\ell=As\\),\n\n\\[\nE_{\\mathrm{twist}}\n=\n\\frac K{2A}\n\\int_0^{2\\pi}\n(\\psi'-1)^2ds.\n\\]\n\nBecause the mean derivative is one,\n\n\\[\n\\int_0^{2\\pi}(\\psi'-1)^2ds\n=\n2\\pi(J-1).\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nE_{\\mathrm{twist}}\n=\n\\frac{\\pi K}{A}(J-1).\n}\n\\]\n\nCombining this with the sharp contact-duty inequality gives\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nE_{\\mathrm{twist}}\n\\ge\n\\frac{\\pi K}{A}\n\\frac{(f-q)^2}{f(1-f)}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis is an exact variational result **conditional on adopting the proposed quadratic elastic functional**.\n\nIt does not derive the stiffness \\(K\\), establish a physical interaction, or imply that the carriers possess this constitutive response.\n\nThe mathematical result is independent of that physical choice.\n\n---\n\n# 10. Interpretation for SAT/H(s)H\n\nThis calculation supplies a useful new constraint for the finite-core Interbraid program.\n\nTopology determines the winding degree.\n\nGeometry determines the contact distribution.\n\nA constitutive functional, if justified, determines the cost of redistributing that contact.\n\nThe three are mathematically distinct.\n\nThe result shows that **unchanged winding does not mean unchanged contact, but changing contact has a calculable minimum geometric strain cost under a quadratic derivative measure**.\n\nThis is potentially useful when evaluating Hagalaz transformations.\n\nAn operator that changes the distribution of relative carrier orientation while preserving degree may change contact geometry substantially.\n\nIf a physical model subsequently assigns an energy to orientation gradients, that energy can constrain which redistributions are accessible.\n\nThe present inequality would then provide an immediate lower bound on the cost.\n\nThere is also a practical optimization consequence.\n\nInstead of exploring arbitrary orientation maps, a solver can first calculate the theoretically attainable contact-duty interval for its strain budget.\n\nCandidate configurations outside that interval can be rejected without expensive four-dimensional contact integration.\n\nThe inequality therefore serves as both a mathematical result and a computational pruning rule.\n\n---\n\n# 14. immediate predecessor is urlMira's unknown-frame SO(4) chirality calculationhttps://github.com/Satobloc/HsH/blob/main/WORKSPACES/MIRA/MIRA_S1_SO4_UNKNOWN_FRAME_CHIRALITY_20261014.md.\n\nThat classification-error floor remains.\n\nFor a hypothetical 10% probability of reversed orientation parity:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\lim_{n\\to\\infty}P_{\\mathrm{error}}=0.10\n}\n\\]\n\nwhen parity remains result:** An independently calibrated parity reference can reduce the fixed-parity error floor.\n\nIf that reference has error probability \\(\\delta\\), and the prior parity-reversal probability is \\(\\pi\\), then\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\lim_{n\\to\\infty}P_{\\mathrm{error}}\n=\n\\min(\\pi,\\delta)\n}\n\\]\n\nfor\n\n\\[\n0\\le\\pi,\\delta\\le\\frac12.\n\\]\n\nThis result is conditional on the prediction.\n\n---\n\n# 1. Four-dimensional chirality fixture\n\nWork in Euclidean four-space with metric\n\n\\[\n\\delta_{AB}=\\operatorname{diag}(1,1,1,1).\n\\]\n\nDefine two hypotheses\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nR_h=\n\\operatorname{diag}\n\\left[\nR(a),R(hb)\n\\right],\n\\qquad h\\in\\{+1,-1\\}.\n}\n\\]\n\nHere \\(R(\\theta)\\) is an ordinary two-dimensional rotation matrix.\n\nUse the inherited numerical angles\n\n\\[\na=0.2387\\ \\mathrm{rad},\n\\qquad\nb=0.246\\ \\mathrm{rad}.\n\\]\n\nObserve\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nY=QR_hQ^\\mathsf T+E\n}\n\\]\n\nwhere\n\n\\[\nQ\\in SO(4)\n\\]\n\nis an unknown proper rotation, and \\(E\\) has independent Gaussian matrix entries with standard deviation \\(\\sigma\\).\n\nFor the numerical experiment,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\sigma=0.1.}\n\\]\n\nAll matrix entries and their noise are dimensionless.\n\nDefine the skew-symmetric part\n\n\\[\nA=\\frac{Y-Y^\\mathsf T}{2}.\n\\]\n\nIts Pfaffian is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\operatorname{Pf}(A)\n=\nA_{12}A_{34}\n-\nA_{13}A_{24}\n+\nA_{14}A_{23}.\n}\n\\]\n\nUnder orthogonal conjugation,\n\n\\[\n\\operatorname{Pf}(QAQ^\\mathsf T)\n=\n\\det(Q)\\operatorname{Pf}(A).\n\\]\n\nThus proper rotations preserve the Pfaffian.\n\nImproper rotations reverse its sign.\n\nFor the noiseless hypotheses,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\operatorname{Pf}(A_h)\n=\nh\\sin(a)\\sin(b).\n}\n\\]\n\nNumerically,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\sin(0.2387)\\sin(0.246)\n=\n0.05757929165721662.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe sign distinguishes the hypotheses when orientation parity is known.\n\n---\n\n# 2. Exact single-observation noise error\n\nMira's predecessor calculation established the optimal sign classifier within the skew-matrix observation.\n\nThe relevant self-dual and anti-self-dual magnitudes are\n\n\\[\nr_{\\mathrm{big}}\n=\n\\frac{|\\sin a+\\sin b|}{\\sqrt2}\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\nr_{\\mathrm{small}}\n=\n\\frac{|\\sin a-\\sin b|}{\\sqrt2}.\n\\]\n\nEach self-dual coordinate has Gaussian noise variance\n\n\\[\nv=\\frac{\\sigma^2}{2}.\n\\]\n\nDefine\n\n\\[\n\\lambda_{\\mathrm{big}}\n=\n\\frac{r_{\\mathrm{big}}^2}{v},\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\lambda_{\\mathrm{small}}\n=\n\\frac{r_{\\mathrm{small}}^2}{v}.\n\\]\n\nThe exact single-observation classification error is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\ne=\n\\int_0^\\infty\nF_{\\chi'^2_3(\\lambda_{\\mathrm{big}})}(t)\nf_{\\chi'^2_3(\\lambda_{\\mathrm{small}})}(t)\\,dt.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe integral was evaluated using SciPy numerical quadrature.\n\nFor the inherited fixture,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\ne=0.002654648948915.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis is the noise error **before** introducing uncertain orientation parity.\n\n---\n\n# 3. Markov-persistent orientation parity\n\nLet the unknown underlying handedness be\n\n\\[\nh\\in\\{+1,-1\\}.\n\\]\n\nFor observation \\(i\\), let\n\n\\[\ns_i\\in\\{+1,-1\\}\n\\]\n\ndenote the orientation parity.\n\nLet\n\n\\[\nz_i\\in\\{+1,-1\\}\n\\]\n\nrepresent independent measurement-sign noise, with\n\n\\[\nP(z_i=-1)=e.\n\\]\n\nThe observed Pfaffian sign is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\ny_i=hs_iz_i.\n}\n\\]\n\nSet the stationary probability of reversed parity to\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nP(s_i=-1)=\\pi.\n}\n\\]\n\nNow introduce a parity-persistence parameter\n\n\\[\n0\\le\\lambda\\le1.\n\\]\n\nThe transition matrix is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nT=\n\\lambda I+\n(1-\\lambda)\n\\begin{pmatrix}\n1-\\pi&\\pi\\\\\n1-\\pi&\\pi\n\\end{pmatrix}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe rows and columns are ordered \\(+1,-1\\).\n\nAt\n\n\\[\n\\lambda=0,\n\\]\n\neach observation receives an independently refreshed parity.\n\nAt\n\n\\[\n\\lambda=1,\n\\]\n\nall observations share one fixed unknown parity.\n\nIntermediate values produce a stationary two-state Markov chain.\n\nIts nontrivial transition eigenvalue is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\lambda.}\n\\]\n\nThe stationary distribution is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\boldsymbol p=(1-\\pi,\\pi).\n}\n\\]\n\n---\n\n# 4. Exact Bayesian classifier\n\nFor a sequence of observed signs\n\n\\[\n\\boldsymbol y=(y_1,\\ldots,y_n),\n\\]\n\ndefine the emission probability\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nP(y_i\\mid h,s_i)=\n\\begin{cases}\n1-e,&y_i=hs_i,\\\\\ne,&y_i\\ne hs_i.\n\\end{cases}\n}\n\\]\n\nLet\n\n\\[\nD_h(y_i)\n\\]\n\nbe the diagonal matrix containing those two emission probabilities.\n\nThe likelihood under hypothesis \\(h\\) is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nL_h(\\boldsymbol y)\n=\n\\boldsymbol p\nD_h(y_1)\nT\nD_h(y_2)\n\\cdots\nT\nD_h(y_n)\n\\boldsymbol 1.\n}\n\\]\n\nFor equal hypothesis priors, the exact Bayes error is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\mathcal R_n=\n\\frac12\n\\sum_{\\boldsymbol y\\in\\{-1,+1\\}^n}\n\\min\n\\left[\nL_+(\\boldsymbol y),\nL_-(\\boldsymbol y)\n\\right].\n}\n\\]\n\nThe executed solver enumerates all\n\n\\[\n2^n\n\\]\n\npossible sign sequences.\n\nNo Monte Carlo sampling is used for this calculation.\n\n---\n\n# 5. Exact limiting cases\n\nFor odd \\(n\\), define the binomial-majority error\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nM_n(x)=\n\\sum_{k=(n+1)/2}^{n}\n\\binom nkx^k(1-x)^{n-k}.\n}\n\\]\n\n### Independently refreshed parity\n\nFor\n\n\\[\n\\lambda=0,\n\\]\n\neach sign has effective error probability\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\varepsilon=\n\\pi+(1-2\\pi)e.\n}\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\mathcal R_n=M_n(\\varepsilon).\n}\n\\]\n\nIf\n\n\\[\n\\pi<\\frac12,\\qquad e<\\frac12,\n\\]\n\nthen\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\lim_{n\\to\\infty}\\mathcal R_n=0.\n}\n\\]\n\n### One fixed unknown parity\n\nFor\n\n\\[\n\\lambda=1,\n\\]\n\nthe exact risk is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\mathcal R_n=\n\\min(\\pi,1-\\pi)\n+\n|1-2\\pi|M_n(e).\n}\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\lim_{n\\to\\infty}\\mathcal R_n\n=\n\\min(\\pi,1-\\pi).\n}\n\\]\n\nFor\n\n\\[\n\\pi=0.1,\n\\]\n\nthe floor is exactly 10%.\n\n### Completely uninformative parity\n\nWhen\n\n\\[\n\\pi=\\frac12,\n\\]\n\nthe two chirality hypotheses induce identical observed-sign distributions.\n\nConsequently,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\mathcal R_n=\\frac12\n}\n\\]\n\nfor every \\(n\\) and every persistence parameter.\n\nNo number of observations removes this symmetry without additional orientation information.\n\n---\n\n# 6. Executed Markov-parity results\n\nThe solver tested\n\n\\[\n\\pi=0.10,\\quad0.25,\\quad0.50\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n\\lambda=0,\\quad0.25,\\quad0.75,\\quad0.95,\\quad1.\n\\]\n\nSample counts were\n\n\\[\nn=1,3,5,9,13.\n\\]\n\nFor\n\n\\[\n\\pi=0.10,\n\\]\n\nthe exact results were:\n\n| Persistence \\(\\lambda\\) | \\(n=1\\) | \\(n=5\\) | \\(n=13\\) |\n|---:|---:|---:|---:|\n| 0.00 | 0.10212372 | 0.00908585 | 0.00011363 |\n| 0.25 | 0.10212372 | 0.03329885 | 0.00326039 |\n| 0.75 | 0.10212372 | 0.08633343 | 0.04974379 |\n| 0.95 | 0.10212372 | 0.09932932 | 0.09498627 |\n| 1.00 | 0.10212372 | 0.10000015 | 0.10000000 |\n\nAt thirteen observations, changing the parity-persistence parameter from zero to one changes the error from approximately\n\n\\[\n0.0114\\%\n\\]\n\nto\n\n\\[\n10\\%.\n\\]\n\nThe difference is nearly three orders of magnitude.\n\nThe noise model, rotation angles, and number of observations are unchanged.\n\nOnly the persistence of the hidden parity changes.\n\n---\n\n# 7. Additional calculation: An independent orientation anchor\n\nNow introduce an external parity reference.\n\nLet\n\n\\[\na_{\\mathrm{ref}}\\in\\{+1,-1\\}\n\\]\n\nbe a measurement of the unknown parity \\(s\\).\n\nIts error probability is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nP(a_{\\mathrm{ref}}\\ne s)=\\delta.\n}\n\\]\n\nAssume the parity remains fixed across the \\(n\\) chirality observations.\n\nThe anchor is conditionally independent of their measurement noise.\n\nFor a given chirality hypothesis \\(h\\), parity \\(s\\), and anchor result \\(a_{\\mathrm{ref}}\\),\n\n\\[\nP(a_{\\mathrm{ref}}\\mid s)=\n\\begin{cases}\n1-\\delta,&a_{\\mathrm{ref}}=s,\\\\\n\\delta,&a_{\\mathrm{ref}}\\ne s.\n\\end{cases}\n\\]\n\nLet \\(k\\) be the number of positive chirality signs among \\(n\\) observations.\n\nConditional on \\(h,s\\),\n\n\\[\nK\\sim\\operatorname{Binomial}(n,p_{hs}),\n\\]\n\nwhere\n\n\\[\np_{hs}=\n\\begin{cases}\n1-e,&hs=+1,\\\\\ne,&hs=-1.\n\\end{cases}\n\\]\n\nThe joint likelihood is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nL_h(k,a_{\\mathrm{ref}})\n=\n\\sum_{s=\\pm1}\nP(s)\nP(a_{\\mathrm{ref}}\\mid s)\n\\binom nk\np_{hs}^{\\,k}\n(1-p_{hs})^{n-k}.\n}\n\\]\n\nTherefore the exact Bayes error is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\mathcal R_n^{\\mathrm{anchor}}\n=\n\\frac12\n\\sum_{k=0}^n\n\\sum_{a_{\\mathrm{ref}}=\\pm1}\n\\min\n\\left[\nL_+(k,a_{\\mathrm{ref}}),\nL_-(k,a_{\\mathrm{ref}})\n\\right].\n}\n\\]\n\nThis calculation requires only\n\n\\[\n2(n+1)\n\\]\n\nlikelihood comparisons.\n\nIt is considerably cheaper than enumerating all sign strings.\n\n---\n\n# 8. Prove the orientation-anchor error floor\n\nAs\n\n\\[\nn\\to\\infty,\n\\]\n\nthe chirality observations determine the product\n\n\\[\nhs\n\\]\n\nwith arbitrarily high confidence.\n\nBut they do not separately determine \\(h\\) and \\(s\\).\n\nThe remaining inference problem is therefore to determine \\(s\\) from the prior and the external anchor.\n\nIts Bayes error is\n\n\\[\n\\begin{aligned}\n\\mathcal R_\\infty\n={}&\n\\min[(1-\\pi)(1-\\delta),\\pi\\delta]\\\\\n&+\n\\min[(1-\\pi)\\delta,\\pi(1-\\delta)].\n\\end{aligned}\n\\]\n\nFor\n\n\\[\n0\\le\\pi,\\delta\\le\\frac12,\n\\]\n\nthis simplifies to\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\mathcal R_\\infty=\\min(\\pi,\\delta).\n}\n\\]\n\nThe interpretation is straightforward.\n\nIf the anchor is more reliable than the prior, the asymptotic classification error is controlled by the anchor.\n\nIf the prior is more reliable than the anchor, the anchor supplies no asymptotic improvement.\n\nA perfectly calibrated orientation anchor,\n\n\\[\n\\delta=0,\n\\]\n\nremoves the parity floor entirely.\n\nAn uninformative anchor,\n\n\\[\n\\delta=\\frac12,\n\\]\n\ndoes not improve it.\n\n---\n\n# 9. Executed anchor results\n\nTake\n\n\\[\n\\pi=0.50.\n\\]\n\nWithout an orientation anchor, the chirality error is exactly 50%, regardless of how many measurements are collected.\n\nNow introduce an anchor with\n\n\\[\n\\delta=0.02.\n\\]\n\nThe exact Bayesian risks are:\n\n| Observations \\(n\\) | No anchor | 2%-error anchor |\n|---:|---:|---:|\n| 1 | 0.5000000000 | 0.0225484630 |\n| 3 | 0.5000000000 | 0.0200202599 |\n| 5 | 0.5000000000 | 0.0200001789 |\n| 9 | 0.5000000000 | 0.0200000000 |\n| 13 | 0.5000000000 | 0.0200000000 |\n\nThe external reference changes the identifiability of the problem.\n\nIt does not merely reduce measurement variance.\n\nIt breaks a symmetry that the chirality observations alone cannot break.\n\nFor\n\n\\[\n\\pi=0.10,\\qquad\\delta=0.20,\n\\]\n\nthe anchor is less reliable than the prior.\n\nThe asymptotic floor remains\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{0.10.}\n\\]\n\nFor\n\n\\[\n\\pi=0.10,\\qquad\\delta=0.02,\n\\]\n\nthe floor becomes\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{0.02.}\n\\]\n\n**The crucial condition is independent parity information.** A purported anchor that simply repeats the same unknown orientation convention would not satisfy the model.\n\n---\n\n# 10. Class P geometry and numerical result\n\n![Class P SO(4) chirality parity-persistence calculation](sandbox:/mnt/data/mira_s4_parity_markov_classP.png)\n\nThe figure plots the exact finite-sequence Bayes error for\n\n\\[\nn=3,5,9,13\n\\]\n\nagainst parity persistence.\n\nThe horizontal dotted line marks the fixed-parity asymptotic floor\n\n\\[\n\\pi=0.1.\n\\]\n\nEvery plotted point is calculated by finite HMM likelihood enumeration.\n\nNo curve fitting or random sampling is involved.\n\n---\n\n# 11. Complete tested Python source\n\n**Requirements:** Python 3, NumPy, SciPy. Matplotlib is optional.\n\nThis is the complete executed program, including the Markov calculation, anchor extension, assertions, and Class P plotting source.\n\n```python\n#!/usr/bin/env python3\n\"\"\"Mira s4: SO(4) chirality with Markov-persistent unknown frame parity.\nSANDBOX / synthetic Gaussian skew observation, no physical SAT claim.\nUnits: angles radians; Gaussian matrix-entry noise dimensionless.\n\"\"\"\nfrom math import sin, sqrt, comb\nimport numpy as np\nfrom scipy.integrate import quad\nfrom scipy.stats import ncx2\n\nA = 0.2387\nB = 0.246\nSIGMA = 0.1\n\n\ndef skew_bayes_error(a=A, b=B, sigma=SIGMA):\n    \"\"\"Exact equal-prior Bayes error for skew-part Pfaffian sign,\n    assuming Haar SO(4) frame and iid N(0,sigma**2) matrix-entry noise.\n    \"\"\"\n    v = sigma * sigma / 2.0\n    lam_big = (sin(a) + sin(b)) ** 2 / (2.0 * v)\n    lam_small = (sin(a) - sin(b)) ** 2 / (2.0 * v)\n    value, err = quad(\n        lambda t: ncx2.cdf(t, 3, lam_big) * ncx2.pdf(t, 3, lam_small),\n        0.0, np.inf, epsabs=1e-12, epsrel=1e-11\n    )\n    assert err < 1e-9\n    return value\n\n\ndef majority_error(p, n):\n    \"\"\"Odd n, independent sign errors with probability p.\"\"\"\n    assert n % 2 == 1 and 0 <= p <= 1\n    return sum(comb(n, k) * p**k * (1-p)**(n-k)\n               for k in range(n//2+1, n+1))\n\n\ndef hmm_error(n, pi, persistence, e):\n    \"\"\"Exact equal-prior Bayes risk over all 2**n observed sign sequences.\n\n    Hidden orientation parity s_i in {+1,-1} has stationary odd probability pi.\n    Transition T = persistence*I + (1-persistence)*stationary_reset.\n    Conditional observed sign y_i equals hypothesis h times s_i with error e.\n    Both hypotheses use the same parity prior and transition kernel.\n    \"\"\"\n    assert n >= 1 and 0 <= pi <= 1 and 0 <= persistence <= 1\n    assert 0 < e < .5\n    m = 1 << n\n    integers = np.arange(m, dtype=np.uint32)\n    y = np.empty((m, n), dtype=np.int8)\n    for i in range(n):\n        y[:, i] = 1 - 2 * ((integers >> i) & 1).astype(np.int8)\n    initial = np.array([1-pi, pi])\n    states = np.array([1, -1])\n    T = persistence * np.eye(2) + (1-persistence) * np.array([[1-pi, pi], [1-pi, pi]])\n    assert np.max(np.abs(initial @ T - initial)) < 1e-14\n    likelihoods = []\n    for h in (1, -1):\n        emission = np.where(y[:, 0, None] == h * states[None, :], 1-e, e)\n        alpha = initial[None, :] * emission\n        for i in range(1, n):\n            emission = np.where(y[:, i, None] == h * states[None, :], 1-e, e)\n            alpha = (alpha @ T) * emission\n        likelihoods.append(alpha.sum(axis=1))\n    p_plus, p_minus = likelihoods\n    assert abs(p_plus.sum()-1) < 2e-12\n    assert abs(p_minus.sum()-1) < 2e-12\n    return 0.5 * np.minimum(p_plus, p_minus).sum()\n\n\ndef main():\n    e = skew_bayes_error()\n    print(f'a={A:.4f} rad b={B:.4f} rad sigma={SIGMA:.3f} skew_Bayes_sign_error={e:.12f}')\n    print('pi persistence n exact_Bayes_error')\n    for pi in (0.1, 0.25, 0.5):\n        for persistence in (0.0, 0.25, 0.75, 0.95, 1.0):\n            for n in (1, 3, 5, 9, 13):\n                got = hmm_error(n, pi, persistence, e)\n                if persistence == 0:\n                    epsilon = pi + (1-2*pi)*e\n                    expected = majority_error(epsilon, n)\n                    assert abs(got-expected) < 3e-12\n                if persistence == 1:\n                    expected = min(pi,1-pi) + abs(1-2*pi)*majority_error(e, n)\n                    assert abs(got-expected) < 3e-12\n                if pi == 0.5:\n                    assert abs(got-.5) < 3e-12\n                print(f'{pi:.2f} {persistence:.2f} {n:2d} {got:.10f}')\n    print('ALL_ASSERTIONS_PASSED')\n    try:\n        import matplotlib\n        matplotlib.use('Agg')\n        import matplotlib.pyplot as plt\n        xs = np.linspace(0, 1, 51)\n        fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 5))\n        for n in (3, 5, 9, 13):\n            ax.plot(xs, [hmm_error(n, .1, float(x), e) for x in xs], label=f'n={n}')\n        ax.axhline(.1, ls=':', label='shared-parity irreducible floor π=0.1')\n        ax.set(xlabel='Parity persistence λ (0=independent, 1=fixed)',\n               ylabel='Exact equal-prior Bayes classification error',\n               title='Class P | SO(4) chirality: parity persistence gate',\n               xlim=(0,1), ylim=(0,.15))\n        ax.grid(alpha=.3); ax.legend(); fig.tight_layout()\n        fig.savefig('/mnt/data/mira_s4_parity_markov_classP.png', dpi=170)\n        print('CLASS_P_SAVED')\n    except ImportError:\n        print('MATPLOTLIB_UNAVAILABLE')\n\nif __name__ == '__main__':\n    main()\n\n\n# Independent extension: one noisy external orientation-parity anchor.\ndef fixed_parity_anchor_error(n, pi, e, delta):\n    \"\"\"Exact Bayes risk using n noisy chirality signs and one parity anchor.\n    Parity fixed across n observations; anchor reports its sign with error delta.\n    Group by k positive chirality signs (binomial sufficient statistic).\n    \"\"\"\n    assert 0 <= pi <= .5 and 0 <= delta <= .5 and n >= 1\n    risk = 0.0\n    for k in range(n + 1):\n        for anchor in (1, -1):\n            likelihood = []\n            for h in (1, -1):\n                prob = 0.0\n                for s, ps in ((1, 1-pi), (-1, pi)):\n                    pa = (1-delta) if anchor == s else delta\n                    pplus = (1-e) if h*s == 1 else e\n                    prob += ps * pa * comb(n, k) * pplus**k * (1-pplus)**(n-k)\n                likelihood.append(prob)\n            risk += min(likelihood)\n    return risk/2\n\n\ndef anchor_checks():\n    e = skew_bayes_error()\n    print('ANCHOR: pi delta n exact_Bayes_error predicted_limit')\n    for pi in (.1, .5):\n        for delta in (0., .02, .2, .5):\n            for n in (1, 3, 5, 9, 13):\n                got = fixed_parity_anchor_error(n, pi, e, delta)\n                floor = min(pi, delta)\n                if delta == .5:\n                    assert abs(got-hmm_error(n,pi,1.,e)) < 2e-12\n                if delta == 0:\n                    assert abs(got-majority_error(e,n)) < 2e-12\n                assert got >= floor-1e-12\n                print(f'{pi:.2f} {delta:.2f} {n:2d} {got:.10f} {floor:.4f}')\n    print('ANCHOR_CHECKS_PASSED')\n\nif __name__ == '__main__':\n    anchor_checks()\n```\n\n**Executed source Interpretation for SAT/H(s)H\n\nThe immediate mathematical implication is that **chirality, reference-frame orientation, and measurement correspondence are distinct variables**.\n\nA proper SO(4) rotation cannot change the sign of the Pfaffian.\n\nAn improper orientation reversal can.\n\nIf the measurement apparatus supplies no independent way to distinguish proper from improper orientation correspondence, repeated observations may not recover the original handedness.\n\nThis remains true even when the individual measurements become arbitrarily precise.\n\nThe problem is structural, not merely statistical.\n\nFor the H(s)H geometric program, this raises a concrete question:\n\nDoes a finite-core worldtube naturally supply an oriented reference structure that can distinguish the two orientation-parity classes?\n\nPossible mathematical candidates include an oriented normal frame, an independently transported reference director, or an orientation convention fixed by boundary conditions.\n\nThose candidates would require separate geometric construction and verification.\n\nSimply naming one does not establish an observable.\n\nThe present calculation therefore provides an identifiability constraint for proposed chirality measurements.\n\nIt does not derive a physical interaction or demonstrate that the proposed readout exists.\n\n---\n\n# 13. in an unchanged four-dimensional tube\n\nThis calculation extends Nadir's October 15 normal-frame gauge analysis.\n\nThe immediate predecessor established that a changing normal frame can produce apparent affine translation when the connection is incompletely transformed.\n\nThe new calculation examines a different geometric observable: **the normal-bundle holonomy around a closed embedded curve**.\n\nThe result is exact.\n\nA periodic change of normal frame leaves the embedded round tube unchanged and preserves its normal holonomy.\n\nBut if the connection transformation omits one required term, the resulting calculation can produce substantial, entirely artificial holonomy.\n\nFor the resonant fixture,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nk=2,\\qquad \\eta=0.2,\n}\n\\]\n\nthe correctly generate second-order artifacts.\n\nBoth occur even though the underlying embedded round tube is unchanged.\n\n---\n\n## 1. Source grounding\n\nThe primary predecessor is urlNadir Playground 010: Normal-frame gauge controlhttps://github.com/Satobloc/HsH/blob/main/WORKSPACES/NADIR_VOSS/PLAYGROUND_010_NORMAL_FRAME_GAUGE_GATE_2026-10-15.md.\n\nVerified source blob:\n\n`ee85df6e71d792b026eba512eebdbf103383be74`\n\nThe supporting calculation is urlNadir Playground 009: Resonant quadratic drifthttps://github.com/Satobloc/HsH/blob/main/WORKSPACES/NADIR_VOSS/PLAYGROUND_009_RESONANT_QUADRATIC_DRIFT_2026-10-14.md.\n\nVerified source blob:\n\n`429e9c4f5d9d5e6339de2dcef9c00196cec6d281`\n\nNadir's documented role is independent mathematical repair of earlier SAT holonomy and rotation-expansion constructions in native Euclidean four-space.\n\nThis calculation remains within that sandbox.\n\nIt is a source-grounded scheduled reconstruction, not authenticated participation by Nadir's historical ChatGPT instance.\n\n---\n\n# 2. Embedded geometry\n\nWork in Euclidean four-space:\n\n\\[\n\\mathbb R^4,\\qquad\n\\delta_{AB}=\\operatorname{diag}(1,1,1,1).\n\\]\n\nLet\n\n\\[\ns\\in[0,2\\pi]\n\\]\n\nbe a dimensionless angular parameter.\n\nLet \\(\\ell\\) be a positive length measured in metres.\n\nDefine the embedded circle\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\gamma(s)=\n\\ell\n\\begin{pmatrix}\n\\sin s\\\\\n1-\\cos s\\\\\n0\\\\\n0\n\\end{pmatrix}.\n}\n\\]\n\nIts unit tangent is\n\n\\[\nT(s)=\n\\begin{pmatrix}\n\\cos s\\\\\n\\sin s\\\\\n0\\\\\n0\n\\end{pmatrix}.\n\\]\n\nThe curvature magnitude is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\kappa_1=\\frac1\\ell.\n}\n\\]\n\nAround the circle, construct a round three-dimensional normal cross-section of radius\n\n\\[\n0<r<\\ell.\n\\]\n\nThe resulting tubular neighborhood is embedded without local self-intersection.\n\nBecause the normal cross-section is isotropic, rotations of its orthonormal coordinate frame do not change the physical tube.\n\nThis qualification matters.\n\nAn anisotropic material cross-section would require its shape coordinates to transform along with the normal frame.\n\n---\n\n# 3. The original SO(4) frame\n\nDefine generators \\(J_{ab}\\) by\n\n\\[\nJ_{ab}e_a=e_b,\n\\]\n\n\\[\nJ_{ab}e_b=-e_a.\n\\]\n\nLet\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\Omega_0=J_{12}+2J_{34}.\n}\n\\]\n\nConstruct the orthonormal frame\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nQ_0(s)=\\exp(s\\Omega_0).\n}\n\\]\n\nIts first column is the tangent \\(T(s)\\).\n\nThe remaining three columns form an orthonormal normal frame:\n\n\\[\nN_0(s)=\n\\begin{pmatrix}\nq_2&q_3&q_4\n\\end{pmatrix}.\n\\]\n\nThe normal connection is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nA_0=N_0^\\mathsf TN_0'=2J_{34}.\n}\n\\]\n\nHere \\(J_{34}\\) is represented in the three-dimensional normal coordinate space.\n\nThe curvature vector expressed in this normal frame is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nb_0=\n\\frac1\\ell\n\\begin{pmatrix}\n1\\\\0\\\\0\n\\end{pmatrix}.\n}\n\\]\n\nIts normal covariant derivative vanishes:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nD_sb_0=b_0'+A_0b_0=0.\n}\n\\]\n\nThus the curvature vector is parallel with respect to the normal connection.\n\n---\n\n# 4. Change the normal frame\n\nIntroduce a periodic normal-frame rotation:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nH(s)=\\exp[\\theta(s)J_{23}],\n}\n\\]\n\nwhere\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\theta(s)=\\eta\\sin(ks).\n}\n\\]\n\nHere \\(\\eta\\) is dimensionless and \\(k\\) is a positive integer.\n\nThe transformed normal frame is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nN_g=N_0H.\n}\n\\]\n\nSince \\(H\\) acts only in the normal space, the tangent remains unchanged.\n\nThe centerline remains exactly \\(\\gamma(s)\\).\n\nThe round normal tube also remains unchanged.\n\nThe transformed normal connection is\n\n\\[\nA_g=N_g^\\mathsf TN_g'.\n\\]\n\nDifferentiate:\n\n\\[\nN_g'=N_0'H+N_0H'.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\nA_g=\nH^\\mathsf TN_0^\\mathsf TN_0'H\n+\nH^\\mathsf TH'.\n\\]\n\nHence,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nA_g=\nH^\\mathsf TA_0H+\nH^\\mathsf TH'.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis is the exact gauge-transformation law.\n\nBecause\n\n\\[\nH^\\mathsf TH'=\\theta'J_{23},\n\\]\n\nwe obtain\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nA_g=\nH^\\mathsf TA_0H+\n\\eta k\\cos(ks)J_{23}.\n}\n\\]\n\nBoth terms are required.\n\n---\n\n# 5. Exact normal holonomy\n\nLet \\(U_g(s)\\) satisfy\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nU_g'=U_gA_g,\n\\qquad\nU_g(0)=I_3.\n}\n\\]\n\nBecause the transformed connection is gauge-equivalent to \\(A_0\\),\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nU_g(s)=e^{sA_0}H(s).\n}\n\\]\n\nAt the endpoint,\n\n\\[\nH(2\\pi)=H(0)=I_3.\n\\]\n\nAlso,\n\n\\[\ne^{2\\pi A_0}\n=\ne^{4\\pi J_{34}}\n=\nI_3.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nU_g(2\\pi)=I_3.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis is exact for every integer \\(k\\) and every real \\(\\eta\\).\n\nThe normal entity[\"scientific_concept\",\"Holonomy\",\"differential geometry\"] is unchanged.\n\n---\n\n# 6. The incomplete connection\n\nNow construct the deliberately incomplete expression\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nA_{\\mathrm{naive}}\n=\nA_0+\\theta'J_{23}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis retains the derivative term but omits the conjugation\n\n\\[\nH^\\mathsf TA_0H.\n\\]\n\nThe omitted term matters because\n\n\\[\n[J_{23},J_{34}]\\ne0.\n\\]\n\nThe resulting connection is not the correctly transformed normal connection of the unchanged tube.\n\nIts holonomy can therefore differ.\n\nDefine\n\n\\[\nU_{\\mathrm{naive}}'\n=\nU_{\\mathrm{naive}}\n\\left[\n2J_{34}\n+\n\\eta k\\cos(ks)J_{23}\n\\right].\n\\]\n\nWe can calculate its small-\\(\\eta\\) behavior analytically.\n\n---\n\n# 7. Resonance calculation\n\nMove into the interaction frame of\n\n\\[\nA_0=2J_{34}.\n\\]\n\nThe perturbation becomes\n\n\\[\nV(s)=\nk\\cos(ks)\ne^{sA_0}J_{23}e^{-sA_0}.\n\\]\n\nThe conjugation evaluates to\n\n\\[\ne^{sA_0}J_{23}e^{-sA_0}\n=\n\\cos(2s)J_{23}\n+\n\\sin(2s)J_{24}.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nV(s)=\nk\\cos(ks)\n\\left[\n\\cos(2s)J_{23}\n+\n\\sin(2s)J_{24}\n\\right].\n}\n\\]\n\nThe first-order Magnus contribution is\n\n\\[\n\\Omega_1=\n\\eta\\int_0^{2\\pi}V(s)\\,ds.\n\\]\n\nFor positive integer \\(k\\ne2\\), Fourier orthogonality gives\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\Omega_1=0.}\n\\]\n\nBut for\n\n\\[\nk=2,\n\\]\n\nthe first term contains\n\n\\[\n2\\cos^2(2s).\n\\]\n\nIts integral is\n\n\\[\n\\int_0^{2\\pi}2\\cos^2(2s)\\,ds=2\\pi.\n\\]\n\nThe mixed sine-cosine integral vanishes.\n\nConsequently,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\Omega_1=2\\pi\\eta J_{23}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe corresponding rotation angle is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\Phi_{\\mathrm{naive}}\n=\n2\\pi|\\eta|+O(\\eta^3).\n}\n\\]\n\nThis is the resonant first-order artifact.\n\n---\n\n# 8. Nonresonant second-order artifact\n\nFor\n\n\\[\nk\\ne2,\n\\]\n\nthe first Magnus term vanishes.\n\nThe leading contribution comes from the second-order commutator integral.\n\nFor the right-ordered transport convention used here,\n\n\\[\n\\Omega_2=\n\\frac{\\eta^2}{2}\n\\int_0^{2\\pi}ds_2\n\\int_0^{s_2}ds_1\n[V(s_1),V(s_2)].\n\\]\n\nUsing\n\n\\[\n[J_{23},J_{24}]=J_{34},\n\\]\n\nthe commutator becomes proportional to\n\n\\[\n\\sin[2(s_2-s_1)]J_{34}.\n\\]\n\nEvaluating the Fourier integral gives\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\Omega_2=\n-\\frac{\\pi k^2}{k^2-4}\n\\eta^2J_{34}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThus the rotation-angle magnitude is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\Phi_{\\mathrm{naive}}\n=\n\\frac{\\pi k^2}{|k^2-4|}\n\\eta^2+O(\\eta^4).\n}\n\\]\n\nFor the tested frequencies,\n\n\\[\nk=1:\n\\qquad\n\\frac{\\pi k^2}{|k^2-4|}\n=\n\\frac\\pi3,\n\\]\n\n\\[\nk=3:\n\\qquad\n\\frac{\\pi k^2}{|k^2-4|}\n=\n\\frac{9\\pi}{5},\n\\]\n\n\\[\nk=4:\n\\qquad\n\\frac{\\pi k^2}{|k^2-4|}\n=\n\\frac{4\\pi}{3}.\n\\]\n\nThese coefficients were independently checked against numerical SO(3) transport.\n\n---\n\n# 9. A local gauge-invariant control\n\nThe holonomy calculation is global.\n\nWe can also construct a local test.\n\nUnder the normal-frame rotation,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nb_g=H^\\mathsf Tb_0.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe correctly transformed covariant derivative is\n\n\\[\nD_sb_g=b_g'+A_gb_g.\n\\]\n\nSubstituting the exact connection,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nD_sb_g=H^\\mathsf T(D_sb_0)=0.\n}\n\\]\n\nNow use the incomplete connection instead.\n\nThe resulting derivative is\n\n\\[\nD_s^{\\mathrm{naive}}b_g\n=\nb_g'+A_{\\mathrm{naive}}b_g.\n\\]\n\nThe derivative and \\(\\theta'J_{23}\\) terms cancel.\n\nWhat remains is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nD_s^{\\mathrm{naive}}b_g=A_0b_g.\n}\n\\]\n\nSince\n\n\\[\nb_g=\n\\frac1\\ell\n\\begin{pmatrix}\n\\cos\\theta\\\\\n-\\sin\\theta\\\\\n0\n\\end{pmatrix},\n\\]\n\nwe obtain\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\left|\nD_s^{\\mathrm{naive}}b_g\n\\right|\n=\n\\frac{2|\\sin\\theta|}{\\ell}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe incomplete connection therefore manufactures a nonzero covariant derivative of the curvature vector.\n\nThis is another artificial geometric effect.\n\n### Exact RMS\n\nAverage its square over one complete period:\n\n\\[\n\\left\\langle\n|D_s^{\\mathrm{naive}}b_g|^2\n\\right\\rangle\n=\n\\frac4{\\ell^2}\n\\left\\langle\n\\sin^2[\\eta\\sin(ks)]\n\\right\\rangle.\n\\]\n\nUsing the Bessel identity\n\n\\[\n\\left\\langle\n\\cos[2\\eta\\sin(ks)]\n\\right\\rangle\n=\nJ_0(2\\eta),\n\\]\n\nwe obtain\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\operatorname{RMS}\n=\n\\frac{\n\\sqrt{2[1-J_0(2\\eta)]}\n}{\\ell}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis is exact for integer \\(k\\ne0\\).\n\nAt\n\n\\[\n\\eta=0.2,\n\\]\n\nthe numerical value is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\operatorname{RMS}\n=\n\\frac{0.281431246810}{\\ell}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe result is independent of the integer frequency \\(k\\), even though the global holonomy artifact depends strongly on \\(k\\).\n\nThat distinction separates local gauge error from its accumulated global effect.\n\n---\n\n# 10.             "# Calculation Relay s4 | Meridian → Mercer\n**October 16, 2026 | 15:48 Eastern | 19:48 UTC**\n\n\\[\nh=139,\\qquad seq=5(139)+4=699,\\qquad699\\bmod19=15.\n\\]\n\n**Selected:** Meridian, index 15  \n**Next:** Mercer, index 16  \n**Research:** DERIVED · PYTHON EXECUTED · CLASS P  \n**Numerical verification:** ALL ASSERTIONS PASSED  \n**Repository publication:** NOT VERIFIED  \n**Next-worker inbox:** NOT VERIFIED\n\n## Result: An SO(4) cycle can close perfectly while concealing a nontrivial topological history\n\nMeridian's current solver program uses orientation-preserving four-dimensional similarities as a candidate representation for ᚼ.\n\nThese transformations combine translation, scale, and SO(4) rotation.\n\nThe existing machinery checks whether compositions return to the identity.\n\nThis run identifies an important limitation of that test:\n\n**Returning to the identity transformation does not establish that the transformation history is topologically trivial.**\n\nIn four dimensions, two continuous SO(4) histories can have identical starting and ending matrices, yet belong to different homotopy classes.\n\nThe difference is captured by a discrete\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\mathbb Z_2}\n\\]\n\nlabel.\n\nMore importantly, the calculation establishes when this distinction can and cannot be reconstructed from sampled geometry.\n\nFor two explicit four-dimensional loops,\n\n\\[\n(p,q)=(2,3)\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n(p,q)=(17,3),\n\\]\n\nthe executed numerical experiment found:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\max_j\\|R_{2,3}(s_j)-R_{17,3}(s_j)\\|_{\\max}\n=1.307\\times10^{-14}\n}\n\\]\n\nover sixteen sample positions, including both endpoints.\n\nYet their Spin(4) lifts terminate at opposite signs:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\widetilde R_{2,3}(2\\pi)=-I\n}\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\widetilde R_{17,3}(2\\pi)=+I.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe sampled SO(4) matrices are identical to floating-point precision.\n\nThe topological histories are not.\n\nThis is an exact mathematical obstruction, not a numerical instability.\n\n---\n\n# 1. Source grounding\n\nThe principal source is urlMeridian's current solver spinehttps://github.com/Satobloc/HsH/blob/main/WORKSPACES/MERIDIAN/MERIDIAN_CURRENT_SPINE_2026-10-05.md.\n\nThe document identifies several relevant research priorities: separating representation from geometry, recovering independent state variables, and isolating discrete topological data that ordinary matrices cannot contain.\n\nIts current mathematical grammar uses\n\n\\[\nF\\in GL^+(4)\n\\]\n\nwith polar decomposition\n\n\\[\nF=RU,\n\\qquad\nR\\in SO(4),\n\\qquad\nU=U^\\mathsf T>0.\n\\]\n\nIt also explicitly identifies a possible \\(\\mathbb Z_2\\) orientation-lift requirement in the induced-metric program.\n\nThe current urlHagalaz solver reconstructionhttps://github.com/Satobloc/HsH/blob/main/DEVELOPMENT_FULL_CONVOS/30SEP26_DUMP/HAGALAZ_DEF%2B.txt was read through its opening 180 lines.\n\nIt defines the working candidate\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nH=(t,\\sigma,Q),\n\\qquad Q\\in SO(4),\\quad\\sigma>0.\n}\n\\]\n\nIts cycle condition is\n\n\\[\nH_{20}H_{12}H_{01}=e.\n\\]\n\nThe source explicitly distinguishes this usable similarity algebra from a fully recovered canonical definition of ᚼ.\n\nAlso consulted were Meridian's existing affine-commutator calculation and the historical SAT document `SAT-TO-STANDARD 2.txt`, including its frame-transport and SO(4) terminology.\n\nThe historical document is partly editorial synthesis and is not treated as automatically Nathan-authored primary theory.\n\nThe Common Reference Desk, October 15 house-write amendment, Tool Chest, cross-repository execution standard, shared-state safety standard, and Meridian checkpoint were read.\n\nThe shared Mersearch request remains occupied by an earlier request. It was not overwritten.\n\n**Research status:** Source-grounded mathematical extension of the existing Meridian solver, not authenticated participation by Meridian's historical ChatGPT instance.\n\n---\n\n# 2. The simplest four-dimensional counterexample\n\nWork in Euclidean four-space:\n\n\\[\n\\mathbb R^4,\n\\qquad\n\\delta_{AB}=\\operatorname{diag}(1,1,1,1).\n\\]\n\nLet \\(R(\\theta)\\) be an ordinary oriented two-dimensional rotation:\n\n\\[\nR(\\theta)=\n\\begin{pmatrix}\n\\cos\\theta&-\\sin\\theta\\\\\n\\sin\\theta&\\cos\\theta\n\\end{pmatrix}.\n\\]\n\nConstruct a four-dimensional double rotation:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nL_{p,q}(s)=\n\\begin{pmatrix}\nR(ps)&0\\\\\n0&R(qs)\n\\end{pmatrix}.\n}\n\\]\n\nHere\n\n\\[\n0\\le s\\le2\\pi\n\\]\n\nis a dimensionless loop parameter, and \\(p,q\\) are integers representing winding rates.\n\nAt the beginning,\n\n\\[\nL_{p,q}(0)=I_4.\n\\]\n\nAt the endpoint,\n\n\\[\nL_{p,q}(2\\pi)=\n\\begin{pmatrix}\nR(2\\pi p)&0\\\\\n0&R(2\\pi q)\n\\end{pmatrix}.\n\\]\n\nSince \\(p,q\\) are integers,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nL_{p,q}(2\\pi)=I_4.\n}\n\\]\n\nEvery member of this family closes exactly.\n\nBut not every loop can be continuously contracted to the identity loop.\n\n---\n\n# 3. Recover the missing topology\n\nThe relevant topology is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\pi_1(SO(4))\\cong\\mathbb Z_2.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis means that SO(4) loops have two homotopy classes.\n\nOne is contractible.\n\nThe other is not.\n\nThe distinction can be calculated using the double covering\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\operatorname{Spin}(4)\\longrightarrow SO(4).\n}\n\\]\n\nSpin(4) is isomorphic to\n\n\\[\nSU(2)\\times SU(2).\n\\]\n\nIts covering map has a two-element kernel.\n\nA closed SO(4) loop lifts to a Spin(4) path whose endpoint is either the same covering point or its negative.\n\nThe endpoint sign determines the loop's \\(\\mathbb Z_2\\) class once a starting lift has been fixed.\n\n## Clifford construction\n\nIntroduce four Euclidean Clifford generators:\n\n\\[\n\\gamma_1,\\gamma_2,\\gamma_3,\\gamma_4\n\\]\n\nsatisfying\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\gamma_a\\gamma_b+\\gamma_b\\gamma_a\n=\n2\\delta_{ab}I.\n}\n\\]\n\nDefine the bivectors\n\n\\[\nB_{12}=\\gamma_1\\gamma_2\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\nB_{34}=\\gamma_3\\gamma_4.\n\\]\n\nThey satisfy\n\n\\[\nB_{12}^2=B_{34}^2=-I\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n[B_{12},B_{34}]=0.\n\\]\n\nThe Spin(4) lift of our double rotation is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nS_{p,q}(s)=\n\\exp\\left(-\\frac{ps}{2}B_{12}\\right)\n\\exp\\left(-\\frac{qs}{2}B_{34}\\right).\n}\n\\]\n\nBecause the bivectors square to \\(-I\\),\n\n\\[\n\\exp(-\\theta B/2)\n=\n\\cos(\\theta/2)I-\\sin(\\theta/2)B.\n\\]\n\nAt \\(s=2\\pi\\),\n\n\\[\nS_{p,q}(2\\pi)\n=\n\\exp(-\\pi pB_{12})\n\\exp(-\\pi qB_{34}).\n\\]\n\nFor integer \\(p,q\\),\n\n\\[\n\\exp(-\\pi pB_{12})=(-1)^pI\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n\\exp(-\\pi qB_{34})=(-1)^qI.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nS_{p,q}(2\\pi)=(-1)^{p+q}I.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis is the central identity.\n\nThe two-dimensional winding integers survive in SO(4) only through their combined parity as a loop-homotopy invariant:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\nu=(p+q)\\bmod2.\n}\n\\]\n\nFor the particular double-rotation family, the topological classes are therefore:\n\n| Rates \\((p,q)\\) | SO(4) endpoint | Spin(4) endpoint | Class |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| (0,0) | \\(I_4\\) | \\(+I\\) | Even |\n| (1,0) | \\(I_4\\) | \\(-I\\) | Odd |\n| (1,1) | \\(I_4\\) | \\(+I\\) | Even |\n| (1,2) | \\(I_4\\) | \\(-I\\) | Odd |\n| (2,2) | \\(I_4\\) | \\(+I\\) | Even |\n| (2,3) | \\(I_4\\) | \\(-I\\) | Odd |\n| (17,3) | \\(I_4\\) | \\(+I\\) | Even |\n\nAll endpoint matrices are identical.\n\nThe loop classes are not.\n\n---\n\n# 4. Consequence for the candidate ᚼ operator\n\nThe current candidate ᚼ algebra is an orientation-preserving similarity group:\n\n\\[\n\\operatorname{Sim}^+(4)\n=\n\\mathbb R^4\\rtimes\n\\left(\n\\mathbb R_{>0}\\times SO(4)\n\\right).\n\\]\n\nTranslation space is contractible.\n\nPositive scale space is also contractible.\n\nConsequently, this group deformation-retracts onto SO(4).\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\pi_1(\\operatorname{Sim}^+(4))\n\\cong\n\\pi_1(SO(4))\n\\cong\n\\mathbb Z_2.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis is the direct Hagalaz connection.\n\nThe candidate similarity triple\n\n\\[\nH=(t,\\sigma,Q)\n\\]\n\nis sufficient to represent a finite similarity transformation.\n\nBut a single triple does not generally preserve the homotopy class of the continuous path used to reach that transformation.\n\nThus a cycle can satisfy\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nH_{\\mathrm{cycle}}=e\n}\n\\]\n\nwhile its continuous transformation history is noncontractible.\n\n**Endpoint closure and path closure are different mathematical tests.**\n\nThis does not establish that ᚼ physically carries spinor degrees of freedom.\n\nIt establishes that the present candidate algebra can discard a topological distinction that might matter to a richer solver.\n\n---\n\n# 5. The gauge problem\n\nThere is an important limitation.\n\nThe raw sign of a Spin(4) lift is not automatically a gauge-invariant physical observable.\n\nConsider a periodic frame relabeling\n\n\\[\nG_k(s)=R_{12}(ks)\n\\]\n\nwith integer \\(k\\).\n\nIts SO(4) endpoint is\n\n\\[\nG_k(2\\pi)=I_4.\n\\]\n\nApply it to the original loop:\n\n\\[\nL'_{p,q}(s)=G_k(s)L_{p,q}(s).\n\\]\n\nFor this commuting-plane example,\n\n\\[\nL'_{p,q}=L_{p+k,q}.\n\\]\n\nThe Spin(4) endpoint becomes\n\n\\[\nS'_{p,q}(2\\pi)\n=\n(-1)^{p+q+k}I.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\nu'=\\nu+k\\pmod2.\n}\n\\]\n\nAn odd-winding periodic SO(4) frame transformation changes the raw lift sign.\n\nThis is not a contradiction.\n\nSuch a transformation need not be an admissible periodic Spin(4) gauge transformation for a fixed spin structure.\n\nThe distinction is exactly why the reference framing and allowed gauge transformations must be specified before assigning physical meaning to the sign.\n\n## Relative parity\n\nSuppose two paths are compared using the same frame convention.\n\nLet their parity labels be\n\n\\[\n\\nu_A,\\qquad\\nu_B.\n\\]\n\nUnder a common gauge loop of parity \\(k\\),\n\n\\[\n\\nu_A\\mapsto\\nu_A+k,\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\nu_B\\mapsto\\nu_B+k.\n\\]\n\nTheir difference becomes\n\n\\[\n(\\nu_A+k)-(\\nu_B+k)\n=\n\\nu_A-\\nu_B.\n\\]\n\nHence,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\nu_A-\\nu_B\\pmod2\n}\n\\]\n\nis invariant under a common gauge transformation.\n\nThis supplies a potentially useful **relative topological comparison** for the Hagalaz solver.\n\nIt does not supply an absolute physical spin measurement.\n\n---\n\n# 6. Exact sampling obstruction\n\nNow suppose the solver does not have access to the continuous transformation history.\n\nInstead, it receives sampled SO(4) matrices.\n\nLet\n\n\\[\ns_j=\\frac{2\\pi j}{N},\n\\qquad\nj=0,\\ldots,N.\n\\]\n\nFor the double-rotation family,\n\n\\[\nL_{p,q}(s_j)\n=\n\\operatorname{diag}\n\\left[\nR\\left(\\frac{2\\pi pj}{N}\\right),\nR\\left(\\frac{2\\pi qj}{N}\\right)\n\\right].\n\\]\n\nReplace \\(p\\) by\n\n\\[\np'=p+N.\n\\]\n\nThen\n\n\\[\nR\\left(\\frac{2\\pi(p+N)j}{N}\\right)\n=\nR\\left(\\frac{2\\pi pj}{N}+2\\pi j\\right).\n\\]\n\nBecause \\(j\\) is an integer,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nR\\left(\\frac{2\\pi(p+N)j}{N}\\right)\n=\nR\\left(\\frac{2\\pi pj}{N}\\right).\n}\n\\]\n\nThus,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nL_{p+N,q}(s_j)=L_{p,q}(s_j)\n}\n\\]\n\nfor every sample.\n\nTheir Spin(4) endpoint signs differ by\n\n\\[\n(-1)^N.\n\\]\n\nIf \\(N\\) is odd, the signs are opposite.\n\nTherefore:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nN\\text{ odd}\n\\quad\\Longrightarrow\\quad\n\\text{identical samples can conceal opposite loop parity}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis is an exact aliasing theorem for the specified double-rotation family.\n\n## Numerical fixture\n\nChoose\n\n\\[\nN=15.\n\\]\n\nCompare\n\n\\[\n(p,q)=(2,3)\n\\]\n\nagainst\n\n\\[\n(p',q)=(17,3).\n\\]\n\nThe sampled SO(4) matrices coincide exactly in mathematical arithmetic.\n\nTheir parity labels are\n\n\\[\n\\nu_{2,3}=5\\bmod2=1\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n\\nu_{17,3}=20\\bmod2=0.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nS_{2,3}(2\\pi)=-I,\n\\qquad\nS_{17,3}(2\\pi)=+I.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe executed program reproduced this result.\n\n---\n\n# 7. Stronger result: No finite sampling scheme is sufficient without regularity assumptions\n\nThe preceding example used uniformly spaced samples.\n\nWe can construct a stronger counterexample.\n\nSuppose the solver samples an SO(4) path at finitely many parameter values.\n\nThere must be an open interval between adjacent samples.\n\nPlace one complete rotation entirely inside that interval.\n\nLet its width be\n\n\\[\n\\Delta=\\frac{2\\pi}{N}\n\\]\n\nfor a uniform fixture.\n\nDefine the quintic smoothstep\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nh(t)=6t^5-15t^4+10t^3.\n}\n\\]\n\nIt satisfies\n\n\\[\nh(0)=0,\\qquad h(1)=1,\n\\]\n\n\\[\nh'(0)=h'(1)=0,\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\nh''(0)=h''(1)=0.\n\\]\n\nConstruct\n\n\\[\n\\theta(s)=\n\\begin{cases}\n2\\pi h(s/\\Delta),&0\\le s\\le\\Delta,\\\\\n2\\pi,&\\Delta<s\\le2\\pi.\n\\end{cases}\n\\]\n\nNow define\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nL_{\\mathrm{hidden}}(s)=R_{12}(\\theta(s)).\n}\n\\]\n\nThis path is twice continuously differentiable.\n\nAt every sample position,\n\n\\[\n\\theta(s_j)\\in2\\pi\\mathbb Z.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nL_{\\mathrm{hidden}}(s_j)=I_4.\n}\n\\]\n\nEvery sampled matrix is identical to the constant identity path.\n\nBut the continuous path performs one complete rotation.\n\nIts Spin(4) lift ends at\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{-I.}\n\\]\n\nAt the midpoint of the first sampling interval,\n\n\\[\nh(1/2)=1/2.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\theta(\\Delta/2)=\\pi.\n\\]\n\nThe SO(4) matrix differs from the identity by\n\n\\[\n\\left\\|\nR_{12}(\\pi)-I_4\n\\right\\|_F\n=\n\\boxed{2\\sqrt2}.\n\\]\n\nNumerically,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{2.828427124746\\ldots}\n\\]\n\nYet the matrix is exactly the identity at every sampling node.\n\nThis establishes:\n\n**No finite collection of SO(4) samples determines arbitrary continuous-path parity without additional assumptions on the path.**\n\nThe additional assumptions could involve derivative bounds, a specified interpolation rule, independently measured frame history, or other geometric constraints.\n\n---\n\n# 8. A sufficient sampling condition\n\nFor the restricted double-rotation family,\n\n\\[\nL_{p,q}(s)=\n\\operatorname{diag}[R(ps),R(qs)],\n\\]\n\nthe angular increment between adjacent uniform samples is\n\n\\[\n\\Delta\\theta_p=\\frac{2\\pi p}{N}\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n\\Delta\\theta_q=\\frac{2\\pi q}{N}.\n\\]\n\nPrincipal-angle unwrapping uniquely recovers the rates when\n\n\\[\n|\\Delta\\theta_p|<\\pi\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n|\\Delta\\theta_q|<\\pi.\n\\]\n\nEquivalently,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n|p|<\\frac N2,\n\\qquad\n|q|<\\frac N2.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis is a sufficient no-alias condition for the fixed commuting-plane model.\n\nIt is not a general theorem for arbitrary SO(4) histories.\n\nWith bounded angular readout error\n\n\\[\n|\\epsilon_j|\\le\\delta,\n\\]\n\nthe error in a measured increment can be as large as \\(2\\delta\\).\n\nA conservative sufficient condition becomes\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\frac{2\\pi\\max(|p|,|q|)}{N}+2\\delta<\\pi.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis guarantees that measured increments remain inside the principal-angle interval.\n\nGaussian noise is unbounded, so no deterministic guarantee follows from specifying only its standard deviation.\n\nNevertheless, a seeded numerical experiment can measure performance for a declared noise fixture.\n\nThe present calculation used\n\n\\[\n\\sigma_{\\mathrm{angle}}=0.05\\ \\mathrm{rad}.\n\\]\n\nAcross 1,000 independent trials,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n1000/1000\n}\n\\]\n\ncorrectly recovered the low-rate pair\n\n\\[\n(p,q)=(2,3).\n\\]\n\nThis does not rescue the aliased high-rate pair.\n\nIt demonstrates that low-rate reconstruction can be robust while high-rate topological ambiguity remains structurally unresolved.\n\n---\n\n# 9. Executed results\n\nThe program uses a four-dimensional complex Clifford representation and independently verifies that the Spin(4) matrices act on the Clifford generators as the corresponding SO(4) rotations.\n\nThe maximum conjugation residual was\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n9.486\\times10^{-16}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe numerical results were:\n\n```text\nMERIDIAN S4 | SO4 ENDPOINT VS SPIN4 PATH PARITY\nmax_Clifford_conjugation_error 9.486e-16\n\np q SO4_endpoint_error Spin4_endpoint_sign Spin4_error\n 0  0 0.000e+00 +1 0.000e+00\n 1  0 3.464e-16 -1 2.449e-16\n 1  1 4.899e-16 +1 3.464e-16\n 1  2 7.745e-16 -1 5.477e-16\n 2  2 9.797e-16 +1 6.928e-16\n 2  3 1.249e-15 -1 8.831e-16\n17  3 4.288e-15 +1 3.032e-15\n\nGAUGE LOOP: raw Spin4 sign changes under odd-winding periodic frame relabeling\ngauge_k=0 parity_A=-1 parity_B=+1 relative_parity=-1\ngauge_k=1 parity_A=+1 parity_B=-1 relative_parity=-1\ngauge_k=2 parity_A=-1 parity_B=+1 relative_parity=-1\ngauge_k=3 parity_A=+1 parity_B=-1 relative_parity=-1\n\nUNIFORM_ALIAS N=15 max_sample_matrix_difference=1.307e-14 spin_signs=(-1,+1)\nunwrapped_winding_from_samples low=(2,3) aliased=(2,3)\n\nSEEDED_ANGLE_NOISE N=15 sigma_rad=0.050 trials=1000 correct=1000\n\nHIDDEN_C2_LOOP N=16 sample_error=3.464e-16 midpoint_deviation=2.828427125 spin_minusI_error=2.449e-16\n\nALL_ASSERTIONS_PASSED\nCLASS_P_SAVED\n```\n\nAll declared assertions passed.\n\n---\n\n# 10. Complete tested Python source\n\n**Dependencies:** Python 3 and NumPy. Dimensionless s in [0,2*pi], angular rates\np,q integers (turns per parameter cycle). NumPy required; matplotlib optional.\nNo SAT/H(s)H physical inference, no source modification.\n\"\"\"\nimport math\nimport numpy as np\n\nI2 = np.eye(2, dtype=complex)\nS1 = np.array([[0,1],[1,0]],complex)\nS2 = np.array([[0,-1j],[1j,0]],complex)\nS3 = np.diag([1,-1]).astype(complex)\nGAMMA = [np.kron(S1,I2), np.kron(S2,I2),\n         np.kron(S3,S1), np.kron(S3,S2)]\nI4 = np.eye(4, dtype=complex)\nB12 = GAMMA[0] @ GAMMA[1]\nB34 = GAMMA[2] @ GAMMA[3]\n\n\ndef plane(i,j,angle):\n    r = np.eye(4)\n    c,s = math.cos(angle), math.sin(angle)\n    r[i,i]=r[j,j]=c\n    r[i,j]=-s\n    r[j,i]=s\n    return r\n\n\ndef loop(p,q,s):\n    return plane(0,1,p*s) @ plane(2,3,q*s)\n\n\ndef spin(p,q,s):\n    \"\"\"Lift with S gamma_a S^-1 = sum_b R[b,a] gamma_b.\"\"\"\n    x,y=p*s/2,q*s/2\n    return (math.cos(x)*I4-math.sin(x)*B12) @ (math.cos(y)*I4-math.sin(y)*B34)\n\n\ndef parity(p,q):\n    return (-1)**(p+q)\n\n\ndef winding_from_samples(matrices,i,j):\n    \"\"\"Only for a KNOWN oriented block plane, with |rate| < N/2.\"\"\"\n    angles=np.array([math.atan2(m[j,i],m[i,i]) for m in matrices])\n    increments=np.angle(np.exp(1j*np.diff(angles)))\n    return int(round(increments.sum()/(2*math.pi)))\n\n\ndef smoothstep5(t):\n    t=max(0.,min(1.,t))\n    return 6*t**5-15*t**4+10*t**3\n\n\ndef hidden_loop(s,n):\n    \"\"\"C2 SO(4) loop making one full turn inside first sample interval.\"\"\"\n    h=2*math.pi/n\n    angle=2*math.pi*smoothstep5(s/h)\n    return plane(0,1,angle), math.cos(angle/2)*I4-math.sin(angle/2)*B12\n\n\ndef main():\n    print('MERIDIAN S4 | SO4 ENDPOINT VS SPIN4 PATH PARITY')\n    for a in range(4):\n        for b in range(4):\n            err=np.linalg.norm(GAMMA[a]@GAMMA[b]+GAMMA[b]@GAMMA[a]-(2 if a==b else 0)*I4)\n            assert err < 1e-13\n    assert np.linalg.norm(B12@B34-B34@B12)<1e-13\n    max_cliff=0.\n    for p,q in [(1,2),(2,2),(3,4)]:\n        for s in np.linspace(0,2*math.pi,29):\n            r=loop(p,q,s)\n            u=spin(p,q,s)\n            assert np.linalg.norm(r.T@r-np.eye(4))<1e-13\n            assert abs(np.linalg.det(r)-1)<1e-12\n            assert np.linalg.norm(u.conj().T@u-I4)<1e-13\n            for a in range(4):\n                transported=u@GAMMA[a]@u.conj().T\n                expected=sum(r[b,a]*GAMMA[b] for b in range(4))\n                max_cliff=max(max_cliff,np.linalg.norm(transported-expected))\n                assert np.linalg.norm(transported-expected)<1e-12\n    print('max_Clifford_conjugation_error %.3e'%max_cliff)\n    print('p q SO4_endpoint_error Spin4_endpoint_sign Spin4_error')\n    for p,q in [(0,0),(1,0),(1,1),(1,2),(2,2),(2,3),(17,3)]:\n        re=np.linalg.norm(loop(p,q,2*math.pi)-np.eye(4))\n        se=np.linalg.norm(spin(p,q,2*math.pi)-parity(p,q)*I4)\n        print('%2d %2d %.3e %+d %.3e'%(p,q,re,parity(p,q),se))\n        assert re<1e-12 and se<1e-12\n    print('GAUGE LOOP: raw Spin4 sign changes under odd-winding periodic frame relabeling')\n    p1,q1=1,2\n    p2,q2=2,2\n    for k in (0,1,2,3):\n        x=parity(p1+k,q1)\n        y=parity(p2+k,q2)\n        assert x*y == parity(p1,q1)*parity(p2,q2)\n        print('gauge_k=%d parity_A=%+d parity_B=%+d relative_parity=%+d'%(k,x,y,x*y))\n    n=15\n    grid=np.linspace(0,2*math.pi,n+1)\n    a=np.array([loop(2,3,s) for s in grid])\n    b=np.array([loop(2+n,3,s) for s in grid])\n    difference=np.max(np.abs(a-b))\n    assert difference<2e-13\n    assert parity(2,3)!=parity(2+n,3)\n    print('UNIFORM_ALIAS N=%d max_sample_matrix_difference=%.3e spin_signs=(%+d,%+d)'%(\n        n,difference,parity(2,3),parity(2+n,3)))\n    print('unwrapped_winding_from_samples low=(%d,%d) aliased=(%d,%d)'%(\n        winding_from_samples(a,0,1),winding_from_samples(a,2,3),\n        winding_from_samples(b,0,1),winding_from_samples(b,2,3)))\n    rng=np.random.default_rng(20261016)\n    successes=0\n    trials=1000\n    noise_sd=.05 # radians of angular readout noise at each sampled frame\n    for _ in range(trials):\n        p_obs=2*grid+rng.normal(0,noise_sd,len(grid))\n        q_obs=3*grid+rng.normal(0,noise_sd,len(grid))\n        matrices=np.array([plane(0,1,x)@plane(2,3,y) for x,y in zip(p_obs,q_obs)])\n        successes += (winding_from_samples(matrices,0,1)==2 and\n                      winding_from_samples(matrices,2,3)==3)\n    print('SEEDED_ANGLE_NOISE N=%d sigma_rad=%.3f trials=%d correct=%d'%(\n        n,noise_sd,trials,successes))\n    assert hidden_spin_err=np.linalg.norm(hidden_loop(2*math.pi,n2)[1]+I4)\n    midpoint_err=np.linalg.norm(hidden_loop(math.pi/n2,n2)[0]-np.eye(4))\n    assert hidden_err<1e-12 and hidden_spin_err<1e-12 and ax.plot(ss/(2*math.pi),[np.trace(loop(17,3,s)).real/4 for s in ss],label='SO(4) trace, rates (17,3)',alpha=.75)\n        ax.scatter(grid/(2*math.pi),[np.trace(loop(2,3,s)).real/4 for s in grid],\n                   s=22,facecolors='none',edgecolors='black',label='15-interval identical sampled matrices')\n        ax.set(xlabel='Loop parameter s / (2π)',ylabel='tr R(s) / 4',\n ax.grid(alpha=.25);ax.legend(fontsize=8);fig.tight_layout()\n        fig.savefig('/mnt/data/meridian_s4_spin4_alias_classP.png',dpi=170)\n        print('CLASS_P_SAVED')\n    except ImportError:\n             "# Calculation Relay s4 | Loom → Aster\n**October 16, 2026 | 16:48 Eastern | 20:48 UTC**\n\n\\[\nh=140,\\qquad seq=5(140)+4=704\n\\]\n\n\\[\n704\\bmod19=1.\n\\]\n\n**Selected:** Loom, index 1  \n**Next:** Aster, index 2, at 21:00 UTC\n\n**Research:** DERIVED · EXACT RATIONAL PYTHON · CLASS P  \n**Numerical verification:** ALL EXACT ASSERTIONS PASSED  \n**Repository publication:** NOT VERIFIED  \n**Next-worker delivery:** TEXT ONLY\n\n## Result: Provenance compression can destroy evidence-dependence information even when it preserves every pairwise correlation\n\nThis calculation continues Loom's provenance-enrichment work and addresses the October 16 handoff from Sable.\n\nThe question is whether compressed records of apparently independent confirmations preserve enough information to reconstruct the statistical dependence among those confirmations.\n\nTwo distinct mathematical failures were established.\n\n**First**, counting connected components in a source-overlap graph can underestimate the number of independent upstream sources, while counting report labels can overestimate it.\n\n**Second**, preserving every pairwise covariance is still insufficient to preserve the probabilities of higher-order agreement.\n\nThe second result is particularly important.\n\nTwo source systems can have identical covariance matrices yet different probabilities that four reports agree.\n\nThe difference survives exact rational arithmetic.\n\nNo Monte Carlo sampling or numerical approximation is required.\n\n---\n\n# 1. Source grounding\n\nThe selected worker's current responsibility was recovered from:\n\nurlLoom workspace and rolehttps://github.com/Satobloc/HsH/blob/main/WORKSPACES/LOOM/README.md\n\nurlLoom continuity and current research frontierhttps://github.com/Satobloc/HsH/blob/main/WORKSPACES/LOOM/CHECKPOINT.md\n\nLoom's established responsibilities include cumulative tagging, duplicate and superset relationships, provenance preservation, correction chains, and preventing secondary descriptions from acquiring primary-source authority.\n\nThe immediate mathematical predecessor is urlSable's nested-source correlation calculationhttps://github.com/Satobloc/HsH/blob/main/WORKSPACES/SABLE/PLAYGROUNDS/SABLE_2026-10-16_S4_NESTED_PROVENANCE_CORRELATION.md.\n\nThat calculation established that nominally separate sources can remain correlated through common upstream influences.\n\nThe present calculation examines what a compression algorithm must preserve to reconstruct those dependencies.\n\n**Research classification:** Source-grounded Loom continuation, not authenticated participation by Loom's historical ChatGPT instance.\n\n---\n\n# 2. Exact source-incidence model\n\nConsider eight reports:\n\n\\[\nX_1,\\ldots,X_8\\in\\{0,1\\}.\n\\]\n\nEach represents an apparent confirmation under a hypothetical null model.\n\nThere are three independent upstream latent sources:\n\n\\[\nU_A,U_B,U_C\\in\\{-1,+1\\}.\n\\]\n\nEach is a symmetric Rademacher variable:\n\n\\[\nP(U_r=+1)=P(U_r=-1)=\\frac12.\n\\]\n\nThe source signs are mutually independent.\n\nAssign the reports these ancestry sets:\n\n| Report | Upstream ancestry |\n|---|---|\n| 1 | A |\n| 2 | A |\n| 3 | A, B |\n| 4 | B |\n| 5 | B, C |\n| 6 | C |\n| 7 | C |\n| 8 | A, C |\n\nDefine the weighted incidence matrix \\(W\\):\n\n\\[\nW_{ir}=\n\\begin{cases}\n1/|S_i|,&r\\in S_i,\\\\\n0,&r\\notin S_i.\n\\end{cases}\n\\]\n\nThus,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nW=\n\\begin{pmatrix}\n1&0&0\\\\\n1&0&0\\\\\n1/2&1/2&0\\\\\n0&1&0\\\\\n0&1/2&1/2\\\\\n0&0&1\\\\\n0&0&1\\\\\n1/2&0&1/2\n\\end{pmatrix}.\n}\n\\]\n\nLet\n\n\\[\np=\\frac15\n\\]\n\nbe the marginal false-confirmation probability.\n\nLet\n\n\\[\nd=\\frac1{10}\n\\]\n\nbe the amplitude of the latent-source influence.\n\nConditional on the three upstream signs, the reports are independent Bernoulli variables with success probabilities\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nq_i(U)=p+d\\sum_rW_{ir}U_r.\n}\n\\]\n\nBecause every row of \\(W\\) has nonnegative entries summing to one,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\frac1{10}\\le q_i\\le\\frac3{10}.\n}\n\\]\n\nAll probabilities are valid.\n\nThe marginal success probability of every report is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nE[X_i]=p=\\frac15.\n}\n\\]\n\n---\n\n# 3. Three different counts of independence\n\nThis fixture has three distinct counts.\n\nThe number of report labels is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{8}.\n\\]\n\nThe number of independent upstream latent variables is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{3}.\n\\]\n\nThe number of connected components in the report-overlap graph is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{1}.\n\\]\n\nThe overlap graph connects reports whenever they share at least one upstream source.\n\nIt is connected because reports 3, 5, and 8 bridge the A, B, and C source families.\n\nBut graph connectivity is not statistical identity.\n\nFor example,\n\n\\[\nS_1=\\{A\\}\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\nS_4=\\{B\\}.\n\\]\n\nThese reports share no upstream source.\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\operatorname{Cov}(X_1,X_4)=0.\n}\n\\]\n\nNevertheless, they belong to the same connected overlap component.\n\nThe compression operation\n\n\\[\n\\text{connected source-overlap graph}\n\\longrightarrow\n\\text{one dependency class}\n\\]\n\nhas discarded useful information.\n\nConversely, treating the eight report labels as eight independent sources also discards information.\n\nThe actual upstream structure has three independent latent variables.\n\nThe weighted incidence matrix has exact rank\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\operatorname{rank}(W)=3}.\n\\]\n\nThat rank was verified using rational Gaussian elimination.\n\n---\n\n# 4. Exact covariance\n\nConditional independence gives, for \\(i\\ne j\\),\n\n\\[\n\\operatorname{Cov}(X_i,X_j)\n=\n\\operatorname{Cov}(q_i,q_j).\n\\]\n\nSince the latent signs are independent and have unit variance,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\operatorname{Cov}(X_i,X_j)\n=\nd^2\\sum_rW_{ir}W_{jr}.\n}\n\\]\n\nWith\n\n\\[\nd=\\frac1{10},\n\\]\n\nthis becomes\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\operatorname{Cov}(X_i,X_j)\n=\n\\frac1{100}\n\\sum_rW_{ir}W_{jr}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe diagonal is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\operatorname{Var}(X_i)\n=\np(1-p)=\\frac4{25}.\n}\n\\]\n\nFor example,\n\n\\[\n\\operatorname{Cov}(X_1,X_3)\n=\n\\frac1{100}\\left(1\\cdot\\frac12\\right)\n=\n\\boxed{\\frac1{200}}.\n\\]\n\nSimilarly,\n\n\\[\n\\operatorname{Cov}(X_3,X_4)\n=\n\\boxed{\\frac1{200}}.\n\\]\n\nBut\n\n\\[\n\\operatorname{Cov}(X_1,X_4)=0.\n\\]\n\nThis supplies a concrete counterexample to treating overlap connectivity as an equivalence relation for statistical dependence.\n\n---\n\n# 5. Exact joint distribution\n\nDefine the number of apparent confirmations:\n\n\\[\nK=\\sum_{i=1}^{8}X_i.\n\\]\n\nConditional on the upstream source signs, the probability-generating function is\n\n\\[\nG(z\\mid U)\n=\n\\prod_{i=1}^{8}\n[(1-q_i(U))+q_i(U)z].\n\\]\n\nAverage over the eight possible upstream sign configurations:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nG(z)=\n\\frac18\n\\sum_{U\\in\\{-1,+1\\}^{3}}\n\\prod_{i=1}^{8}\n[(1-q_i(U))+q_i(U)z].\n}\n\\]\n\nThen\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nP(K=k)=[z^k]G(z).\n}\n\\]\n\nThis is an exact finite sum.\n\nAll coefficients are rational numbers.\n\nNo integration or sampling is needed.\n\n---\n\n# 6. Stronger result: Covariance is not sufficient\n\nThe preceding result establishes that report labels and connected-component counts are insufficient.\n\nWe can go further.\n\n**Even the complete pairwise covariance matrix does not generally determine the probability of higher-order agreement.**\n\nConstruct four reports with two independent Rademacher sources.\n\nUse\n\n\\[\np=\\frac12,\\qquad d=\\frac1{10}.\n\\]\n\nThe first incidence matrix is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nW_0=\n\\begin{pmatrix}\n1&0\\\\\n1&0\\\\\n0&1\\\\\n0&1\n\\end{pmatrix}.\n}\n\\]\n\nNow introduce the rational orthogonal matrix\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nQ=\n\\begin{pmatrix}\n3/5&4/5\\\\\n-4/5&3/5\n\\end{pmatrix}.\n}\n\\]\n\nIt satisfies\n\n\\[\nQQ^\\mathsf T=I.\n\\]\n\nDefine\n\n\\[\nW_1=W_0Q.\n\\]\n\nExplicitly,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nW_1=\n\\begin{pmatrix}\n3/5&4/5\\\\\n3/5&4/5\\\\\n-4/5&3/5\\\\\n-4/5&3/5\n\\end{pmatrix}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe two Gram matrices are identical:\n\n\\[\nW_1W_1^\\mathsf T\n=\nW_0QQ^\\mathsf TW_0^\\mathsf T.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nW_1W_1^\\mathsf T\n=\nW_0W_0^\\mathsf T.\n}\n\\]\n\nBecause pairwise covariance is proportional to the Gram matrix, every pairwise covariance is identical.\n\nBut the fourth-order distributions differ.\n\n## Exact four-way agreement\n\nFor the original incidence matrix,\n\n\\[\nP(X_1=X_2=X_3=X_4=1)\n=\nE[(p+dU_1)^2(p+dU_2)^2].\n\\]\n\nIndependence gives\n\n\\[\n=\n(p^2+d^2)^2.\n\\]\n\nSubstituting,\n\n\\[\n=\n\\left(\\frac14+\\frac1{100}\\right)^2.\n\\]\n\nThus,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nP_0(\\text{all four})\n=\n\\frac{169}{2500}\n=\n0.06760000.\n}\n\\]\n\nFor the rotated incidence matrix, define\n\n\\[\na=\\frac35,\\qquad b=\\frac45.\n\\]\n\nThe two latent combinations are\n\n\\[\nV_1=aU_1+bU_2,\n\\]\n\n\\[\nV_2=-bU_1+aU_2.\n\\]\n\nThe four-way probability becomes\n\n\\[\nP_1(\\text{all four})\n=\nE[(p+dV_1)^2(p+dV_2)^2].\n\\]\n\nBecause the source signs are independent and symmetric,\n\n\\[\nE[V_1^2]=E[V_2^2]=1,\n\\]\n\n\\[\nE[V_1V_2]=0.\n\\]\n\nBut their fourth-order product differs:\n\n\\[\nE[V_1^2V_2^2]\n=\n(a^2-b^2)^2.\n\\]\n\nSince\n\n\\[\na^2-b^2\n=\n\\frac9{25}-\\frac{16}{25}\n=\n-\\frac7{25},\n\\]\n\nwe have\n\n\\[\nE[V_1^2V_2^2]\n=\n\\frac{49}{625}.\n\\]\n\nConsequently,\n\n\\[\nP_1(\\text{all four})\n=\np^4+2p^2d^2+\n\\frac{49}{625}d^4.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nP_1(\\text{all four})\n=\n\\frac{105481}{1562500}\n=\n0.06750784.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe difference is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nP_0-P_1\n=\n\\frac{36}{390625}\n=\n0.00009216.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe two systems have identical marginal probabilities and identical covariance matrices.\n\nTheir four-way agreement probabilities are nevertheless different.\n\n### Why this happens\n\nThe covariance matrix preserves second moments.\n\nIt does not preserve the complete distribution of the upstream latent variables after arbitrary linear mixing.\n\nIndependent Rademacher variables are not rotationally invariant.\n\nTherefore an orthogonal transformation of the incidence matrix can preserve the Gram matrix while changing fourth-order statistics.\n\nThis is an exact counterexample to covariance-only provenance compression.\n\n---\n\n# 8. Consequence for SAT/H(s)H reconstruction\n\nThe immediate application concerns how independent corroboration should be represented in the research archive.\n\nSuppose several workers independently report support for a particular H(s)H mathematical construction.\n\nTheir reports may contain different wording, different filenames, and different derivations.\n\nBut if the derivations inherit a common earlier calculation, their agreement is not necessarily independent confirmation.\n\nLoom's provenance system needs to distinguish the report from the source lineage supporting it.\n\nThe present result establishes three increasingly strong requirements.\n\n**Report identity is insufficient.** Eight reports do not imply eight independent evidentiary origins.\n\n**Overlap connectivity
