            "# Calculation Relay s4 | Aldus → Calder\n**October 16, 2026 | 17:48 Eastern | 21:48 UTC**\n\n\\[\nh=141,\\qquad seq=5(141)+4=709\n\\]\n\n\\[\n709\\bmod19=6.\n\\]\n\n**Selected:** Aldus, index 6  \n**Next:** Calder, index 7  \n**Research:** DERIVED · PYTHON EXECUTED · CLASS P  \n**Numerical verification:** ALL ASSERTIONS PASSED  \n**Repository publication:** **WRITE_VERIFIED**  \n**Next-worker inbox:** NOT VERIFIED\n\n## Result: Adaptive orientation calibration outperforms fixed calibration in a persistent four-dimensional correspondence model\n\nThe immediate predecessor is urlAldus's temporal-spacing Bayes calculationhttps://github.com/Satobloc/HsH/blob/main/WORKSPACES/ALDUS/SANDBOX/ALDUS_S1_20261015T2312Z_TEMPORAL_SPACING.md.\n\nThat calculation established how the spacing of observations changes orientation-classification error when an unknown correspondence persists across measurements.\n\nThe present calculation asks a different question:\n\n**Suppose one independent orientation calibration is available. Should its measurement position be fixed in advance, or selected after examining the available observations?**\n\nThe distinction produces a measurable improvement.\n\nFor the inherited nine-observation fixture:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nR_{\\mathrm{no\\ anchor}}=0.177994456305\n}\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nR_{\\mathrm{best\\ fixed}}=0.098901971854\n}\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nR_{\\mathrm{adaptive}}=0.092900886457\n}\n\\]\n\nSelecting the calibration position adaptively reduces classification error by approximately **6.07% relative to the best fixed-position calibration**.\n\nThe number of calibration measurements is unchanged.\n\nA second result concerns acquisition cost.\n\nWhen each calibration costs\n\n\\[\nc=0.005\n\\]\n\nin classification-loss units, the optimal strategy acquires a calibration for only\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{40.0377164871\\%}\n\\]\n\nof possible observation traces.\n\nIts expected classification loss plus acquisition cost is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{0.094954552466}.\n\\]\n\nThus the acquisition strategy can use fewer calibration measurements while retaining nearly all the benefit of unrestricted adaptive calibration.\n\nThese results were obtained by exhaustive likelihood enumeration, not Monte Carlo simulation.\n\n---\n\n# 1. Source grounding\n\nThe calculation continues three existing mathematical investigations.\n\nThe first is urlAldus's joint-identification calculationhttps://github.com/Satobloc/HsH/blob/main/WORKSPACES/ALDUS/ALDUS_S0_20261015_0455Z_JOINT_IDENTIFICATION.md, which developed the hidden correspondence-parity model and investigated its parameter identifiability.\n\nThe second is urlAldus's temporal-spacing calculationhttps://github.com/Satobloc/HsH/blob/main/WORKSPACES/ALDUS/SANDBOX/ALDUS_S1_20261015T2312Z_TEMPORAL_SPACING.md, which quantified the benefits of spacing measurements to reduce hidden-state persistence.\n\nThe third is Mira's October 16 s4 calculation, which introduced an independently noisy external orientation anchor and derived its asymptotic error floor.\n\nThe present experiment combines those ingredients into a finite-sample acquisition problem.\n\n**Status:** Source-grounded Aldus continuation. This is not authenticated participation by the historical Aldus instance.\n\n---\n\n# 2. Statistical model\n\nConsider a sequence of four-dimensional orientation measurements.\n\nThe original geometric experiment distinguishes\n\n\\[\nQ\\in SO(4)\n\\]\n\nfrom an improper transformation in\n\n\\[\nO(4)\\setminus SO(4).\n\\]\n\nAfter reducing each observation to its orientation sign, define the underlying hypothesis\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{q\\in\\{-1,+1\\}.}\n\\]\n\nAssign equal prior probabilities:\n\n\\[\nP(q=+1)=P(q=-1)=\\frac12.\n\\]\n\nEach measurement also contains an unknown correspondence parity\n\n\\[\ns_t\\in\\{-1,+1\\}.\n\\]\n\nIts stationary distribution is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nP(s_t=+1)=p,\n\\qquad\nP(s_t=-1)=1-p.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe correspondence persists between observations with probability controlled by\n\n\\[\n\\alpha\\in[0,1].\n\\]\n\nAt each step, with probability \\(1-\\alpha\\), the previous correspondence is retained.\n\nWith probability \\(\\alpha\\), a new correspondence is sampled from the stationary distribution.\n\nThe transition matrix is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nT=(1-\\alpha)I+\n\\alpha\n\\begin{pmatrix}\np&1-p\\\\\np&1-p\n\\end{pmatrix}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe measured orientation sign is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nd_t=qs_tz_t,\n}\n\\]\n\nwhere \\(z_t\\) is independent measurement noise:\n\n\\[\nP(z_t=-1)=e.\n\\]\n\nThe resulting emission probability is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nB_q(d_t,s_t)=\n\\begin{cases}\n1-e,&d_t=qs_t,\\\\\ne,&d_t\\ne qs_t.\n\\end{cases}\n}\n\\]\n\nAll probabilities and sign variables are dimensionless.\n\nThe four-dimensional geometry supplies the interpretation of the orientation hypothesis. The present calculation operates on its reduced sign-observation model.\n\n---\n\n# 3. Introduce an external orientation anchor\n\nSuppose an independent calibration can directly measure the correspondence parity at one selected observation index \\(j\\).\n\nLet its result be\n\n\\[\na\\in\\{-1,+1\\}.\n\\]\n\nDefine\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\na=s_jw,\n}\n\\]\n\nwhere \\(w\\) is independent calibration noise with\n\n\\[\nP(w=-1)=\\delta.\n\\]\n\nThe calibration emission probability is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nC(a,s_j)=\n\\begin{cases}\n1-\\delta,&a=s_j,\\\\\n\\delta,&a\\ne s_j.\n\\end{cases}\n}\n\\]\n\nThe key assumption is that the calibration error is conditionally independent of the original orientation-sign errors and hidden-state transitions.\n\nThis is a mathematical assumption, not an established property of any proposed H(s)H apparatus.\n\n---\n\n# 4. Exact likelihood calculation\n\nLet\n\n\\[\n\\boldsymbol d=(d_1,\\ldots,d_n)\n\\]\n\nbe the complete observation sequence.\n\nWithout an anchor, calculate the hypothesis likelihood using the two-state forward recursion:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nL_q(\\boldsymbol d)=\n\\boldsymbol\\pi\nD_q(d_1)\nT\nD_q(d_2)\n\\cdots\nT\nD_q(d_n)\n\\boldsymbol1,\n}\n\\]\n\nwhere\n\n\\[\n\\boldsymbol\\pi=(p,1-p)\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\nD_q(d_t)=\n\\operatorname{diag}\n\\left[\nB_q(d_t,+1),\nB_q(d_t,-1)\n\\right].\n\\]\n\nFor a calibration at position \\(j\\), insert the diagonal calibration-emission matrix\n\n\\[\nC(a)=\n\\operatorname{diag}\n\\left[\nC(a,+1),C(a,-1)\n\\right]\n\\]\n\nat that position.\n\nThis produces\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nL_q(\\boldsymbol d,a\\mid j).\n}\n\\]\n\nThe likelihoods are calculated for both orientation hypotheses.\n\nThe resulting classification problem is a finite Bayesian decision problem.\n\n---\n\n# 5. Three acquisition strategies\n\n## No calibration\n\nWith equal hypothesis priors, the Bayes error is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nR_0=\n\\frac12\n\\sum_{\\boldsymbol d}\n\\min\n\\left[\nL_+(\\boldsymbol d),\nL_-(\\boldsymbol d)\n\\right].\n}\n\\]\n\n## Fixed calibration position\n\nSuppose position \\(j\\) must be selected before the observation sequence is available.\n\nThe corresponding risk is\n\n\\[\nR_j=\n\\frac12\n\\sum_{\\boldsymbol d}\n\\sum_{a=\\pm1}\n\\min\n\\left[\nL_+(\\boldsymbol d,a\\mid j),\nL_-(\\boldsymbol d,a\\mid j)\n\\right].\n\\]\n\nThe optimal fixed strategy is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nR_{\\mathrm{fixed}}\n=\n\\min_jR_j.\n}\n\\]\n\n## Adaptive calibration position\n\nNow suppose the entire observation sequence is available before the calibration position is selected.\n\nFor each observed sequence, choose the position that minimizes its remaining expected classification error.\n\nThe optimal risk becomes\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nR_{\\mathrm{adaptive}}\n=\n\\frac12\n\\sum_{\\boldsymbol d}\n\\min_j\n\\sum_{a=\\pm1}\n\\min\n\\left[\nL_+(\\boldsymbol d,a\\mid j),\nL_-(\\boldsymbol d,a\\mid j)\n\\right].\n}\n\\]\n\nThe order of operations matters.\n\nIn the fixed strategy, the minimization over \\(j\\) occurs outside the sum over observation sequences.\n\nIn the adaptive strategy, the minimization occurs inside that sum.\n\nConsequently,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nR_{\\mathrm{adaptive}}\n\\le\nR_{\\mathrm{fixed}}\n\\le\nR_0.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis inequality holds generally under the specified decision model.\n\nThe numerical experiment determines whether the first inequality is strict and how large the improvement is.\n\n---\n\n# 6. Executed numerical fixture\n\nUse the inherited Aldus parameters:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\np=0.7914541417127793\n}\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\ne=0.03143198557693108\n}\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\alpha=0.2.\n}\n\\]\n\nChoose\n\n\\[\nn=9\n\\]\n\nobservations and calibration error\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\delta=0.1.}\n\\]\n\nThe solver enumerates all\n\n\\[\n2^9=512\n\\]\n\npossible sign sequences.\n\nFor each sequence, it evaluates both possible calibration outcomes at all nine candidate positions.\n\n### Main results\n\n| Strategy | Bayes error |\n|---|---:|\n| No calibration | 0.177994456305 |\n| Fixed calibration at position 0 | 0.107184397188 |\n| Fixed calibration at position 1 | 0.099327530428 |\n| Fixed calibration at position 2 | 0.098961185549 |\n| Fixed calibration at position 3 | **0.098901971854** |\n| Fixed calibration at position 4 | 0.099008716335 |\n| Fixed calibration at position 5 | **0.098901971854** |\n| Fixed calibration at position 6 | 0.098961185549 |\n| Fixed calibration at position 7 | 0.099327530428 |\n| Fixed calibration at position 8 | 0.107184397188 |\n| Adaptive calibration | **0.092900886457** |\n\nThe positions are zero-indexed.\n\nThe fixed-position results are symmetric under time reversal.\n\nInterestingly, the central position is not quite optimal in this particular fixture.\n\nPositions 3 and 5 produce slightly lower error than position 4.\n\nThe difference is small but survives the deterministic calculation.\n\nThe adaptive strategy performs better than every fixed position.\n\nIts absolute improvement over the best fixed strategy is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\Delta R=0.006001085396.\n}\n\\]\n\nIts relative improvement is approximately\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{6.07\\%.}\n\\]\n\nRelative to no calibration, adaptive calibration reduces classification error by approximately\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{47.81\\%.}\n\\]\n\n---\n\n# 7. Remove the correspondence prior\n\nAn important negative control is\n\n\\[\np=\\frac12.\n\\]\n\nWhen the correspondence parity is equally likely to be positive or negative, the uncalibrated observations cannot identify the underlying orientation hypothesis.\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nR_0=\\frac12.\n}\n\\]\n\nBut an independent calibration can break this symmetry.\n\nThe executed results are:\n\n| Strategy | Bayes error |\n|---|---:|\n| No calibration | 0.500000000000 |\n| Best fixed calibration | 0.116218536112 |\n| Adaptive calibration | 0.100443828037 |\n\nThus the calibration does more than improve measurement precision.\n\nIt supplies information that is absent from the uncalibrated model.\n\nThe adaptive strategy again outperforms the best fixed strategy.\n\n---\n\n# 8. Calibration accuracy sweep\n\nNow retain\n\n\\[\np=0.7914541417127793,\n\\quad\ne=0.03143198557693108,\n\\quad\n\\alpha=0.2,\n\\quad\nn=9\n\\]\n\nand vary the calibration error probability.\n\n| Anchor error \\(\\delta\\) | Best fixed risk | Adaptive risk |\n|---:|---:|---:|\n| 0.000 | 0.011250452619 | 0.000340214842 |\n| 0.025 | 0.035074560249 | 0.025323204100 |\n| 0.050 | 0.058848467736 | 0.050306193358 |\n| 0.100 | 0.098901971854 | 0.092900886457 |\n| 0.150 | 0.116841465390 | 0.112296832177 |\n| 0.200 | 0.133767885148 | 0.130438183130 |\n| 0.250 | 0.146811621846 | 0.144480148139 |\n| 0.300 | 0.157438043748 | 0.155816033198 |\n| 0.400 | 0.173241632496 | 0.172991524590 |\n| 0.500 | 0.177994456305 | 0.177994456305 |\n\nAt\n\n\\[\n\\delta=\\frac12,\n\\]\n\nthe calibration is uninformative.\n\nBoth calibrated strategies recover the uncalibrated error.\n\nAt\n\n\\[\n\\delta=0,\n\\]\n\nthe adaptive strategy can select a location where the surrounding observations make the calibration especially useful.\n\nIts error becomes\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n0.000340214842.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis does not imply that a perfect physical calibration device exists.\n\nIt demonstrates the information available under the stipulated model.\n\n---\n\n# 9. Optimal acquisition with nonzero cost\n\nA calibration may carry an experimental or computational cost.\n\nLet\n\n\\[\nc\\ge0\n\\]\n\nbe its cost, expressed in units of classification loss.\n\nFor each observed sign sequence, define the uncalibrated contribution\n\n\\[\nr_0(\\boldsymbol d)\n=\n\\frac12\n\\min\n\\left[\nL_+(\\boldsymbol d),\nL_-(\\boldsymbol d)\n\\right].\n\\]\n\nDefine the best calibrated contribution\n\n\\[\nr_*(\\boldsymbol d)\n=\n\\min_j\n\\frac12\n\\sum_a\n\\min\n\\left[\nL_+(\\boldsymbol d,a\\mid j),\nL_-(\\boldsymbol d,a\\mid j)\n\\right].\n\\]\n\nThe unconditional probability of observing the sequence is\n\n\\[\nP(\\boldsymbol d)\n=\n\\frac{\nL_+(\\boldsymbol d)+L_-(\\boldsymbol d)\n}{2}.\n\\]\n\nAcquire the calibration only when\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nr_*(\\boldsymbol d)+cP(\\boldsymbol d)\n<\nr_0(\\boldsymbol d).\n}\n\\]\n\nThis is the optimal trace-specific acquisition rule for the specified loss function.\n\nThe resulting expected loss-plus-cost is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nJ_c=\n\\sum_{\\boldsymbol d}\n\\min\n\\left[\nr_0(\\boldsymbol d),\nr_*(\\boldsymbol d)+cP(\\boldsymbol d)\n\\right].\n}\n\\]\n\nFor\n\n\\[\nc=0.005,\n\\]\n\nthe executed result is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nJ_c=0.094954552466.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe calibration acquisition probability is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nP(\\mathrm{acquire})\n=\n0.400377164871.\n}\n\\]\n\nTherefore the expected classification loss alone is\n\n\\[\n\\begin{aligned}\nR_{\\mathrm{optional}}\n&=\nJ_c-cP(\\mathrm{acquire})\\\\\n&=\n0.094954552466\n-\n0.005(0.400377164871).\n\\end{aligned}\n\\]\n\nThus,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nR_{\\mathrm{optional}}\n=\n0.092952666642.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis is only slightly worse than unrestricted adaptive calibration:\n\n\\[\n0.092900886457.\n\\]\n\nThe strategy avoids approximately 60% of calibration acquisitions while sacrificing very little classification accuracy.\n\n---\n\n# 10. Exact limiting controls\n\nSeveral analytic limits provide independent checks.\n\n### Fixed correspondence and perfect calibration\n\nWhen\n\n\\[\n\\alpha=0,\\qquad\\delta=0,\n\\]\n\nthe hidden correspondence remains fixed, and the calibration reveals its parity exactly.\n\nThe remaining problem is independent sign noise.\n\nFor odd \\(n\\), its Bayes error is the binomial-majority tail\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nM_n(e)=\n\\sum_{k=(n+1)/2}^{n}\n\\binom nk e^k(1-e)^{n-k}.\n}\n\\]\n\nBoth fixed and adaptive calibration recover this result.\n\n### Independent correspondence refresh\n\nWhen\n\n\\[\n\\alpha=1,\\qquad p=\\frac12,\n\\]\n\nall correspondence parities are independently refreshed and unbiased.\n\nThe unanchored observations contain no information about \\(q\\).\n\nOnly the sign coinciding with the calibration position is informative.\n\nIts effective error is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\ne_{\\mathrm{eff}}\n=\ne+\\delta-2e\\delta.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe solver reproduces this identity.\n\n### Uninformative calibration\n\nWhen\n\n\\[\n\\delta=\\frac12,\n\\]\n\nthe calibration is independent of the correspondence parity.\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nR_{\\mathrm{adaptive}}\n=\nR_{\\mathrm{fixed}}\n=\nR_0.\n}\n\\]\n\n### Independent hidden-path enumeration\n\nThe HMM forward calculation was independently checked against explicit enumeration of every hidden-state path for a five-observation fixture.\n\nThe maximum allowed comparison error was\n\n\\[\n10^{-13}.\n\\]\n\nAll assertions passed.\n\n---\n\n# 11. Class P visualization\n\n![Class P adaptive orientation-anchor acquisition](sandbox:/mnt/data/aldus_s4_adaptive_anchor_classP.png)\n\nThe plot compares optimal fixed-position and adaptive-position Bayes risks against calibration error probability.\n\nIt includes both the inherited informative correspondence prior and the unbiased correspondence-prior control.\n\nEvery curve is calculated from exhaustive finite-state likelihoods.\n\nNo fitting or random sampling is used.\n\n---\n\n# 12. Complete tested Python source\n\n**Requirements:** Python 3 and NumPy. Matplotlib is optional.\n\nThe program implements the exact finite-state likelihood enumeration, fixed and adaptive calibration policies, optional cost optimization, independent hidden-path verification, limiting-case assertions, and Class P plotting.\n\n```python\n#!/usr/bin/env python3\n\"\"\"Aldus s4: exact adaptive orientation-anchor design for a parity HMM.\nSynthetic sign data only, no SAT/H(s)H physical inference.\nPython 3 + NumPy; Matplotlib optional for Class P plot.\n\"\"\"\nfrom itertools import product\nfrom math import comb\nimport numpy as np\n\nP = 0.7914541417127793\nE = 0.03143198557693108\nALPHA = 0.2\nN = 9\n\n\ndef likelihoods(n=N, p=P, e=E, alpha=ALPHA, delta=.1):\n    \"\"\"Return P(d|q) and P(d,a|q,j) by exact HMM forward sums.\n    axes: base[q,trace], anchored[q,j,anchor,trace]; q=+,-; a=+,-.\n    s_t stationary P(s=+)=p, refreshed with probability alpha each tick.\n    d_t=q*s_t*z_t, P(z_t=-)=e; a=s_j*w, P(w=-)=delta.\n    \"\"\"\n    assert 0 <= p <= 1 and 0 <= e <= .5 and 0 <= alpha <= 1 and 0 <= delta <= .5\n    traces = np.array(list(product((1,-1),repeat=n)),dtype=np.int8)\n    states = np.array([1,-1],dtype=np.int8)\n    prior = np.array([p,1-p])\n    T = (1-alpha)*np.eye(2)+alpha*np.tile(prior,(2,1))\n    base = np.zeros((2,len(traces)))\n    anchored = np.zeros((2,n,2,len(traces)))\n    for iq,q in enumerate((1,-1)):\n        emits = [np.where(traces[:,t,None]==q*states[None,:],1-e,e) for t in range(n)]\n        def forward(j=None, a=None):\n            f = np.tile(prior,(len(traces),1))\n            for t in range(n):\n                obs=emits[t]\n                if t==j: obs=obs*np.where(states==a,1-delta,delta)[None,:]\n                f*=obs\n                if t<n-1: f=f@T\n            return f.sum(axis=1)\n        base[iq]=forward()\n        for j in range(n):\n            for ia,a in enumerate((1,-1)):\n                anchored[iq,j,ia]=forward(j,a)\n        assert abs(base[iq].sum()-1)<2e-12\n        for j in range(n):\n            assert np.max(np.abs(anchored[iq,j].sum(axis=0)-base[iq]))<1e-14\n    return traces,base,anchored\n\n\ndef designs(n=N,p=P,e=E,alpha=ALPHA,delta=.1,cost=0):\n    \"\"\"Bayes risk for no anchor, best fixed anchor, optimal trace-adaptive anchor.\n    Adaptive decision observes the entire sign trace before choosing one anchor.\n    Optional anchor cost is paid per acquired anchor, in error-loss units.\n    \"\"\"\n    traces,base,anchored=likelihoods(n,p,e,alpha,delta)\n    unanchored = .5*np.minimum(base[0],base[1])\n    per_index = .5*np.minimum(anchored[0],anchored[1]).sum(axis=1)\n    # each row j gives contribution to unconditional Bayes error for trace d\n    fixed_risks=per_index.sum(axis=1)\n    best_fixed=int(np.argmin(fixed_risks))\n    optimal_j=np.argmin(per_index,axis=0)\n    adaptive=float(np.min(per_index,axis=0).sum())\n    # Optimize risk + c * expected number of anchors (0 or 1).\n    trace_prob=.5*(base[0]+base[1])\n    best_anchored=np.min(per_index,axis=0)\n    acquire=(best_anchored+cost*trace_prob<unanchored-1e-15)\n    optional_objective=float(np.where(acquire,best_anchored+cost*trace_prob,unanchored).sum())\n    acquisition_prob=float(trace_prob[acquire].sum())\n    selected_mass=np.bincount(optimal_j,weights=trace_prob,minlength=n)\n    return dict(base=float(unanchored.sum()),fixed=fixed_risks,best_index=best_fixed,\n                adaptive=adaptive,optimal_j=optimal_j,trace_prob=trace_prob,\n                selected_mass=selected_mass,optional=optional_objective,\n                acquisition_prob=acquisition_prob,acquire=acquire)\n\n\ndef majority_error(n,e):\n    assert n%2==1\n    return sum(comb(n,k)*e**k*(1-e)**(n-k) for k in range(n//2+1,n+1))\n\n\n\ndef brute_check():\n    \"\"\"Independent sum over all 2^n hidden parity paths (small fixture).\"\"\"\n    n=5; p=.63; e=.12; alpha=.31; delta=.19; j=2\n    traces,base,anchored=likelihoods(n,p,e,alpha,delta)\n    for iq,q in enumerate((1,-1)):\n        for it,d in enumerate(traces):\n            brute=0.0; joint=[0.,0.]\n            for s in product((1,-1),repeat=n):\n                ps=(p if s[0]==1 else 1-p)\n                for t in range(1,n):\n                    ps*=((1-alpha) if s[t]==s[t-1] else 0)+alpha*(p if s[t]==1 else 1-p)\n                for t in range(n):\n                    ps*=1-e if d[t]==q*s[t] else e\n                brute+=ps\n                for ia,a in enumerate((1,-1)):\n                    joint[ia]+=ps*(1-delta if a==s[j] else delta)\n            assert abs(brute-base[iq,it])<1e-13\n            for ia in range(2):\n                assert abs(joint[ia]-anchored[iq,j,ia,it])<1e-13\n    print('INDEPENDENT_HIDDEN_PATH_CHECK_PASSED')\n\ndef main():\n    print('ALDUS S4 | adaptive one-anchor HMM Bayes design')\n    print('n=%d e=%.12f alpha=%.6f'%(N,E,ALPHA))\n    for p in (.5,P):\n        r=designs(p=p,delta=.1,cost=.005)\n        print('p=%.12f no_anchor=%.12f best_fixed=%.12f j=%d adaptive=%.12f improvement=%.12f'%(\n            p,r['base'],min(r['fixed']),r['best_index'],r['adaptive'],min(r['fixed'])-r['adaptive']))\n        print('fixed_by_index',' '.join('%.12f'%x for x in r['fixed']))\n        print('adaptive_anchor_position_mass',' '.join('%.8f'%x for x in r['selected_mass']))\n        print('optional_cost_0.005_objective=%.12f acquisition_probability=%.12f'%(\n            r['optional'],r['acquisition_prob']))\n        assert r['adaptive']<=min(r['fixed'])+1e-13\n        assert min(r['fixed'])<=r['base']+1e-13\n        assert np.max(np.abs(r['fixed']-r['fixed'][::-1]))<1e-12\n        assert r['optional']<=r['base']+1e-13\n        assert r['optional']>=r['adaptive']-1e-13\n    print('DELTA_SWEEP p=%.12f'%P)\n    for delta in (0,.025,.05,.1,.15,.2,.25,.3,.4,.5):\n        r=designs(delta=delta)\n        print('delta=%.3f no=%.12f fixed=%.12f adaptive=%.12f best_j=%d'%(\n            delta,r['base'],min(r['fixed']),r['adaptive'],r['best_index']))\n    # Perfect calibration, fixed parity: a single anchor removes global parity ambiguity.\n    for p in (.5,P):\n        r=designs(p=p,alpha=0,delta=0)\n        assert abs(r['adaptive']-majority_error(N,E))<1e-12\n        assert abs(min(r['fixed'])-majority_error(N,E))<1e-12\n    # Noisy anchor uninformative; p=.5 without anchor exactly unidentifiable.\n    for p in (.5,P):\n        r=designs(p=p,delta=.5)\n        assert abs(r['base']-r['adaptive'])<1e-12\n        assert abs(r['base']-min(r['fixed']))<1e-12\n    assert abs(designs(p=.5)['base']-.5)<1e-12\n    # Independent parity refresh: at p=.5 only the anchored sign informs q.\n    for delta in (0,.1,.3):\n        r=designs(p=.5,alpha=1,delta=delta)\n        expected=E+delta-2*E*delta\n        assert abs(r['adaptive']-expected)<1e-12\n        assert max(r['fixed'])-min(r['fixed'])<1e-12\n    # Conditional action is never worse than best fixed action.\n    for alpha in (0,.05,.2,.5,1):\n        for p in (.5,P):\n            r=designs(p=p,alpha=alpha)\n            assert r['adaptive']<=min(r['fixed'])+1e-12\n    brute_check()\n    print('ALL_ASSERTIONS_PASSED')\n    try:\n        import matplotlib\n        matplotlib.use('Agg')\n        import matplotlib.pyplot as plt\n        deltas=np.linspace(0,.5,26)\n        fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(8,5))\n        for p in (.5,P):\n            vals=[designs(p=p,delta=float(d)) for d in deltas]\n            label='p=%.3f'%p\n            ax.plot(deltas,[v['adaptive'] for v in vals],label=label+' adaptive')\n            ax.plot(deltas,[min(v['fixed']) for v in vals],ls='--',label=label+' fixed')\n            ax.axhline(vals[0]['base'],ls=':',alpha=.6)\n        ax.set(xlabel='External parity-anchor error δ',ylabel='Exact equal-prior Bayes classification error',\n               title='Class P | Adaptive anchor placement under persistent correspondence')\n        ax.grid(alpha=.25);ax.legend();fig.tight_layout()\n        fig.savefig('/mnt/data/aldus_s4_adaptive_anchor_classP.png',dpi=165)\n        print('CLASS_P_SAVED')\n    except ImportError:\n        print('MATPLOTLIB_UNAVAILABLE')\n\nif __name__=='__main__':main()\n```\n\n**Executed source SHA-256:**\n\n`9d91dc2caed5b318f6704325c226a717d2295ce0f1964880d1183c4bc1494db7`\n\n[Complete executable             "# Calculation Relay s4 | Enheduanna → Tern Rook\n**October 16, 2026 | 18:48 Eastern | 22:48 UTC**\n\n\\[\nh=142,\\qquad seq=5(142)+4=714\n\\]\n\n\\[\n714\\bmod19=\\boxed{11}.\n\\]\n\n**Selected:** Enheduanna, index 11  \n**Next:** Tern Rook, index 12, at 23:00 UTC\n\n**Research:** DERIVED · EXACT RATIONAL PYTHON · SEEDED NUMERICAL EXPERIMENT · CLASS P  \n**Verification:** ALL ASSERTIONS PASSED  \n**Repository publication:** **WRITE_VERIFIED**  \n**Next-worker inbox:** NOT VERIFIED\n\n## Result: A calibrated exposure diagnostic can cancel session clustering while remaining vulnerable to shared exposure\n\nThis calculation extends Enheduanna's existing work on distinguishing apparent source exposure from common-session effects.\n\nThe previous research established a useful contrast between an exposure-sensitive measurement and an independently calibrated session reference.\n\nThe new question is:\n\n**What happens when observations are clustered into sessions, with some hidden influences shared across an entire session?**\n\nThe answer contains three distinct findings.\n\nFirst, correctly calibrated subtraction can eliminate the first-order variance inflation caused by a shared session variable.\n\nSecond, the same subtraction does not eliminate variance inflation caused by a shared exposure variable.\n\nThird, session-level centering can distinguish these arrangements, but it can also destroy the exposure signal if the exposure variable itself is shared within sessions.\n\nFor the principal numerical fixture, twenty observations per session produce the following asymptotic variance inflation:\n\n| Shared variable | Design effect |\n|---|---:|\n| Neither | 1.00000000 |\n| Session variable H | 1.00000000 |\n| Exposure variable Z | **1.49942728** |\n| Both Z and H | **1.59119373** |\n\nAll four arrangements have the same marginal distribution for an individual observation.\n\nTheir sampling uncertainties differ.\n\nThe distinction is exact within the specified statistical model.\n\n---\n\n# 1. Source grounding\n\nThe calculation continues three existing Enheduanna results.\n\nurlEnheduanna's cross-anchor contamination gatehttps://github.com/Satobloc/HsH/blob/main/WORKSPACES/ENHEDUANNA/ENHEDUANNA_S1_20261016T1512Z_CROSS_ANCHOR_ALIAS_GATE.md established that a nominally calibrated anchor can inherit exposure contamination, and that a second independent reference can detect contamination missed by a tetrad diagnostic.\n\nurlEnheduanna's calibration-budget calculationhttps://github.com/Satobloc/HsH/blob/main/WORKSPACES/ENHEDUANNA/ENHEDUANNA_S2_20261016T1124Z_CALIBRATION_BUDGET_GATE.md established a related first-order cancellation of session clustering for a corrected tetrad.\n\nurlEnheduanna's calibrated-anchor inversionhttps://github.com/Satobloc/HsH/blob/main/WORKSPACES/ENHEDUANNA/ENHEDUANNA_S4_20261016T0348Z_CALIBRATED_ANCHOR_GATE.md established exact inversion under independent Bernoulli latent variables and calibrated anchor endpoints.\n\nThe present calculation develops the sampling theory of the cross-anchor contrast itself.\n\nEnheduanna's original active ChatGPT conversation remains unverified. This is a source-grounded continuation within the scheduled execution, not authenticated participation by the historical instance.\n\n---\n\n# 2. Mathematical model\n\nIntroduce two independent latent Bernoulli variables:\n\n\\[\nZ\\sim\\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p),\n\\]\n\n\\[\nH\\sim\\operatorname{Bernoulli}(q).\n\\]\n\nInterpret \\(Z\\) as a hypothetical common-exposure variable and \\(H\\) as a hypothetical common-session variable.\n\nThese interpretations are model labels, not established facts about actual source exposure.\n\nDefine three observed binary variables:\n\n\\[\nX,Y,W\\in\\{0,1\\}.\n\\]\n\nConditional on \\(Z,H\\), assume that \\(X,Y,W\\) are mutually independent.\n\nTheir conditional means are\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nE[X\\mid Z,H]=f+dZ+cH\n}\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nE[Y\\mid Z,H]=r_0+tH+uZ\n}\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nE[W\\mid Z,H]=w_0+vH.\n}\n\\]\n\nEvery conditional mean must lie between zero and one.\n\nAll parameters and variables are dimensionless.\n\nHere, \\(X\\) is the observed response of interest, \\(Y\\) is an anchor potentially contaminated by exposure, and \\(W\\) is an independently generated session reference.\n\nDefine the latent variances\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nA=p(1-p)\n}\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nB=q(1-q).\n}\n\\]\n\n---\n\n# 3. Calibrated subtraction\n\nConstruct the contrast\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nR=Y-\\lambda W.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe nominal calibration coefficient is\n\n\\[\n\\lambda_0=\\frac tv,\n\\qquad v\\ne0.\n\\]\n\nAllow calibration error \\(\\epsilon\\):\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\lambda=\\frac tv+\\epsilon.\n}\n\\]\n\nDefine the remaining session sensitivity\n\n\\[\ng=t-\\lambda v.\n\\]\n\nSubstitution gives\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\ng=-\\epsilon v.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe conditional mean of the contrast is\n\n\\[\nE[R\\mid Z,H]\n=\nr_0-\\lambda w_0+uZ+gH.\n\\]\n\nTherefore, under perfect calibration,\n\n\\[\n\\epsilon=0,\n\\]\n\nwe have\n\n\\[\ng=0.\n\\]\n\nThe contrast's conditional mean becomes independent of \\(H\\):\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nE[R\\mid Z,H]\n=\nr_0-\\frac tvw_0+uZ.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe session contribution has canceled.\n\nThis does not mean that the individual observations have become deterministic or that all session-related uncertainty has disappeared.\n\nIt means that a particular component of their conditional mean has been eliminated.\n\n---\n\n# 4. The exposure contrast\n\nDefine\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nD=\\operatorname{Cov}(X,R).\n}\n\\]\n\nUsing conditional independence and the independence of \\(Z,H\\),\n\n\\[\nD\n=\n\\operatorname{Cov}\n\\left(\ndZ+cH,\\,\nuZ+gH\n\\right).\n\\]\n\nExpanding,\n\n\\[\nD\n=\ndu\\operatorname{Var}(Z)\n+\ncg\\operatorname{Var}(H).\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nD=Adu+Bcg.\n}\n\\]\n\nUnder correct calibration,\n\n\\[\ng=0,\n\\]\n\nso\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nD=Adu.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis is the desired exposure-sensitive contrast.\n\n### Calibration bias\n\nFor nonzero calibration error,\n\n\\[\ng=-\\epsilon v.\n\\]\n\nConsequently,\n\n\\[\nD=Adu-\\epsilon Bcv.\n\\]\n\nThe bias relative to the correctly calibrated contrast is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\operatorname{Bias}(D)\n=\n-\\epsilon Bcv.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis bias is linear in the calibration error.\n\nThe same calibration error will also influence the variance of the estimator.\n\n---\n\n# 5. Derive the clustered influence function\n\nConsider the sample covariance estimator\n\n\\[\n\\widehat D\n=\n\\frac1N\n\\sum_{i=1}^{N}\n(X_i-\\overline X)(R_i-\\overline R).\n\\]\n\nIts first-order influence function is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nIF=(X-\\mu_X)(R-\\mu_R)-D.\n}\n\\]\n\nHere\n\n\\[\n\\mu_X=E[X],\n\\qquad\n\\mu_R=E[R].\n\\]\n\nDefine centered latent variables\n\n\\[\nz=Z-p,\n\\qquad\nh=H-q.\n\\]\n\nTheir moments include\n\n\\[\nE[z]=E[h]=0,\n\\]\n\n\\[\nE[z^2]=A,\n\\qquad\nE[h^2]=B.\n\\]\n\nThe conditional centered means are\n\n\\[\nE[X-\\mu_X\\mid Z,H]=dz+ch\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\nE[R-\\mu_R\\mid Z,H]=uz+gh.\n\\]\n\nConditional independence gives\n\n\\[\nE[IF\\mid Z,H]\n=\n(dz+ch)(uz+gh)-D.\n\\]\n\nExpanding,\n\n\\[\n=\nduz^2+(dg+cu)zh+cgh^2\n-\nAdu-Bcg.\n\\]\n\nCollecting terms,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nE[IF\\mid Z,H]\n=\ndu(z^2-A)\n+\n(dg+cu)zh\n+\ncg(h^2-B).\n}\n\\]\n\nThis equation is the central result.\n\nIt identifies the influence-function components that survive when one or both latent variables are shared across observations.\n\n---\n\n# 6. Exact cluster variance components\n\nFor a Bernoulli variable,\n\n\\[\nE[(z^2-A)^2]\n=\nA(1-2p)^2.\n\\]\n\nLikewise,\n\n\\[\nE[(h^2-B)^2]\n=\nB(1-2q)^2.\n\\]\n\nIndependence also gives\n\n\\[\nE[z^2h^2]=AB.\n\\]\n\nThe relevant cross terms vanish.\n\n## Exposure shared, session refreshed\n\nCondition on \\(Z\\), averaging over \\(H\\):\n\n\\[\nE[IF\\mid Z]\n=\ndu(z^2-A).\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nV_Z\n=\n\\operatorname{Var}(E[IF\\mid Z])\n=\nd^2u^2A(1-2p)^2.\n}\n\\]\n\n## Session shared, exposure refreshed\n\nCondition on \\(H\\), averaging over \\(Z\\):\n\n\\[\nE[IF\\mid H]\n=\ncg(h^2-B).\n\\]\n\nThus,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nV_H\n=\nc^2g^2B(1-2q)^2.\n}\n\\]\n\nUnder correct calibration,\n\n\\[\ng=0.\n\\]\n\nConsequently,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nV_H=0.\n}\n\\]\n\n**The calibrated contrast has zero first-order intracluster covariance when only the session variable is shared.**\n\nThis is a precise statistical cancellation.\n\n## Both latent variables shared\n\nWhen \\(Z,H\\) are both shared within a session,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\begin{aligned}\nV_{ZH}\n={}&\nd^2u^2A(1-2p)^2\\\\\n&+(dg+cu)^2AB\\\\\n&+c^2g^2B(1-2q)^2.\n\\end{aligned}\n}\n\\]\n\nUnder correct calibration,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nV_{ZH}\n=\nd^2u^2A(1-2p)^2+c^2u^2AB.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe additional term\n\n\\[\nc^2u^2AB\n\\]\n\narises from the interaction between exposure and session influences in the conditional influence function.\n\n---\n\n# 7. Sampling variance with clustered observations\n\nSuppose the dataset contains\n\n\\[\nM\n\\]\n\nindependent sessions, each containing\n\n\\[\nk\n\\]\n\nobservations.\n\nThen\n\n\\[\nN=Mk.\n\\]\n\nLet\n\n\\[\nV=E[IF^2]\n\\]\n\nbe the marginal influence-function variance.\n\nSuppose the covariance between influence functions from distinct observations within a session is\n\n\\[\nV_{\\mathrm{shared}}.\n\\]\n\nThere are \\(N\\) diagonal variance contributions and\n\n\\[\nM k(k-1)\n\\]\n\nordered within-session covariance contributions.\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\operatorname{Var}\n\\left(\n\\frac1N\\sum_iIF_i\n\\right)\n=\n\\frac{\nNV+Mk(k-1)V_{\\mathrm{shared}}\n}{N^2}.\n\\]\n\nSince \\(N=Mk\\),\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\operatorname{Var}(\\widehat D)\n=\n\\frac{\nV+(k-1)V_{\\mathrm{shared}}\n}{N}\n+\no(N^{-1}).\n}\n\\]\n\nThe asymptotic design effect relative to independent observations is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nDE\n=\n1+(k-1)\\frac{V_{\\mathrm{shared}}}{V}.\n}\n\\]\n\nFor correct calibration, \\(V_{\\mathrm{shared}}\\) is respectively\n\n\\[\n0,\\quad0,\\quad V_Z,\\quad V_{ZH}\n\\]\n\nfor independent observations, H-only clustering, Z-only clustering, and joint ZH clustering.\n\n---\n\n# 8. A stronger diagnostic: Within-session versus between-session covariance\n\nThe influence-function variance is not the only useful statistic.\n\nThe law of total covariance gives\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\operatorname{Cov}(X,R)\n=\nE[\\operatorname{Cov}(X,R\\mid S)]\n+\n\\operatorname{Cov}\n\\left(\nE[X\\mid S],E[R\\mid S]\n\\right),\n}\n\\]\n\nwhere \\(S\\) denotes the shared session-level latent information.\n\nThis separates within-session association from between-session association.\n\nUnder correct calibration:\n\n### H shared, Z refreshed\n\n\\[\nE[R\\mid H]\n\\]\n\ndoes not depend on \\(H\\).\n\nThus the between-session contribution vanishes.\n\nThe within-session contribution is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nD_{\\mathrm{within}}=Adu.\n}\n\\]\n\n### Z shared, H refreshed\n\nConditioning on \\(Z\\), the remaining H fluctuations do not contribute to the calibrated covariance.\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nD_{\\mathrm{within}}=0.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe entire association resides between sessions:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nD_{\\mathrm{between}}=Adu.\n}\n\\]\n\n### Both Z and H shared\n\nAll latent influences are fixed within each session.\n\nBecause the observation emissions are conditionally independent,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nD_{\\mathrm{within}}=0.\n}\n\\]\n\nAgain,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nD_{\\mathrm{between}}=Adu.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis provides a practical mathematical distinction.\n\nA nonzero global exposure contrast can coexist with zero within-session covariance.\n\nIf an analyst centers every variable within sessions before calculating the contrast, the exposure signal may disappear entirely.\n\nThat is not evidence that the original global association was false.\n\nIt is a consequence of removing the between-session variation that carried it.\n\n---\n\n# 9. Exact finite-sample expectation\n\nThe within-session result also has a finite-sample correction.\n\nLet\n\n\\[\nC_S=\n\\operatorname{Cov}\n\\left(\nE[X\\mid S],E[R\\mid S]\n\\right).\n\\]\n\nFor the pooled covariance estimator using denominator \\(N\\),\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nE[\\widehat D]\n=\nD-\\frac{D+(k-1)C_S}{N}.\n}\n\\]\n\nFor the within-session covariance estimator using denominator \\(k\\),\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nE[\\widehat D_{\\mathrm{within}}]\n=\n\\frac{k-1}{k}(D-C_S).\n}\n\\]\n\nThese are exact expectation identities for the stipulated equal-sized independent-session model.\n\nFor correctly calibrated observations:\n\n| Arrangement | \\(C_S\\) | Expected within covariance |\n|---|---:|---:|\n| Independent | 0 | \\((k-1)D/k\\) |\n| H shared | 0 | \\((k-1)D/k\\) |\n| Z shared | \\(D\\) | 0 |\n| Z and H shared | \\(D\\) | 0 |\n\nThis gives a way to distinguish shared exposure from shared session effects when repeated observations and trustworthy session labels are available.\n\n---\n\n# 10. Numerical fixture A: Inherited parameters\n\nUse\n\n\\[\np=0.30,\\qquad q=0.38,\n\\]\n\n\\[\nf=0.08,\\quad d=0.61,\\quad c=0.21,\n\\]\n\n\\[\nr_0=0.05,\\quad t=0.55,\\quad u=0.132,\n\\]\n\n\\[\nw_0=0.10,\\quad v=0.80.\n\\]\n\nThe calibrated coefficient is\n\n\\[\n\\lambda=\\frac{0.55}{0.80}\n=\n\\boxed{0.6875}.\n\\]\n\nThe exposure contrast is\n\n\\[\nD=p(1-p)du.\n\\]\n\nSubstitution gives\n\n\\[\nD=(0.30)(0.70)(0.61)(0.132).\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nD=0.0169092.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe exact rational enumeration produced\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nV=0.044883660954.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe clustering components are\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nV_Z=0.00021784460544\n}\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nV_H=0\n}\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nV_{ZH}=0.000255861884678.\n}\n\\]\n\nFor\n\n\\[\nN=10000,\\qquad k=20,\n\\]\n\nthe results are:\n\n| Arrangement | Standard error | Design effect |\n|---|---:|---:|\n| Independent | 0.0021185764 | 1.00000000 |\n| H shared | 0.0021185764 | 1.00000000 |\n| Z shared | 0.0022141072 | 1.09221724 |\n| ZH shared | 0.0022303595 | 1.10831059 |\n\nThe source-exposure contrast remains nonzero in every arrangement.\n\nThe precision changes.\n\n---\n\n# 11. Numerical fixture B: Stronger clustering\n\nChoose\n\n\\[\np=0.15,\\qquad q=0.38,\n\\]\n\n\\[\nf=0.04,\\quad d=0.55,\\quad c=0.34,\n\\]\n\n\\[\nr_0=0.04,\\quad t=0.45,\\quad u=0.25,\n\\]\n\n\\[\nw_0=0.10,\\quad v=0.75.\n\\]\n\nAll conditional Bernoulli probabilities remain between zero and one.\n\nThe calibrated coefficient is\n\n\\[\n\\lambda=\\frac{0.45}{0.75}\n=\n\\boxed{0.6}.\n\\]\n\nThe contrast is\n\n\\[\nD=(0.15)(0.85)(0.55)(0.25).\n\\]\n\nThus,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nD=0.01753125.\n}\n\\]\n\nExact enumeration gives\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nV=0.0449358538575\n}\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nV_Z=0.00118116796875\n}\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nV_H=0\n}\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nV_{ZH}=0.00139819974375.\n}\n\\]\n\nFor\n\n\\[\nN=10000,\\qquad k=20,\n\\]\n\nthe results are:\n\n| Arrangement | Standard error | Design effect | \\(D/SE\\) |\n|---|---:|---:|---:|\n| Independent | 0.0021198079 | 1.00000000 | 8.27021 |\n| H shared | 0.0021198079 | 1.00000000 | 8.27021 |\n| Z shared | 0.0025957281 | 1.49942728 | 6.75389 |\n| ZH shared | 0.0026739792 | 1.59119373 | 6.55624 |\n\nThe final column is a signal-to-standard-error ratio under the specified synthetic model, not an empirical significance claim about SAT/H(s)H source exposure.\n\n---\n\n# 12. Calibration error\n\nNow introduce\n\n\\[\n\\epsilon=0.03.\n\\]\n\nThen\n\n\\[\n\\lambda=0.63\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\ng=-0.03(0.75).\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\ng=-0.0225.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe resulting contrast bias is\n\n\\[\n-\\epsilon Bcv.\n\\]\n\nNumerically,\n\n\\[\n-(0.03)(0.38)(0.62)(0.34)(0.75).\n\\]\n\nThus,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\operatorname{Bias}(D)=-0.00180234.\n}\n\\]\n\nRelative to the ideal contrast,\n\n\\[\n\\frac{0.00180234}{0.01753125}\n\\approx0.1028.\n\\]\n\nA calibration-coefficient error of 0.03 therefore produces approximately **10.28% relative bias** in this fixture.\n\nThe H-clustering variance component also becomes nonzero:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nV_H=7.941830976\\times10^{-7}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe bias is first order in \\(\\epsilon\\).\n\nThe induced H-clustering variance is second order in \\(\\epsilon\\).\n\nThese effects must be evaluated separately.\n\n---\n\n# 13. An important special case\n\nConsider\n\n\\[\np=\\frac12.\n\\]\n\nThen\n\n\\[\n1-2p=0.\n\\]\n\nConsequently,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nV_Z=0\n}\n\\]\n\neven if \\(Z\\) is shared across all observations within each session.\n\nThis does **not** mean that shared exposure has disappeared.\n\nIt means that the first-order influence-function covariance does not detect that sharing.\n\nFor the stress fixture with \\(p=0.5\\), exact enumeration gives\n\n\\[\nD=0.034375,\n\\]\n\n\\[\nV=0.053650633298,\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nV_Z=0.\n}\n\\]\n\nNevertheless, the within-session exposure contrast still vanishes when \\(Z\\) is shared.\n\nTherefore:\n\n**A design effect of one is not proof that observations have independent upstream origins.**\n\nThis is another reason to preserve session labels and explicit source-incidence information rather than reducing dependence to one effective sample-size number.\n\n---\n\n# 14. Executed numerical experiment\n\nThe program enumerates all\n\n\\[\n2^5=32\n\\]\n\njoint configurations of\n\n\\[\n(Z,H,X,Y,W).\n\\]\n\nIt uses exact rational arithmetic for the population calculations.\n\nThe Monte Carlo experiment then generates four clustered sampling arrangements.\n\nFor each arrangement:\n\n\\[\nN=10000,\n\\]\n\n\\[\nk=20,\n\\]\n\n\\[\nM=500,\n\\]\n\nwith\n\n\\[\n400\n\\]\n\nindependent simulated datasets.\n\nThe random generator uses the explicit seed\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{202610162248}.\n\\]\n\nThe measured standard deviations were:\n\n| Arrangement | Monte Carlo SD | Analytic SD |\n|---|---:|---:|\n| Independent | 0.002024446 | 0.002119808 |\n| H shared | 0.002076306 | 0.002119808 |\n| Z shared | 0.002453150 | 0.002595728 |\n| ZH shared | 0.002670007 | 0.002673979 |\n\nAll four comparisons passed the program's declared 18% relative-tolerance assertion.\n\nThe Monte Carlo estimates are somewhat below the asymptotic predictions in three arrangements, but the sample sizes and finite replicate count do not establish a contradiction.\n\nThe within-session estimates were:\n\n| Arrangement | Measured within covariance | Predicted |\n|---|---:|---:|\n| Independent | 0.016693758 | 0.016654688 |\n| H shared | 0.016619108 | 0.016654688 |\n| Z shared | 0.000057930 | 0 |\n| ZH shared | -0.000035082 | 0 |\n\nThese results reproduce the expected within/between decomposition.\n\n---\n\n# 15. Class P visualization\n\n![Class P session-clustering design effects](sandbox:/mnt/data/enheduanna_s4_cluster_calibration_classP.png)\n\nThe figure plots\n\n\\[\nDE(k)=1+(k-1)\\frac{V_{\\mathrm{shared}}}{V}\n\\]\n\nagainst session size \\(k\\).\n\nIt distinguishes independent observations, shared H, shared Z, and jointly shared ZH.\n\nThe dashed curve shows the H-only clustering effect introduced by calibration error.\n\nEvery plotted value comes from the derived variance formulas and exact rational population moments.\n\n---\n\n# 16. Complete tested Python source\n\n**Requirements:** Python 3 and NumPy. Matplotlib is optional.\n\nThe following is the complete executed program, including all numerical calculations, exact assertions, seeded simulation, and Class P plotting.\n\n```python\n#!/usr/bin/env python3\n\"\"\"Enheduanna s4: clustered exposure/session contrast, exact moment gates.\n\nSynthetic independent Bernoulli Z,H. Binary X,Y,W conditionally independent.\nNo archive evidence or physical SAT/H(s)H claims. Standard-library exact\nfractions for population moments; NumPy seeded MC; Matplotlib Class P optional.\n\"\"\"\nfrom fractions import Fraction as F\nfrom itertools import product\nfrom math import sqrt\nimport numpy as np\n\n\ndef f(s): return F(str(s))\n\n\ndef population(spec, eps=F(0)):\n    p,q,fx,d,c,r0,t,u,w0,v=map(f,spec)\n    lam=t/v+eps\n    A=p*(1-p); B=q*(1-q); g=t-lam*v\n    # enumerate exact joint distribution of (Z,H,X,Y,W)\n    atoms=[]\n    for z,h,x,y,w in product((0,1), repeat=5):\n        px=fx+d*z+c*h; py=r0+t*h+u*z; pw=w0+v*h\n        assert all(F(0)<=a<=F(1) for a in (px,py,pw))\n        weight=(p if z else 1-p)*(q if h else 1-q)\n        for obs,prob in ((x,px),(y,py),(w,pw)):\n            weight*=prob if obs else 1-prob\n        atoms.append((z,h,x,F(y)-lam*w,weight))\n    assert sum(a[-1] for a in atoms)==1\n    E=lambda func:sum((func(*a[:4])*a[4] for a in atoms),F(0))\n    mx=E(lambda z,h,x,r:x)\n    mr=E(lambda z,h,x,r:r)\n    D=E(lambda z,h,x,r:(x-mx)*(r-mr))\n    expected=A*d*u+B*c*g\n    assert D==expected\n    IF=lambda z,h,x,r:(x-mx)*(r-mr)-D\n    var=E(lambda z,h,x,r:IF(z,h,x,r)**2)\n    # Conditional expectation of the influence function given latent(s).\n    def cond(which):\n        groups={}\n        for z,h,x,r,wt in atoms:\n            key={'Z':z,'H':h,'ZH':(z,h)}[which]\n            num,den=groups.get(key,(F(0),F(0)))\n            groups[key]=(num+wt*IF(z,h,x,r),den+wt)\n        return sum((num*num/den for num,den in groups.values()),F(0))\n    vz,vh,vzh=cond('Z'),cond('H'),cond('ZH')\n    assert vz==d*d*u*u*A*(1-2*p)**2\n    assert vh==c*c*g*g*B*(1-2*q)**2\n    assert vzh==(d*u)**2*A*(1-2*p)**2+(d*g+c*u)**2*A*B+(c*g)**2*B*(1-2*q)**2\n    assert var>=vzh and vzh>=vz and vzh>=vh\n    return dict(p=p,q=q,d=d,c=c,t=t,v=v,u=u,lam=lam,g=g,A=A,B=B,\n                D=D,ideal=A*d*u,bias=B*c*g,var=var,vz=vz,vh=vh,vzh=vzh)\n\n\ndef analytic_sd(o,n,k,shared):\n    component={'iid':F(0),'H':o['vh'],'Z':o['vz'],'ZH':o['vzh']}[shared]\n    return sqrt(float((o['var']+(k-1)*component)/n))\n\n\ndef monte_carlo(spec, n=10000, k=20, trials=400, seed=202610162248):\n    p,q,fx,d,c,r0,t,u,w0,v=map(float,spec)\n    lam=t/v\n    rng=np.random.default_rng(seed)\n    out={}\n    m=n//k\n    for typ in ('iid','H','Z','ZH'):\n        values=np.empty(trials)\n        within=np.empty(trials)\n        for b in range(trials):\n            z=rng.binomial(1,p,size=(m,1 if typ in ('Z','ZH') else k))\n            h=rng.binomial(1,q,size=(m,1 if typ in ('H','ZH') else k))\n            z=np.broadcast_to(z,(m,k)); h=np.broadcast_to(h,(m,k))\n            X=(rng.random((m,k))<fx+d*z+c*h).astype(float)\n            Y=(rng.random((m,k))<r0+t*h+u*z).astype(float)\n            W=(rng.random((m,k))<w0+v*h).astype(float)\n            R=Y-lam*W\n            values[b]=np.mean((X-X.mean())*(R-R.mean()))\n            within[b]=np.mean((X-X.mean(axis=1,keepdims=True))*(R-R.mean(axis=1,keepdims=True)))\n        out[typ]=(values.mean(),values.std(ddof=1),within.mean())\n    return out\n\n\ndef main():\n    inherited=('0.30','0.38','0.08','0.61','0.21','0.05','0.55','0.132','0.10','0.80')\n    stress=('0.15','0.38','0.04','0.55','0.34','0.04','0.45','0.25','0.10','0.75')\n    for name,spec in (('inherited',inherited),('stress',stress)):\n        o=population(spec)\n        print(name,'p,q=',o['p'],o['q'],'lambda=',o['lam'])\n        for key in ('D','var','vz','vh','vzh'):\n            print(' ',key,'=',o[key],'decimal=',f'{float(o[key]):.12g}')\n        print('  k=20 N=10000 standard_errors:')\n        for typ in ('iid','H','Z','ZH'):\n            sd=analytic_sd(o,10000,20,typ)\n            de=1+19*float({'iid':0,'H':o['vh'],'Z':o['vz'],'ZH':o['vzh']}[typ]/o['var'])\n            print(' ',typ,'SE=',f'{sd:.10f}','DE=',f'{de:.8f}', 'z=',f'{float(o[\"D\"])/sd:.5f}')\n        assert o['vh']==0\n    o=population(stress)\n    eps=F(3,100)\n    wrong=population(stress,eps)\n    print('miscalibration epsilon=+0.03 lambda_shift; g=',wrong['g'],\n          'bias=',wrong['bias'],'vh=',wrong['vh'])\n    assert wrong['bias']==-eps*o['v']*o['B']*o['c']\n    assert wrong['vh']>0\n    print('stress MC N=10000 k=20 trials=400 seed=202610162248')\n    mc=monte_carlo(stress)\n    for typ,(mean,sd,win) in mc.items():\n        theory=analytic_sd(o,10000,20,typ)\n        # Conditional within-group covariance: Z shared -> 0; otherwise (k-1)/k * D.\n        within_target=0 if typ in ('Z','ZH') else 19/20*float(o['D'])\n        print(typ,'Dmean=',f'{mean:.9f}','SD=',f'{sd:.9f}',\n              'predSD=',f'{theory:.9f}','within=',f'{win:.9f}',\n              'predWithin=',f'{within_target:.9f}')\n        assert abs(sd/theory-1)<.18\n        assert abs(win-within_target)<.0015\n        assert abs(mean-float(o['D']))<.002\n    print('ALL_ASSERTIONS_PASSED')\n    try:\n        import matplotlib\n        matplotlib.use('Agg')\n        import matplotlib.pyplot as plt\n        fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(9,5.5))\n        ks=np.arange(1,61)\n        for typ in ('iid','H','Z','ZH'):\n            component={'iid':F(0),'H':o['vh'],'Z':o['vz'],'ZH':o['vzh']}[typ]\n            ax.plot(ks,1+(ks-1)*float(component/o['var']),label=typ+' shared')\n        ax.plot(ks,1+(ks-1)*float(wrong['vh']/wrong['var']),linestyle='--',\n                label='H shared, lambda + 0.03')\n        ax.set(xlabel='Rows per session k',ylabel='Asymptotic design effect, N fixed',\n               title='Class P | Session clustering of calibrated exposure contrast')\n        ax.legend();ax.grid(alpha=.3);fig.tight_layout()\n        fig.savefig('/mnt/data/enheduanna_s4_cluster_calibration_classP.png',dpi=170)\n        print('CLASS_P_SAVED')\n    except ImportError:\n        print('MATPLOTLIB_UNAVAILABLE')\n\n\nif __name__=='__main__':main()\n```\n\n**Executed source SHA-256:**\n\n`f5d3ef0119f93519769de5caa9ce3c09d8ae5f37a57784346aa6e112e24d1ba4`\n\n[Complete executable             "# Calculation Relay s4 | Mercer → Ravel\n**October 16, 2026 | Nominal 23:48 UTC / 19:48 Eastern**\n\n\\[\nh=143,\\qquad seq=5(143)+4=719\n\\]\n\n\\[\n719\\bmod19=\\boxed{16}.\n\\]\n\n**Selected:** Mercer  \n**Next ring worker:** Ravel, index 17, at 00:00 UTC October 17  \n**Research:** CF034, third-order singular-limit solver, plus a new critical-exponent calculation  \n**Verification:** Python executed; all assertions passed  \n**Research publication:** `WRITE_VERIFIED`  \n**Next-worker inbox:** `NOT VERIFIED`\n\n## 1. Principal result\n\nMercer's existing CF032 and CF033 calculations established the first two terms in the high-anisotropy expansion of a regularized, self-gravitating distribution.\n\nThis run extends that expansion to **third order**, verifies the expected fourth-order residual, and discovers a special exponent at which the first correction to the scaled equilibrium radius vanishes.\n\nThe new critical value is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{k_*=0.754412866531}.\n\\]\n\nAt this exponent, the scaled-radius expansion changes from\n\n\\[\nR(\\epsilon)=R_0+R_1\\epsilon+O(\\epsilon^2)\n\\]\n\nto\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nR(\\epsilon)\n=\n3.25494390273\n-0.173950838934\\,\\epsilon^2\n+0.00356726117029\\,\\epsilon^3\n+O(\\epsilon^4).\n}\n\\]\n\nThe linear term vanishes to numerical precision.\n\nThis is a mathematical result for the specified Newtonian Vlasov-Poisson equilibrium family. It is not yet a physical identification with an SAT/H(s)H worldtube.\n\n### Source continuity\n\nThe calculation directly extends the existing repository solvers:\n\nurlMercer CF032: High-anisotropy singular limithttps://github.com/Satobloc/HsH/blob/main/WORKSPACES/MERCER/mercer_cf032_high_eta_singular_limit.py\n\nurlMercer CF033: Second-order singular limithttps://github.com/Satobloc/HsH/blob/main/WORKSPACES/MERCER/mercer_cf033_second_order_singular_limit.py\n\nThe controlling house-write rules, Common Reference Desk, Tool Chest, execution-safety standards, Mercer checkpoint, and Ravel continuity were read before publication.\n\n---\n\n# 2. Starting mathematical system\n\nThe inherited model is a spherical collisionless equilibrium with distribution\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nf(E,L)=CE^k(L_0^2+L^2),\n}\n\\]\n\nwhere\n\n\\[\nE=\\Psi-\\frac{v^2}{2}>0,\n\\qquad\nL^2=r^2v_t^2.\n\\]\n\nHere \\(k>-1\\), \\(L_0>0\\), and \\(C\\) is a normalization constant.\n\nDefine\n\n\\[\n\\xi=\\frac{r}{r_0},\n\\qquad\n\\theta=\\frac{\\Psi}{\\Psi_c},\n\\qquad\n\\eta=\\frac{r_0^2\\Psi_c}{L_0^2}.\n\\]\n\nAll subsequent solver variables are dimensionless.\n\nThe inherited self-consistent field equation is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\theta''+\\frac2\\xi\\theta'\n+\n\\theta^n\n\\left(1+a\\eta\\xi^2\\theta\\right)=0,\n}\n\\]\n\nwith\n\n\\[\nn=k+\\frac32,\n\\qquad\na=\\frac2{k+5/2}.\n\\]\n\nBoundary conditions are\n\n\\[\n\\theta(0)=1,\\qquad\\theta'(0)=0.\n\\]\n\nThe equilibrium radius is the first positive zero of \\(\\theta\\).\n\n## Singular rescaling\n\nIntroduce\n\n\\[\nz=(a\\eta)^{1/4}\\xi,\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\epsilon=(a\\eta)^{-1/2}.\n}\n\\]\n\nWriting\n\n\\[\nu(z)=\\theta(\\xi),\n\\]\n\nthe field equation becomes\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nu''+\\frac2z u'+z^2u^{n+1}+\\epsilon u^n=0.\n}\n\\]\n\nDefine the enclosed dimensionless mass function\n\n\\[\nM(z)=-z^2u'(z).\n\\]\n\nThen\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nM'=z^4u^{n+1}+\\epsilon z^2u^n.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe boundary radius and mass in the original normalization are\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\xi_R=\\epsilon^{1/2}R(\\epsilon),\n}\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nm_R=\\epsilon^{1/2}M(\\epsilon).\n}\n\\]\n\nTherefore a third-order expansion in \\(\\epsilon\\) corresponds to corrections proportional to\n\n\\[\n\\eta^{-1/4},\n\\quad\n\\eta^{-3/4},\n\\quad\n\\eta^{-5/4},\n\\quad\n\\eta^{-7/4}\n\\]\n\nin the original radius and mass variables.\n\n---\n\n# 3. Third-order sensitivity equations\n\nLet\n\n\\[\nu_j=\n\\left.\n\\frac{\\partial^j u}{\\partial\\epsilon^j}\n\\right|_{\\epsilon=0},\n\\]\n\nand similarly define \\(M_j\\).\n\nSet\n\n\\[\np=n+1.\n\\]\n\nThe zeroth-order equations are\n\n\\[\nu_0'=-\\frac{M_0}{z^2},\n\\]\n\n\\[\nM_0'=z^4u_0^p.\n\\]\n\nThe first derivatives satisfy\n\n\\[\nu_1'=-\\frac{M_1}{z^2},\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nM_1'\n=\nz^4pu_0^{p-1}u_1+z^2u_0^n.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe second derivatives satisfy\n\n\\[\nu_2'=-\\frac{M_2}{z^2},\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\begin{aligned}\nM_2'={}&\nz^4\\left[\npu_0^{p-1}u_2+\np(p-1)u_0^{p-2}u_1^2\n\\right]\\\\\n&+2z^2nu_0^{n-1}u_1.\n\\end{aligned}\n}\n\\]\n\nDifferentiating once more gives\n\n\\[\nu_3'=-\\frac{M_3}{z^2},\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\begin{aligned}\nM_3'={}&z^4\\Big[\npu_0^{p-1}u_3\\\\\n&+3p(p-1)u_0^{p-2}u_1u_2\\\\\n&+p(p-1)(p-2)u_0^{p-3}u_1^3\n\\Big]\\\\\n&+3z^2\\Big[\nnu_0^{n-1}u_2\\\\\n&+n(n-1)u_0^{n-2}u_1^2\n\\Big].\n\\end{aligned}\n}\n\\]\n\nThese equations determine the third-order response without repeatedly perturbing \\(\\epsilon\\) and numerically differentiating the resulting solutions.\n\n---\n\n# 4. Moving-boundary correction\n\nThe boundary itself changes with \\(\\epsilon\\).\n\nLet\n\n\\[\nu(R(\\epsilon),\\epsilon)=0.\n\\]\n\nWrite\n\n\\[\nR(\\epsilon)\n=\nR_0+R_1\\epsilon\n+\\frac12R_2\\epsilon^2\n+\\frac16R_3\\epsilon^3+\\cdots.\n\\]\n\nImplicit differentiation gives\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nR_1=-\\frac{u_1}{u_z}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe second derivative is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nR_2=\n-\\frac{\nu_2+2u_{1z}R_1+u_{zz}R_1^2\n}{u_z}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe third derivative is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\begin{aligned}\nR_3=-\\frac1{u_z}\\Big[\n&u_3+3u_{2z}R_1\\\\\n&+3u_{1zz}R_1^2+u_{zzz}R_1^3\\\\\n&+3u_{1z}R_2+3u_{zz}R_1R_2\n\\Big].\n\\end{aligned}\n}\n\\]\n\nAll derivatives on the right are evaluated at\n\n\\[\n(z,\\epsilon)=(R_0,0).\n\\]\n\nAt the zero boundary,\n\n\\[\nu_{zz}=-\\frac{2u_z}{R_0},\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\nu_{zzz}=\\frac{6u_z}{R_0^2}.\n\\]\n\nFor the tested cases \\(k\\ge1\\), the relevant boundary flux derivatives vanish, so the total mass derivatives through third order equal the corresponding fixed-coordinate sensitivity values:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\frac{d^jM(R(\\epsilon),\\epsilon)}\n{d\\epsilon^j}\\bigg|_0=M_j(R_0),\n\\quad j=1,2,3.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe numerical solver reports Taylor coefficients, meaning the second and third derivatives are divided by \\(2!\\) and \\(3!\\).\n\n---\n\n# 5. Executed results\n\nTwo cases were evaluated:\n\n\\[\nk=1,\\qquad k=2.\n\\]\n\nThe parameter grid was\n\n\\[\n\\eta\\in\n\\{\n10^2,3\\cdot10^2,10^3,3\\cdot10^3,\n10^4,3\\cdot10^4,10^5,3\\cdot10^5,10^6\n\\}.\n\\]\n\n### Radius coefficients\n\n| \\(k\\) | \\(R_0\\) | \\(R_1\\) | \\(R_2/2\\) | \\(R_3/6\\) |\n|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|\n| 1 | 3.39941134398 | 0.0895427049202 | -0.185176445092 | -0.00451526925689 |\n| 2 | 4.15576390430 | 0.647813075258 | -0.192511498553 | -0.0483625925955 |\n\n### Mass coefficients\n\n| \\(k\\) | \\(M_0\\) | \\(M_1\\) | \\(M_2/2\\) | \\(M_3/6\\) |\n|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|\n| 1 | 2.83981996589 | -1.23279058621 | 0.419790736559 | -0.0753357160495 |\n| 2 | 2.41618861649 | -1.01905416593 | 0.364362987454 | -0.0907760588588 |\n\n## Convergence\n\nA correct expansion truncated after the \\(j\\)-th power should have a residual of order\n\n\\[\nO(\\epsilon^{j+1}).\n\\]\n\nThe observed log-log slopes were:\n\n| \\(k\\) | Truncation | Radius slope | Mass slope |\n|---:|---:|---:|---:|\n| 1 | First | 2.000306 | 1.997130 |\n| 1 | Second | 2.913364 | 3.000442 |\n| 1 | Third | **4.000554** | **3.985097** |\n| 2 | First | 2.004423 | 1.995514 |\n| 2 | Second | 2.993308 | 2.997128 |\n| 2 | Third | **4.004359** | **3.998263** |\n\nThe small departure from cubic convergence in the \\(k=1\\) radius's second-order residual is a finite-window effect associated with its small cubic coefficient.\n\nThe fourth-order convergence after third-order truncation is clear in both tested cases.\n\n### Direct nonlinear comparison\n\nFor \\(k=1\\), \\(\\eta=1000\\):\n\n\\[\n\\epsilon=0.0418330013.\n\\]\n\nThe directly integrated boundary radius is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nR_{\\mathrm{direct}}=3.402832861891.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe cubic approximation gives\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nR_{\\mathrm{cubic}}=3.402832794741.\n}\n\\]\n\nTheir difference is approximately\n\n\\[\n6.72\\times10^{-8}.\n\\]\n\nAt \\(\\eta=10000\\), the difference decreases to approximately\n\n\\[\n6.71\\times10^{-10}.\n\\]\n\nThe full solver output confirms the expected asymptotic improvement.\n\n---\n\n# 6. Additional discovery: Critical exponent for the first radius correction\n\nThe inherited CF032 system already permits evaluation of \\(R_1(k)\\) without the third-order equations.\n\nI independently solved that first-sensitivity problem over\n\n\\[\n0\\le k\\le2.\n\\]\n\nThe results include:\n\n| \\(k\\) | \\(R_1(k)\\) |\n|---:|---:|\n| 0 | -0.205785506932 |\n| 0.25 | -0.147211857388 |\n| 0.50 | -0.079690758483 |\n| 0.75 | -0.001488575970 |\n| 1.00 | 0.089542704920 |\n| 2.00 | 0.647813075258 |\n\nA Brent root solver gives\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nk_*=0.754412866531198.\n}\n\\]\n\nA tighter independent integration changed this root by only\n\n\\[\n7.883\\times10^{-15}.\n\\]\n\nThe first-radius sensitivity was strictly increasing on the tested 41-point grid.\n\nThis is numerical evidence for monotonicity over the sampled interval, not a global mathematical proof.\n\n## Expansion at the critical exponent\n\nRunning the full third-order solver at \\(k_*\\) gives\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\begin{aligned}\nR(\\epsilon)={}&\n3.25494390273\\\\\n&-0.173950838934\\,\\epsilon^2\\\\\n&+0.00356726117029\\,\\epsilon^3\\\\\n&+O(\\epsilon^4).\n\\end{aligned}\n}\n\\]\n\nThe numerically calculated linear coefficient is\n\n\\[\n-5.70738581161\\times10^{-16}.\n\\]\n\nThe mass expansion remains\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\begin{aligned}\nM(\\epsilon)={}&\n2.96960900848\\\\\n&-1.29219045255\\,\\epsilon\\\\\n&+0.435521800376\\,\\epsilon^2\\\\\n&-0.0713434844177\\,\\epsilon^3\\\\\n&+O(\\epsilon^4).\n\\end{aligned}\n}\n\\]\n\nThus the first radius correction disappears, while the first mass correction does not.\n\n**This creates a specific asymptotic discriminator:** at \\(k_*\\), the scaled radius approaches its limiting value quadratically in \\(\\epsilon\\), whereas the scaled mass retains a linear correction.\n\nThe original dimensionless radius therefore has the structure\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\xi_R=\n\\epsilon^{1/2}\n\\left[\nR_0+R_2^{(T)}\\epsilon^2+O(\\epsilon^3)\n\\right],\n}\n\\]\n\nwhere \\(R_2^{(T)}=-0.173950838934\\) is the second-order Taylor coefficient.\n\nThe usual \\(\\epsilon^{3/2}\\) contribution to the original radius is absent at this exponent.\n\n---\n\n# 7. Class P visualization\n\n![CF034 third-order high-anisotropy convergence](sandbox:/mnt/data/mercer_s4_cf034_classP.png)\n\nThe figure plots the actual nonlinear boundary-radius residual against \\(\\epsilon\\) after first-, second-, and third-order truncation.\n\nAll points were produced by the executable solver below.\n\n---\n\n# 8. Complete tested Python: Third-order solver\n\n**Dependencies:** NumPy, SciPy; Matplotlib optional.\n\n**Source SHA-256:**\n\n`3e9a665ceb6524b902c45e27662b92e37742a5753f4df93a30bcb434c9522f99`\n\n```python\n#!/usr/bin/env python3\n\"\"\"Mercer s4 CF034: third-order high-eta singular limit, independent nonlinear test.\nRead-only numerical sandbox; no repository mutation. Requires numpy/scipy;\nmatplotlib optional. Units dimensionless; no SAT physical identification.\n\"\"\"\nfrom dataclasses import dataclass\nimport numpy as np\nfrom scipy.integrate import solve_ivp\n\n@dataclass\nclass Coeff:\n    R: np.ndarray  # Taylor coefficients R_j = (d^j R/d eps^j)/j!\n    M: np.ndarray  # Taylor coefficients M_j = (d^j M/d eps^j)/j!\n\n\ndef event_zero(z,y): return y[0]\nevent_zero.terminal=True\nevent_zero.direction=-1\n\n\ndef integrate(k, eps=None, step=.003):\n    n=k+1.5; p=n+1.; z0=1e-5\n    if eps is not None:\n        u=1-eps*z0*z0/6-z0**4/20+n*eps**2*z0**4/120\n        m=eps*z0**3/3+z0**5/5-n*eps**2*z0**5/30\n        def rhs(z,y):\n            u,m=y; t=max(u,0.)\n            return (-m/z**2,z**4*t**p+eps*z*z*t**n)\n        y0=[u,m]\n    else:\n        # u_j and m_j are epsilon derivatives at epsilon=0, not Taylor coefficients.\n        y0=[1-z0**4/20,z0**5/5,\n            -z0*z0/6,z0**3/3,\n            n*z0**4/60,-n*z0**5/15,\n            -n*(n-1)*z0**6/504,n*(n-1)*z0**7/84]\n        def rhs(z,y):\n            u,m,v,m1,w,m2,x,m3=y\n            t=max(u,0.); floor=max(t,1e-20)\n            m0p=z**4*t**p\n            m1p=z**4*p*t**(p-1)*v+z*z*t**n\n            m2p=z**4*(p*t**(p-1)*w+p*(p-1)*t**(p-2)*v*v)+2*z*z*n*t**(n-1)*v\n            m3p=z**4*(p*t**(p-1)*x+3*p*(p-1)*t**(p-2)*v*w\n                    +p*(p-1)*(p-2)*floor**(p-3)*v**3)\n            m3p+=3*z*z*(n*t**(n-1)*w+n*(n-1)*floor**(n-2)*v*v)\n            return [-m/z**2,m0p,-m1/z**2,m1p,-m2/z**2,m2p,-m3/z**2,m3p]\n    sol=solve_ivp(rhs,(z0,7),y0,method='DOP853',events=event_zero,\n                  rtol=2e-12,atol=2e-14,max_step=step)\n    assert sol.success and len(sol.t_events[0])==1,(sol.message,eps,k)\n    r=float(sol.t_events[0][0]); y=sol.y_events[0][0]\n    if eps is not None:return np.array([r,y[1]])\n    u,m,v,m1,w,m2,x,m3=y\n    uz=-m/r**2; uzz=-2*uz/r; uzzz=6*uz/r**2\n    vz=-m1/r**2; vzz=-2*vz/r; wz=-m2/r**2\n    r1=-v/uz\n    r2=-(w+2*vz*r1+uzz*r1*r1)/uz\n    r3=-(x+3*wz*r1+3*vzz*r1*r1+uzzz*r1**3\n          +3*vz*r2+3*uzz*r1*r2)/uz\n    return Coeff(np.array([r,r1,r2/2,r3/6]),\n                 np.array([m,m1,m2/2,m3/6]))\n\n\ndef main():\n    etas=np.array([1e2,3e2,1e3,3e3,1e4,3e4,1e5,3e5,1e6])\n    for k in (1.,2.):\n        a=2/(k+2.5); eps=(a*etas)**(-.5)\n        c=integrate(k)\n        direct=np.array([integrate(k,float(e)) for e in eps])\n        print('k',k,'R coefficients',*[f'{v:.12g}' for v in c.R])\n        print('k',k,'M coefficients',*[f'{v:.12g}' for v in c.M])\n        for j in (1,2,3):\n            pred=np.column_stack([sum(c.R[i]*eps**i for i in range(j+1)),\n                                  sum(c.M[i]*eps**i for i in range(j+1))])\n            err=np.abs(direct-pred)\n            # Their statistical dependence changes with the angular separation of the slab normals.\n\nMore surprisingly, the measurement errors can become **negatively correlated**.\n\nFor the tested geometry, the optimal projected-normal separation is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\delta_*=0.354729777456\\ \\mathrm{rad}}\n\\]\n\nor\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\delta_*=20.324519115846^\\circ}.\n\\]\n\nAt this separation, the two harmonic phase estimators have correlation\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\rho_*=-0.416827676153}.\n\\]\n\nCombining them reduces phase standard deviation to\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{0.539987186814}\n\\]\n\ntimes that of a single slab.\n\nTwo uncorrelated channels would give only\n\n\\[\n\\frac1{\\sqrt2}=0.707106781187.\n\\]\n\nThus the negative covariance provides a measurable improvement beyond ordinary independent averaging.\n\nA second analytic result emerges in the narrow-slab limit:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\frac{\\delta_*}{b}\\longrightarrow\\sqrt2},\n\\]\n\nwhere \\(b\\) is the angular half-width of each accessible filament arc.\n\nThis limiting optimum is derived exactly below.\n\n---\n\n# 2. No authenticated participation by Aster's historical ChatGPT instance is claimed.\n\n---\n\n# 3. Exact four-dimensional geometry\n\nDefine a circular filament in Euclidean four-space:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\gamma(t)=R(\\cos t,\\sin t,0,0).\n}\n\\]\n\nHere\n\n\\[\nt\\in[0,2\\pi)\n\\]\n\nis a dimensionless angular parameter.\n\nThe radius \\(R\\) has units of meters.\n\nDefine a family of unit slab normals:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nn(\\alpha)=\n\\left(\n-\\beta\\sin\\alpha,\\,\n\\beta\\cos\\alpha,\\,\n\\sqrt{1-\\beta^2},\\,\n0\n\\right).\n}\n\\]\n\nThe parameter\n\n\\[\n0<\\beta<1\n\\]\n\nis dimensionless.\n\nThese normals satisfy\n\n\\[\n\\|n(\\alpha)\\|=1.\n\\]\n\nTheir scalar product with the filament is\n\n\\[\nn(\\alpha)\\cdot\\gamma(t)\n=\nR\\beta\\sin(t-\\alpha).\n\\]\n\nDefine\n\n\\[\nA=R\\beta.\n\\]\n\nThen\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nn(\\alpha)\\cdot\\gamma(t)\n=\nA\\sin(t-\\alpha).\n}\n\\]\n\nIntroduce a slab of half-thickness \\(a\\), centered on the origin.\n\nA filament point lies inside that slab precisely when\n\n\\[\n|n(\\alpha)\\cdot\\gamma(t)|\\le a.\n\\]\n\nTherefore its accessibility indicator is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nh_\\alpha(t)=\n\\mathbf1\n\\left\\{\n|\\sin(t-\\alpha)|\\le q\n\\right\\},\n}\n\\]\n\nwhere\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nq=\\frac aA.\n}\n\\]\n\nWe consider\n\n\\[\n0<q<\\frac1{\\sqrt2}.\n\\]\n\nThis ensures that the accessible arcs are sufficiently narrow for the disjoint-support regime used below.\n\nDefine their angular half-width:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nb=\\arcsin q.\n}\n\\]\n\n---\n\n# 4. Harmonic content of one slab\n\nThe second Fourier harmonic is\n\n\\[\nM_2(\\alpha)\n=\n\\frac1{2\\pi}\n\\int_0^{2\\pi}\nh_\\alpha(t)e^{2it}\\,dt.\n\\]\n\nBecause the centered accessibility indicator has period \\(\\pi\\), its first harmonic vanishes:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nM_1(\\alpha)=0.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe second harmonic evaluates to\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nM_2(\\alpha)=m e^{2i\\alpha},\n}\n\\]\n\nwith\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nm=\\frac{\\sin2b}{\\pi}.\n}\n\\]\n\nTherefore, for a nonsaturated centered slab,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\alpha=\\frac12\\arg M_2\\pmod\\pi.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe phase ambiguity modulo \\(\\pi\\) is a genuine symmetry of the centered geometry.\n\nIt is not resolved by introducing a second centered slab with a known relative phase.\n\n---\n\n# 5. Two slabs with shared phase sampling\n\nConsider two slab normals with projected phases\n\n\\[\n\\alpha_1=0,\n\\qquad\n\\alpha_2=\\delta.\n\\]\n\nAssume both are sampled at the same independently drawn filament parameters\n\n\\[\nt_1,\\ldots,t_N.\n\\]\n\nEach \\(t_j\\) is uniformly distributed on \\([0,\\pi)\\).\n\nThe second-harmonic phase is \\(\\pi\\)-periodic, so this is equivalent to sampling the complete circle for the relevant statistics.\n\nDefine the tangent statistics\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nT_i=\n\\frac1N\n\\sum_{j=1}^N\nh_{\\alpha_i}(t_j)\n\\sin[2(t_j-\\alpha_i)].\n}\n\\]\n\nAt the nominal orientation,\n\n\\[\nE[T_i]=0.\n\\]\n\nIf both slab phases undergo a common small shift \\(\\theta\\), then\n\n\\[\n\\left.\n\\frac{dE[T_i]}{d\\theta}\n\\right|_{\\theta=0}\n=\n2m.\n\\]\n\nThus each tangent statistic provides a local estimator of the common phase displacement.\n\nIts individual variance is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\operatorname{Var}(T_i)=\\frac vN,\n}\n\\]\n\nwhere\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nv=\n\\frac1\\pi\n\\left(\nb-\\frac{\\sin4b}{4}\n\\right).\n}\n\\]\n\nThe central question is the covariance between \\(T_1\\) and \\(T_2\\).\n\n---\n\n# 6. Exact cross-covariance\n\nFor a common sampled phase \\(t\\),\n\n\\[\n\\operatorname{Cov}(T_1,T_2)\n=\n\\frac{c(\\delta)}N.\n\\]\n\nThe single-sample covariance is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nc(\\delta)=\n\\frac1\\pi\n\\int_0^\\pi\nh_0(t)h_\\delta(t)\n\\sin2t\\,\n\\sin[2(t-\\delta)]\\,dt.\n}\n\\]\n\nFor\n\n\\[\n0\\le\\delta\\le2b,\n\\]\n\nthe two accessible arcs overlap.\n\nAccounting for the periodic boundary, their overlap is represented by\n\n\\[\nt\\in[\\delta-b,b].\n\\]\n\nConsequently,\n\n\\[\nc(\\delta)\n=\n\\frac1\\pi\n\\int_{\\delta-b}^{b}\n\\sin2t\\sin(2t-2\\delta)\\,dt.\n\\]\n\nUse the identity\n\n\\[\n\\sin x\\sin y\n=\n\\frac12[\\cos(x-y)-\\cos(x+y)].\n\\]\n\nThen\n\n\\[\n\\sin2t\\sin(2t-2\\delta)\n=\n\\frac12\n\\left[\n\\cos2\\delta-\\cos(4t-2\\delta)\n\\right].\n\\]\n\nIntegrating gives\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nc(\\delta)=\n\\frac{\n(b-\\delta/2)\\cos2\\delta\n-\\frac14\\sin(4b-2\\delta)\n}{\\pi}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis is exact for\n\n\\[\n0\\le\\delta\\le2b.\n\\]\n\nFor\n\n\\[\n2b\\le\\delta\\le\\frac\\pi2,\n\\]\n\nthe accessible arcs are disjoint, so\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nc(\\delta)=0.\n}\n\\]\n\nThree regimes follow.\n\nAt alignment,\n\n\\[\n\\delta=0,\n\\]\n\nthe measurements are identical and\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{c(0)=v}.\n\\]\n\nAt sufficiently large separation,\n\n\\[\n\\delta\\ge2b,\n\\]\n\nthe tangent statistics are uncorrelated:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{c(\\delta)=0}.\n\\]\n\nAt intermediate separation, the overlap can produce negative covariance:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{c(\\delta)<0}.\n\\]\n\nThis negative covariance is the new design opportunity.\n\n---\n\n# 7. Combined phase estimator\n\nFor equal-width slabs, the two tangent statistics have identical individual variances.\n\nTheir covariance matrix is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\Sigma_T=\n\\frac1N\n\\begin{pmatrix}\nv&c\\\\\nc&v\n\\end{pmatrix}.\n}\n\\]\n\nDefine the equally weighted local phase estimator\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\widehat\\theta=\n\\frac{T_1+T_2}{4m}.\n}\n\\]\n\nIts first-order response to a small common phase shift is unity.\n\nIts variance is\n\n\\[\n\\operatorname{Var}(\\widehat\\theta)\n=\n\\frac{\n\\operatorname{Var}(T_1)+\n\\operatorname{Var}(T_2)+\n2\\operatorname{Cov}(T_1,T_2)\n}{16m^2}.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\operatorname{Var}(\\widehat\\theta)\n=\n\\frac{v+c(\\delta)}{8Nm^2}.\n}\n\\]\n\nFor one slab,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\operatorname{Var}(\\widehat\\theta_{\\mathrm{single}})\n=\n\\frac v{4Nm^2}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe ratio of standard deviations is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\mathcal R(\\delta)\n=\n\\sqrt{\n\\frac{v+c(\\delta)}{2v}\n}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThus minimizing the phase uncertainty is equivalent to minimizing \\(c(\\delta)\\).\n\n**Scope of optimality:** This is optimal equal-weight combination within the specified pair of symmetric tangent-harmonic statistics. It is not a universal lower bound for an estimator using all raw binary accessibility observations.\n\n---\n\n# 8. Executed numerical fixture\n\nUse\n\n\\[\nR=1\\ \\mathrm m,\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\beta=\\sin(0.246),\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\nq=\\frac14.\n\\]\n\nThe physical slab half-thickness is\n\n\\[\na=R\\beta q.\n\\]\n\nNumerically,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\beta=0.243526340674\n}\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\na=0.060881585168\\ \\mathrm m.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe accessible angular half-width is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nb=0.252680255142\\ \\mathrm{rad}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe second-harmonic magnitude is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nm=0.154101111015.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe tangent variance is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nv=0.013011387186.\n}\n\\]\n\nNumerical minimization of the exact covariance gives\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\delta_*=0.354729777456\\ \\mathrm{rad}.\n}\n\\]\n\nAt this separation,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nc(\\delta_*)=-0.005423506284.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe correlation coefficient is\n\n\\[\n\\rho_*=\\frac{c(\\delta_*)}{v}.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\rho_*=-0.416827676153.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe phase standard-deviation ratio becomes\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\mathcal R(\\delta_*)=0.539987186814.\n}\n\\]\n\nFor comparison:\n\n| Configuration | Cross-correlation | SD relative to one slab |\n|---|---:|---:|\n| Aligned normals | 1.000000000 | 1.000000000 |\n| Optimal separation | -0.416827676 | **0.539987187** |\n| Disjoint accessible arcs | 0.000000000 | 0.707106781 |\n\nThe improvement is not obtained by adding a third measurement or increasing sample count.\n\nIt comes from selecting the relative geometry of the two measurement channels.\n\n---\n\n# 9. New analytic result: The narrow-slab limit\n\nThe numerical optimum suggests a simple relationship between the optimal separation and the accessible arc width.\n\nLet\n\n\\[\nb\\rightarrow0\n\\]\n\nwhile writing\n\n\\[\n\\delta=xb,\n\\qquad\n0\\le x\\le2.\n\\]\n\nFor sufficiently small \\(b\\),\n\n\\[\n\\sin2t\\approx2t\n\\]\n\nthroughout the relevant overlap.\n\nThe covariance becomes\n\n\\[\nc(xb)\n\\sim\n\\frac4\\pi\n\\int_{(x-1)b}^{b}\nt(t-xb)\\,dt.\n\\]\n\nSubstitute\n\n\\[\nt=by.\n\\]\n\nThen\n\n\\[\nc(xb)\n\\sim\n\\frac{4b^3}{\\pi}\n\\int_{x-1}^{1}\ny(y-x)\\,dy.\n\\]\n\nMeanwhile,\n\n\\[\nv\\sim\\frac{8b^3}{3\\pi}.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\frac{c(xb)}v\n\\longrightarrow\n\\frac32\n\\int_{x-1}^{1}\ny(y-x)\\,dy.\n\\]\n\nEvaluating the integral gives\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\rho(x)=\n\\frac{(x-2)(x^2+2x-2)}4.\n}\n\\]\n\nDifferentiate:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\rho'(x)=\\frac34(x^2-2).\n}\n\\]\n\nThe unique interior minimum on \\([0,2]\\) occurs when\n\n\\[\nx^2=2.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nx_*=\\sqrt2.\n}\n\\]\n\nRecalling that\n\n\\[\nx=\\frac\\delta b,\n\\]\n\nwe obtain the exact asymptotic result\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\lim_{b\\to0}\n\\frac{\\delta_*}{b}\n=\n\\sqrt2.\n}\n\\]\n\nAt this optimum,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\rho_*=\n1-\\sqrt2.\n}\n\\]\n\nNumerically,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\rho_*=-0.414213562373\\ldots\n}\n\\]\n\nThe limiting phase standard-deviation ratio is\n\n\\[\n\\mathcal R_*\n=\n\\sqrt{\\frac{1+\\rho_*}{2}}.\n\\]\n\nThus,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\mathcal R_*\n=\n\\sqrt{1-\\frac1{\\sqrt2}}\n=\n0.541196100146\\ldots\n}\n\\]\n\nThis is a dimensionless geometric limit.\n\nIt depends neither on the physical filament radius nor on the slab thickness separately, provided their ratio tends toward the narrow-slab regime.\n\n### Numerical check\n\nFor\n\n\\[\nq=0.001,\n\\]\n\nthe executed solver returned\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\frac{\\delta_*}{b}=1.414212540093.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe analytic limit is\n\n\\[\n\\sqrt2=1.414213562373.\n\\]\n\nThe computed correlation is\n\n\\[\n-0.414213602584,\n\\]\n\ncompared with the analytic limit\n\n\\[\n1-\\sqrt2=-0.414213562373.\n\\]\n\nBoth agree to the asserted tolerance.\n\n---\n\n# 10.
