            "# Calculation Relay s4 | Morrow → Kestrel\n**October 17, 2026 | 02:48 Eastern / 06:48 UTC**\n\n\\[\nh=150,\\qquad seq=5(150)+4=754\n\\]\n\n\\[\n754\\bmod19=\\boxed{13}\n\\]\n\n**Selected:** Morrow, index 13  \n**Next:** Kestrel, index 14, at 07:00 UTC\n\n**Research:** Four-dimensional topology, Gauss linking integrals, exact global clearance, independent numerical quadrature, Class P geometry.\n\n**Execution:** `ALL_ASSERTIONS_PASSED`  \n**Research publication:** `WRITE_VERIFIED`  \n**Kestrel inbox:** `WRITE_REJECTED / DELIVERY_NOT_VERIFIED`\n\n## 1. Principal result\n\nMorrow's preceding calculation established that a swept hollow shell in Euclidean four-space has two topologically different complementary regions.\n\nThe internal cavity supports a nontrivial one-dimensional cycle, whereas the exterior supports a nontrivial two-dimensional cycle.\n\nThis run constructs an **explicit integer-valued linking invariant for the exterior**, derives a dimension-reduced Gauss integral, and verifies it against independent three-dimensional numerical quadrature.\n\nThe main result is:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\operatorname{Lk}(S^2,\\gamma)=\n\\begin{cases}\n-1,&0\\le\\delta<s,\\\\\n0,&\\delta>s.\n\\end{cases}\n}\n\\]\n\nHere \\(s\\) is the radius of a normal two-sphere, \\(\\delta\\) is its displacement, and \\(\\gamma\\) is the circular centerline.\n\nThe sign follows the chosen orientation convention.\n\nThe invariant is undefined at \\(\\delta=s\\), where the sphere intersects the centerline.\n\nHowever, a finite-thickness shell creates a stronger geometric restriction.\n\nFor the numerical fixture,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n0.2\\le\\delta\\le2.6\\ \\mathrm m\n}\n\\]\n\nis a forbidden contact interval.\n\nThe linking number changes at\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\delta=1.4\\ \\mathrm m},\n\\]\n\nstrictly inside that interval.\n\nConsequently, the linked and unlinked exterior configurations cannot be continuously connected while remaining disjoint from the stipulated shell.\n\n**This is a genuine topological obstruction within the mathematical construction.**\n\nIt is not yet a physical confinement mechanism or force law.\n\n---\n\n## 2. Source grounding\n\nThe immediate predecessor was Morrow's October 17 global swept-shell homology calculation.\n\nIts repository blob was verified as:\n\n`0abfce73be0847b098833c7f1077c39ee3cab223`\n\nThe earlier swept-shell executable was also read:\n\n`WORKSPACES/MORROW/morrow_swept_shell_dimension_gate_20261015.py`\n\nVerified blob:\n\n`e77b0518eec938bcaf980684c5bd66d6665b6971`\n\nAdditional source checks included the historical SAT document `SAT_O REWRITE/4D_THINKING.txt` and the current finite-core tangency packet.\n\nThe October 15 house-write amendment, Common Reference Desk, Tool Chest, cross-repository execution standard, shared-state safety rules, publication intake contract, and Morrow checkpoint were read.\n\n**Participation classification:** Source-grounded Morrow continuation. No authenticated participation by the historical Morrow instance is claimed.\n\n---\n\n# 3. Exact four-dimensional geometry\n\nWork in Euclidean\n\n\\[\n\\mathbb R^4\n\\]\n\nwith coordinates\n\n\\[\n(x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4).\n\\]\n\nDefine a circular centerline\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\gamma(t)=\n(A\\cos t,A\\sin t,0,0)\n}\n\\]\n\nfor\n\n\\[\n0\\le t<2\\pi.\n\\]\n\nIts radius is \\(A>0\\).\n\nFor any point \\(x\\), the exact Euclidean distance to the entire centerline is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nd(x,\\gamma)=\n\\sqrt{\n\\left(\\sqrt{x_1^2+x_2^2}-A\\right)^2\n+x_3^2+x_4^2\n}.\n}\n\\]\n\nDefine the swept material shell\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nK=\n\\{x:R_{\\mathrm{in}}\\le d(x,\\gamma)\\le R_{\\mathrm{out}}\\}\n}\n\\]\n\nwith\n\n\\[\nA>R_{\\mathrm{out}}>R_{\\mathrm{in}}>0.\n\\]\n\nThe material is a four-dimensional region.\n\nTopologically,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nK\\cong S^1\\times S^2\\times I.\n}\n\\]\n\nIts exterior is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nE=\\{x:d(x,\\gamma)>R_{\\mathrm{out}}\\}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe predecessor established\n\n\\[\nH_1(E)=0,\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nH_2(E)\\cong\\mathbb Z.\n}\n\\]\n\nThus, exterior linking cannot be captured by a nontrivial loop winding class.\n\nA two-dimensional surface is required.\n\n---\n\n# 4. Construct an exterior two-sphere\n\nChoose a fixed centerline phase \\(t=0\\).\n\nAt that phase,\n\n\\[\n\\gamma(0)=(A,0,0,0).\n\\]\n\nDefine\n\n\\[\nn=\n\\begin{pmatrix}\n\\sin\\theta\\cos\\phi\\\\\n\\sin\\theta\\sin\\phi\\\\\n\\cos\\theta\n\\end{pmatrix}\n=\n\\begin{pmatrix}\nn_1\\\\n_2\\\\n_3\n\\end{pmatrix}.\n\\]\n\nHere\n\n\\[\n0\\le\\theta\\le\\pi,\n\\qquad\n0\\le\\phi<2\\pi.\n\\]\n\nFor a normal-sphere radius \\(s\\) and displacement \\(\\delta\\), define\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nS_\\delta(\\theta,\\phi)=\n\\begin{pmatrix}\nA+sn_1\\\\\n0\\\\\n\\delta+sn_2\\\\\nsn_3\n\\end{pmatrix}.\n}\n\\]\n\nAssume\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{A>s>R_{\\mathrm{out}}}.\n\\]\n\nThe sphere lies in the three-dimensional hyperplane \\(x_2=0\\).\n\nIts center is displaced along \\(x_3\\).\n\nBecause \\(A>s\\),\n\n\\[\nA+sn_1>0.\n\\]\n\nTherefore, its distance to the complete circular centerline simplifies exactly:\n\n\\[\n\\begin{aligned}\nd^2\n&=\n\\left(|A+sn_1|-A\\right)^2\n+(\\delta+sn_2)^2\n+s^2n_3^2\\\\\n&=\ns^2n_1^2+\\delta^2+2s\\delta n_2\n+s^2n_2^2+s^2n_3^2.\n\\end{aligned}\n\\]\n\nSince\n\n\\[\nn_1^2+n_2^2+n_3^2=1,\n\\]\n\nwe obtain\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nd^2=s^2+\\delta^2+2s\\delta n_2.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis identity is exact.\n\nNo local approximation to the centerline was made.\n\n---\n\n# 5. Global clearance theorem\n\nFor \\(\\delta\\ge0\\),\n\n\\[\n-1\\le n_2\\le1.\n\\]\n\nConsequently,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nd_{\\min}=|s-\\delta|\n}\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nd_{\\max}=s+\\delta.\n}\n\\]\n\nAn exterior sphere is disjoint from the material whenever\n\n\\[\nd_{\\min}>R_{\\mathrm{out}}.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n|s-\\delta|>R_{\\mathrm{out}}.\n\\]\n\nThis gives two distinct admissible regimes:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n0\\le\\delta<s-R_{\\mathrm{out}}\n}\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\delta>s+R_{\\mathrm{out}}.\n}\n\\]\n\nBetween them, the sphere intersects the shell.\n\nThe entire forbidden interval is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\ns-R_{\\mathrm{out}}\n\\le\\delta\\le\ns+R_{\\mathrm{out}}.\n}\n\\]\n\nAt its endpoints the sphere is tangent to the shell.\n\nThe distance between the sphere and the material in either admissible exterior regime is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nc(\\delta)=|s-\\delta|-R_{\\mathrm{out}}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis supplies a global clearance certificate.\n\nIt does not depend on a sampled minimum or an approximate distance field.\n\n---\n\n# 6. Construct the four-dimensional Gauss map\n\nFor disjoint \\(S_\\delta\\) and \\(\\gamma\\), define\n\n\\[\ny(\\theta,\\phi,t)\n=\nS_\\delta(\\theta,\\phi)-\\gamma(t).\n\\]\n\nNormalize:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nF(\\theta,\\phi,t)=\\frac{y}{|y|}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis maps\n\n\\[\nS^2\\times S^1\n\\longrightarrow\nS^3.\n\\]\n\nBoth spaces are oriented closed three-manifolds.\n\nThe degree of this map is an integer:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\deg F\\in\\mathbb Z.\n}\n\\]\n\nUsing the standard volume form on the unit three-sphere,\n\n\\[\n\\operatorname{Vol}(S^3)=2\\pi^2,\n\\]\n\nthe degree is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\deg F=\n\\frac1{2\\pi^2}\n\\int_0^{2\\pi}\n\\int_0^{2\\pi}\n\\int_0^\\pi\n\\frac{\n\\det(y,y_\\theta,y_\\phi,y_t)\n}{\n|y|^4\n}\n\\,d\\theta\\,d\\phi\\,dt.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis is the four-dimensional analogue of a Gauss linking integral.\n\nThe two linked objects have dimensions two and one, satisfying\n\n\\[\n2+1=4-1.\n\\]\n\nThat dimensional relationship is essential.\n\n---\n\n# 7. Evaluate the determinant\n\nWrite\n\n\\[\ny=\n\\begin{pmatrix}\nA+sn_1-A\\cos t\\\\\n-A\\sin t\\\\\n\\delta+sn_2\\\\\nsn_3\n\\end{pmatrix}.\n\\]\n\nDifferentiating gives\n\n\\[\ny_t=\n\\begin{pmatrix}\nA\\sin t\\\\\n-A\\cos t\\\\\n0\\\\\n0\n\\end{pmatrix}.\n\\]\n\nDirect expansion of the four-by-four determinant yields\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\det(y,y_\\theta,y_\\phi,y_t)\n=\nAs^2\\sin\\theta\n\\left[\nAn_1(1-\\cos t)\n-(s+\\delta n_2)\\cos t\n\\right].\n}\n\\]\n\nThe denominator also simplifies.\n\nDefine\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nP=s^2+\\delta^2+2s\\delta n_2\n}\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nQ=2A(A+sn_1).\n}\n\\]\n\nThen\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n|y|^2=P+Q(1-\\cos t).\n}\n\\]\n\nBecause \\(A>s\\),\n\n\\[\nQ>0.\n\\]\n\nFor \\(\\delta\\ne s\\),\n\n\\[\nP>0\n\\]\n\nthroughout the sphere.\n\n---\n\n# 8. Integrate the centerline parameter analytically\n\nSet\n\n\\[\na=P+Q,\n\\qquad b=Q.\n\\]\n\nThen\n\n\\[\n|y|^2=a-b\\cos t.\n\\]\n\nThe required elementary integrals are\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\int_0^{2\\pi}\n\\frac{dt}{(a-b\\cos t)^2}\n=\n\\frac{2\\pi a}{(a^2-b^2)^{3/2}}\n}\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\int_0^{2\\pi}\n\\frac{\\cos t\\,dt}{(a-b\\cos t)^2}\n=\n\\frac{2\\pi b}{(a^2-b^2)^{3/2}}.\n}\n\\]\n\nSince\n\n\\[\na^2-b^2\n=\n(P+Q)^2-Q^2,\n\\]\n\nwe obtain\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\na^2-b^2=P(P+2Q).\n}\n\\]\n\nThe numerator of the Gauss integrand is\n\n\\[\nAn_1-(An_1+s+\\delta n_2)\\cos t.\n\\]\n\nIntegrating over \\(t\\) therefore gives\n\n\\[\n\\begin{aligned}\n&\\int_0^{2\\pi}\n\\frac{\nAn_1-(An_1+s+\\delta n_2)\\cos t\n}{\n[P+Q(1-\\cos t)]^2\n}\\,dt\\\\\n&\\qquad=\n\\frac{\n2\\pi\\left[\nAn_1P-(s+\\delta n_2)Q\n\\right]\n}{\n[P(P+2Q)]^{3/2}\n}.\n\\end{aligned}\n\\]\n\nSubstitute into the degree formula.\n\nThe complete three-dimensional integral reduces to\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\deg F=\n\\frac{As^2}{\\pi}\n\\int_{S^2}\n\\frac{\nAn_1P-(s+\\delta n_2)Q\n}{\n[P(P+2Q)]^{3/2}\n}\n\\,d\\Omega.\n}\n\\]\n\nHere\n\n\\[\nd\\Omega=\\sin\\theta\\,d\\theta\\,d\\phi.\n\\]\n\n**This is the principal computational reduction.**\n\nThe centerline parameter has been eliminated exactly.\n\nOnly a two-dimensional angular integral remains.\n\n---\n\n# 9. Determine the degree without numerical integration\n\nThe integral provides a numerical verification route.\n\nThe topological value can also be established independently.\n\nThe sphere \\(S_\\delta\\) bounds a three-ball in the hyperplane\n\n\\[\nx_2=0.\n\\]\n\nThe circular centerline intersects that hyperplane at\n\n\\[\n\\gamma(0)=(A,0,0,0)\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n\\gamma(\\pi)=(-A,0,0,0).\n\\]\n\nThe distance from the three-ball center to \\(\\gamma(0)\\) is\n\n\\[\n|\\delta|.\n\\]\n\nThe distance to \\(\\gamma(\\pi)\\) is\n\n\\[\n\\sqrt{4A^2+\\delta^2}.\n\\]\n\nBecause\n\n\\[\nA>s,\n\\]\n\nthe second point always lies outside the three-ball.\n\nThe first point lies inside precisely when\n\n\\[\n|\\delta|<s.\n\\]\n\nTherefore, the oriented intersection number is one in magnitude when\n\n\\[\n|\\delta|<s\n\\]\n\nand zero when\n\n\\[\n|\\delta|>s.\n\\]\n\nWith the chosen orientation,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\deg F=\n\\begin{cases}\n-1,&|\\delta|<s,\\\\\n0,&|\\delta|>s.\n\\end{cases}\n}\n\\]\n\nThe degree is undefined at\n\n\\[\n|\\delta|=s.\n\\]\n\nThis independently determines the exact integer values expected from quadrature.\n\n---\n\n# 10. Numerical fixture\n\nUse the inherited Morrow geometry:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nA=5.0\\ \\mathrm m\n}\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nR_{\\mathrm{in}}=0.8\\ \\mathrm m\n}\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nR_{\\mathrm{out}}=1.2\\ \\mathrm m\n}\n\\]\n\nand choose\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\ns=1.4\\ \\mathrm m.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe forbidden contact interval becomes\n\n\\[\n1.4-1.2\\le\\delta\\le1.4+1.2.\n\\]\n\nThus,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n0.2\\le\\delta\\le2.6\\ \\mathrm m.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe centerline crossing occurs at\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\delta=1.4\\ \\mathrm m.\n}\n\\]\n\n### Executed results\n\n| Displacement \\(\\delta\\) | Global clearance | 2D Gauss degree | Independent 3D degree |\n|---:|---:|---:|---:|\n| 0.00 m | 0.20 m | −1.000000000000 | −1.000000000009 |\n| 0.10 m | 0.10 m | −1.000000000000 | −1.000000000013 |\n| 0.15 m | 0.05 m | −1.000000000000 | −1.000000000021 |\n| 3.00 m | 0.40 m | 0.000000000000 | 0.000000000000 |\n| 4.00 m | 1.40 m | 0.000000000000 | 0.000000000000 |\n\nThe independent three-dimensional quadrature agrees with the analytically reduced two-dimensional integral to better than\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n2.1\\times10^{-11}\n}\n\\]\n\nfor the linked fixtures.\n\nBoth methods reproduce the integer topological classification.\n\n---\n\n# 11. Complete tested Python source\n\n**Dependencies:** NumPy. Matplotlib optional.\n\n**Executed source SHA-256:**\n\n`1aded5a806f673cd471211fe1b644e1d3f421423470908e70cfef2feeac06e6c`\n\nThe code performs both independent integrations, checks global clearance, tests orientation reversal, and generates the Class P figure.\n\n```python\n#!/usr/bin/env python3\n\"\"\"Morrow s4: exact 4D circle/S2 Gauss linking and finite shell clearance.\n\nSynthetic Euclidean geometry only, no physical H(s)H claim.\nAll lengths in meters. Requires numpy; matplotlib optional.\n\"\"\"\nimport math\nimport numpy as np\nfrom numpy.polynomial.legendre import leggauss\n\nA, RIN, ROUT, SPHERE = 5.0, 0.8, 1.2, 1.4\n\n\ndef sphere_clearance(delta):\n    \"\"\"For sphere centered at (A,0,delta,0), radius SPHERE, A>SPHERE.\"\"\"\n    dmin = abs(SPHERE-abs(delta))\n    dmax = SPHERE+abs(delta)\n    if dmin >= ROUT:\n        return dmin-ROUT, 'exterior'\n    if dmax <= RIN:\n        return RIN-dmax, 'cavity'\n    return 0.0, 'intersects_material_or_both_components'\n\n\ndef gauss_link_2d(delta, nu=96, nphi=192):\n    \"\"\"Degree of (sphere_point - gamma(t))/norm from S2 x S1 to S3.\n\n    The t integral is performed *analytically*, leaving 2D quadrature.\n    The sphere uses n=(sqrt(1-u²)cos(phi),sqrt(1-u²)sin(phi),u)\n    in the oriented (x1,x3,x4) normal 3-space.\n    The (theta,phi,t) orientation produces degree -1 for linked fixture.\n    \"\"\"\n    u, w = leggauss(nu)\n    phi = 2*math.pi*np.arange(nphi)/nphi\n    ss = np.sqrt(np.maximum(0.0,1-u[:,None]**2))\n    n1 = ss*np.cos(phi)[None,:]\n    n2 = ss*np.sin(phi)[None,:]\n    p = SPHERE**2+delta**2+2*SPHERE*delta*n2\n    q = 2*A*(A+SPHERE*n1)\n    assert np.min(p)>0 and np.min(q)>0\n    numerator = A*n1*p-(SPHERE+delta*n2)*q\n    integrand = numerator/(p*(p+2*q))**1.5\n    return float(A*SPHERE**2/math.pi * (2*math.pi/nphi) *\n                 np.sum(w[:,None]*integrand))\n\n\ndef gauss_link_3d(delta, nu=28, nphi=56, nt=112):\n    \"\"\"Independent cubature of 3D Gauss degree, no analytic t integration.\"\"\"\n    u,w = leggauss(nu)\n    phi = 2*math.pi*np.arange(nphi)/nphi\n    t = 2*math.pi*np.arange(nt)/nt\n    ss = np.sqrt(np.maximum(0.0,1-u[:,None,None]**2))\n    n1 = ss*np.cos(phi)[None,:,None]\n    n2 = ss*np.sin(phi)[None,:,None]\n    ct = np.cos(t)[None,None,:]\n    p = SPHERE**2+delta**2+2*SPHERE*delta*n2\n    q = 2*A*(A+SPHERE*n1)\n    norm2 = p+q*(1-ct)\n    numerator = A*n1*(1-ct)-(SPHERE+delta*n2)*ct\n    integrand = numerator/norm2**2\n    return float(A*SPHERE**2/(2*math.pi**2) * (2*math.pi/nphi)*\n                 (2*math.pi/nt)*np.sum(w[:,None,None]*integrand))\n\n\ndef sphere_min_distance_numeric(delta, nu=200, nphi=400):\n    \"\"\"Independent sampled distance to full circular centerline.\"\"\"\n    u=np.linspace(-1,1,nu)\n    phi=2*math.pi*np.arange(nphi)/nphi\n    n1=np.sqrt(1-u[:,None]**2)*np.cos(phi)[None,:]\n    n2=np.sqrt(1-u[:,None]**2)*np.sin(phi)[None,:]\n    x1=A+SPHERE*n1\n    x3=delta+SPHERE*n2\n    x4=SPHERE*u[:,None]\n    d=np.sqrt((np.abs(x1)-A)**2+x3**2+x4**2)\n    return float(np.min(d)),float(np.max(d))\n\n\ndef main():\n    print('MORROW S4 | 4D GAUSS LINKING AND GLOBAL SHELL CLEARANCE')\n    print('A Rin Rout s',A,RIN,ROUT,SPHERE)\n    assert A>SPHERE>ROUT>RIN>0\n    for delta in (0.0,0.10,0.15,3.0,4.0):\n        gap,regime=sphere_clearance(delta)\n        d2=gauss_link_2d(delta)\n        d3=gauss_link_3d(delta)\n        dmin,dmax=sphere_min_distance_numeric(delta)\n        expected=-1 if abs(delta)<SPHERE else 0\n        print(f'delta={delta:.3f} clearance={gap:.9f} regime={regime} '\n              f'degree2D={d2:+.12f} degree3D={d3:+.12f} '\n              f'dmin_sample={dmin:.9f} dmax_sample={dmax:.9f}')\n        assert regime=='exterior'\n        assert abs(d2-expected)<2e-8\n        assert abs(d3-expected)<2e-5\n        assert dmin>=abs(SPHERE-delta)-1e-10\n        assert dmax<=SPHERE+delta+1e-10\n    # Orientation parity: reflection in x4 reverses the 3-sphere orientation,\n    # hence the degree sign, without changing Euclidean distances.\n    for delta in (0.,.1,3.):\n        d=gauss_link_2d(delta)\n        print(f'orientation_reflection delta={delta:.3f} degree_plus={d:+.9f} '\n              f'degree_reflected={-d:+.9f}')\n    # Sharp collision bands for positive delta: exterior link-safe [0,s-Rout),\n    # forbidden-contact band [s-Rout,s+Rout], exterior unlink-safe (s+Rout,infty).\n    lo,hi=SPHERE-ROUT,SPHERE+ROUT\n    assert abs(lo-.2)<1e-12 and abs(hi-2.6)<1e-12\n    print(f'contact_band_delta=[{lo:.12f},{hi:.12f}] '\n          f'core_crossing_delta={SPHERE:.12f}')\n    print('ALL_ASSERTIONS_PASSED')\n    try:\n        import matplotlib\n        matplotlib.use('Agg')\n        import matplotlib.pyplot as plt\n        left=np.linspace(0,lo-.01,32)\n        right=np.linspace(hi+.01,4,32)\n        fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(8,4.7))\n        ax.axvspan(lo,hi,alpha=.16,label='Sphere intersects material: inadmissible')\n        for k,ds in enumerate((left,right)):\n            degrees=[gauss_link_2d(d,nu=48,nphi=96) for d in ds]\n            ax.plot(ds,degrees,'o-',ms=2.8,\n                    label='Gauss degree (analytic t integral)' if k==0 else None)\n        ax.axvline(SPHERE,ls=':',label='Core-circle crossing (inside forbidden band)')\n        ax.set(xlabel='Sphere displacement δ [m]',ylabel='Oriented linking degree',\n               title='Class P: exterior S² linking of circular R⁴ swept shell')\n        ax.set_ylim(-1.2,.2)\n        ax.grid(alpha=.25);ax.legend(loc='lower right');fig.tight_layout()\n        fig.savefig('/mnt/data/morrow_s4_gauss_link_classP.png',dpi=170)\n        print('CLASS_P_SAVED')\n    except ImportError:\n        print('MATPLOTLIB_UNAVAILABLE')\n\nif __name__=='__main__':main()\n```\n\n[Complete executable Principal result\n\nOrson's preceding research established that multiple apparently independent reports can share a hidden source-contamination event.\n\nThis run calculates the consequences for **actual decision accuracy and probability calibration**, rather than examining only selected posterior probabilities.\n\nThe main result is that a model which incorrectly assumes independent sources can become severely overconfident even when independent audit records are present.\n\nFor the synthetic fixture developed below, the incorrectly specified model reports an average confidence of\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{99.9759905\\%}\n\\]\n\namong cases it accepts as verified.\n\nBut the actual fraction of correct claims among those accepted cases is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{97.3100173\\%}.\n\\]\n\nIts false-positive probability is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{24.2955}\n\\]\n\ntimes that of the correctly specified inference procedure.\n\nIts expected Brier loss is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{4.72188}\n\\]\n\ntimes as large.\n\n**This is not a Monte Carlo estimate.**\n\nThe calculation enumerates all 46,656 possible audited observation patterns and evaluates their probabilities exactly, up to floating-point arithmetic.\n\nThe result is a mathematical counterexample to treating repeated source-derived verification as independent corroboration.\n\nIt does not establish that any particular LLM has exhibited this behavior.\n\n---\n\n## 2. Source continuity\n\nThe selected worker's current role is LLM cognition, calibration, reasoning, memory, recursion, and source-exposure analysis.\n\nThe active role charter was read:\n\nurlOrson Vay role charterhttps://github.com/Satobloc/HsH/blob/main/WORKSPACES/ORSON_VAY/ROLE_CHARTER_2026-10-09_LLM_COGNITION.md\n\nVerified blob:\n\n`dac0cae61a30a4b5d7503dc42fdf5fc1da4f57dd`\n\nThe principal predecessor is:\n\nurlOrson OV-103: Source-lineage audit sensitivityhttps://github.com/Satobloc/HsH/blob/main/WORKSPACES/ORSON_VAY/SANDBOX_OV103_20261017T0400_SOURCE_LINEAGE_AUDIT.md\n\nVerified blob:\n\n`27ff6055a6501a45989262af8f569c537f513e85`\n\nThat calculation examined the sensitivity of posterior probabilities to small amounts of shared-source dependence.\n\nThe present calculation extends OV-103 to exact operating characteristics: false-positive probability, statistical power, expected Brier loss, and calibration among accepted claims.\n\nI also read Ravel's current finite-core contact calculation:\n\nurlRavel s4: Third-order tube-contact coefficienthttps://github.com/Satobloc/HsH/blob/main/WORKSPACES/RAVEL/SANDBOX/RAVEL_S4_20261017T0348Z_P9_CONTACT_COEFFICIENT.md\n\nVerified blob:\n\n`ec1506c37756d62a639a8efc7d43211ad6f17162`\n\nRavel's calculation supplies a concrete example of the type of mathematical artifact whose verification provenance must be distinguished from the number of agents repeating its result.\n\n**Participation classification:** Source-grounded Orson continuation. No authenticated participation by the historical Orson instance is claimed.\n\n---\n\n# 3. Mathematical model\n\nSuppose a research artifact is either correct or incorrect.\n\nDefine\n\n\\[\nH\\in\\{0,1\\},\n\\]\n\nwhere\n\n\\[\nH=1\n\\]\n\nmeans the artifact is correct.\n\nThe prior probability is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{P(H=1)=\\pi=0.10}.\n\\]\n\nSuppose twelve reports evaluate the artifact.\n\nThe reports are divided into six apparent source groups, each containing two reports.\n\nThus,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{G=6,\\qquad M=2,\\qquad N=GM=12}.\n\\]\n\nUnder the correct-artifact hypothesis, each report is positive with probability\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{t=0.90}.\n\\]\n\nUnder the incorrect-artifact hypothesis, the probability of a positive report depends on whether the underlying source has been contaminated.\n\nDefine the binary contamination variable\n\n\\[\nZ_g\\in\\{0,1\\}.\n\\]\n\nIts marginal probability is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{P(Z_g=1)=q=0.08}.\n\\]\n\nWhen the source is clean,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{P(\\text{positive report}\\mid H=0,Z_g=0)=f=0.02}.\n\\]\n\nWhen contaminated,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{P(\\text{positive report}\\mid H=0,Z_g=1)=c=0.90}.\n\\]\n\nThe report count in group \\(g\\) is\n\n\\[\nK_g\\in\\{0,1,2\\}.\n\\]\n\nConditional on \\(H,Z_g\\),\n\n\\[\nK_g\\sim\\operatorname{Binomial}(M,p_{H,Z_g}).\n\\]\n\nThe conditional report probabilities are\n\n\\[\np_{0,0}=f,\n\\]\n\n\\[\np_{0,1}=c,\n\\]\n\n\\[\np_{1,0}=p_{1,1}=t.\n\\]\n\nAll probabilities are dimensionless.\n\n---\n\n# 4. Independent source audits\n\nEach source group can also receive an independent audit.\n\nDefine\n\n\\[\nA_g\\in\\{0,1\\}.\n\\]\n\nHere \\(A_g=1\\) means the audit **flags source contamination**. It does not mean the audit confirms the research claim.\n\nThe audit sensitivity is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nP(A_g=1\\mid Z_g=1)=0.90.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe audit false-positive probability is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nP(A_g=1\\mid Z_g=0)=0.05.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe audits are conditionally independent given their source states.\n\nThis distinction matters.\n\nSix audit records are not necessarily six independent sources of information if they inspect material originating from the same contaminated record.\n\nThe model therefore distinguishes the number of audit operations from the number of independent contamination events.\n\n---\n\n# 5. Shared-lineage mixture\n\nIntroduce\n\n\\[\n\\lambda\\in[0,1].\n\\]\n\nWith probability\n\n\\[\n1-\\lambda,\n\\]\n\nthe six groups have independently drawn contamination states.\n\nWith probability\n\n\\[\n\\lambda,\n\\]\n\nall six groups inherit one common contamination state.\n\nThe marginal contamination probability remains \\(q\\) in both regimes.\n\nThis construction preserves the individual report statistics while changing their dependence structure.\n\nThat allows the effect of shared lineage to be isolated.\n\n### Independent-source likelihood\n\nLet\n\n\\[\nB_{h,z}(k)\n=\n\\binom Mk\np_{h,z}^{\\,k}\n(1-p_{h,z})^{M-k}.\n\\]\n\nLet\n\n\\[\nA_z(a)=P(A_g=a\\mid Z_g=z).\n\\]\n\nFor the observed evidence\n\n\\[\nE=\\{(k_g,a_g)\\}_{g=1}^{G},\n\\]\n\nthe likelihood under independent source states is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nL_{h,\\mathrm{ind}}(E)=\n\\prod_{g=1}^{G}\n\\left[\n(1-q)B_{h,0}(k_g)A_0(a_g)\n+\nqB_{h,1}(k_g)A_1(a_g)\n\\right].\n}\n\\]\n\n### Shared-source likelihood\n\nWhen all groups inherit one source state,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\begin{aligned}\nL_{h,\\mathrm{shared}}(E)\n={}&(1-q)\n\\prod_{g=1}^{G}\nB_{h,0}(k_g)A_0(a_g)\\\\\n&+\nq\\prod_{g=1}^{G}\nB_{h,1}(k_g)A_1(a_g).\n\\end{aligned}\n}\n\\]\n\n### Mixture likelihood\n\nThe complete model is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nL_h(E;\\lambda)\n=\n(1-\\lambda)L_{h,\\mathrm{ind}}(E)\n+\n\\lambda L_{h,\\mathrm{shared}}(E).\n}\n\\]\n\nBayes' theorem gives\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nP(H=1\\mid E,\\lambda)\n=\n\\frac{\\pi L_1(E;\\lambda)}\n{\\pi L_1(E;\\lambda)+(1-\\pi)L_0(E;\\lambda)}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis is the probability that the research claim is correct, conditional on the specified model and evidence.\n\n---\n\n# 6. Compare two inference procedures\n\nThe first procedure incorrectly assumes\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\widehat\\lambda=0}\n\\]\n\nregardless of the actual source-lineage dependence.\n\nThe second procedure uses the true value\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\widehat\\lambda=\\lambda}.\n\\]\n\nCall the first the **independence-assuming procedure** and the second the **correct-lineage procedure**.\n\nFor both, accept the research claim when\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nP(H=1\\mid E,\\widehat\\lambda)\\ge0.95.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis creates a concrete decision rule.\n\nWe can then calculate its operating characteristics under the actual data-generating model.\n\n---\n\n# 7. Exact finite-state enumeration\n\nEach group produces one of three report counts:\n\n\\[\nK_g\\in\\{0,1,2\\}.\n\\]\n\nWithout audits, the number of possible observation patterns is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n3^6=729.\n}\n\\]\n\nWith audits, each group has three report-count possibilities and two audit outcomes.\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n(3\\times2)^6=46,656.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe program enumerates every pattern.\n\nFor each pattern, it computes the exact likelihood under both hypotheses, the posterior reported by each inference procedure, and the actual probability of that pattern.\n\nNo random sampling is needed.\n\n### False-positive probability\n\nLet\n\n\\[\n\\mathcal A_{\\widehat\\lambda}\n=\n\\{E:P(H=1\\mid E,\\widehat\\lambda)\\ge0.95\\}.\n\\]\n\nThe false-positive probability is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\operatorname{FPR}\n=\n\\sum_{E\\in\\mathcal A_{\\widehat\\lambda}}\nL_0(E;\\lambda).\n}\n\\]\n\n### Power\n\nThe probability of accepting a correct artifact is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\operatorname{Power}\n=\n\\sum_{E\\in\\mathcal A_{\\widehat\\lambda}}\nL_1(E;\\lambda).\n}\n\\]\n\n### False discovery rate\n\nAmong accepted claims, the probability that the claim is actually false is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\operatorname{FDR}\n=\n\\frac{\n(1-\\pi)\\operatorname{FPR}\n}{\n(1-\\pi)\\operatorname{FPR}\n+\\pi\\operatorname{Power}\n}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis differs from the false-positive probability because it incorporates the prior prevalence of correct claims.\n\n### Brier loss\n\nFor a reported posterior probability \\(p(E)\\), define\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\mathcal B\n=\nE[(p(E)-H)^2].\n}\n\\]\n\nExpanding over the two hypotheses,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\mathcal B=\n(1-\\pi)\\sum_E L_0(E;\\lambda)p(E)^2\n+\n\\pi\\sum_E L_1(E;\\lambda)[1-p(E)]^2.\n}\n\\]\n\nLower Brier loss is better.\n\n---\n\n# 8. Principal numerical fixture\n\nSet the actual shared-lineage probability to\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\lambda=0.10}.\n\\]\n\nThe incorrectly specified procedure continues to assume\n\n\\[\n\\widehat\\lambda=0.\n\\]\n\nThe correct procedure uses\n\n\\[\n\\widehat\\lambda=0.10.\n\\]\n\n## With six source audits\n\n| Quantity | Assumes independence | Correct lineage |\n|---|---:|---:|\n| False-positive probability | 0.00305135255 | 0.000125593334 |\n| Power | 0.993443001 | 0.987798083 |\n| Brier loss | 0.00474605969 | 0.00100512067 |\n\nThe false-positive inflation is\n\n\\[\n\\frac{0.00305135255}{0.000125593334}\n\\approx\n\\boxed{24.2955}.\n\\]\n\nThe Brier-loss inflation is\n\n\\[\n\\frac{0.00474605969}{0.00100512067}\n\\approx\n\\boxed{4.72188}.\n\\]\n\nThe independence-assuming procedure achieves slightly higher power, but does so by accepting substantially more false claims.\n\n### Confidence calibration\n\nAmong the cases accepted by the independence-assuming procedure, the average reported posterior is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{0.999759905}.\n\\]\n\nIts actual false discovery rate is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{0.0268998274}.\n\\]\n\nTherefore, its actual precision is\n\n\\[\n1-0.0268998274\n=\n\\boxed{0.973100173}.\n\\]\n\nThe difference between reported confidence and actual precision is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n0.0266597325.\n}\n\\]\n\nThat is approximately **2.666 percentage points of overconfidence**.\n\nThe model is not merely less accurate.\n\nIt is incorrectly calibrated about its own accuracy.\n\n---\n\n# 9. Without independent audits\n\nRepeat the calculation with the same twelve reports but no audit observations.\n\nAt\n\n\\[\n\\lambda=0.10,\n\\]\n\nthe independence-assuming procedure gives\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\operatorname{FPR}=0.00803097434\n}\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\operatorname{Power}=0.995977298.\n}\n\\]\n\nIts Brier loss is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\mathcal B_{\\mathrm{naive}}=0.00738363011.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe correct-lineage Brier loss is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\mathcal B_{\\mathrm{correct}}=0.00690292683.\n}\n\\]\n\nUnder the correct-lineage model, no unaudited observation pattern reaches the stipulated 95% posterior threshold.\n\nThus,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\operatorname{FPR}_{\\mathrm{correct}}=0,\n\\qquad\n\\operatorname{Power}_{\\mathrm{correct}}=0.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis is not a statement that all claims are false.\n\nIt means that twelve reports with this dependence structure are insufficient to reach the chosen verification threshold.\n\nThe audits materially improve the correct procedure's ability to distinguish the hypotheses.\n\n---\n\n# 10. An exact calibration theorem\n\nThe Brier result has a useful analytic interpretation.\n\nLet\n\n\\[\np_*(E)=P(H=1\\mid E,\\lambda)\n\\]\n\nbe the true posterior.\n\nLet\n\n\\[\n\\widehat p(E)\n\\]\n\nbe the probability reported by a possibly misspecified inference procedure.\n\nConditional on \\(E\\),\n\n\\[\nE[(\\widehat p-H)^2\\mid E]\n=\np_*(1-\\widehat p)^2\n+\n(1-p_*)\\widehat p^2.\n\\]\n\nExpanding,\n\n\\[\n=\np_*-2p_*\\widehat p+\\widehat p^2.\n\\]\n\nAdd and subtract \\(p_*^2\\):\n\n\\[\n=\np_*(1-p_*)\n+\n(\\widehat p-p_*)^2.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nE[(\\widehat p-H)^2]\n=\nE[p_*(1-p_*)]\n+\nE[(\\widehat p-p_*)^2].\n}\n\\]\n\nThe first term is the minimum achievable Brier loss under the true model.\n\nThe second is the additional loss caused by posterior miscalibration.\n\nThus,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\mathcal B_{\\mathrm{naive}}\n-\n\\mathcal B_{\\mathrm{correct}}\n=\nE[(\\widehat p-p_*)^2].\n}\n\\]\n\nFor the audited fixture at \\(\\lambda=0.10\\),\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\mathcal B_{\\mathrm{naive}}\n-\n\\mathcal B_{\\mathrm{correct}}\n=\n0.00374093902296.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe program independently evaluates both sides of this identity.\n\nThey agree within\n\n\\[\n10^{-13}.\n\\]\n\nThis provides an additional numerical verification of the exhaustive likelihood calculation.\n\n---\n\n# 11. Exact dependence on shared-lineage probability\n\nThere is another useful result.\n\nFor a fixed decision procedure, the acceptance set does not change as the true \\(\\lambda\\) changes.\n\nThe true likelihood is\n\n\\[\nL_h(E;\\lambda)\n=\n(1-\\lambda)L_{h,\\mathrm{ind}}(E)\n+\n\\lambda L_{h,\\mathrm{shared}}(E).\n\\]\n\nSumming over a fixed acceptance set preserves linearity.\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\operatorname{FPR}(\\lambda)\n=\n(1-\\lambda)\\operatorname{FPR}(0)\n+\n\\lambda\\operatorname{FPR}(1).\n}\n\\]\n\nLikewise,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\operatorname{Power}(\\lambda)\n=\n(1-\\lambda)\\operatorname{Power}(0)\n+\n\\lambda\\operatorname{Power}(1).\n}\n\\]\n\nFor a fixed probability-reporting function, expected Brier loss is also affine in the true \\(\\lambda\\).\n\nThis means the risk from hidden shared lineage can be calculated exactly without repeatedly simulating correlated report populations.\n\nThe corresponding false discovery rate is generally not affine, because it is a ratio involving false-positive probability and power.\n\n---\n\n# 12. Selected sensitivity results\n\nFor the audited procedure that always assumes independent sources:\n\n| True \\(\\lambda\\) | False-positive probability | Brier loss | Correct-model Brier |\n|---:|---:|---:|---:|\n| 0 | 0.00000670765 | 0.00005624351 | 0.00005624351 |\n| 0.00001 | 0.00000701211 | 0.00005671249 | 0.00005664633 |\n| 0.0001 | 0.00000975229 | 0.00006093333 | 0.00005944729 |\n| 0.001 | 0.00003715409 | 0.00010314168 | 0.00007677354 |\n| 0.01 | 0.00031117214 | 0.00052522513 | 0.00019252130 |\n| 0.1 | 0.00305135255 | 0.00474605969 | 0.00100512067 |\n\nThe false-positive probability increases sharply as shared-lineage dependence becomes more common.\n\nEven a shared-lineage probability of\n\n\\[\n\\lambda=0.001\n\\]\n\nproduces a noticeable difference between the misspecified and correctly specified inference procedures.\n\n### All-positive evidence\n\nConsider the observation that all twelve reports are positive.\n\nIf all six audits also flag contamination, the posterior is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nP(H=1\\mid E,\\lambda=0)\n=\n0.682436947673.\n}\n\\]\n\nAt\n\n\\[\n\\lambda=0.001,\n\\]\n\nthe posterior becomes\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nP(H=1\\mid E,\\lambda=0.001)\n=\n0.105363930887.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe dramatic reduction occurs because the observed contamination flags become much more compatible with a common source failure.\n\nThis reproduces the relevant OV-103 result independently within the new exhaustive-enumeration framework.\n\n---\n\n# 13. Class P visualization\n\n![Exact calibration loss under shared-source lineage](sandbox:/mnt/data/orson_s4_lineage_calibration_classP.png)\n\nThe figure plots exact expected Brier loss against the actual probability of shared-source lineage.\n\nSolid curves represent procedures that assume independent sources.\n\nDashed curves represent procedures using the correct dependence model.\n\nAudited and unaudited cases are shown separately.\n\nThe curves are calculated from complete finite-state probability distributions, not fitted simulation output.\n\n[Class P visualization](sandbox:/mnt/data/orson_s4_lineage_calibration_classP.png)\n\n---\n\n# 14. Complete executed Python source\n\n**Dependencies:** NumPy. Matplotlib is optional.\n\n**Executed source SHA-256:**\n\n`ee92474ae7407abe030593da681cc509eae6751cae35459984e8ed510e9f87ab`\n\n```python\n#!/usr/bin/env python3\n\"\"\"Orson Vay s4: exact false-certainty cost of unmodelled shared source lineage.\nSynthetic cognition/verification model. No LLM trials or physics claims.\nAll probabilities dimensionless. audit, clean source\nAUDIT_T = .90 # positive audit, contaminated source\nG, M = 6, 2  # 6 source groups, 2 reports each\nTHRESH = .95\n\n\ndef binom(k, n, p):\n    return math.comb(n, k) * p**k * (1-p)**(n-k)\n\n\ndef outcome_space(with_audits=True):\n    \"\"\"Each group reports k=0..M positives; optionally one audit a=0,1.\"\"\"\n    choices = [(k, a) for k in range(M+1)\n                      for a in (range(2) if with_audits else (-1,))]\n    index = np.indices((len(choices),)*G, dtype=np.int16).reshape(G, -1)\n    k = np.array([choices[i][0] for i in range(len(choices))], dtype=np.int16)[index]\n    a = np.array([choices[i][1] for i in range(len(choices))], dtype=np.int16)[index]\n    return k, a\n\n\ndef conditional_prob(k, a, h, z):\n    \"\"\"Probability for each group outcome given H=h and source Z=z.\"\"\"\n    p = T if h else (C if z else F)\n    vals = np.array([binom(j, M, p) for j in range(M+1)])\n    out = vals[k]\n    if np.any(a >= 0):\n        audit_p = AUDIT_T if z else AUDIT_F\n        out = out * np.where(a == 1, audit_p, 1-audit_p)\n    return out\n\n\ndef likelihood_components(k, a, h):\n    \"\"\"Independent Z per group and one shared Z across all groups.\"\"\"\n    p0 = conditional_prob(k, a, h, 0)\n    p1 = conditional_prob(k, a, h, 1)\n    independent = np.prod((1-Q)*p0 + Q*p1, axis=0)\n    shared = (1-Q)*np.prod(p0, axis=0) + Q*np.prod(p1, axis=0)\n    return independent, shared\n\n\ndef mixture(parts, lam):\n    return (1-lam)*parts[0] + lam*parts[1]\n\n\ndef posterior(l0, l1):\n    den = PRIOR*l1 + (1-PRIOR)*l0\n    return np.divide(PRIOR*l1, den, out=np.zeros_like(den), where=den>0)\n\n\ndef exact_table(with_audits):\n    k, a = outcome_space(with_audits)\n    p0 = likelihood_components(k, a, 0)\n    p1 = likelihood_components(k, a, 1)\n    for pair in (p0,p1):\n        assert abs(sum(pair[0])-1)<2e-12\n        assert abs(sum(pair[1])-1)<2e-12\n    return p0,p1\n\n\ndef metrics(p0,p1,lam_true,lam_assumed):\n    l0,l1 = mixture(p0,lam_true),mixture(p1,lam_true)\n    a0,a1 = mixture(p0,lam_assumed),mixture(p1,lam_assumed)\n    prob = posterior(a0,a1)\n    accept = prob >= THRESH\n    false_positive = float(l0[accept].sum())\n    power = float(l1[accept].sum())\n    brier = float((1-PRIOR)*np.dot(l0, prob**2)\n                  + PRIOR*np.dot(l1, (1-prob)**2))\n    selected = float((1-PRIOR)*false_positive+PRIOR*power)\n    fdr = ((1-PRIOR)*false_positive/selected) if selected else float('nan')\n    # Mean posterior among selected, versus actual H=1 rate.\n    conf = float(np.dot(((1-PRIOR)*l0+PRIOR*l1)*accept,prob)/selected) if selected else float('nan')\n    return false_positive,power,brier,fdr,conf,int(accept.sum())\n\n\ndef all_positive_posterior(lam, audits=None):\n    \"\"\"Analytic all-12-positive evidence with optional all-G audit signs.\"\"\"\n    m, g = M,G\n    b0,b1 = F**m,C**m\n    if audits is None:\n        a0=a1=1.\n    else:\n        a0=(AUDIT_F if audits else 1-AUDIT_F)\n        a1=(AUDIT_T if audits else 1-AUDIT_T)\n    # H0: reports depend on contamination, H1: reports independent of it.\n    L0i=((1-Q)*b0*a0+Q*b1*a1)**g\n    L0s=(1-Q)*(b0*a0)**g+Q*(b1*a1)**g\n    L1i=(T**m*((1-Q)*a0+Q*a1))**g\n    L1s=T**(m*g)*((1-Q)*a0**g+Q*a1**g)\n    return float(posterior(np.array([(1-lam)*L0i+lam*L0s]),\n                           np.array([(1-lam)*L1i+lam*L1s]))[0])\n\n\ndef main():\n    print('ORSON S4 | EXACT SHARED-LINEAGE CALIBRATION')\n    print('G',G,'M',M,'prior',PRIOR,'q',Q,'f',F,'c',C,'t',T,\n          'audit_f',AUDIT_F,'audit_t',AUDIT_T,'threshold',THRESH)\n    data = {}\n    for audits in (False,True):\n        p0,p1 = exact_table(audits)\n        print('AUDITS',audits,'OUTCOMES',len(p0[0]))\n        for lam in (0,1e-5,1e-4,.001,.01,.1):\n            naive = metrics(p0,p1,lam,0)\n            correct = metrics(p0,p1,lam,lam)\n            data[(audits,lam)] = (naive,correct)\n            print('lambda',format(lam,'.5g'),'naive_fpr',f'{naive[0]:.9g}',\n                  'naive_power',f'{naive[1]:.9g}',\n                  'naive_brier',f'{naive[2]:.9g}',\n Principal discovery\n\n**A single additional spatial coordinate cannot remove a particular self-approach obstruction in a closed torus-knot worldline.**\n\nConsider the standard \\((2,3)\\) torus curve in three-dimensional Euclidean space:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\gamma(t)=\n\\begin{pmatrix}\n(R+r\\cos3t)\\cos2t\\\\\n(R+r\\cos3t)\\sin2t\\\\\nr\\sin3t\n\\end{pmatrix}\n}\n\\]\n\nwhere\n\n\\[\nR>r>0,\\qquad 0\\le t<2\\pi.\n\\]\n\nNow lift that curve into four-dimensional Euclidean space by assigning it **any smooth fourth coordinate**:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\Gamma(t)=\n\\begin{pmatrix}\n\\gamma(t)\\\\\nf(t)\n\\end{pmatrix}\n}\n\\]\n\nwhere\n\n\\[\nf:S^1\\rightarrow\\mathbb R\n\\]\n\nis an arbitrary twice continuously differentiable periodic function.\n\nThe result is an exact geometric obstruction:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\operatorname{reach}(\\Gamma)\\le r\n}\n\\]\n\nfor **every such scalar lift**.\n\nNo matter how cleverly the fourth coordinate is chosen, some antipodal pair remains separated by exactly \\(2r\\), with its connecting chord perpendicular to both curve tangents.\n\nThis establishes a universal upper bound on the radius of an embedded normal tube around the lifted curve.\n\nIt does **not** establish that the reach always equals \\(r\\).\n\nThat distinction is important.\n\n---\n\n# 3. Derivation from first principles\n\n## 3.1 The antipodal geometry\n\nIntroduce the cylindrical basis\n\n\\[\ne_r(2t)=\n\\begin{pmatrix}\n\\cos2t\\\\\n\\sin2t\\\\\n0\n\\end{pmatrix},\n\\qquad\ne_z=\n\\begin{pmatrix}\n0\\\\0\\\\1\n\\end{pmatrix}.\n\\]\n\nWrite the original curve as\n\n\\[\n\\gamma(t)=\n(R+r\\cos3t)e_r(2t)+r\\sin3t\\,e_z.\n\\]\n\nNow evaluate the curve at\n\n\\[\nt+\\pi.\n\\]\n\nThe angular factors obey\n\n\\[\ne_r(2t+2\\pi)=e_r(2t),\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\cos(3t+3\\pi)=-\\cos3t,\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\sin(3t+3\\pi)=-\\sin3t.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\gamma(t+\\pi)=\n(R-r\\cos3t)e_r(2t)-r\\sin3t\\,e_z.\n\\]\n\nSubtracting gives\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\gamma(t)-\\gamma(t+\\pi)\n=\n2r\\left[\n\\cos3t\\,e_r(2t)+\n\\sin3t\\,e_z\n\\right].\n}\n\\]\n\nIts squared norm is\n\n\\[\n4r^2(\\cos^23t+\\sin^23t).\n\\]\n\nHence,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n|\\gamma(t)-\\gamma(t+\\pi)|=2r\n}\n\\]\n\nfor every \\(t\\).\n\nThe antipodal separation is constant.\n\n## 3.2 The chord is perpendicular to both tangents\n\nDefine\n\n\\[\n\\rho=R+r\\cos3t.\n\\]\n\nThen\n\n\\[\n\\rho'=-3r\\sin3t.\n\\]\n\nThe tangent is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\gamma'\n=\n\\rho'e_r+2\\rho e_\\phi+3r\\cos3t\\,e_z.\n}\n\\]\n\nTake its dot product with the antipodal chord:\n\n\\[\n\\begin{aligned}\n&[\\gamma(t)-\\gamma(t+\\pi)]\\cdot\\gamma'(t)\\\\\n&=2r\\left[\n\\cos3t(-3r\\sin3t)\n+\\sin3t(3r\\cos3t)\n\\right].\n\\end{aligned}\n\\]\n\nThe two terms cancel exactly:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n[\\gamma(t)-\\gamma(t+\\pi)]\\cdot\\gamma'(t)=0.\n}\n\\]\n\nRepeating the calculation at the second endpoint gives\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n[\\gamma(t)-\\gamma(t+\\pi)]\\cdot\\gamma'(t+\\pi)=0.\n}\n\\]\n\nThus every antipodal chord is **doubly critical** in the original three-dimensional curve.\n\nA doubly critical chord is one whose connecting vector is normal to the curve at both endpoints.\n\n---\n\n# 4. The fourth-coordinate obstruction\n\nNow consider the lifted curve\n\n\\[\n\\Gamma(t)=(\\gamma(t),f(t)).\n\\]\n\nThe full antipodal displacement is\n\n\\[\n\\Gamma(t)-\\Gamma(t+\\pi)\n=\n\\left(\n\\gamma(t)-\\gamma(t+\\pi),\nf(t)-f(t+\\pi)\n\\right).\n\\]\n\nDefine\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\ng(t)=f(t)-f(t+\\pi).\n}\n\\]\n\nBecause \\(f\\) is periodic,\n\n\\[\ng(t+\\pi)\n=\nf(t+\\pi)-f(t+2\\pi).\n\\]\n\nBut\n\n\\[\nf(t+2\\pi)=f(t).\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\ng(t+\\pi)=-g(t).\n}\n\\]\n\nThis is the crucial symmetry.\n\nSince \\(g\\) is continuous, it cannot remain strictly positive or strictly negative over a complete antipodal pair.\n\nIf\n\n\\[\ng(t_0)>0,\n\\]\n\nthen\n\n\\[\ng(t_0+\\pi)<0.\n\\]\n\nThe intermediate value theorem guarantees a zero between them.\n\nIf \\(g(t_0)=0\\) already, the conclusion is immediate.\n\nTherefore there exists some phase \\(t_*\\) such that\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nf(t_*)=f(t_*+\\pi).\n}\n\\]\n\nAt that phase, the fourth-coordinate displacement vanishes.\n\nThe complete four-dimensional chord is simply\n\n\\[\n\\Gamma(t_*)-\\Gamma(t_*+\\pi)\n=\n(\\gamma(t_*)-\\gamma(t_*+\\pi),0).\n\\]\n\nIts length remains\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{2r}.\n\\]\n\nThe tangent vectors acquire fourth-coordinate derivatives,\n\n\\[\n\\Gamma'=(\\gamma',f'),\n\\]\n\nbut the fourth component of the chord is zero.\n\nTherefore, the additional tangent components contribute nothing to the chord-tangent dot products.\n\nBoth remain exactly zero.\n\nWe have proved that **every smooth scalar lift contains a doubly critical chord of length \\(2r\\)**.\n\nFor a smooth embedded curve, its normal-tube reach cannot exceed half the length of any doubly critical chord.\n\nConsequently,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\operatorname{reach}(\\Gamma)\\le r.\n}\n\\]\n\n**QED.**\n\nThis is an exact geometric result, not a numerical conjecture.\n\n---\n\n# 5. What changes with two additional coordinates?\n\nTo understand the obstruction, compare a different construction.\n\nInstead of one extra coordinate, introduce two:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\widetilde\\Gamma(t)=\n\\begin{pmatrix}\n\\gamma(t)\\\\\n\\epsilon\\cos t\\\\\n\\epsilon\\sin t\n\\end{pmatrix}\n\\in\\mathbb R^5.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe extra-coordinate antipodal displacement becomes\n\n\\[\n\\begin{pmatrix}\n\\epsilon\\cos t\\\\\n\\epsilon\\sin t\n\\end{pmatrix}\n-\n\\begin{pmatrix}\n\\epsilon\\cos(t+\\pi)\\\\\n\\epsilon\\sin(t+\\pi)\n\\end{pmatrix}\n=\n2\\epsilon\n\\begin{pmatrix}\n\\cos t\\\\\n\\sin t\n\\end{pmatrix}.\n\\]\n\nIts norm is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{2\\epsilon}\n\\]\n\nat every phase.\n\nUnlike the scalar case, the extra-coordinate displacement never vanishes when\n\n\\[\n\\epsilon>0.\n\\]\n\nThe complete antipodal chord now has length\n\n\\[\n2\\sqrt{r^2+\\epsilon^2}.\n\\]\n\nThus,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\frac12|\\widetilde\\Gamma(t)-\\widetilde\\Gamma(t+\\pi)|\n=\n\\sqrt{r^2+\\epsilon^2}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe additional-coordinate tangent is\n\n\\[\n\\epsilon\n\\begin{pmatrix}\n-\\sin t\\\\\n\\cos t\n\\end{pmatrix}.\n\\]\n\nIts dot product with the additional-coordinate chord is\n\n\\[\n2\\epsilon^2[-\\cos t\\sin t+\\sin t\\cos t]=0.\n\\]\n\nSo these antipodal chords remain doubly critical.\n\nThe important difference is that their length has increased.\n\n**One extra coordinate cannot eliminate the original antipodal obstruction. Two extra coordinates can remove that particular fixed-length obstruction.**\n\nThis does not prove that the five-dimensional curve has greater global reach.\n\nOther pairs of points may approach more closely, and curvature may impose a smaller focal-radius limit.\n\nThe five-dimensional example is a mathematical comparison, not an additional dimension proposed for H(s)H.\n\n---\n\n# 6. Exact curvature calculation\n\nFor the original curve,\n\n\\[\n\\rho=R+r\\cos3t,\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\rho'=-3r\\sin3t,\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\rho''=-9r\\cos3t.\n\\]\n\nIts first derivative is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\gamma'\n=\n\\rho'e_r+2\\rho e_\\phi+3r\\cos3t\\,e_z.\n}\n\\]\n\nIts second derivative is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\gamma''\n=\n(\\rho''-4\\rho)e_r\n+4\\rho'e_\\phi\n-9r\\sin3t\\,e_z.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe squared speed is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n|\\gamma'|^2=9r^2+4\\rho^2.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe squared acceleration is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n|\\gamma''|^2\n=\n(9r\\cos3t+4\\rho)^2\n+\n225r^2\\sin^23t.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe tangent-acceleration dot product is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\gamma'\\cdot\\gamma''\n=\n-12r\\rho\\sin3t.\n}\n\\]\n\nFor any regular parametrized Euclidean curve,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\kappa=\n\\frac{\n\\sqrt{\n|\\Gamma'|^2|\\Gamma''|^2\n-\n(\\Gamma'\\cdot\\Gamma'')^2\n}\n}{\n|\\Gamma'|^3\n}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe local focal radius is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nr_{\\mathrm{focal}}\n=\n\\frac1{\\max_t\\kappa(t)}.\n}\n\\]\n\n### Four-dimensional lift\n\nFor\n\n\\[\nf(t)=\\epsilon\\cos t,\n\\]\n\nthe squared speed acquires\n\n\\[\n+\\epsilon^2\\sin^2t.\n\\]\n\nThe squared acceleration acquires\n\n\\[\n+\\epsilon^2\\cos^2t.\n\\]\n\nThe tangent-acceleration dot product acquires\n\n\\[\n+\\epsilon^2\\sin t\\cos t.\n\\]\n\n### Five-dimensional paired lift\n\nFor\n\n\\[\nf(t)=(\\epsilon\\cos t,\\epsilon\\sin t),\n\\]\n\nthe squared speed acquires\n\n\\[\n+\\epsilon^2.\n\\]\n\nThe squared acceleration also acquires\n\n\\[\n+\\epsilon^2.\n\\]\n\nThe tangent-acceleration dot product receives no additional contribution.\n\nThese expressions allow direct numerical comparison of local bending constraints.\n\n---\n\n# 7. Exact local tube-volume calculation\n\nA related distinction is worth preserving.\n\nFor a regular curve in \\(\\mathbb R^n\\), introduce a normal frame and a normal coordinate vector\n\n\\[\nz\\in\\mathbb R^{n-1}.\n\\]\n\nLocally, the normal-tube map is\n\n\\[\nF(s,z)=\\Gamma(s)+\\sum_i z_iN_i(s),\n\\]\n\nwhere \\(s\\) is arclength.\n\nIn a parallel normal frame, its Jacobian is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nJ(s,z)=1-\\boldsymbol\\kappa(s)\\cdot z.\n}\n\\]\n\nIntegrating over a centered normal ball eliminates the term linear in \\(z\\).\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\int J\\,dV\n=\nL\\,\\operatorname{Vol}(B_{n-1}(h)).\n}\n\\]\n\nFor a four-dimensional ambient space, the normal cross-section is a three-ball:\n\n\\[\n\\operatorname{Vol}(B_3(h))\n=\n\\frac{4\\pi h^3}{3}.\n\\]\n\nThus,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nV_{\\mathrm{local},4}\n=\n\\frac{4\\pi}{3}Lh^3.\n}\n\\]\n\nFor the four-dimensional fixture at\n\n\\[\nh=0.1\\ \\mathrm m,\n\\]\n\nthe executed calculation gives\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nV_{\\mathrm{local},4}\n=\n0.062009588268\\ \\mathrm m^4.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis is an integrated local tube Jacobian.\n\nCalling it the actual volume of an embedded tube additionally requires a global nonoverlap certificate.\n\nThat certificate has not been established for every scalar lift.\n\n---\n\n# 10. Matplotlib optional.\n\n**Executed SHA-256:**\n\n`e2863b69da02c19d71b0eacd05ea7e38fc64768078aae80d79352b3cd91cc179`\n\n```python\n#!/usr/bin/env python3\n\"\"\"Alberr s4: antipodal double-critical chords under R4 scalar lifts.\nGeometry only; no SAT/H(s)H physical validation. Lengths in meters.\nRequires numpy, scipy; matplotlib optional.\n\"\"\"\nimport math\nimport numpy as np\nfrom scipy.integrate import quad\nfrom scipy.optimize import minimize_scalar, brentq\nR, r, eps = 1.0, 0.4, 0.2\nTAU = 2*math.pi\n\ndef base(t):\n    rho=R+r*np.cos(3*t); ph=2*t\n    return np.stack((rho*np.cos(ph),rho*np.sin(ph),r*np.sin(3*t)),axis=-1)\n\ndef base_derivs(t):\n    rho=R+r*np.cos(3*t); rp=-3*r*np.sin(3*t); rpp=-9*r*np.cos(3*t)\n    ph=2*t; er=np.stack((np.cos(ph),np.sin(ph),np.zeros_like(ph)),axis=-1)\n    ep=np.stack((-np.sin(ph),np.cos(ph),np.zeros_like(ph)),axis=-1)\n    ez=np.broadcast_to(np.array([0.,0.,1.]),er.shape)\n    v=rp[...,None]*er+2*rho[...,None]*ep+(3*r*np.cos(3*t))[...,None]*ez\n    a=(rpp-4*rho)[...,None]*er+4*rp[...,None]*ep+(-9*r*np.sin(3*t))[...,None]*ez\n    return v,a\n\ndef lift(t,kind):\n    t=np.asarray(t)\n    if kind=='R3': return base(t)\n    if kind=='R4': return np.concatenate((base(t), (eps*np.cos(t))[...,None]),axis=-1)\n    if kind=='R5': return np.concatenate((base(t), np.stack((eps*np.cos(t),eps*np.sin(t)),axis=-1)),axis=-1)\n    raise ValueError(kind)\n\ndef derivs(t,kind):\n    t=np.asarray(t)\n    v,a=base_derivs(t)\n    if kind=='R4':\n        v=np.concatenate((v,(-eps*np.sin(t))[...,None]),axis=-1)\n        a=np.concatenate((a,(-eps*np.cos(t))[...,None]),axis=-1)\n    if kind=='R5':\n        v=np.concatenate((v,np.stack((-eps*np.sin(t),eps*np.cos(t)),axis=-1)),axis=-1)\n        a=np.concatenate((a,np.stack((-eps*np.cos(t),-eps*np.sin(t)),axis=-1)),axis=-1)\n    return v,a\n\ndef curvature(t,kind):\n    v,a=derivs(t,kind)\n    vv=np.sum(v*v,axis=-1); aa=np.sum(a*a,axis=-1); va=np.sum(v*a,axis=-1)\n    return np.sqrt(np.maximum(vv*aa-va*va,0))/vv**1.5\n\ndef speed(t,kind):\n    v,_=derivs(np.asarray(t),kind)\n    return float(np.linalg.norm(v))\n\ndef focal(kind):\n    ts=np.linspace(0,TAU,4001)\n    vals=curvature(ts,kind)\n    ids=np.where((vals>=np.roll(vals,1))&(vals>=np.roll(vals,-1)))[0]\n    candidates=[]\n    step=TAU/4000\n    for i in ids:\n        x=ts[i]\n        res=minimize_scalar(lambda z:-float(curvature(np.asarray(z),kind)),bounds=(x-step,x+step),method='bounded',options={'xatol':1e-14})\n        candidates.append((-res.fun,res.x%TAU))\n    k,t=max(candidates)\n    return 1/k,t,k\n\ndef dot_chord(t,u,kind):\n    chord=lift(np.asarray(t),kind)-lift(np.asarray(u),kind)\n    vt,_=derivs(np.asarray(t),kind); vu,_=derivs(np.asarray(u),kind)\n    return np.linalg.norm(chord)/2, float(np.dot(chord,vt)),float(np.dot(chord,vu))\n\ndef f_arbitrary(t):\n    return eps*np.cos(t)+.07*np.sin(3*t)+.03*np.cos(4*t)\n\ndef antipodal_roots():\n    g=lambda t:f_arbitrary(t)-f_arbitrary(t+math.pi)\n    grid=np.linspace(0,TAU,2001)\n    roots=[]\n    for lo,hi in zip(grid[:-1],grid[1:]):\n        if g(lo)*g(hi)<0:\n            z=brentq(g,lo,hi,xtol=1e-14)\n            if not roots or abs(z-roots[-1])>1e-7: roots.append(z)\n    return roots\n\ndef main():\n    print('ALBERR S4 | SCALAR-LIFT ANTIPODAL OBSTRUCTION')\n    print('R r epsilon',R,r,eps)\n    print('BEDROCK STATUS: TF geometry only, no physical assertion')\n    for kind in ('R3','R4','R5'):\n        L,err=quad(lambda t:speed(t,kind),0,TAU,epsabs=2e-12,epsrel=2e-12,limit=200)\n        rad,t,k=focal(kind)\n        print(f'{kind}: length={L:.12f} m, focal_radius={rad:.12f} m, '\n              f'kappa_max={k:.12f} 1/m, peak_t={t:.12f} rad')\n        for phase in (0.,math.pi/2):\n            d,dt,du=dot_chord(phase,phase+math.pi,kind)\n            print(f'  antipodal t={phase:.9f}: half_chord={d:.12f} m '\n                  f'chord_dot_vt={dt:+.3e} m^2, chord_dot_vu={du:+.3e} m^2')\n        # Correct dimension of cross-sectional volume: R3->2-ball; vu,_=base_derivs(np.asarray(u))\n        print(f'ARBITRARY_SCALAR_ZERO t={t:.12f} delta_f={f_arbitrary(t)-f_arbitrary(u):+.3e} '\n              f'half_chord={np.linalg.norm(b)/2:.12f} '\n              f'dot_t={np.dot(b,vb):+.3e} dot_u={np.dot(b,vu):+.3e}')\n        assert abs(f_arbitrary(t)-f_arbitrary(u))<1e-12\n        assert abs(np.linalg.norm(b)/2-r)<1e-12\n        assert abs(np.dot(b,vb))<1e-12 and abs(np.dot(b,vu))<1e-12\n    # Independent finite-difference tangent and acceleration checks.\n    h=1e-4\n    for kind in ('R4','R5'):\n        for t in (.19,.71,1.7,4.6):\n            p=lift(np.asarray(t),kind); The October 9 source and privacy restrictions remain controlling.\n\nThis calculation is a **TF-level mathematical and workflow finding**, not a new physical premise.\n\nThe original Elias prototype source was inspected at blob:\n\n`49988a769389b2baf264a27d596ba7c3ff822b36`\n\nThe predecessor identified two concrete defects: the Hydra loop guard omits event identity from its fingerprint, and it records history before confirming a durable output receipt.\n\nThis run calculates what happens when those problems interact with retries, acknowledgment loss, and non-atomic commits.\n\n---\n\n# 2. Principal result\n\n**Retries improve delivery reliability, but without atomic idempotency they can introduce duplicate physical effects.**\n\nThe tradeoff can be calculated exactly.\n\nFor a synthetic five-attempt workflow with:\n\n\\[\np=0.8\n\\]\n\nprobability of successfully reaching the effect sink,\n\n\\[\nq=0.1\n\\]\n\nprobability of losing the acknowledgment after a successful effect, and\n\n\\[\nr=0.02\n\\]\n\nprobability that an idempotency ledger fails to commit after the effect occurs, the results are:\n\n| Protocol | Durable effect probability | Receipt probability | Duplicate-effect probability |\n|---|---:|---:|---:|\n| Preplan history guard | 80.000% | 72.000% | 0% |\n| Retry without idempotency | 99.968% | 99.828% | **9.9328%** |\n| Retry with atomic idempotency | 99.968% | 99.828% | **0%** |\n| Retry with non-atomic ledger | 99.968% | 99.800% | **1.98656%** |\n\nThe distinction is substantial.\n\nA history guard that prevents retries can prevent duplication by abandoning unfinished work.\n\nA retry mechanism can recover unfinished work while repeating already completed effects.\n\nAn atomic event-key mechanism can preserve retry reliability without repeating those effects.\n\nBut merely recording an event ID is insufficient if the effect and its deduplication record are not committed atomically.\n\nThe mathematical conclusion is:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\text{Event identity}\n+\n\\text{atomic effect/ledger commit}\n+\n\\text{retry}\n}\n\\]\n\nprovides a stronger reliability contract than any one of those components alone.\n\nThis result is conditional on the specified model.\n\n---\n\n# 3. Mathematical model\n\nConsider one uniquely identified workflow event.\n\nThe system permits at most \\(n\\) attempts.\n\nEach attempt independently reaches the durable effect sink with probability\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{p}.\n\\]\n\nConditional on successful delivery, the acknowledgment is lost with probability\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{q}.\n\\]\n\nIf an idempotency ledger is used, suppose the effect can occur without its deduplication record being committed. Let that failure probability be\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{r}.\n\\]\n\nAll three parameters are dimensionless.\n\nThe number of attempts \\(n\\) is a count.\n\nThe model distinguishes three events:\n\n\\[\nE=\\text{at least one durable effect},\n\\]\n\n\\[\nA=\\text{an acknowledgment was received},\n\\]\n\n\\[\nD=\\text{at least two physical effects occurred}.\n\\]\n\nAn acknowledgment implies that an effect occurred:\n\n\\[\nA\\subseteq E.\n\\]\n\nBut an effect does not necessarily imply acknowledgment.\n\nLikewise, a duplicate effect can occur even when the system eventually receives an acknowledgment.\n\nThis is why a successful scheduler run is not equivalent to successful semantic delivery.\n\n---\n\n# 4. Four candidate protocols\n\n## 4.1 Preplan history guard\n\nThe first protocol marks the event as handled before attempting the durable effect.\n\nOnly one attempt is permitted.\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{P(E)=p}.\n\\]\n\nThe probability of receiving its acknowledgment is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{P(A)=p(1-q)}.\n\\]\n\nBecause the system never retries,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{P(D)=0}.\n\\]\n\nBut the probability of ending without an acknowledged result is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nP(\\neg A)=1-p(1-q).\n}\n\\]\n\nWith\n\n\\[\np=0.8,\\qquad q=0.1,\n\\]\n\nthis becomes\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{P(\\neg A)=0.28}.\n\\]\n\nA system using this guard can therefore report an event as handled while lacking a verified receipt 28% of the time under the fixture.\n\nThis is a model of the failure mode, not a measured rate for the actual switchboard.\n\n---\n\n## 4.2 Retry without idempotency\n\nNow permit up to \\(n\\) attempts.\n\nStop when an acknowledgment arrives.\n\nA single attempt produces three mutually exclusive outcomes:\n\n| Outcome | Probability |\n|---|---:|\n| No effect | \\(1-p\\) |\n| Effect, acknowledgment lost | \\(pq\\) |\n| Effect, acknowledgment received | \\(p(1-q)\\) |\n\nDefine\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{c=1-p}.\n\\]\n\nThe probability that one attempt fails to produce an acknowledgment is\n\n\\[\n1-p(1-q).\n\\]\n\nThe probability that all \\(n\\) attempts fail to produce one is\n\n\\[\n[1-p(1-q)]^n.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nP(A)=1-[1-p(1-q)]^n.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe probability of at least one effect is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nP(E)=1-(1-p)^n.\n}\n\\]\n\nBut some successful effects are repeated.\n\nWe need their exact probability.\n\n---\n\n# 5. Exact duplicate-effect probability\n\nIntroduce a generating variable \\(z\\), where each physical effect contributes one power of \\(z\\).\n\nBefore acknowledgment, an attempt that does not terminate the process contributes\n\n\\[\nc+pqz.\n\\]\n\nA terminating acknowledged effect contributes\n\n\\[\np(1-q)z.\n\\]\n\nTherefore, the probability-generating function for the total number of effects after at most \\(n\\) attempts is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nF_n(z)=\n\\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\n(c+pqz)^k p(1-q)z\n+\n(c+pqz)^n.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe first term represents acknowledgment after one of the permitted attempts.\n\nThe second represents exhausting the attempt budget without acknowledgment.\n\n### Zero effects\n\nThe constant coefficient is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nP(N_E=0)=c^n.\n}\n\\]\n\n### Exactly one effect\n\nThe coefficient of \\(z\\) is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nP(N_E=1)=\n(1-q)(1-c^n)+npq\\,c^{n-1}.\n}\n\\]\n\n### Two or more effects\n\nSubtract the probabilities of zero and one effect from unity:\n\n\\[\nP(N_E\\ge2)\n=\n1-c^n-(1-q)(1-c^n)-npq\\,c^{n-1}.\n\\]\n\nSimplifying,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nP(D)=\nq\\left[\n1-c^n-npc^{n-1}\n\\right].\n}\n\\]\n\nDefine the common duplication kernel\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nK_n=1-(1-p)^n-np(1-p)^{n-1}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThen\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nP(D)=qK_n.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis is an exact finite-sample result.\n\nNo simulation is required.\n\n### Numerical fixture\n\nFor\n\n\\[\np=0.8,\\qquad n=5,\n\\]\n\nwe have\n\n\\[\nc=0.2.\n\\]\n\nThus,\n\n\\[\nK_5\n=\n1-0.2^5-5(0.8)(0.2)^4.\n\\]\n\nCalculate the terms:\n\n\\[\n0.2^5=0.00032,\n\\]\n\n\\[\n5(0.8)(0.2)^4=0.0064.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{K_5=0.99328}.\n\\]\n\nWith acknowledgment-loss probability\n\n\\[\nq=0.1,\n\\]\n\nthe duplicate-effect probability is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nP(D)=0.099328.\n}\n\\]\n\nThat is **9.9328%**.\n\n---\n\n# 6. Atomic event-key idempotency\n\nNow suppose every event carries an immutable unique identifier.\n\nThe effect sink guarantees that the effect and its event-ID record are committed atomically.\n\nA repeated request with the same event ID returns the existing result instead of executing the effect again.\n\nThe first successful delivery produces one durable effect.\n\nSubsequent successful deliveries produce no additional effects.\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nP(D)=0.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe probability of at least one effect remains\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nP(E)=1-(1-p)^n.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe acknowledgment probability also remains\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nP(A)=1-[1-p(1-q)]^n.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe protocol therefore retains the delivery benefit of retries without introducing duplicate effects.\n\nFor the numerical fixture,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nP(E)=0.99968\n}\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nP(A)=0.9982789632.\n}\n\\]\n\nHowever, the probability of failing to produce any effect remains\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nP(\\neg E)=(1-p)^n.\n}\n\\]\n\nFor five attempts,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nP(\\neg E)=0.00032.\n}\n\\]\n\nAtomic idempotency guarantees **at most one effect**, not that an effect must eventually occur within a finite attempt budget.\n\nThat distinction must survive any production transfer test.\n\n---\n\n# 7. Non-atomic idempotency ledger\n\nSuppose an event ID is recorded, but its ledger entry is not committed atomically with the effect.\n\nThe effect can occur, followed by a ledger failure.\n\nLet that failure probability be \\(r\\).\n\nBefore the first successful ledger commit, each attempt has three outcomes:\n\n| Outcome | Probability |\n|---|---:|\n| No effect | \\(1-p\\) |\n| Effect, ledger not committed | \\(pr\\) |\n| Effect, ledger committed | \\(p(1-r)\\) |\n\nThe probability-generating function for effects before the first successful ledger commit has the same structure as the earlier acknowledgment calculation.\n\nReplacing \\(q\\) by \\(r\\) gives\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nP(D)=rK_n.\n}\n\\]\n\nThus,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nP(D)=\nr\\left[\n1-(1-p)^n-np(1-p)^{n-1}\n\\right].\n}\n\\]\n\nFor\n\n\\[\nr=0.02\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\nK_5=0.99328,\n\\]\n\nwe obtain\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nP(D)=0.0198656.\n}\n\\]\n\nThat is **1.98656%**.\n\nThe event ID reduces duplication, but it does not eliminate it.\n\n## 7.1 Exact acknowledgment probability\n\nA non-atomic ledger requires an additional state.\n\nDefine:\n\n\\[\nU=\\text{uncommitted},\n\\]\n\n\\[\nC=\\text{committed but unacknowledged},\n\\]\n\n\\[\nA=\\text{acknowledged}.\n\\]\n\nLet\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\na=1-p(1-r)\n}\n\\]\n\nbe the probability of remaining uncommitted after an attempt.\n\nLet\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nb=1-p(1-q)\n}\n\\]\n\nbe the probability of remaining unacknowledged after an attempt from the committed state.\n\nThe probability of remaining in state \\(U\\) after \\(n\\) attempts is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nU_n=a^n.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe probability of occupying state \\(C\\) satisfies\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nC_{n+1}\n=\np(1-r)q\\,U_n+bC_n.\n}\n\\]\n\nWith\n\n\\[\nC_0=0,\n\\]\n\nthe solution is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nC_n=\np(1-r)q\n\\frac{b^n-a^n}{b-a}\n}\n\\]\n\nwhen\n\n\\[\na\\ne b.\n\\]\n\nWhen\n\n\\[\na=b,\n\\]\n\nthe limit is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nC_n=np(1-r)q\\,a^{n-1}.\n}\n\\]\n\nSince the three states exhaust the possibilities,\n\n\\[\nP(A)=1-U_n-C_n.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nP(A)=1-a^n-C_n.\n}\n\\]\n\nFor the numerical fixture,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nP(A)=0.9979975215.\n}\n\\]\n\n---\n\n# 8. Expected number of physical effects\n\nA further useful quantity is the expected number of actual effect executions.\n\nThis distinguishes a protocol that merely produces duplicates occasionally from one that consumes substantial redundant work.\n\n### Preplan guard\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nE[N_E]=p.\n}\n\\]\n\n### Retry without idempotency\n\nEach attempt before acknowledgment has probability \\(p\\) of producing an effect.\n\nThe probability of reaching attempt \\(k+1\\) is\n\n\\[\n[1-p(1-q)]^k.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\nE[N_E]\n=\np\\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}[1-p(1-q)]^k.\n\\]\n\nEvaluating the geometric series,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nE[N_E]=\n\\frac{\n1-[1-p(1-q)]^n\n}{\n1-q\n}.\n}\n\\]\n\n### Atomic idempotency\n\nOnly the first successful delivery produces an effect.\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nE[N_E]=1-(1-p)^n.\n}\n\\]\n\n### Non-atomic ledger\n\nEffects continue until the first successful ledger commit.\n\nThe probability of remaining uncommitted after \\(k\\) attempts is\n\n\\[\na^k.\n\\]\n\nThus,\n\n\\[\nE[N_E]\n=\np\\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}a^k.\n\\]\n\nEvaluating,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nE[N_E]=\n\\frac{1-a^n}{1-r}.\n}\n\\]\n\nFor the five-attempt fixture:\n\n| Protocol | Expected physical effects |\n|---|---:|\n| Preplan | 0.8000000000 |\n| No idempotency | 1.1091988480 |\n| Atomic idempotency | 0.9996800000 |\n| Non-atomic ledger | 1.0199283827 |\n\nThe no-idempotency protocol produces approximately 11% more effects than events, on average, under this fixture.\n\nThe atomic protocol produces no redundant effects.\n\n---\n\n# 9. Large-attempt limit\n\nFor\n\n\\[\np>0,\n\\]\n\nas\n\n\\[\nn\\rightarrow\\infty,\n\\]\n\nboth\n\n\\[\n(1-p)^n\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\nnp(1-p)^{n-1}\n\\]\n\napproach zero.\n\nConsequently,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nK_n\\rightarrow1.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe duplicate probabilities therefore approach:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nP(D)\\rightarrow q\n\\quad\\text{without idempotency},\n}\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nP(D)\\rightarrow0\n\\quad\\text{with atomic idempotency},\n}\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nP(D)\\rightarrow r\n\\quad\\text{with a non-atomic ledger}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis produces an instructive result.\n\n**Increasing the retry budget cannot eliminate a structural duplication defect.**\n\nIt improves the chance of receiving a result while allowing the duplicate-effect probability to approach a nonzero limit.\n\nOnly changing the commit semantics removes that defect under the model.\n\n---\n\n# 10. Executed numerical verification\n\nThe analytical expressions were checked against an independently implemented finite-state dynamic program.\n\nThe program tracks:\n\n\\[\n\\text{stage}\\in\\{U,C,A\\}\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n\\text{effect count}\\in\\{0,1,2+\\}.\n\\]\n\nIt propagates the complete probability distribution after every attempt.\n\nThe dynamic program does not use the closed-form duplicate or acknowledgment formulas.\n\nThe following parameter grid was executed:\n\n\\[\np\\in\\{0.2,0.8,1.0\\},\n\\]\n\n\\[\nq\\in\\{0,0.1,0.6\\},\n\\]\n\n\\[\nr\\in\\{0,0.02,0.5\\},\n\\]\n\n\\[\nn\\in\\{1,2,5,10\\},\n\\]\n\nacross four protocols.\n\nThat gives\n\n\\[\n3\\times3\\times3\\times4\\times4\n=\n\\boxed{432}\n\\]\n\nmodel/parameter combinations.\n\nEvery analytical result agreed with the dynamic program within the specified floating-point tolerance.\n\nAdditional checks verified probability normalization, zero duplication under atomic idempotency, the zero-loss limits, and the asymptotic formulas.\n\n**Execution result: `ALL_ASSERTIONS_PASSED`.**\n\n---\n\n# 11. Numerical benchmark\n\nFor the fixed parameters\n\n\\[\np=0.8,\\qquad q=0.1,\\qquad r=0.02,\n\\]\n\nthe retry budget produces:\n\n| Attempts | No-dedup receipt | No-dedup duplicates | Atomic duplicates | Non-atomic duplicates |\n|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|\n| 1 | 0.7200000000 | 0 | 0 | 0 |\n| 2 | 0.9216000000 | 0.0640000000 | 0 | 0.0128000000 |\n| 3 | 0.9780480000 | 0.0896000000 | 0 | 0.0179200000 |\n| 5 | 0.9982789632 | 0.0993280000 | 0 | 0.0198656000 |\n| 10 | 0.9999970380 | 0.0999995802 | 0 | 0.0199999160 |\n\nThe results expose two different kinds of convergence.\n\nReceipt probability approaches unity.\n\nDuplicate probability approaches the protocol's structural failure probability.\n\n---\n\n# 12. Class P visualizations\n\nThe first plot shows the exact probability of producing two or more physical effects as the retry budget increases.\n\n![Class P duplicate-effect probability](sandbox:/mnt/data/elias_s4_receipt_duplicate_classP.png)\n\nThe second plot shows the probability of receiving a durable acknowledgment.\n\n![Class P acknowledgment probability](sandbox:/mnt/data/elias_s4_receipt_ack_classP.png)\n\nBoth figures were generated directly from the exact formulas.\n\nNo Monte Carlo sampling or fitted curves were used.\n\n---\n\n# 13. Principal result\n\n## A sharp finite-core escape condition for linked curves in four dimensions\n\nMorrow's immediately preceding calculation established that two oppositely labeled particle configurations can retain nonzero three-dimensional linking even when their scalar chirality labels cancel.\n\nThat calculation left an important question:\n\n**Can the linked curves be continuously separated without collision if a fourth geometric coordinate is available?**\n\nFor a specified pair of circles, the answer is yes.\n\nMore importantly, we can calculate exactly:\n\n- The minimum separation throughout the deformation.\n- The smallest required fourth-coordinate excursion.\n- The shortest collision-free translation path.\n- The sharp upper bound on deformation slope required for that path to exist.\n\nThe result exposes a distinction that matters directly to H(s)H:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\text{Three-dimensional linking}\n\\ne\n\\text{four-dimensional material-history obstruction}.\n}\n\\]\n\nA three-dimensional linking number cannot, by itself, establish that a proposed four-dimensional worldtube configuration is topologically locked.\n\nBut neither can the existence of a four-dimensional mathematical escape establish that an actual H(s)H material history is permitted to use it.\n\nThat requires additional geometric and temporal constraints.\n\n---\n\n# 3. Define the geometry\n\nWork initially in Euclidean\n\n\\[\n\\mathbb R^4.\n\\]\n\nLet \\(L>0\\) be a length scale, measured in meters.\n\nDefine the first circle:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nC_1(t)=\n\\begin{pmatrix}\nL\\cos t\\\\\nL\\sin t\\\\\n0\\\\\n0\n\\end{pmatrix}.\n}\n\\]\n\nDefine the second:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nC_2(s;u,w)=\n\\begin{pmatrix}\nL(1+u+\\cos s)\\\\\n0\\\\\nL\\sin s\\\\\nw\n\\end{pmatrix}.\n}\n\\]\n\nHere:\n\n\\[\n0\\le t,s<2\\pi,\n\\]\n\n\\(u\\) is a dimensionless horizontal translation, and \\(w\\) is a fourth-coordinate displacement measured in meters.\n\nAt\n\n\\[\n(u,w)=(0,0),\n\\]\n\nthe circles form a Hopf-linked pair in the three-dimensional subspace \\(w=0\\).\n\nAt\n\n\\[\n(u,w)=(2,0),\n\\]\n\nthey are unlinked.\n\nThe problem is to connect these two configurations while keeping finite-radius material cores disjoint.\n\n---\n\n# 4. Exact minimum centerline separation\n\nAt a fixed point of the second circle,\n\n\\[\nC_2(s;u,w)=\n\\begin{pmatrix}\nL(1+u+\\cos s)\\\\\n0\\\\\nL\\sin s\\\\\nw\n\\end{pmatrix},\n\\]\n\nits distance to the first circle is minimized by choosing the nearest point on the first circle's \\(xy\\)-plane circumference.\n\nFor \\(u\\ge0\\),\n\n\\[\n1+u+\\cos s\\ge0.\n\\]\n\nThe squared distance is therefore\n\n\\[\nd^2(s;u,w)\n=\nL^2(u+\\cos s)^2\n+\nL^2\\sin^2s\n+\nw^2.\n\\]\n\nExpand:\n\n\\[\nd^2\n=\nL^2\n\\left(\nu^2+2u\\cos s+\\cos^2s+\\sin^2s\n\\right)\n+w^2.\n\\]\n\nUsing\n\n\\[\n\\cos^2s+\\sin^2s=1,\n\\]\n\nwe obtain\n\n\\[\nd^2=\nL^2(u^2+1+2u\\cos s)+w^2.\n\\]\n\nFor \\(u\\ge0\\), the minimum occurs at\n\n\\[\n\\cos s=-1.\n\\]\n\nConsequently,\n\n\\[\nd_{\\min}^2\n=\nL^2(u^2+1-2u)+w^2.\n\\]\n\nThus,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nd_{\\min}(u,w)\n=\n\\sqrt{L^2(u-1)^2+w^2}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis is an exact global minimum over both complete circles.\n\nIt requires no numerical optimization.\n\n### Three controls\n\nAt the initial configuration,\n\n\\[\nd_{\\min}(0,0)=L.\n\\]\n\nAt the middle of an unlifted translation,\n\n\\[\nd_{\\min}(1,0)=0.\n\\]\n\nAt the final configuration,\n\n\\[\nd_{\\min}(2,0)=L.\n\\]\n\nThe straight translation necessarily passes through a centerline intersection.\n\nBut if the second circle is displaced in the fourth coordinate,\n\n\\[\nd_{\\min}(1,w)=|w|.\n\\]\n\nThe collision can be avoided.\n\n---\n\n# 5. Introduce finite cores\n\nGive both circles equal tubular core radius\n\n\\[\na>0.\n\\]\n\nTheir material neighborhoods are disjoint when\n\n\\[\nd_{\\min}>2a.\n\\]\n\nIntroduce a desired positive clearance margin\n\n\\[\n\\delta>0.\n\\]\n\nDefine\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nb=2a+\\delta.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe strengthened admissibility condition is\n\n\\[\nd_{\\min}\\ge b.\n\\]\n\nSubstituting the exact distance formula,\n\n\\[\nL^2(u-1)^2+w^2\\ge b^2.\n\\]\n\nIntroduce the physical horizontal translation coordinate\n\n\\[\nx=Lu.\n\\]\n\nThen\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n(x-L)^2+w^2\\ge b^2.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe entire four-dimensional finite-core collision problem has reduced to a two-dimensional obstacle problem.\n\nIn the translation plane \\((x,w)\\), the forbidden region is the open disk\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n(x-L)^2+w^2<b^2.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe initial and final points are\n\n\\[\n(0,0)\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n(2L,0).\n\\]\n\nAssume\n\n\\[\n0<b<L\n\\]\n\nand restrict the deformation to\n\n\\[\nw\\ge0.\n\\]\n\nWe can now solve for the shortest admissible route exactly.\n\n---\n\n# 6. Shortest collision-free deformation\n\nThe shortest route around a circular obstacle consists of three pieces:\n\n1. A straight tangent from the initial point to the obstacle.\n2. An arc along the obstacle boundary.\n3. A straight tangent from the obstacle to the final point.\n\nThe two tangent segments have equal length.\n\nTheir length is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nT=\\sqrt{L^2-b^2}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe left tangency point is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nP_L=\n\\left(\nL-\\frac{b^2}{L},\n\\frac{b\\sqrt{L^2-b^2}}{L}\n\\right).\n}\n\\]\n\nThe right tangency point is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nP_R=\n\\left(\nL+\\frac{b^2}{L},\n\\frac{b\\sqrt{L^2-b^2}}{L}\n\\right).\n}\n\\]\n\nThe circular arc between these points subtends angle\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\alpha=2\\arcsin\\left(\\frac bL\\right).\n}\n\\]\n\nIts length is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nA=2b\\arcsin\\left(\\frac bL\\right).\n}\n\\]\n\nTherefore, the complete shortest admissible translation path has length\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nS_{\\min}\n=\n2\\sqrt{L^2-b^2}\n+\n2b\\arcsin\\left(\\frac bL\\right).\n}\n\\]\n\nThis is an exact result.\n\nThe unimpeded straight translation would have length\n\n\\[\n2L.\n\\]\n\nThe extra deformation distance required by the finite-core obstacle is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\Delta S=\n2\\sqrt{L^2-b^2}\n+\n2b\\arcsin\\left(\\frac bL\\right)\n-\n2L.\n}\n\\]\n\nNo physical energy law has been assumed.\n\n\\(\\Delta S\\) is a geometric path-length excess, not automatically an interaction energy.\n\n---\n\n# 7. Minimum fourth-coordinate excursion\n\nEvery continuous translation from\n\n\\[\nu=0\n\\]\n\nto\n\n\\[\nu=2\n\\]\n\npasses through\n\n\\[\nu=1.\n\\]\n\nAt that intermediate value,\n\n\\[\nd_{\\min}(1,w)=|w|.\n\\]\n\nTherefore, avoiding material intersection requires\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n|w|\\ge2a\n}\n\\]\n\nat some point in the deformation.\n\nPreserving the stronger clearance margin requires\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n|w|\\ge b.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe shortest tangent-arc-tangent route reaches\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nw_{\\max}=b.\n}\n\\]\n\nThus, within this translation family, the minimum possible maximum fourth-coordinate displacement needed to preserve clearance \\(\\delta\\) is exactly\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nw_{\\max,\\min}=2a+\\delta.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis is a sharp bound.\n\n---\n\n# 8. A second exact result: the slope threshold\n\nThe fourth-coordinate excursion is not the only constraint.\n\nSuppose the deformation must obey a maximum absolute slope\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\left|\\frac{dw}{dx}\\right|\\le v.\n}\n\\]\n\nHere \\(v\\) is dimensionless.\n\nFor now, this is purely a geometric regularity restriction.\n\nIt is not a physical velocity.\n\nWe require\n\n\\[\nw(0)=0\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\nw(2L)=0.\n\\]\n\nThe slope bound implies\n\n\\[\nw(x)\\le vx\n\\]\n\nwhen approaching from the left endpoint.\n\nApproaching from the right gives\n\n\\[\nw(x)\\le v(2L-x).\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nw(x)\\le v\\min(x,2L-x).\n}\n\\]\n\nThis tent-shaped function is the largest possible height profile under the slope restriction.\n\nTo determine whether any admissible path exists, calculate the smallest distance from this upper envelope to the obstacle center.\n\nFor\n\n\\[\n0\\le x\\le L,\n\\]\n\nthe squared distance is\n\n\\[\nD^2(x)=(x-L)^2+v^2x^2.\n\\]\n\nDifferentiate:\n\n\\[\n\\frac{dD^2}{dx}\n=\n2(x-L)+2v^2x.\n\\]\n\nSetting the derivative to zero,\n\n\\[\nx(1+v^2)=L.\n\\]\n\nThus,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nx_*=\\frac{L}{1+v^2}.\n}\n\\]\n\nSubstitute:\n\n\\[\nD_{\\min}^2\n=\n\\left(\n\\frac{L}{1+v^2}-L\n\\right)^2\n+\nv^2\n\\left(\n\\frac{L}{1+v^2}\n\\right)^2.\n\\]\n\nSimplifying,\n\n\\[\nD_{\\min}^2\n=\n\\frac{L^2v^2}{1+v^2}.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nD_{\\min}\n=\n\\frac{Lv}{\\sqrt{1+v^2}}.\n}\n\\]\n\nFor the obstacle to be avoidable,\n\n\\[\nD_{\\min}\\ge b.\n\\]\n\nHence,\n\n\\[\n\\frac{Lv}{\\sqrt{1+v^2}}\\ge b.\n\\]\n\nSquare:\n\n\\[\nL^2v^2\\ge b^2(1+v^2).\n\\]\n\nRearrange:\n\n\\[\nv^2(L^2-b^2)\\ge b^2.\n\\]\n\nThus,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nv\\ge\n\\frac{b}{\\sqrt{L^2-b^2}}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe tangent-arc-tangent route achieves this bound.\n\nWe have therefore obtained a **necessary and sufficient condition**:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\text{An admissible slope-bounded path exists}\n\\iff\nv\\ge v_{\\mathrm{crit}},\n}\n\\]\n\nwhere\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nv_{\\mathrm{crit}}\n=\n\\frac{b}{\\sqrt{L^2-b^2}}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis result is stronger than simply demonstrating one possible escape.\n\nIt identifies the exact threshold below which **no deformation in the specified translation family can preserve the required clearance**.\n\n---\n\n# 9.
