Requires numpy; matplotlib for optional Class P plot.\n\"\"\"\nimport math\nimport numpy as np\n\nL, CORE, CLEAR = 1.0, .15, .10\nB = 2*CORE + CLEAR\nassert 0 < B < L\n\n\ndef curves(u, w, t):\n    \"\"\"Two circles; second translated in x and fourth coordinate w.\"\"\"\n    x = np.stack((L*np.cos(t), L*np.sin(t), 0*t, 0*t), axis=-1)\n    y = np.stack((L*(1+u+np.cos(t)), 0*t, L*np.sin(t), 0*t+w), axis=-1)\n    return x, y\n\n\ndef exact_gap(u, w):\n    return math.hypot(L*(u-1), w)\n\n\ndef path(b=B, N=1201):\n    \"\"\"Shortest obstacle-avoiding route in (u, w/L) half-plane.\n    Physical arclength coordinates (xshift,w), both in metres.\n    The forbidden circle is centered at (L,0), radius b.\n    \"\"\"\n    a = math.asin(b/L)\n    tangent = math.sqrt(L*L-b*b)\n    arc = 2*b*a\n    total = 2*tangent+arc\n    s = np.linspace(0, total, N)\n    p = np.empty((N,2))\n    left = np.array([L-b*b/L, b*tangent/L])\n    right = np.array([L+b*b/L, b*tangent/L])\n    for j, z in enumerate(s):\n        if z <= tangent:\n            p[j] = left*(z/tangent)\n        elif z <= tangent+arc:\n            theta = math.pi/2+a-(z-tangent)/b\n            p[j] = (L+b*math.cos(theta), b*math.sin(theta))\n        else:\n            p[j] = right+(np.array([2*L,0])-right)*((z-tangent-arc)/tangent)\n    return s, p, total\n\n\ndef sampled_gap(u, w, n=512):\n    \"\"\"Independent brute-force pairwise circle sampling, not exact formula.\"\"\"\n    t = np.linspace(0, 2*math.pi, n, endpoint=False)\n    c1, c2 = curves(u, w, t)\n    # Blocked to avoid excessive temporary allocations.\n    best = math.inf\n    for k in range(0, n, 64):\n        delta = c1[k:k+64,None,:]-c2[None,:,:]\n        best = min(best, float(np.linalg.norm(delta, axis=-1).min()))\n    return best\n\n\ndef link_number_3d(u, n=400):\n    \"\"\"Gauss integral only at endpoints w=0, never on lifted 4D stages.\"\"\"\n    t=(np.arange(n)+.5)*2*math.pi/n\n    x,y=curves(u,0,t)\n    dx=np.stack((-L*np.sin(t),L*np.cos(t),0*t),axis=-1)\n    dy=np.stack((-L*np.sin(t),0*t,L*np.cos(t)),axis=-1)\n    d=x[:,None,:3]-y[None,:,:3]\n    triple=np.sum(np.cross(dx[:,None,:],dy[None,:,:])*d,axis=-1)\n    return float(np.sum(triple/np.linalg.norm(d,axis=-1)**3)*(2*math.pi/n)**2/(4*math.pi))\n\n\ndef independent_so4(seed=20261017):\n    rng=np.random.default_rng(seed)\n    a=rng.normal(size=(4,4)); q,_=np.linalg.qr(a)\n    if np.linalg.det(q)<0: q[:,0]*=-1\n    return q\n\n\ndef main():\n    s, p, total=path()\n    tangent=math.sqrt(L*L-B*B)\n    analytic=2*tangent+2*B*math.asin(B/L)\n    assert abs(total-analytic)<1e-13\n    gaps=np.hypot(p[:,0]-L,p[:,1])\n    assert np.min(gaps)>=B-1e-12\n    assert abs(gaps.min()-B)<1e-11\n    assert abs(p[0,0])<1e-14 and abs(p[-1,0]-2*L)<1e-14\n    assert abs(p[:,1].max()-B)<2e-5\n    assert np.min(p[:,1])>=-1e-14\n    assert np.max(np.abs(np.linalg.norm(np.diff(p,axis=0),axis=1)-np.diff(s)))<2e-6\n    print('KESTREL S4 | R4 LINKED-CIRCLE FINITE-CORE UNLINKING COMPARATOR')\n    print('L CORE CLEAR B',L,CORE,CLEAR,B)\n    print('tangent_length',f'{tangent:.12f}','arc_length',f'{2*B*math.asin(B/L):.12f}')\n    print('shortest_translation_path',f'{total:.12f}','straight_path',f'{2*L:.12f}')\n    print('path_length_excess',f'{total-2*L:.12f}')\n    # Exact Lipschitz/slope threshold for all u in [0,2L].\n    vcrit = B/math.sqrt(L*L-B*B)\n    print('minimum_max_abs_slope',f'{vcrit:.12f}')\n    for v in (0., .25, vcrit, .5, 1.):\n        ugrid=np.linspace(0,2*L,10001)\n        # Every |dw/du|<=v path with zero endpoints obeys this tent bound.\n        upper=v*np.minimum(ugrid,2*L-ugrid)\n        minpossible=np.hypot(ugrid-L,upper).min()\n        exactmin=L*v/math.sqrt(1+v*v)\n        print('slope_bound',f'{v:.12f}', 'best_possible_min_gap',\n              f'{exactmin:.12f}','grid',f'{minpossible:.12f}')\n        assert abs(minpossible-exactmin)<3e-7\n        assert (exactmin>=B-1e-12)==(v>=vcrit-1e-12)\n    # The constructed tangent-arc-tangent route saturates the sharp bound.\n    slopes=np.abs(np.diff(p[:,1])/np.diff(p[:,0]))\n    assert slopes.max()<vcrit+1e-8\n\n    print('minimum_centerline_gap',f'{gaps.min():.12f}','minimum_material_clearance',f'{gaps.min()-2*CORE:.12f}')\n    print('minimum_required_max_fourth_lift',f'{2*CORE:.12f}',\n          'actual_max_fourth_lift',f'{p[:,1].max():.12f}')\n    for u,w in ((0.,0.),(.5,0.),(1.,0.),(1.,B),(2.,0.)):\n        print('control',u,w,'exact',f'{exact_gap(u,w):.12f}',\n              'sampled',f'{sampled_gap(u,w):.12f}')\n        assert abs(sampled_gap(u,w)-exact_gap(u,w))<1e-10\n    for u,w in (tuple(p[j]) for j in (0,100,350,600,850,1100,1200)):\n        numeric=sampled_gap(u,w,n=384)\n        analytic_gap=exact_gap(u,w)\n        assert numeric>=analytic_gap-1e-12\n        assert numeric-analytic_gap<2e-5\n    print('Gauss_link_initial',f'{link_number_3d(0):+.12f}')\n    print('Gauss_link_final',f'{link_number_3d(2):+.12f}')\n    assert abs(abs(link_number_3d(0))-1)<1e-9\n    assert abs(link_number_3d(2))<1e-9\n    q=independent_so4()\n    assert abs(np.linalg.det(q)-1)<1e-12\n    for u,w in ((0.,0.),(1.,B),(2.,0.)):\n        t=np.linspace(0,2*math.pi,256,endpoint=False)\n        x,y=curves(u,w,t)\n        xx,yy=x@q,y@q\n        old=np.linalg.norm(x[:,None,:]-y[None,:,:],axis=-1).min()\n        new=np.linalg.norm(xx[:,None,:]-yy[None,:,:],axis=-1).min()\n        assert abs(old-new)<1e-12\n    # Independent arclength numerical quadrature of the exact path.\n    numer=float(np.linalg.norm(np.diff(p,axis=0),axis=1).sum())\n    print('polyline_length',f'{numer:.12f}','absolute_error',f'{abs(numer-total):.3e}')\n    assert abs(numer-total)<2e-6\n    print('SO4_AND_BRUTE_FORCE_CHECKS_PASSED')\n    print('ALL_ASSERTIONS_PASSED')\n    try:\n        import matplotlib\n        matplotlib.use('Agg')\n        import matplotlib.pyplot as plt\n        fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(8,5.2))\n        t=np.linspace(0,math.pi,500)\n        ax.fill(L+B*np.cos(t),B*np.sin(t),alpha=.16,label='forbidden centerline-gap disk')\n        ax.plot(L+B*np.cos(t),B*np.sin(t),ls=':',label='gap = 2 core radii + margin')\n        ax.plot(p[:,0],p[:,1],lw=2,label='shortest safe R4 translation')\n        ax.scatter([0,2*L],[0,0],s=35)\n        ax.set(xlabel='x translation [m]',ylabel='fourth-coordinate translation [m]',\n               title='Class P: finite-core Hopf-link escape in Euclidean R4')\n        ax.set_aspect('equal');ax.grid(alpha=.25);ax.legend();fig.tight_layout()\n        fig.savefig('/mnt/data/kestrel_s4_r4_unlink_classP.png',dpi=160)\n        plt.close(fig)\n        fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(8,4.8))\n        ax.plot(s,gaps-2*CORE,label='exact material clearance')\n        ax.axhline(CLEAR,ls=':',label='prescribed margin')\n        ax.set(xlabel='translation-path arclength [m]',ylabel='core-to-core clearance [m]',\n               title='Class P: minimum clearance along unlinking isotopy')\n        ax.grid(alpha=.25);ax.legend();fig.tight_layout()\n        fig.savefig('/mnt/data/kestrel_s4_r4_unlink_clearance_classP.png',dpi=160)\n        plt.close(fig)\n        print('CLASS_P_PLOTS_SAVED')\n    except ImportError:\n        print('MATPLOTLIB_UNAVAILABLE')\n\nif __name__=='__main__': main()\n```\n\n[Complete executable Python](sandbox:/mnt/data/kestrel_s4_r4_unlink_clearance.py)\n\n---\n\n# 13. BEDROCK review\n\nI independently read the complete live urlBEDROCK.mdhttps://github.com/Satobloc/HsH/blob/main/BEDROCK.md.\n\n**Verified source blob:** `ea2126ab88a6625177d2c488b75fee0e27a70ca2`\n\nI also consulted urlSTATE_OF_THE_THEORY.mdhttps://github.com/Satobloc/HsH/blob/main/STATE_OF_THE_THEORY.md, the October 9 internal-first directive, Sable's README and continuity checkpoint, the original SAT *Fundamental Intuitions Extended* extraction, and the August 2024 discussion of forces across temporal points.\n\nThe authority distinctions remain intact: ND, FB, WB, TF, OC, and SS. No quarantined material was accessed.\n\n**One material translation ambiguity emerged.**\n\nBR-005 defines the straight vacuum filament as aligned with the time normal:\n\n\\[\n\\theta_4=0.\n\\]\n\nBut under the proposed Householder-induced Lorentz metric, a vector aligned with that normal is **timelike**, not metric-null.\n\nThis need not contradict BEDROCK. The term *null/vacuum* may designate the unwound vacuum configuration rather than a null spacetime interval.\n\nHowever, those meanings cannot be silently identified.\n\nThe calculation below makes the distinction exact.\n\n---\n\n# 2. Principal result\n\n## A radial time-normal field produces a curved Lorentz metric from flat Euclidean four-space\n\nBegin with the four-dimensional Euclidean metric\n\n\\[\n\\delta_{ab}.\n\\]\n\nLet\n\n\\[\nx\\in\\mathbb R^4,\\qquad r=\\sqrt{x_ax_a}>0.\n\\]\n\nDefine the radial Euclidean unit vector field\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nu^a(x)=\\frac{x^a}{r}.\n}\n\\]\n\nConstruct the Householder metric\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\ng_{ab}=\\delta_{ab}-2u_au_b.\n}\n\\]\n\nAt every point, this metric has signature\n\n\\[\n(-,+,+,+).\n\\]\n\nNevertheless, it is **not generally flat**.\n\nFor this particular radial field, I obtain\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nR=\\frac{12}{r^2}\n}\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nR_{abcd}R^{abcd}=\\frac{48}{r^4}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThese are exact results.\n\nThe important distinction is:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\text{Lorentz signature is algebraic; curvature depends on spatial variation.}\n}\n\\]\n\nThe metric signature follows immediately from the Householder construction.\n\nThe curvature requires derivatives of the time-normal field.\n\nA constant time normal produces flat Minkowski geometry.\n\nA radial time normal produces nonzero curvature.\n\nThat gives us a concrete mathematical test for the SAT/H(s)H metric-induction program.\n\n---\n\n# 3. Derivation\n\n## 3.1 Householder properties\n\nDefine the projector orthogonal to \\(u\\):\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nP_{ab}=\\delta_{ab}-u_au_b.\n}\n\\]\n\nBecause\n\n\\[\nu_au^a=1,\n\\]\n\nwe have\n\n\\[\nP_{ab}u^b=0.\n\\]\n\nThe induced metric can be rewritten\n\n\\[\ng=P-u\\otimes u.\n\\]\n\nApplying the metric twice gives\n\n\\[\ng^2=I.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\ng^{-1}=g.\n}\n\\]\n\nIts determinant is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\det g=-1}\n\\]\n\nin Cartesian Euclidean coordinates.\n\nThe radial direction has eigenvalue \\(-1\\), while the three orthogonal directions have eigenvalue \\(+1\\).\n\nThus the signature is Lorentzian.\n\nThis conclusion holds for any smooth Euclidean unit vector field \\(u\\), not just the radial example.\n\n---\n\n## 3.2 Derivatives of the time normal\n\nFor\n\n\\[\nu_a=\\frac{x_a}{r},\n\\]\n\ndifferentiate:\n\n\\[\n\\partial_cu_a\n=\n\\frac{\\delta_{ac}}r-\\frac{x_ax_c}{r^3}.\n\\]\n\nUsing\n\n\\[\nx_a=ru_a,\n\\]\n\nwe obtain\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\partial_cu_a=\\frac{P_{ac}}r.\n}\n\\]\n\nDifferentiate the metric:\n\n\\[\n\\partial_cg_{ab}\n=\n-2\\left[\n(\\partial_cu_a)u_b+\nu_a(\\partial_cu_b)\n\\right].\n\\]\n\nSubstitute the projector expression:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\partial_cg_{ab}\n=\n-\\frac2r\n\\left(\nP_{ac}u_b+u_aP_{bc}\n\\right).\n}\n\\]\n\nThis derivative is nonzero because the radial direction changes across Euclidean space.\n\n---\n\n## 3.3 Christoffel symbols\n\nThe Levi-Civita connection is\n\n\\[\n\\Gamma^a{}_{bc}\n=\n\\frac12g^{ad}\n\\left(\n\\partial_bg_{dc}\n+\n\\partial_cg_{db}\n-\n\\partial_dg_{bc}\n\\right).\n\\]\n\nSubstituting the metric derivatives and simplifying gives\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\Gamma^a{}_{bc}\n=\n\\frac2r u^aP_{bc}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis is the first substantial result.\n\nThe entire connection is determined by the radial field and its orthogonal projector.\n\nIt also has a useful property:\n\n\\[\n\\Gamma^a{}_{bc}u^bu^c=0.\n\\]\n\nConsequently, radial integral curves of \\(u\\) are geodesics of the induced metric.\n\n---\n\n# 4. Exact Riemann curvature\n\nUse the convention\n\n\\[\nR^a{}_{bcd}\n=\n\\partial_c\\Gamma^a{}_{db}\n-\n\\partial_d\\Gamma^a{}_{cb}\n+\n\\Gamma^a{}_{ce}\\Gamma^e{}_{db}\n-\n\\Gamma^a{}_{de}\\Gamma^e{}_{cb}.\n\\]\n\nSubstitute\n\n\\[\n\\Gamma^a{}_{bc}\n=\n\\frac2r u^aP_{bc}.\n\\]\n\nThe quadratic connection terms vanish because\n\n\\[\nP_{ab}u^b=0.\n\\]\n\nAfter differentiating the remaining terms, the Riemann tensor becomes\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nR^a{}_{bcd}\n=\n\\frac2{r^2}\n\\left(\nP^a{}_cP_{bd}\n-\nP^a{}_dP_{bc}\n\\right).\n}\n\\]\n\nThis expression is exact.\n\nIt has no components involving the radial direction.\n\nThe curvature is entirely associated with directions tangent to the three-dimensional hyperspheres\n\n\\[\nr=\\text{constant}.\n\\]\n\n## 4.1 Ricci tensor\n\nContract the first and third indices:\n\n\\[\nR_{bd}=R^a{}_{bad}.\n\\]\n\nSince\n\n\\[\nP^a{}_a=3\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\nP^a{}_dP_{ab}=P_{db},\n\\]\n\nwe obtain\n\n\\[\nR_{bd}\n=\n\\frac2{r^2}(3P_{bd}-P_{bd}).\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nR_{ab}=\\frac4{r^2}P_{ab}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe radial Ricci contraction vanishes:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nR_{ab}u^au^b=0.\n}\n\\]\n\n## 4.2 Scalar curvature\n\nContract again:\n\n\\[\nR=g^{ab}R_{ab}.\n\\]\n\nBecause the projector has rank three,\n\n\\[\ng^{ab}P_{ab}=3.\n\\]\n\nHence,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nR=\\frac{12}{r^2}.\n}\n\\]\n\nUnits:\n\n\\[\n[R]=\\mathrm m^{-2}.\n\\]\n\n## 4.3 Quadratic invariants\n\nThe squared Ricci tensor is\n\n\\[\nR_{ab}R^{ab}\n=\n3\\left(\\frac4{r^2}\\right)^2.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nR_{ab}R^{ab}=\\frac{48}{r^4}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe Kretschmann scalar is\n\n\\[\n\\mathcal K=R_{abcd}R^{abcd}.\n\\]\n\nFor the present curvature tensor,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\mathcal K=\\frac{48}{r^4}.\n}\n\\]\n\nBoth quantities have units\n\n\\[\n\\mathrm m^{-4}.\n\\]\n\nAn additional identity follows:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\mathcal K-4R_{ab}R^{ab}+R^2=0.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe four-dimensional Euler curvature density vanishes pointwise away from the origin, despite the nonzero Riemann tensor.\n\n---\n\n# 5. The induced Einstein tensor\n\nThe Einstein tensor is\n\n\\[\nG_{ab}=R_{ab}-\\frac12Rg_{ab}.\n\\]\n\nSubstitute the expressions already derived:\n\n\\[\nG_{ab}\n=\n\\frac4{r^2}P_{ab}\n-\n\\frac6{r^2}g_{ab}.\n\\]\n\nSince\n\n\\[\ng=P-u\\otimes u,\n\\]\n\nwe obtain\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nG_{ab}\n=\n\\frac1{r^2}\n\\left(\n6u_au_b-2P_{ab}\n\\right).\n}\n\\]\n\nIts radial timelike contraction is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nG_{ab}u^au^b=\\frac6{r^2}.\n}\n\\]\n\nIts eigenvalue in each orthogonal spatial direction is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n-\\frac2{r^2}.\n}\n\\]\n\nIf one formally imposed the Einstein field equations, this would correspond to an effective isotropic equation-of-state ratio\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\frac p\\rho=-\\frac13.\n}\n\\]\n\nThat is a property of the constructed metric under the stated interpretation.\n\nIt is **not** a claim that SAT/H(s)H contains such matter or that its cosmology has been derived.\n\nThe important negative result is that the radial Householder metric is **not an Einstein-vacuum solution**.\n\nAn additional dynamical equation or constitutive structure would be needed to establish a physical gravitational model.\n\n---\n\n# 6. Radial expansion and the Raychaudhuri equation\n\nThe induced metric has a particularly simple expression in four-dimensional spherical coordinates:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nds^2=-dr^2+r^2d\\Omega_3^2.\n}\n\\]\n\nHere \\(d\\Omega_3^2\\) is the metric on the unit three-sphere.\n\nThe radial direction is timelike.\n\nThe hypersurfaces\n\n\\[\nr=\\text{constant}\n\\]\n\nare spacelike three-spheres.\n\nTheir scale factor is\n\n\\[\na(r)=r.\n\\]\n\nThe radial congruence has expansion\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\Theta=\\nabla_au^a=\\frac3r.\n}\n\\]\n\nIts shear and vorticity vanish.\n\nIts acceleration also vanishes:\n\n\\[\nu^a\\nabla_au^b=0.\n\\]\n\nDifferentiate the expansion along the radial flow:\n\n\\[\n\\frac{d\\Theta}{dr}\n=\n-\\frac3{r^2}.\n\\]\n\nFor a geodesic, shear-free, vorticity-free timelike congruence, the Raychaudhuri equation reduces to\n\n\\[\n\\frac{d\\Theta}{dr}\n=\n-\\frac{\\Theta^2}{3}\n-\nR_{ab}u^au^b.\n\\]\n\nWe already found\n\n\\[\nR_{ab}u^au^b=0.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n-\\frac{\\Theta^2}{3}\n=\n-\\frac{(3/r)^2}{3}\n=\n-\\frac3{r^2}.\n\\]\n\nThus,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\frac{d\\Theta}{dr}\n=\n-\\frac{\\Theta^2}{3}\n=\n-\\frac3{r^2}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe congruence satisfies the Raychaudhuri equation exactly.\n\nThis is a useful consistency check independent of the scalar-curvature calculation.\n\n---\n\n# 7. A singularity distinction\n\nThe radial unit field is undefined at\n\n\\[\nr=0.\n\\]\n\nBoth curvature invariants diverge there:\n\n\\[\nR\\sim r^{-2},\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\mathcal K\\sim r^{-4}.\n\\]\n\nBut their integrated behavior differs.\n\nThe four-dimensional spherical volume element is\n\n\\[\ndV=2\\pi^2r^3\\,dr.\n\\]\n\nFor a shell\n\n\\[\na<r<b,\n\\]\n\nthe volume is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nV=\\frac{\\pi^2}{2}(b^4-a^4).\n}\n\\]\n\nThe integrated scalar curvature is\n\n\\[\n\\int R\\,dV\n=\n\\int_a^b\n\\frac{12}{r^2}\n2\\pi^2r^3\\,dr.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\int R\\,dV\n=\n12\\pi^2(b^2-a^2).\n}\n\\]\n\nAs\n\n\\[\na\\rightarrow0,\n\\]\n\nthis integral remains finite.\n\nNow consider the Kretschmann scalar:\n\n\\[\n\\int\\mathcal K\\,dV\n=\n\\int_a^b\n\\frac{48}{r^4}\n2\\pi^2r^3\\,dr.\n\\]\n\nThus,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\int\\mathcal K\\,dV\n=\n96\\pi^2\\ln\\left(\\frac ba\\right).\n}\n\\]\n\nAs\n\n\\[\na\\rightarrow0,\n\\]\n\nthis diverges logarithmically.\n\n**The scalar-curvature integral can remain finite even when the quadratic curvature integral diverges.**\n\nThat matters for any proposed finite-core regularization.\n\nA finite integrated scalar curvature is not sufficient evidence that the underlying geometry is nonsingular.\n\n---\n\n# 8. BEDROCK θ₄ consistency test\n\nThis is the most important interpretation boundary in the calculation.\n\nLet \\(v\\) be a Euclidean unit tangent vector making angle \\(\\theta\\) with the time normal \\(u\\).\n\nThen\n\n\\[\nu\\cdot v=\\cos\\theta.\n\\]\n\nUnder the induced metric,\n\n\\[\ng(v,v)\n=\n\\delta(v,v)-2(u\\cdot v)^2.\n\\]\n\nBecause\n\n\\[\n\\delta(v,v)=1,\n\\]\n\nwe obtain\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\ng(v,v)=1-2\\cos^2\\theta.\n}\n\\]\n\nEvaluate three orientations.\n\n| Angle from time normal | Induced metric norm | Classification |\n|---|---:|---|\n| \\(0^\\circ\\) | \\(-1\\) | Timelike |\n| \\(45^\\circ\\) | \\(0\\) | Null |\n| \\(90^\\circ\\) | \\(+1\\) | Spacelike |\n\nBEDROCK BR-005 says that the straight vacuum filament has\n\n\\[\n\\theta_4=0.\n\\]\n\nUnder the Householder metric, that direction is timelike.\n\nThe metric-null direction instead occurs at\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\theta=45^\\circ.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis yields a precise unresolved translation question:\n\n**Does SAT's “null/vacuum” designation mean absence of excitation or winding, or does it require a null interval in the induced Lorentz metric?**\n\nThe first interpretation is compatible with the construction.\n\nThe second is not, without modifying the metric or the geometric identification.\n\nI am recording this as a **TF-level consistency flag**, not modifying BR-005.\n\n---\n\n# 9. Executed numerical results\n\nThe analytical tensors were independently checked using numerical differentiation of the metric connection.\n\nThe Python program evaluated 15 Cartesian points, including three fixed fixtures and twelve seeded pseudorandom points.\n\nFor each point, it independently constructed the Christoffel symbols from metric derivatives, calculated the Riemann tensor by centered finite differences, and compared the resulting contractions with the analytical formulas.\n\n### Numerical error bounds\n\n| Check | Maximum observed absolute error |\n|---|---:|\n| Christoffel symbols | \\(8.882\\times10^{-16}\\) |\n| Riemann components | \\(6.018\\times10^{-10}\\) |\n| Scalar curvature | \\(3.606\\times10^{-9}\\) |\n| Kretschmann scalar | \\(9.600\\times10^{-9}\\) |\n\nAll numerical assertions passed.\n\n### Curvature fixtures\n\n| Radius | Scalar curvature | Kretschmann scalar | \\(G(u,u)\\) |\n|---:|---:|---:|---:|\n| 0.4 m | 75.000000 | 1875.000000 | 37.500000 |\n| 1.0 m | 12.000000 | 48.000000 | 6.000000 |\n| 2.0 m | 3.000000 | 3.000000 | 1.500000 |\n\nThe scalar curvature and Einstein-tensor entries have units \\(\\mathrm m^{-2}\\). Class P geometry\n\n![Exact curvature invariants for radial Householder metric](sandbox:/mnt/data/sable_s4_radial_householder_classP.png)\n\nThe plot shows the different radial scaling laws:\n\n\\[\nR\\propto r^{-2},\n\\]\n\n\\[\nG(u,u)\\propto r^{-2},\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\mathcal K\\propto r^{-4}.\n\\]\n\nThe plotted curves were generated directly from the analytical formulas.\n\n[Class P plot](sandbox:/mnt/data/sable_s4_radial_householder_classP.png)\n\n---\n\n# 11. Complete tested Python source\n\n**Dependencies:** NumPy and SciPy. Matplotlib is optional.\n\n**Executed source SHA-256:**\n\n`95240ed24c0bbe3a38fed99cc6284929c1216a06d8c1f22ae260daad8d35ed56`\n\n```python\n#!/usr/bin/env python3\n\"\"\"Sable s4: Householder Lorentz metric from radial Euclidean unit field.\nTF mathematical comparator only. Four Euclidean Cartesian coordinates in metres.\nDependencies numpy, scipy; matplotlib optional. No external source data.\n\"\"\"\nimport math\nimport numpy as np\nfrom scipy.integrate import quad\n\nDIM=4\nI=np.eye(DIM)\n\ndef fields(x):\n    x=np.asarray(x,dtype=float)\n    r=float(np.linalg.norm(x))\n    if r<=0: raise ValueError('Radial unit flow undefined at origin')\n    u=x/r\n    P=I-np.outer(u,u)\n    g=I-2*np.outer(u,u)\n    return r,u,P,g\n\ndef metric_derivative(x):\n    r,u,P,g=fields(x)\n    # D[c,i,j] = partial_c g_ij\n    return -2/r*(np.einsum('ic,j->cij',P,u)+np.einsum('i,jc->cij',u,P))\n\ndef gamma_metric(x):\n    r,u,P,g=fields(x)\n    D=metric_derivative(x)\n    G=np.zeros((DIM,DIM,DIM))\n    for a in range(DIM):\n        for b in range(DIM):\n            for c in range(DIM):\n                G[a,b,c]=.5*sum(g[a,d]*(D[b,d,c]+D[c,d,b]-D[d,b,c]) for d in range(DIM))\n    return G\n\ndef gamma_closed(x):\n    r,u,P,g=fields(x)\n    return (2/r)*np.einsum('a,bc->abc',u,P)\n\ndef riemann_closed(x):\n    r,u,P,g=fields(x)\n    # R^a_{bcd} = partial_c Gamma^a_{db} - partial_d Gamma^a_{cb} + ...\n    return (2/r**2)*(np.einsum('ac,db->abcd',P,P)-np.einsum('ad,cb->abcd',P,P))\n\ndef riemann_finite_difference(x, step=1e-5):\n    x=np.asarray(x,dtype=float)\n    G=gamma_metric(x)\n    DG=np.empty((DIM,DIM,DIM,DIM))\n    for c in range(DIM):\n        h=step*max(1.,float(np.linalg.norm(x)))\n        delta=np.zeros(DIM);delta[c]=h\n        DG[c]=(gamma_metric(x+delta)-gamma_metric(x-delta))/(2*h)\n    R=np.zeros((DIM,DIM,DIM,DIM))\n    for a in range(DIM):\n        for b in range(DIM):\n            for c in range(DIM):\n Principal result\n\n## Relative chirality can remain identifiable when absolute chirality is not\n\nMira's earlier calculation established that the sign of a four-dimensional skew matrix's Pfaffian is invariant under proper SO(4) rotations but reverses under an orientation-reversing O(4) transformation.\n\nConsequently, when the parity of an observation frame is completely unknown, **absolute chirality cannot be identified**.\n\nThis run establishes a useful extension:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\text{Two observations sharing an unknown orientation parity can retain identifiable relative chirality.}\n}\n\\]\n\nThe result is exact under the specified observation model.\n\nMore strongly, the product of the two observed Pfaffian signs is the **Bayes-optimal discriminator of relative chirality**, assuming independent isotropic noise and equal independent chirality priors.\n\nThe absolute orientation remains unidentified.\n\nThe relative orientation does not.\n\nThis is a mathematical example of information surviving the loss of a shared reference convention.\n\n---\n\n# 3. Four-dimensional chirality\n\nLet \\(A\\) be a real \\(4\\times4\\) antisymmetric matrix:\n\n\\[\nA^\\mathsf T=-A.\n\\]\n\nIts Pfaffian is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\operatorname{Pf}(A)\n=\nA_{12}A_{34}\n-\nA_{13}A_{24}\n+\nA_{14}A_{23}.\n}\n\\]\n\nFor any orthogonal transformation \\(Q\\),\n\n\\[\nQ^\\mathsf TQ=I,\n\\]\n\nthe Pfaffian transforms according to\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\operatorname{Pf}(QAQ^\\mathsf T)\n=\n\\det(Q)\\operatorname{Pf}(A).\n}\n\\]\n\nTherefore:\n\n\\[\n\\det(Q)=+1\n\\quad\\Longrightarrow\\quad\n\\operatorname{Pf}(QAQ^\\mathsf T)=\\operatorname{Pf}(A),\n\\]\n\nwhile\n\n\\[\n\\det(Q)=-1\n\\quad\\Longrightarrow\\quad\n\\operatorname{Pf}(QAQ^\\mathsf T)=-\\operatorname{Pf}(A).\n\\]\n\nProper SO(4) rotations preserve Pfaffian sign.\n\nImproper O(4) transformations reverse it.\n\n---\n\n# 4. The common-parity theorem\n\nConsider two antisymmetric observations\n\n\\[\nA_1,\\qquad A_2.\n\\]\n\nSuppose their observation frames have the same unknown orientation parity.\n\nThe two frames may otherwise differ by arbitrary proper SO(4) rotations.\n\nLet\n\n\\[\nO\\in\\{+1,-1\\}\n\\]\n\ndenote their common orientation parity.\n\nLet the underlying chirality labels be\n\n\\[\nh_1,h_2\\in\\{+1,-1\\}.\n\\]\n\nIn the absence of measurement noise, the observed Pfaffian signs are\n\n\\[\nz_1=Oh_1,\n\\]\n\n\\[\nz_2=Oh_2.\n\\]\n\nMultiply:\n\n\\[\nz_1z_2=O^2h_1h_2.\n\\]\n\nBecause\n\n\\[\nO^2=1,\n\\]\n\nwe obtain\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nz_1z_2=h_1h_2.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe unknown parity cancels.\n\nThus the relative chirality\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nH=h_1h_2\n}\n\\]\n\nis observable even when neither absolute chirality is.\n\nThis requires the parity ambiguity to be **shared**.\n\nIf the two measurements have independently unknown orientation parities, the cancellation no longer follows.\n\n---\n\n# 5. Add measurement noise\n\nFollowing Mira's earlier synthetic fixture, let the two underlying rotation angles be\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\alpha=0.2387\\ \\mathrm{rad},\n\\qquad\n\\beta=0.246\\ \\mathrm{rad}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThese are mathematical fixture parameters, not independently validated physical constants.\n\nFor a single observation, the skew matrix separates into self-dual and anti-self-dual three-vector components.\n\nDefine their noiseless lengths:\n\n\\[\nr_{\\mathrm{big}}\n=\n\\frac{\\sin\\alpha+\\sin\\beta}{\\sqrt2},\n\\]\n\n\\[\nr_{\\mathrm{small}}\n=\n\\frac{|\\sin\\alpha-\\sin\\beta|}{\\sqrt2}.\n\\]\n\nLet the original matrix-entry noise have standard deviation\n\n\\[\n\\sigma.\n\\]\n\nThe corresponding independent skew-component variance is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nv=\\frac{\\sigma^2}{2}.\n}\n\\]\n\nDefine the noncentrality parameters\n\n\\[\n\\lambda_{\\mathrm{big}}\n=\n\\frac{r_{\\mathrm{big}}^2}{v},\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\lambda_{\\mathrm{small}}\n=\n\\frac{r_{\\mathrm{small}}^2}{v}.\n\\]\n\nThe exact probability of an incorrect Pfaffian-sign decision under known orientation parity is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\ne(\\sigma)=\n\\int_0^\\infty\nF_{\\chi'^2_3(\\lambda_{\\mathrm{big}})}(t)\nf_{\\chi'^2_3(\\lambda_{\\mathrm{small}})}(t)\n\\,dt.\n}\n\\]\n\nHere \\(F\\) is the noncentral chi-square cumulative distribution function and \\(f\\) is its density.\n\nThis expression comes from comparing the squared lengths of the two noisy three-vector components.\n\nFor the earlier isotropic observation model, the Pfaffian-sign rule is Bayes-optimal within the skew observation.\n\n---\n\n# 6. Exact Bayesian discrimination of relative chirality\n\nLet\n\n\\[\nf_i^+(x_i)\n\\]\n\ndenote the likelihood of observation \\(x_i\\) under positive effective chirality.\n\nLet\n\n\\[\nf_i^-(x_i)\n\\]\n\ndenote the likelihood under negative effective chirality.\n\nAssume equal independent priors on the two underlying chirality labels.\n\nBecause the common unknown orientation parity can reverse both labels simultaneously, the likelihood for **equal relative chirality** is proportional to\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nL_{\\mathrm{same}}\n=\nf_1^+f_2^+\n+\nf_1^-f_2^-.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe likelihood for **opposite relative chirality** is proportional to\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nL_{\\mathrm{opposite}}\n=\nf_1^+f_2^-\n+\nf_1^-f_2^+.\n}\n\\]\n\nSubtract:\n\n\\[\nL_{\\mathrm{same}}-L_{\\mathrm{opposite}}\n=\nf_1^+f_2^+\n+\nf_1^-f_2^-\n-\nf_1^+f_2^-\n-\nf_1^-f_2^+.\n\\]\n\nFactor:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nL_{\\mathrm{same}}-L_{\\mathrm{opposite}}\n=\n(f_1^+-f_1^-)\n(f_2^+-f_2^-).\n}\n\\]\n\nMira's predecessor established that the sign of each likelihood difference is the sign of the corresponding observed Pfaffian.\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\widehat H\n=\n\\operatorname{sgn}\n\\left[\n\\operatorname{Pf}(A_1)\n\\operatorname{Pf}(A_2)\n\\right]\n}\n\\]\n\nis the Bayes-optimal relative-chirality decision under the model.\n\nThis remains true even when the common frame parity is entirely unknown.\n\n---\n\n# 7. Exact error probability\n\nLet\n\n\\[\ne_1=e(\\sigma_1),\n\\qquad\ne_2=e(\\sigma_2).\n\\]\n\nThe relative-chirality decision is wrong precisely when one individual sign is wrong and the other is correct.\n\nThus,\n\n\\[\nP(\\mathrm{error})\n=\ne_1(1-e_2)+(1-e_1)e_2.\n\\]\n\nExpanding,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nE_{12}=e_1+e_2-2e_1e_2.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis formula is exact under conditional independence.\n\nSeveral useful limits follow.\n\nIf both observations are perfect,\n\n\\[\ne_1=e_2=0,\n\\]\n\nthen\n\n\\[\nE_{12}=0.\n\\]\n\nIf one observation is completely uninformative,\n\n\\[\ne_2=\\frac12,\n\\]\n\nthen\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nE_{12}=\\frac12.\n}\n\\]\n\nIf one observation is perfect,\n\n\\[\ne_1=0,\n\\]\n\nthen\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nE_{12}=e_2.\n}\n\\]\n\nA reliable reference observation therefore allows the second observation's relative chirality to be estimated nearly as accurately as its own absolute chirality could be estimated under a known orientation frame.\n\n---\n\n# 8. Executed numerical results\n\nThe Python calculation used\n\n\\[\n\\alpha=0.2387,\n\\qquad\n\\beta=0.246.\n\\]\n\nThree noise levels were tested:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\sigma_1=0.10,\\quad\n\\sigma_2=0.15,\\quad\n\\sigma_3=0.20.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe exact individual skew-sign errors are:\n\n| Observation | Noise \\(\\sigma\\) | Known-parity error |\n|---|---:|---:|\n| 1 | 0.10 | 0.002654648949 |\n| 2 | 0.15 | 0.051828925756 |\n| 3 | 0.20 | 0.142366826706 |\n\nWith balanced, completely unknown absolute parity, each individual absolute-chirality error is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{0.5}.\n\\]\n\nBut the relative errors are substantially smaller:\n\n| Relative pair | Exact Bayes error |\n|---|---:|\n| \\(H_{12}\\) | **0.054208399498** |\n| \\(H_{13}\\) | **0.144265607761** |\n| \\(H_{23}\\) | **0.179438313079** |\n\nThe first pair therefore retains approximately **94.58% classification accuracy** despite having no calibrated absolute orientation parity.\n\n---\n\n# 9. Independent Monte Carlo verification\n\nThe script generated\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{250{,}000}\n\\]\n\nsynthetic triples.\n\nRandom seed:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{202610171248}.\n\\]\n\nEach synthetic observation had independently randomized proper SO(4) orientation, represented through its self-dual and anti-self-dual three-vector components.\n\nAll three observations shared one unknown orientation parity.\n\nThe numerical results were:\n\n| Pair | Exact error | Monte Carlo error | Standardized discrepancy |\n|---|---:|---:|---:|\n| 1–2 | 0.054208399 | 0.054392000 | 0.405 |\n| 1–3 | 0.144265608 | 0.144848000 | 0.829 |\n| 2–3 | 0.179438313 | 0.179496000 | 0.075 |\n\nAll discrepancies were below one standard error.\n\n**Execution:** `ALL_ASSERTIONS_PASSED`.\n\n---\n\n# 10. Three-observation consistency and correlated errors\n\nFor three observations, define\n\n\\[\nH_{12}=h_1h_2,\n\\]\n\n\\[\nH_{13}=h_1h_3,\n\\]\n\n\\[\nH_{23}=h_2h_3.\n\\]\n\nTheir product is\n\n\\[\nH_{12}H_{13}H_{23}\n=\nh_1^2h_2^2h_3^2.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nH_{12}H_{13}H_{23}=1.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe observed relative-sign estimates obey the same algebraic identity.\n\nHowever, this identity alone does **not** verify that the observation frames share parity. Any three binary signs satisfy the corresponding pair-product identity.\n\nIt is a consistency identity, not an independent parity-calibration test.\n\n### Shared-reference error covariance\n\nDefine\n\n\\[\nW_{12}\n\\]\n\nas the indicator that the estimated relative chirality between observations 1 and 2 is wrong.\n\nDefine\n\n\\[\nW_{13}\n\\]\n\nsimilarly.\n\nBoth error indicators depend on observation 1.\n\nConsequently, they are correlated.\n\nUnder independent individual sign errors,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\operatorname{Cov}(W_{12},W_{13})\n=\ne_1(1-e_1)(1-2e_2)(1-2e_3).\n}\n\\]\n\nFor the numerical fixture,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\operatorname{Cov}(W_{12},W_{13})\n=\n0.001697439391.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe Monte Carlo result was\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n0.001993427584.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe difference is consistent with sampling fluctuations at the tested sample size.\n\nThis matters because multiple relative-chirality measurements sharing a reference cannot be treated as statistically independent evidence.\n\nDoing so would overstate the information recovered.\n\n---\n\n# 11. What happens when common parity drifts?\n\nThe common-parity requirement is the central vulnerability.\n\nSuppose the second observation's parity differs from the first with probability\n\n\\[\nd.\n\\]\n\nThen the relative-sign decision is wrong when either the original relative decision is wrong or the parity relationship flips, but not both.\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nE_{12}(d)\n=\nd+(1-2d)E_{12}(0).\n}\n\\]\n\nFor the first numerical pair:\n\n\\[\nE_{12}(0)=0.054208399498.\n\\]\n\nThe independently executed arithmetic gives:\n\n| Parity mismatch probability \\(d\\) | Relative error |\n|---:|---:|\n| 0 | 0.054208399498 |\n| 0.02 | 0.072040063518 |\n| 0.05 | 0.098787559548 |\n| 0.10 | 0.143366719598 |\n| 0.25 | 0.277104199749 |\n| 0.50 | 0.500000000000 |\n\nAt\n\n\\[\nd=\\frac12,\n\\]\n\nthe relative chirality becomes unidentifiable under this observation model.\n\nThus, the next experimental requirement is not merely measuring two skew structures.\n\nIt is establishing that their orientation conventions are meaningfully related.\n\n---\n\n# 12. Principal result\n\n## Nonzero normal holonomy generated entirely by embedded four-dimensional geometry\n\nNadir's preceding work established an important negative control.\n\nA rotating normal frame can create apparent connection coefficients even when the underlying geometry has trivial holonomy. Omitting the gauge-completion terms can then manufacture artificial geometric effects.\n\nThe next question is:\n\n**Can a genuinely curved normal connection be generated directly by an embedded object in Euclidean four-space, without imposing an independent connection?**\n\nYes.\n\nFor a particular exact embedding, I obtain\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\Theta(R)=\n\\frac{2\\pi a^2R^2}{1+a^2R^2}\n}\n\\]\n\nfor the normal-bundle holonomy angle around a circular path of radius \\(R\\).\n\nThe associated normal curvature is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nK_N(r)=\n\\frac{2a^2}{(1+a^2r^2)^3}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe induced Gaussian curvature is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nK(r)=\n-\\frac{2a^2}{(1+a^2r^2)^3}.\n}\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{K+K_N=0.}\n\\]\n\nThese are exact results.\n\nUnlike Nadir's previous pure-gauge example, the curvature is nonzero. The holonomy cannot be eliminated by merely changing the normal frame.\n\nThis gives the H(s)H playground a concrete example of geometric transport generated by an embedding rather than an arbitrarily prescribed rotation law.\n\n---\n\n# 3. Construct the surface\n\nWork in Euclidean\n\n\\[\n\\mathbb R^4\n\\]\n\nwith coordinates measured in meters.\n\nLet\n\n\\[\na>0\n\\]\n\nhave units\n\n\\[\n[a]=\\mathrm m^{-1}.\n\\]\n\nDefine the two-dimensional embedded surface\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nF(x,y)=\n\\begin{pmatrix}\nx\\\\\ny\\\\\n\\frac a2(x^2-y^2)\\\\\naxy\n\\end{pmatrix}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis is the real representation of the complex quadratic graph\n\n\\[\nw=\\frac a2z^2,\n\\]\n\nwhere\n\n\\[\nz=x+iy.\n\\]\n\nThe complex notation is only a convenient mathematical representation.\n\nIt does not introduce an additional physical dimension or carrier.\n\nDefine\n\n\\[\nr^2=x^2+y^2\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nD=1+a^2r^2.\n}\n\\]\n\n---\n\n# 4. Exact induced metric\n\nDifferentiate the embedding.\n\n\\[\nF_x=\n\\begin{pmatrix}\n1\\\\\n0\\\\\nax\\\\\nay\n\\end{pmatrix},\n\\]\n\n\\[\nF_y=\n\\begin{pmatrix}\n0\\\\\n1\\\\\n-ay\\\\\nax\n\\end{pmatrix}.\n\\]\n\nTheir Euclidean inner products are\n\n\\[\nF_x\\cdot F_x=D,\n\\]\n\n\\[\nF_y\\cdot F_y=D,\n\\]\n\n\\[\nF_x\\cdot F_y=0.\n\\]\n\nTherefore, the induced metric is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nds^2=D(dx^2+dy^2).\n}\n\\]\n\nThe induced area element is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\ndA_{\\mathrm{surface}}=D\\,dx\\,dy.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe surface is conformally flat.\n\nThat does not imply that its intrinsic curvature vanishes.\n\n---\n\n# 5. Construct the normal frame\n\nThe normalized tangent vectors are\n\n\\[\nt_1=\n\\frac1{\\sqrt D}\n\\begin{pmatrix}\n1\\\\0\\\\ax\\\\ay\n\\end{pmatrix},\n\\]\n\n\\[\nt_2=\n\\frac1{\\sqrt D}\n\\begin{pmatrix}\n0\\\\1\\\\-ay\\\\ax\n\\end{pmatrix}.\n\\]\n\nChoose orthonormal normals\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nn_1=\n\\frac1{\\sqrt D}\n\\begin{pmatrix}\n-ax\\\\\nay\\\\\n1\\\\\n0\n\\end{pmatrix}\n}\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nn_2=\n\\frac1{\\sqrt D}\n\\begin{pmatrix}\n-ay\\\\\n-ax\\\\\n0\\\\\n1\n\\end{pmatrix}.\n}\n\\]\n\nDirect multiplication gives\n\n\\[\nn_1\\cdot n_2=0,\n\\]\n\n\\[\nn_1\\cdot n_1=n_2\\cdot n_2=1.\n\\]\n\nBoth normals are orthogonal to both tangents.\n\nThus\n\n\\[\n(t_1,t_2,n_1,n_2)\n\\]\n\nforms an orthonormal frame in \\(\\mathbb R^4\\).\n\n---\n\n# 6. Derive the normal connection\n\nDefine the normal connection one-form by\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nA_i=n_1\\cdot\\partial_i n_2.\n}\n\\]\n\nDifferentiate \\(n_2\\).\n\nFor the \\(x\\) direction,\n\n\\[\n\\partial_xn_2\n=\n\\frac1{\\sqrt D}\n\\begin{pmatrix}\n0\\\\-a\\\\0\\\\0\n\\end{pmatrix}\n-\n\\frac{a^2x}{D}n_2.\n\\]\n\nBecause\n\n\\[\nn_1\\cdot n_2=0,\n\\]\n\nthe second term contributes nothing.\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nA_x=-\\frac{a^2y}{D}.\n}\n\\]\n\nSimilarly,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nA_y=\\frac{a^2x}{D}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe complete connection is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nA=\n\\frac{a^2}{D}\n(-y\\,dx+x\\,dy).\n}\n\\]\n\nNo independent connection field has been inserted.\n\nIt follows from the derivatives of the embedded surface's normal vectors.\n\n---\n\n# 7. Calculate normal curvature\n\nFor an SO(2) normal bundle, the curvature two-form is\n\n\\[\n\\mathcal F=dA.\n\\]\n\nThus,\n\n\\[\n\\mathcal F_{xy}\n=\n\\partial_xA_y-\\partial_yA_x.\n\\]\n\nCalculate\n\n\\[\n\\partial_xA_y\n=\n\\frac{a^2}{D}\n-\n\\frac{2a^4x^2}{D^2},\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n\\partial_yA_x\n=\n-\\frac{a^2}{D}\n+\n\\frac{2a^4y^2}{D^2}.\n\\]\n\nSubtracting,\n\n\\[\n\\mathcal F_{xy}\n=\n\\frac{2a^2}{D}\n-\n\\frac{2a^4r^2}{D^2}.\n\\]\n\nSince\n\n\\[\nD-a^2r^2=1,\n\\]\n\nwe obtain\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\mathcal F_{xy}=\\frac{2a^2}{D^2}.\n}\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\mathcal F=\n\\frac{2a^2}{(1+a^2r^2)^2}\n\\,dx\\wedge dy.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe curvature has units\n\n\\[\n[\\mathcal F_{xy}]=\\mathrm m^{-2}.\n\\]\n\nThe scalar normal curvature relative to the induced area element is\n\n\\[\nK_N=\\frac{\\mathcal F_{xy}}D.\n\\]\n\nHence,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nK_N=\n\\frac{2a^2}{D^3}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis is nonzero for every finite \\(r\\) when \\(a>0\\).\n\nThe normal connection is therefore not pure gauge.\n\n---\n\n# 8. Exact closed-loop holonomy\n\nConsider the circular path\n\n\\[\nx=R\\cos\\phi,\n\\]\n\n\\[\ny=R\\sin\\phi,\n\\]\n\nwith\n\n\\[\n0\\le\\phi\\le2\\pi.\n\\]\n\nAlong this circle,\n\n\\[\ndx=-R\\sin\\phi\\,d\\phi,\n\\]\n\n\\[\ndy=R\\cos\\phi\\,d\\phi.\n\\]\n\nCalculate\n\n\\[\n-y\\,dx+x\\,dy.\n\\]\n\nSubstitution gives\n\n\\[\nR^2\\sin^2\\phi\\,d\\phi\n+\nR^2\\cos^2\\phi\\,d\\phi.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n-y\\,dx+x\\,dy=R^2d\\phi.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe connection becomes\n\n\\[\nA=\n\\frac{a^2R^2}{1+a^2R^2}\\,d\\phi.\n\\]\n\nIntegrate around the complete circle:\n\n\\[\n\\Theta(R)=\\oint A.\n\\]\n\nThus,\n\n\\[\n\\Theta(R)=\n\\int_0^{2\\pi}\n\\frac{a^2R^2}{1+a^2R^2}\n\\,d\\phi.\n\\]\n\nThe integrand is constant.\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\Theta(R)=\n\\frac{2\\pi a^2R^2}{1+a^2R^2}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis is the exact accumulated normal-frame rotation angle under the stated convention.\n\n---\n\n# 9. Independent Stokes derivation\n\nThe connection result can be checked without integrating the connection itself.\n\nBy Stokes' theorem,\n\n\\[\n\\oint_{\\partial\\Sigma}A\n=\n\\int_\\Sigma dA.\n\\]\n\nFor a disk of radius \\(R\\),\n\n\\[\n\\int_\\Sigma dA\n=\n\\int_0^{2\\pi}\n\\int_0^R\n\\frac{2a^2}{(1+a^2r^2)^2}\nr\\,dr\\,d\\phi.\n\\]\n\nIntegrate over \\(\\phi\\):\n\n\\[\n=\n4\\pi a^2\n\\int_0^R\n\\frac{r}{(1+a^2r^2)^2}\n\\,dr.\n\\]\n\nLet\n\n\\[\nu=1+a^2r^2.\n\\]\n\nThen\n\n\\[\ndu=2a^2r\\,dr.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\int_\\Sigma dA\n=\n2\\pi\n\\int_1^{1+a^2R^2}u^{-2}\\,du.\n\\]\n\nEvaluate:\n\n\\[\n=\n2\\pi\n\\left[\n1-\\frac1{1+a^2R^2}\n\\right].\n\\]\n\nSimplifying,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\int_\\Sigma dA=\n\\frac{2\\pi a^2R^2}{1+a^2R^2}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis agrees exactly with the line integral.\n\n---\n\n# 10. Intrinsic and normal curvature\n\nThe metric is\n\n\\[\nds^2=D(dx^2+dy^2).\n\\]\n\nFor a conformal two-dimensional metric\n\n\\[\nds^2=e^{2\\psi}(dx^2+dy^2),\n\\]\n\nthe Gaussian curvature is\n\n\\[\nK=-e^{-2\\psi}\\Delta\\psi.\n\\]\n\nHere,\n\n\\[\ne^{2\\psi}=D,\n\\]\n\nso\n\n\\[\n\\psi=\\frac12\\log D.\n\\]\n\nThe Euclidean Laplacian gives\n\n\\[\n\\Delta\\log D\n=\n\\frac{4a^2}{D^2}.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\nK\n=\n-\\frac1{2D}\n\\frac{4a^2}{D^2}.\n\\]\n\nHence,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nK=-\\frac{2a^2}{D^3}.\n}\n\\]\n\nWe already obtained\n\n\\[\nK_N=\\frac{2a^2}{D^3}.\n\\]\n\nThus,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nK+K_N=0.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis identity is a geometric property of the chosen holomorphic embedding.\n\nIt is not asserted as a general identity for arbitrary H(s)H worldtubes.\n\n---\n\n# 11. Shape-operator verification\n\nThe second derivatives of the embedding are\n\n\\[\nF_{xx}=\n\\begin{pmatrix}\n0\\\\0\\\\a\\\\0\n\\end{pmatrix},\n\\]\n\n\\[\nF_{xy}=\n\\begin{pmatrix}\n0\\\\0\\\\0\\\\a\n\\end{pmatrix},\n\\]\n\n\\[\nF_{yy}=\n\\begin{pmatrix}\n0\\\\0\\\\-a\\\\0\n\\end{pmatrix}.\n\\]\n\nProjecting onto the two normal directions and expressing the result in the orthonormal tangent frame gives\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nS_1=\n\\frac a{D^{3/2}}\n\\begin{pmatrix}\n1&0\\\\\n0&-1\n\\end{pmatrix}\n}\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nS_2=\n\\frac a{D^{3/2}}\n\\begin{pmatrix}\n0&1\\\\\n1&0\n\\end{pmatrix}.\n}\n\\]\n\nTheir determinants are\n\n\\[\n\\det S_1=-\\frac{a^2}{D^3},\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\det S_2=-\\frac{a^2}{D^3}.\n\\]\n\nThe Gauss equation gives\n\n\\[\nK=\\det S_1+\\det S_2.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nK=-\\frac{2a^2}{D^3}.\n}\n\\]\n\nNow calculate their commutator:\n\n\\[\n[S_1,S_2]=S_1S_2-S_2S_1.\n\\]\n\nThis gives\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n[S_1,S_2]\n=\n\\frac{2a^2}{D^3}\n\\begin{pmatrix}\n0&1\\\\\n-1&0\n\\end{pmatrix}.\n}\n\\]\n\nIts upper-right entry is exactly\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\frac{2a^2}{D^3}=K_N.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe normal-curvature result is therefore independently recovered from the shape operators.\n\n---\n\n# 12. Finite-core regularity\n\nThe eigenvalues of either shape operator are\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\kappa_\\pm=\n\\pm\\frac a{D^{3/2}}.\n}\n\\]\n\nFor an arbitrary unit normal direction, the corresponding shape operator has the same eigenvalue magnitudes.\n\nBecause\n\n\\[\nD\\ge1,\n\\]\n\nwe have\n\n\\[\n|\\kappa_\\pm|\\le a.\n\\]\n\nConsider a normal offset of radius \\(\\rho\\).\n\nLocal focal singularities can occur when\n\n\\[\n1-\\rho\\kappa=0.\n\\]\n\nA sufficient condition for avoiding these local singularities is\n\n\\[\n\\rho|\\kappa|<1.\n\\]\n\nSince\n\n\\[\n|\\kappa|\\le a,\n\\]\n\nwe obtain\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\rho<\\frac1a.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis is a useful finite-core regularity bound.\n\nIt does **not** prove global tubular injectivity.\n\nDifferent normal fibers could still intersect globally, and that question would require an additional calculation.\n\n---\n\n# 13. Gauge invariance\n\nRotate the normal frame through an angle \\(\\chi\\):\n\n\\[\nn_1'=\\cos\\chi\\,n_1+\\sin\\chi\\,n_2,\n\\]\n\n\\[\nn_2'=-\\sin\\chi\\,n_1+\\cos\\chi\\,n_2.\n\\]\n\nUnder this transformation,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nA'=A-d\\chi.\n}\n\\]\n\nIf \\(\\chi\\) is periodic around the loop,\n\n\\[\n\\chi(2\\pi)=\\chi(0),\n\\]\n\nthen\n\n\\[\n\\oint A'=\\oint A.\n\\]\n\nThe accumulated angle is unchanged.\n\nIf the frame makes an integer winding,\n\n\\[\n\\chi=m\\phi,\n\\]\n\nthen\n\n\\[\n\\oint A'=\\oint A-2\\pi m.\n\\]\n\nThe unwrapped angle changes, but the SO(2) monodromy remains identical:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\ne^{i(\\Theta-2\\pi m)}=e^{i\\Theta}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis distinction matters for the Hagalaz and holonomy programs.\n\nThe unwrapped connection integral is not an absolute gauge-invariant real number without a specified framing convention.\n\nThe associated SO(2) holonomy is gauge invariant.\n\n---\n\n# 14. Numerical fixture\n\nChoose\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\na=0.8\\ \\mathrm m^{-1},\n}\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nR=0.75\\ \\mathrm m,\n}\n\\]\n\nand finite-core probe radius\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\rho=0.20\\ \\mathrm m.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe local focal threshold is\n\n\\[\n\\frac1a=1.25\\ \\mathrm m.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\rho<\\frac1a.\n\\]\n\nThe chosen offset satisfies the local regularity condition.\n\nFor the loop,\n\n\\[\na^2R^2=0.36.\n\\]\n\nThus,\n\n\\[\nD=1.36.\n\\]\n\nThe exact holonomy is\n\n\\[\n\\Theta=\n\\frac{2\\pi(0.36)}{1.36}.\n\\]\n\nNumerically,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\Theta=1.663196110724\\ \\mathrm{rad}.\n}\n\\]\n\nAt\n\n\\[\nR=\\frac1a=1.25\\ \\mathrm m,\n\\]\n\nwe obtain\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\Theta=\\pi.}\n\\]\n\nAs\n\n\\[\nR\\rightarrow\\infty,\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\Theta\\rightarrow2\\pi.}\n\\]\n\nThe unwrapped angle approaches one complete revolution, while the SO(2) monodromy approaches the identity.\n\n---\n\n# 15. Principal calculation\n\n## A nonsingular curved Lorentz metric induced by a smooth time-normal field in Euclidean four-space\n\nMeridian's previous work established that a preferred Euclidean direction can generate a Lorentzian metric through\n\n\\[\ng=\\delta-2u\\otimes u.\n\\]\n\nSable's preceding radial-field calculation produced nonzero curvature but a singularity at the origin.\n\nThe present calculation asks whether a smooth field can produce curvature **without requiring that singularity**.\n\nThe answer is yes.\n\nI constructed a globally smooth time-normal field, derived its curvature invariants, calculated its Misner-Sharp mass and Einstein tensor, and independently verified the results through four-dimensional Cartesian numerical differentiation.\n\nThe construction also produces a regular central geometry with an effective de Sitter-like limit.\n\nThat is a mathematical result, not a claim that SAT/H(s)H has derived de Sitter spacetime or a physical cosmological constant.\n\n---\n\n# 3. Define the four-dimensional geometry\n\nUse Euclidean coordinates\n\n\\[\nX=(t,x,y,z)\\in\\mathbb R^4,\n\\]\n\nall measured in meters.\n\nDefine the spatial radius\n\n\\[\nr=\\sqrt{x^2+y^2+z^2}.\n\\]\n\nLet\n\n\\[\n\\kappa>0\n\\]\n\nhave dimensions\n\n\\[\n[\\kappa]=\\mathrm m^{-1}.\n\\]\n\nIntroduce\n\n\\[\nq=\\kappa^2r^2,\n\\qquad\nD=1+q.\n\\]\n\nDefine the Euclidean unit vector field\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nu(X)=\n\\frac{(1,\\kappa x,\\kappa y,\\kappa z)}\n{\\sqrt{1+\\kappa^2r^2}}.\n}\n\\]\n\nIts Euclidean norm is exactly one:\n\n\\[\n\\delta(u,u)=1.\n\\]\n\nUnlike the fully radial field\n\n\\[\nu=\\frac{X}{|X|},\n\\]\n\nthis field remains smooth at the origin.\n\nAt\n\n\\[\nr=0,\n\\]\n\nwe have\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nu=(1,0,0,0).\n}\n\\]\n\nThus the central time normal is aligned with the first coordinate axis.\n\nConstruct\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\ng_{ab}=\\delta_{ab}-2u_au_b.\n}\n\\]\n\nBecause \\(u\\) is Euclidean-unit,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\ng^2=I,\\qquad g^{-1}=g,\\qquad\\det g=-1.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe eigenvalues are\n\n\\[\n(-1,+1,+1,+1).\n\\]\n\nThe metric is Lorentzian everywhere.\n\nThere is no signature degeneracy at the origin.\n\n---\n\n# 4. Exact spherical-coordinate metric\n\nWrite the Euclidean background as\n\n\\[\nd\\sigma^2=dt^2+dr^2+r^2d\\Omega_2^2.\n\\]\n\nThe preferred unit covector is\n\n\\[\nu^\\flat=\n\\frac{dt+\\kappa r\\,dr}{\\sqrt D}.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\nds_g^2\n=\nd\\sigma^2-2(u^\\flat)^2.\n\\]\n\nExpand:\n\n\\[\nds_g^2\n=\ndt^2+dr^2+r^2d\\Omega_2^2\n-\n\\frac2D(dt+\\kappa r\\,dr)^2.\n\\]\n\nCollect terms:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nds_g^2=\n\\frac{\n(q-1)dt^2\n-4\\kappa r\\,dt\\,dr\n+(1-q)dr^2\n}{D}\n+r^2d\\Omega_2^2.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe two-dimensional radial-temporal block is\n\n\\[\nh_{AB}=\n\\frac1D\n\\begin{pmatrix}\nq-1&-2\\kappa r\\\\\n-2\\kappa r&1-q\n\\end{pmatrix}.\n\\]\n\nIts determinant is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\det h=-1.}\n\\]\n\nIt is its own inverse:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{h^{-1}=h.}\n\\]\n\nThis is a useful algebraic simplification.\n\nThe metric is stationary and spherically symmetric, but not static in the displayed coordinates.\n\n---\n\n# 5. Curvature derivation\n\n## 5.1 Two-dimensional base curvature\n\nDirect calculation of the Levi-Civita connection of \\(h_{AB}\\) gives\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nR_h=\n\\frac{4\\kappa^2(1-3q)}{D^3}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe squared gradient of the areal radius is\n\n\\[\n(\\nabla r)^2=h^{rr}.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n(\\nabla r)^2=\\frac{1-q}{D}.\n}\n\\]\n\nSince\n\n\\[\n\\sqrt{|\\det h|}=1,\n\\]\n\nthe base Laplacian is\n\n\\[\n\\Delta_h r\n=\n\\partial_A(h^{Ar}).\n\\]\n\nThe metric is time-independent, so\n\n\\[\n\\Delta_h r=\\partial_rh^{rr}.\n\\]\n\nDifferentiate:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\Delta_h r=\n-\\frac{4\\kappa^2r}{D^2}.\n}\n\\]\n\n## 5.2 Four-dimensional scalar curvature\n\nFor a spherical warped product with areal radius \\(r\\),\n\n\\[\nR_4=\nR_h+\n\\frac2{r^2}\\left[1-(\\nabla r)^2\\right]\n-\\frac4r\\Delta_h r.\n\\]\n\nSubstitute the preceding expressions.\n\nFirst,\n\n\\[\n1-(\\nabla r)^2\n=\n1-\\frac{1-q}{D}\n=\n\\frac{2q}{D}.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\nR_4=\n\\frac{4\\kappa^2(1-3q)}{D^3}\n+\n\\frac{4q}{r^2D}\n+\n\\frac{16\\kappa^2}{D^2}.\n\\]\n\nBecause\n\n\\[\nq=\\kappa^2r^2,\n\\]\n\nthe middle term becomes\n\n\\[\n\\frac{4\\kappa^2}{D}.\n\\]\n\nCombining over the common denominator gives\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nR_4=\n\\frac{4\\kappa^2(q^2+3q+6)}{D^3}.\n}\n\\]\n\nUnits:\n\n\\[\n[R_4]=\\mathrm m^{-2}.\n\\]\n\nAt the origin,\n\n\\[\nq=0,\\qquad D=1.\n\\]\n\nThus,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nR_4(0)=24\\kappa^2.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe scalar curvature is finite.\n\n---\n\n# 6. Quadratic curvature invariants\n\nThe squared Hessian of the areal radius is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n(\\nabla_A\\nabla_Br)\n(\\nabla^A\\nabla^Br)\n=\n\\frac{8\\kappa^4r^2}{D^4}.\n}\n\\]\n\nFor this spherical warped product, the Kretschmann scalar is\n\n\\[\n\\mathcal K=\nR_h^2+\n\\frac8{r^2}\n(\\nabla_A\\nabla_Br)\n(\\nabla^A\\nabla^Br)\n+\n\\frac4{r^4}\n\\left[1-(\\nabla r)^2\\right]^2.\n\\]\n\nSubstitution and simplification yield\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\mathcal K=\n\\frac{\n16\\kappa^4\n(q^4+4q^3+19q^2+6q+6)\n}{D^6}.\n}\n\\]\n\nAt the origin,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\mathcal K(0)=96\\kappa^4.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis is finite.\n\nThe squared Ricci tensor is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nR_{ab}R^{ab}\n=\n\\frac{\n8\\kappa^4\n(q^4+8q^3+23q^2+18q+18)\n}{D^6}.\n}\n\\]\n\nIn four dimensions,\n\n\\[\nC_{abcd}C^{abcd}\n=\n\\mathcal K\n-2R_{ab}R^{ab}\n+\\frac{R_4^2}{3}.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nC_{abcd}C^{abcd}\n=\n\\frac{\n16\\kappa^4q^2(q-3)^2\n}{3D^6}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe Weyl invariant vanishes at the center:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nC_{abcd}C^{abcd}\\big|_{r=0}=0.\n}\n\\]\n\nIt also vanishes at the isolated radius\n\n\\[\nq=3.\n\\]\n\nThat does not mean the entire geometry is conformally flat.\n\nAll three curvature invariants have been derived analytically and independently checked numerically.\n\n---\n\n# 7. Exact Misner-Sharp mass\n\nThe Misner-Sharp mass in geometrized units is\n\n\\[\nm(r)=\\frac r2\n\\left[\n1-(\\nabla r)^2\n\\right].\n\\]\n\nSubstitute\n\n\\[\n(\\nabla r)^2=\\frac{1-q}{D}.\n\\]\n\nThen\n\n\\[\nm(r)\n=\n\\frac r2\n\\left[\n1-\\frac{1-q}{D}\n\\right].\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nm(r)=\\frac{\\kappa^2r^3}{1+\\kappa^2r^2}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis has units of length when \\(G=c=1\\).\n\nNear the origin,\n\n\\[\nm(r)\\sim\\kappa^2r^3.\n\\]\n\nThis is the expected regular cubic behavior for a finite central effective density.\n\nAt large radius,\n\n\\[\nm(r)\\sim r.\n\\]\n\nConsequently, the metric is **not asymptotically flat**.\n\nThis is an important limitation, not a numerical defect.\n\n---\n\n# 8. Exact Einstein tensor\n\nUse the orthonormal frame defined by the preferred timelike direction \\(u\\), its orthogonal radial direction \\(v\\), and two angular directions.\n\nThe effective energy-density component is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nG(u,u)=\n\\frac{2\\kappa^2(q+3)}{D^2}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe radial pressure component is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nG(v,v)=\n-\\frac{2\\kappa^2(q+3)}{D^2}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe angular components are equal:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nG_{\\mathrm{angular}}=\n\\frac{2\\kappa^2(q-3)}{D^3}.\n}\n\\]\n\nIf we formally write\n\n\\[\nG_{ab}=8\\pi T_{ab}\n\\]\n\nin geometrized units, these correspond to\n\n\\[\n8\\pi\\rho=\n\\frac{2\\kappa^2(q+3)}{D^2},\n\\]\n\n\\[\np_r=-\\rho,\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n8\\pi p_t=\n\\frac{2\\kappa^2(q-3)}{D^3}.\n\\]\n\nThis is an effective source associated with the metric.\n\nNo physical material has been derived.\n\n## Mass-density identity\n\nDifferentiate\n\n\\[\nm(r)=\\frac{\\kappa^2r^3}{D}.\n\\]\n\nWe obtain\n\n\\[\n\\frac{dm}{dr}\n=\n\\frac{\n\\kappa^2r^2(3+q)\n}{D^2}.\n\\]\n\nBut\n\n\\[\n\\frac{r^2}{2}G(u,u)\n=\n\\frac{\n\\kappa^2r^2(3+q)\n}{D^2}.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\frac{dm}{dr}\n=\n\\frac{r^2}{2}G(u,u).\n}\n\\]\n\nThis identity holds exactly.\n\nIt provides a direct bridge between the induced metric and Meridian's earlier mass-constraint work.\n\n---\n\n# 9. Central regularity and effective stress\n\nAt\n\n\\[\nr=0,\n\\]\n\nwe obtain\n\n\\[\n8\\pi\\rho=6\\kappa^2,\n\\]\n\n\\[\n8\\pi p_r=-6\\kappa^2,\n\\]\n\n\\[\n8\\pi p_t=-6\\kappa^2.\n\\]\n\nThus,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\np_r=p_t=-\\rho\n}\n\\]\n\nat the center.\n\nThe Einstein tensor there is proportional to the metric:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nG_{ab}(0)=-6\\kappa^2g_{ab}(0).\n}\n\\]\n\nThe center therefore has a regular de Sitter-like curvature structure with effective\n\n\\[\n\\Lambda_{\\mathrm{eff}}=6\\kappa^2.\n\\]\n\nThis is a local mathematical identification.\n\nIt is not a proposed SAT cosmological constant.\n\n### Energy-condition diagnostics\n\nFor the formal effective source,\n\n\\[\n\\rho+p_r=0.\n\\]\n\nAlso,\n\n\\[\n8\\pi(\\rho+p_t)\n=\n\\frac{2\\kappa^2q(q+5)}{D^3}\n\\ge0.\n\\]\n\nAnd\n\n\\[\n8\\pi(\\rho-p_t)\n=\n\\frac{2\\kappa^2(q^2+3q+6)}{D^3}\n>0.\n\\]\n\nThus the formal stress tensor satisfies the weak and dominant energy conditions.\n\nThe strong-energy-condition combination is\n\n\\[\n\\rho+p_r+2p_t=2p_t.\n\\]\n\nIt changes sign at\n\n\\[\nq=3.\n\\]\n\nThis is another exact property of the construction.\n\n---\n\n# 10. Radial null expansions\n\nA useful geometric diagnostic occurs at\n\n\\[\nr=\\frac1\\kappa.\n\\]\n\nThere,\n\n\\[\n(\\nabla r)^2=0.\n\\]\n\nHowever, the metric determinant remains nonzero and all calculated curvature invariants remain finite.\n\nTo distinguish this from a physical event-horizon claim, calculate the radial null expansions.\n\nChoose the preferred timelike vector \\(u\\) as the future orientation.\n\nLet \\(v\\) be the outward orthogonal radial unit vector.\n\nDefine the null vectors\n\n\\[\n\\ell_\\pm=u\\pm v.\n\\]\n\nTheir expansions are\n\n\\[\n\\Theta_\\pm=\\frac2r\\ell_\\pm(r).\n\\]\n\nFor the present field,\n\n\\[\nu(r)=\\frac{\\kappa r}{\\sqrt D},\n\\]\n\n\\[\nv(r)=\\frac1{\\sqrt D}.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\Theta_\\pm=\n\\frac{2(\\kappa r\\pm1)}\n{r\\sqrt{1+\\kappa^2r^2}}.\n}\n\\]\n\nAt\n\n\\[\nr=\\frac1\\kappa,\n\\]\n\nwe obtain\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\Theta_-=0,\n\\qquad\n\\Theta_+>0.\n}\n\\]\n\nFor\n\n\\[\nr>\\frac1\\kappa,\n\\]\n\nboth expansions are positive.\n\nWith the stated time orientation, the exterior region is anti-trapped rather than a conventional black-hole trapped region.\n\nThis demonstrates why the zero of \\(g^{rr}\\) must not automatically be identified with a black-hole event horizon.\n\n---\n\n# 11. Exact distance degeneracy\n\nTake two arbitrary points\n\n\\[\nz=x+iy,\n\\qquad\nw=x'+iy'.\n\\]\n\nThe squared Euclidean distance between their embedded images is\n\n\\[\n\\|F_a(z)-F_a(w)\\|^2.\n\\]\n\nThe first two coordinates contribute\n\n\\[\n|z-w|^2.\n\\]\n\nThe last two coordinates contribute\n\n\\[\n\\frac{a^2}{4}|z^2-w^2|^2.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\|F_a(z)-F_a(w)\\|^2\n=\n|z-w|^2+\n\\frac{a^2}{4}|z^2-w^2|^2.\n\\]\n\nFactor\n\n\\[\nz^2-w^2=(z-w)(z+w).\n\\]\n\nThen\n\n\\[\n|z^2-w^2|^2\n=\n|z-w|^2|z+w|^2.\n\\]\n\nThus,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\|F_a(z)-F_a(w)\\|^2\n=\n|z-w|^2\n\\left[\n1+\\frac{a^2}{4}|z+w|^2\n\\right].\n}\n\\]\n\nBecause \\(S\\) is orthogonal,\n\n\\[\nS^\\mathsf TS=I.\n\\]\n\nConsequently,\n\n\\[\n\\|SF_a(z)-SF_a(w)\\|^2\n=\n\\|F_a(z)-F_a(w)\\|^2.\n\\]\n\nHence,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nd_{\\widetilde F}(z,w)=d_F(z,w)\n}\n\\]\n\nfor every pair of points.\n\nThis is not merely a finite-sampling degeneracy.\n\nEven the complete continuous distance function cannot distinguish the two orientations.\n\n---\n\n# 5. Their intrinsic geometry is identical\n\nDifferentiate the original embedding:\n\n\\[\nF_x=(1,0,ax,ay),\n\\]\n\n\\[\nF_y=(0,1,-ay,ax).\n\\]\n\nTheir inner products give\n\n\\[\nF_x\\cdot F_x=1+a^2r^2,\n\\]\n\n\\[\nF_y\\cdot F_y=1+a^2r^2,\n\\]\n\n\\[\nF_x\\cdot F_y=0.\n\\]\n\nDefine\n\n\\[\nD=1+a^2r^2.\n\\]\n\nThe induced metric is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nds^2=D(dx^2+dy^2).\n}\n\\]\n\nBecause the reflection preserves inner products, the reflected surface has exactly the same induced metric.\n\nIts Gaussian curvature is also identical:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nK=-\\frac{2a^2}{D^3}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThus neither intrinsic distances nor intrinsic Gaussian curvature distinguish the two embeddings.\n\n---\n\n# 6. Their oriented normal curvatures differ\n\nFor the original surface, use the orthonormal normal frame\n\n\\[\nn_1=\n\\frac1{\\sqrt D}\n(-ax,ay,1,0),\n\\]\n\n\\[\nn_2=\n\\frac1{\\sqrt D}\n(-ay,-ax,0,1).\n\\]\n\nThe normal connection is\n\n\\[\nA=n_1\\cdot dn_2.\n\\]\n\nDirect differentiation gives\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nA=\\frac{a^2}{D}(-y\\,dx+x\\,dy).\n}\n\\]\n\nIts curvature is\n\n\\[\ndA=\n\\frac{2a^2}{D^2}\\,dx\\wedge dy.\n\\]\n\nRelative to the induced area element, the scalar normal curvature is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nK_N=\\frac{2a^2}{D^3}.\n}\n\\]\n\nNow reflect the surface.\n\nThe transformed tangent vectors are\n\n\\[\n\\widetilde t_i=St_i.\n\\]\n\nTo preserve the chosen orientation of the complete four-dimensional orthonormal frame, choose\n\n\\[\n\\widetilde n_1=Sn_1,\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\widetilde n_2=-Sn_2.\n\\]\n\nThe extra minus sign compensates for\n\n\\[\n\\det S=-1.\n\\]\n\nThe transformed normal connection becomes\n\n\\[\n\\widetilde A\n=\n\\widetilde n_1\\cdot d\\widetilde n_2.\n\\]\n\nSubstitute:\n\n\\[\n\\widetilde A\n=\n(Sn_1)\\cdot d(-Sn_2).\n\\]\n\nSince \\(S\\) is constant and orthogonal,\n\n\\[\n\\widetilde A\n=\n-n_1\\cdot dn_2.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\widetilde A=-A.\n}\n\\]\n\nIts curvature satisfies\n\n\\[\nd\\widetilde A=-dA.\n\\]\n\nHence,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\widetilde K_N=-K_N.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe Gaussian curvature remains unchanged.\n\nThe oriented normal curvature reverses.\n\n---\n\n# 7. Exact holonomy reversal\n\nFor a circle of radius \\(R\\), Nadir's preceding derivation gives\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\Theta(R)=\n\\frac{2\\pi a^2R^2}{1+a^2R^2}.\n}\n\\]\n\nUnder the reflection,\n\n\\[\n\\widetilde A=-A.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\widetilde\\Theta(R)\n=\n\\oint\\widetilde A\n=\n-\\oint A.\n\\]\n\nThus,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\widetilde\\Theta(R)=-\\Theta(R).\n}\n\\]\n\nThe SO(2) holonomy matrices are inverses:\n\n\\[\nH(\\widetilde F)=H(F)^{-1}.\n\\]\n\nTheir traces are identical:\n\n\\[\n\\operatorname{tr}H(F)=2\\cos\\Theta,\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\operatorname{tr}H(\\widetilde F)=2\\cos(-\\Theta).\n\\]\n\nBecause cosine is even,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\operatorname{tr}H(F)\n=\n\\operatorname{tr}H(\\widetilde F).\n}\n\\]\n\nEven the trace of the normal holonomy fails to distinguish the two orientations.\n\nAn oriented normal-frame reference supplies additional information that distances and unoriented holonomy traces do not.\n\n---\n\n# 8. Relative orientation survives a shared ambiguity\n\nSuppose two surfaces have holonomies\n\n\\[\n\\Theta_1,\\qquad\\Theta_2.\n\\]\n\nDefine their signed holonomy observables\n\n\\[\nh_i=\\operatorname{sgn}(\\sin\\Theta_i).\n\\]\n\nAssume neither sine vanishes.\n\nLet the unknown common ambient orientation parity be\n\n\\[\n\\eta\\in\\{-1,+1\\}.\n\\]\n\nThe observed signs are\n\n\\[\nz_1=\\eta h_1,\n\\]\n\n\\[\nz_2=\\eta h_2.\n\\]\n\nMultiply:\n\n\\[\nz_1z_2=\\eta^2h_1h_2.\n\\]\n\nBecause\n\n\\[\n\\eta^2=1,\n\\]\n\nwe obtain\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nz_1z_2=h_1h_2.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe absolute signs are ambiguous.\n\nTheir relative sign is not.\n\nHowever, if the observations use independently unknown orientation parities,\n\n\\[\nz_1=\\eta_1h_1,\n\\]\n\n\\[\nz_2=\\eta_2h_2,\n\\]\n\nthen\n\n\\[\nz_1z_2=\\eta_1\\eta_2h_1h_2.\n\\]\n\nThe parity factors no longer necessarily cancel.\n\nIf \\(\\eta_1,\\eta_2\\) are independent, uniformly random signs, their product is also uniformly random.\n\nIn that case, the relative sign is unidentifiable from these observations.\n\n---\n\n# 9. Exact statistical noise model\n\nNow add measurement noise.\n\nLet an observed phase be\n\n\\[\nY=\\eta\\Theta+\\epsilon,\n\\]\n\nwhere\n\n\\[\n\\epsilon\\sim\\mathcal N(0,\\sigma^2).\n\\]\n\nThe phase is interpreted modulo \\(2\\pi\\).\n\nWe classify its orientation by\n\n\\[\n\\widehat h=\\operatorname{sgn}(\\sin Y).\n\\]\n\nTo calculate its error exactly, determine the probability that the noisy sine is positive.\n\nThe sine is positive on intervals\n\n\\[\n(2k\\pi,(2k+1)\\pi)\n\\]\n\nfor integers \\(k\\).\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\nP_+(\\Theta,\\sigma)\n=\n\\sum_{k=-\\infty}^{\\infty}\nP\\left(\n2k\\pi<\\Theta+\\epsilon<(2k+1)\\pi\n\\right).\n\\]\n\nUsing the standard normal cumulative distribution function \\(\\Phi\\),\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nP_+(\\Theta,\\sigma)\n=\n\\sum_{k=-\\infty}^{\\infty}\n\\left[\n\\Phi\\left(\n\\frac{(2k+1)\\pi-\\Theta}{\\sigma}\n\\right)\n-\n\\Phi\\left(\n\\frac{2k\\pi-\\Theta}{\\sigma}\n\\right)\n\\right].\n}\n\\]\n\nThis is an exact wrapped-Gaussian expression.\n\nFor\n\n\\[\n\\sin\\Theta>0,\n\\]\n\nthe sign-error probability is\n\n\\[\ne=1-P_+.\n\\]\n\nFor\n\n\\[\n\\sin\\Theta<0,\n\\]\n\nit is\n\n\\[\ne=P_+.\n\\]\n\nThus,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\ne(\\Theta,\\sigma)=\n\\begin{cases}\n1-P_+(\\Theta,\\sigma),&\\sin\\Theta>0,\\\\\nP_+(\\Theta,\\sigma),&\\sin\\Theta<0.\n\\end{cases}\n}\n\\]\n\nNo small-angle approximation has been made.\n\n---\n\n# 10. Exact relative-sign error\n\nLet the two individual sign-error probabilities be\n\n\\[\ne_1,\\qquad e_2.\n\\]\n\nAssume independent phase noise.\n\nThe relative-sign estimate is wrong precisely when one individual sign is wrong and the other is correct.\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\nE_{12}\n=\ne_1(1-e_2)+(1-e_1)e_2.\n\\]\n\nExpanding,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nE_{12}=e_1+e_2-2e_1e_2.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis is the exact error probability of the specified sign-product estimator.\n\nIt is not a claim that the estimator is globally Bayes-optimal for every possible continuous-phase observation model.\n\n## Add parity drift\n\nSuppose the orientation parity differs between observations with probability\n\n\\[\nd.\n\\]\n\nA parity mismatch reverses the relative-sign estimate.\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\nE_{12}(d)\n=\n(1-d)E_{12}(0)\n+\nd[1-E_{12}(0)].\n\\]\n\nSimplifying,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nE_{12}(d)\n=\nd+(1-2d)E_{12}(0).\n}\n\\]\n\nAt\n\n\\[\nd=\\frac12,\n\\]\n\nwe obtain\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nE_{12}=\\frac12.\n}\n\\]\n\nComplete independent parity ambiguity destroys the relative-sign information.\n\n---\n\n# 11. Executed numerical results\n\nTwo mathematical fixtures were used.\n\n### Fixture 1\n\n\\[\na_1=0.8\\ \\mathrm m^{-1},\n\\]\n\n\\[\nR_1=1.15\\ \\mathrm m,\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\sigma_1=0.30\\ \\mathrm{rad}.\n\\]\n\nThe exact holonomy is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\Theta_1=2.880246990899\\ \\mathrm{rad}.\n}\n\\]\n\nIts sine is\n\n\\[\n\\sin\\Theta_1=+0.258380753676.\n\\]\n\nThe exact sign-error probability is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\ne_1=0.191835525236.\n}\n\\]\n\n### Fixture 2\n\n\\[\na_2=1.4\\ \\mathrm m^{-1},\n\\]\n\n\\[\nR_2=2.4\\ \\mathrm m,\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\sigma_2=0.45\\ \\mathrm{rad}.\n\\]\n\nThe exact holonomy is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\Theta_2=5.771924948244\\ \\mathrm{rad}.\n}\n\\]\n\nIts sine is\n\n\\[\n\\sin\\Theta_2=-0.489276830195.\n\\]\n\nThe exact sign-error probability is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\ne_2=0.127950218819.\n}\n\\]\n\nTherefore, the true relative sign is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nh_1h_2=-1.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe exact relative-sign error under common parity is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nE_{12}(0)=0.270694949192.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis corresponds to approximately **72.93% classification accuracy**.\n\n---\n\n# 12. abs(np.linalg.det(fr)-1)<2e-14\n            # n1 dot partial_i n2 under ambient reflection plus normal orientation correction.\n            h=1e-5\n            for coord in (0,1):\n                xp,yp=(x+h,y) if coord==0 else (x,y+h)\n                xm,ym=(x-h,y) if coord==0 else (x,y-h)\n                deriv=(frame(xp,yp,a)[3]-frame(xm,ym,a)[3])/(2*h)\n Principal discovery\n\n## A braid can be unwound in three-dimensional space without its constituent worldlines ever touching\n\nThis is an important mathematical discriminator for the H(s)H interbraid program.\n\nConsider two particle histories.\n\nOne remains spatially stationary.\n\nThe other completes one revolution around it.\n\nIn a two-dimensional spatial plane, the relative trajectory has winding number\n\n\\[\nB=1.\n\\]\n\nIf both particles are restricted to that plane, the winding cannot be removed continuously without their positions coinciding.\n\nBut ordinary three-dimensional space provides another direction.\n\n**I constructed an exact continuous deformation that removes the winding while keeping both complete four-dimensional worldlines disjoint, preserving their endpoints, and maintaining timelike tangents.**\n\nThe construction also works for sufficiently thin finite-core Euclidean worldtubes.\n\nThis does not establish that an H(s)H interbraid can physically unwind.\n\nInstead, it identifies an additional requirement:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\text{Geometric winding}\n\\neq\n\\text{topologically protected interbraid}\n}\n\\]\n\nunless the admissible geometry supplies the necessary protection.\n\nThat protection may arise from the complete interlocked worldtube structure, rather than from the centerline winding alone.\n\n---\n\n# 3. Exact construction\n\nWork in four-dimensional coordinates\n\n\\[\nX=(\\tau,x,y,z),\n\\]\n\nwhere\n\n\\[\n\\tau=ct\n\\]\n\nis measured in meters.\n\nLet\n\n\\[\nR>0\n\\]\n\nbe the spatial separation and\n\n\\[\nk>0\n\\]\n\nan angular rate in radians per meter.\n\nDefine\n\n\\[\n\\phi=k\\tau.\n\\]\n\nOne complete revolution occupies\n\n\\[\n0\\leq\\phi\\leq2\\pi.\n\\]\n\nIntroduce a deformation parameter\n\n\\[\ns\\in[0,1].\n\\]\n\nDefine\n\n\\[\n\\beta=\\frac{\\pi s}{2},\n\\]\n\n\\[\na=\\cos\\beta,\n\\qquad\nb=\\sin\\beta.\n\\]\n\nNow construct the relative spatial vector\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\mathbf r_s(\\phi)\n=\nR\n\\begin{pmatrix}\nb^2+a^2\\cos\\phi\\\\\na\\sin\\phi\\\\\nab(1-\\cos\\phi)\n\\end{pmatrix}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe two complete histories are\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nX_1(\\tau)=(\\tau,0,0,0)\n}\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nX_{2,s}(\\tau)=\n(\\tau,\\mathbf r_s(k\\tau)).\n}\n\\]\n\nThe parameter \\(s\\) labels different complete four-dimensional configurations.\n\nIt is not a second physical time coordinate.\n\n---\n\n# 4. The endpoints are fixed\n\nAt the beginning of the revolution,\n\n\\[\n\\phi=0.\n\\]\n\nThen\n\n\\[\n\\cos\\phi=1,\n\\qquad\n\\sin\\phi=0.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\mathbf r_s(0)\n=\nR\n\\begin{pmatrix}\na^2+b^2\\\\0\\\\0\n\\end{pmatrix}.\n\\]\n\nSince\n\n\\[\na^2+b^2=1,\n\\]\n\nwe obtain\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\mathbf r_s(0)=(R,0,0).\n}\n\\]\n\nExactly the same holds at\n\n\\[\n\\phi=2\\pi.\n\\]\n\nThus,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\mathbf r_s(0)=\\mathbf r_s(2\\pi)=(R,0,0)\n}\n\\]\n\nfor every value of \\(s\\).\n\nThe deformation cannot escape by moving its endpoints.\n\n---\n\n# 5. The particles never coincide\n\nCalculate the squared spatial separation:\n\n\\[\n\\|\\mathbf r_s\\|^2\n=\nR^2\n\\left[\n(b^2+a^2\\cos\\phi)^2\n+a^2\\sin^2\\phi\n+a^2b^2(1-\\cos\\phi)^2\n\\right].\n\\]\n\nExpanding and collecting terms gives\n\n\\[\n\\|\\mathbf r_s\\|^2\n=\nR^2(a^2+b^2)^2.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\|\\mathbf r_s\\|=R.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe separation is constant throughout the deformation.\n\nThere is no spatial collision.\n\n### Complete four-dimensional clearance\n\nNow compare arbitrary points on the two histories.\n\nThey need not have equal time coordinates.\n\nTheir squared Euclidean distance is\n\n\\[\nd^2(\\tau_1,\\tau_2)\n=\n(\\tau_1-\\tau_2)^2\n+\n\\|\\mathbf r_s(k\\tau_2)\\|^2.\n\\]\n\nSince the spatial norm is \\(R\\),\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nd^2(\\tau_1,\\tau_2)\n=\n(\\tau_1-\\tau_2)^2+R^2.\n}\n\\]\n\nConsequently,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nd_{\\min}=R.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis is the global minimum over every pair of points in the complete histories.\n\nTherefore, Euclidean tubular neighborhoods of radius \\(\\rho\\) remain disjoint whenever\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n2\\rho<R.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis establishes a finite-core version of the counterexample, subject to the stated Euclidean tube definition.\n\n---\n\n# 6. The braid disappears\n\nAt\n\n\\[\ns=0,\n\\]\n\nwe have\n\n\\[\na=1,\\qquad b=0.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\mathbf r_0(\\phi)=\nR(\\cos\\phi,\\sin\\phi,0).\n}\n\\]\n\nThe relative vector completes one revolution in the \\(xy\\)-plane.\n\nIts planar winding number is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{B=1}.\n\\]\n\nAt\n\n\\[\ns=1,\n\\]\n\nwe have\n\n\\[\na=0,\\qquad b=1.\n\\]\n\nThen\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\mathbf r_1(\\phi)=(R,0,0).\n}\n\\]\n\nThe relative vector is stationary.\n\nIts planar winding number is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{B=0}.\n\\]\n\nYet the complete deformation is continuous.\n\nHow?\n\nThe relative vector leaves the original plane.\n\n### The critical configuration\n\nAt\n\n\\[\ns=\\frac12,\n\\]\n\nwe have\n\n\\[\na=b=\\frac1{\\sqrt2}.\n\\]\n\nAt\n\n\\[\n\\phi=\\pi,\n\\]\n\nthe relative vector becomes\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\mathbf r_{1/2}(\\pi)=(0,0,R).\n}\n\\]\n\nIts projection into the original \\(xy\\)-plane is zero.\n\nBut its actual three-dimensional separation is still \\(R\\).\n\nThe projected winding number becomes undefined at this intermediate configuration.\n\nIt can then reappear as zero.\n\n**No physical centerline intersection occurs.**\n\nThis is the essential distinction.\n\n---\n\n# 7. A constructive route toward protecting interbraid\n\nThe counterexample suggests a useful quantitative condition.\n\nSuppose two finite-core objects have radius \\(\\rho\\).\n\nRequire that their spatial separation always satisfy\n\n\\[\n|\\mathbf r|>2\\rho.\n\\]\n\nNow impose a geometric confinement condition\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n|r_z|<2\\rho.\n}\n\\]\n\nIf their planar projection vanished, we would have\n\n\\[\nr_x=r_y=0.\n\\]\n\nThen\n\n\\[\n|\\mathbf r|=|r_z|<2\\rho,\n\\]\n\ncontradicting the nonintersection requirement.\n\nTherefore, the planar relative vector can never pass through the origin.\n\nIts winding number is conserved under continuous deformations respecting those constraints.\n\nThus,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\begin{aligned}\n|\\mathbf r|&>2\\rho,\\\\\n|r_z|&<2\\rho\n\\end{aligned}\n\\quad\\Longrightarrow\\quad\nB\\text{ is conserved}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis is a **sufficient geometric protection condition**.\n\nIt is not a proposed physical law.\n\nMore generally, if the relative separation is bounded below by \\(d_0\\), any deformation that changes planar winding must permit a transverse excursion of at least \\(d_0\\).\n\nFor the executed fixture,\n\n\\[\nd_0=1\\ \\mathrm m.\n\\]\n\nThe constructed homotopy reaches exactly that transverse displacement.\n\n### Why this matters\n\nIt gives us a mathematical distinction between two situations.\n\nA freely deformable pair of centerlines in three-dimensional space does not possess a protected braid integer.\n\nA geometrically constrained pair can.\n\nThat means H(s)H must specify what makes the interbraid **an interlock rather than merely a projected winding**.\n\nThe answer may involve complete finite-core structures, linked shells, additional excluded regions, or constraints inherited from the timesheet and neighboring worldtubes.\n\nThose possibilities remain to be derived.\n\nNo arbitrary scale-dependent suppression or braid-erasure mechanism is introduced.\n\n---\n\n# 13. Exact step-response discriminator\n\nChoose a unit step source at\n\n\\[\n\\tau_0.\n\\]\n\nDefine\n\n\\[\nd=\\tau-\\tau_0-r.\n\\]\n\nThe null-linked response is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nu_B=\\frac{H(d)}r.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe memory response is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nu_C=\n\\frac{H(d)}r\n\\left(1-e^{-d/\\ell}\\right).\n}\n\\]\n\nFor the numerical fixture,\n\n\\[\nr=2.0\\ \\mathrm m,\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\ell=0.5\\ \\mathrm m.\n\\]\n\nThe executed results are:\n\n| Time after causal arrival, m | Null response | Memory response | Memory fraction of static |\n|---:|---:|---:|---:|\n| −0.1 | 0 | 0 | 0 |\n| 0.0 | 0.500000 | 0 | 0 |\n| 0.1 | 0.500000 | 0.090635 | 0.181269 |\n| 0.5 | 0.500000 | 0.316060 | 0.632121 |\n| 1.0 | 0.500000 | 0.432332 | 0.864665 |\n| 2.0 | 0.500000 | 0.490842 | 0.981684 |\n| 5.0 | 0.500000 | 0.499977 | 0.999955 |\n\nBoth models are causal.\n\nBoth approach the same stationary response.\n\nTheir transient behavior differs substantially.\n\n---\n\n# 12. Frequency-domain discriminator\n\nUse the Fourier convention\n\n\\[\nf(\\tau)=f_\\omega e^{-i\\omega\\tau}.\n\\]\n\nThe null-linked transfer function is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nH_B(\\omega,r)=\n\\frac{e^{i\\omega r}}r.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe exponential-memory transfer function is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nH_C(\\omega,r)=\n\\frac{e^{i\\omega r}}\n{r(1-i\\omega\\ell)}.\n}\n\\]\n\nDivide:\n\n\\[\n\\frac{H_C}{H_B}\n=\n\\frac1{1-i\\omega\\ell}.\n\\]\n\nThe amplitude ratio is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\left|\\frac{H_C}{H_B}\\right|\n=\n\\frac1{\\sqrt{1+(\\omega\\ell)^2}}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe additional phase is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\Delta\\varphi=\n\\arctan(\\omega\\ell).\n}\n\\]\n\nWith\n\n\\[\n\\ell=0.5\\ \\mathrm m,\n\\]\n\nthe executed results are:\n\n| \\(\\omega\\), rad/m | Amplitude ratio | Additional phase, rad |\n|---:|---:|---:|\n| 0.0 | 1.000000000000 | 0 |\n| 0.5 | 0.970142500145 | 0.244978663127 |\n| 1.0 | 0.894427191000 | 0.463647609001 |\n| 2.0 | 0.707106781187 | 0.785398163397 |\n| 4.0 | 0.447213595500 | 1.107148717794 |\n| 8.0 | 0.242535625036 | 1.325817663668 |\n\n**Result:** The models are indistinguishable in their stationary scalar response but distinguishable by their frequency-dependent transfer functions.\n\nThis is an exact property of the two defined kernels.\n\nIt does not establish that either kernel is the correct H(s)H electromagnetic mechanism.\n\n---\n\n# 13.
