Principal result\n\n## A straight worldtube can be the stable vacuum reference while a geometric coupling selects a finite-pitch helix\n\nThe calculation addresses a specific unfinished SAT → H(s)H question:\n\n**What mathematical conditions would cause a straight finite-core worldtube to acquire a stable helical geometry without winding around another object?**\n\nI constructed a minimal variational model with four properties.\n\nFirst, the straight tube is stable when its ordinary bending, tension, and localization coefficients are positive.\n\nSecond, a handed geometric coupling can destabilize a finite band of helical modes.\n\nThird, a positive quartic term can stabilize a finite-amplitude coil.\n\nFourth, the resulting configuration can be realized by two distinct, nonintersecting four-dimensional worldtubes possessing cumulative relative winding.\n\nThe important result is stronger than finding one stationary helix.\n\nFor the declared functional, **the selected finite-amplitude helix is a global energy minimizer among all periodic transverse configurations**.\n\nThat conclusion follows from Fourier diagonalization and an analytical lower bound, not just numerical optimization.\n\nThe outstanding physical question is whether SAT/H(s)H's inherited geometry actually supplies the required coupling.\n\n---\n\n# 3. Define the native four-dimensional geometry\n\nUse coordinates\n\n\\[\nX=(w,x,y,z),\n\\]\n\nwith\n\n\\[\nds^2=dw^2+dx^2+dy^2+dz^2.\n\\]\n\nAll coordinates are measured in meters.\n\nThe distinguished propagation direction is\n\n\\[\nu=(1,0,0,0).\n\\]\n\nRepresent a worldtube centerline by\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nX(w)=\n\\begin{pmatrix}\nw\\\\\nx(w)\\\\\ny(w)\\\\\n0\n\\end{pmatrix}.\n}\n\\]\n\nDefine the transverse displacement\n\n\\[\n\\mathbf q(w)=\n\\begin{pmatrix}\nx(w)\\\\\ny(w)\n\\end{pmatrix}.\n\\]\n\nThe straight vacuum-aligned reference is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\mathbf q(w)=0}.\n\\]\n\nNo separate carrier is required.\n\nThe centerline itself acquires curvature when \\(\\mathbf q\\) becomes nonzero.\n\n---\n\n# 4. Construct a trial geometric energy\n\nDefine\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nE[\\mathbf q]=\n\\int_0^L\n\\left[\n\\frac A2|\\mathbf q''|^2\n+\\frac T2|\\mathbf q'|^2\n+\\frac M2|\\mathbf q|^2\n-\\frac D2(x'y''-y'x'')\n+\\frac g4|\\mathbf q|^4\n\\right]dw.\n}\n\\]\n\nHere primes denote differentiation with respect to \\(w\\).\n\nThe coefficients have dimensions:\n\n| Parameter | Meaning in this mathematical fixture | Units |\n|---|---|---|\n| \\(A\\) | Bending coefficient | \\(U\\,\\mathrm m\\) |\n| \\(T\\) | Longitudinal tension coefficient | \\(U/\\mathrm m\\) |\n| \\(M\\) | Transverse localization coefficient | \\(U/\\mathrm m^3\\) |\n| \\(D\\) | Handed geometric coupling | \\(U\\) |\n| \\(g\\) | Quartic stabilization coefficient | \\(U/\\mathrm m^5\\) |\n\nHere \\(U\\) is an arbitrary energy unit.\n\nThe functional is defined relative to the distinguished \\(w\\) coordinate. It is not asserted to be a reparametrization-invariant fundamental action.\n\n**Crucially, \\(D\\) is not a newly established physical force.** It is a trial coefficient whose possible origin must be investigated in inherited worldtube interactions.\n\n---\n\n# 5. Substitute a circular helix\n\nLet\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\mathbf q(w)=\nR\n\\begin{pmatrix}\n\\cos kw\\\\\n\\sin kw\n\\end{pmatrix}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThen\n\n\\[\n|\\mathbf q'|^2=R^2k^2,\n\\]\n\n\\[\n|\\mathbf q''|^2=R^2k^4.\n\\]\n\nThe handed term is\n\n\\[\nx'y''-y'x''=R^2k^3.\n\\]\n\nAlso,\n\n\\[\n|\\mathbf q|^4=R^4.\n\\]\n\nSubstitution gives\n\n\\[\n\\frac EL=\n\\frac{R^2}{2}\n\\left(\nAk^4-Dk^3+Tk^2+M\n\\right)\n+\n\\frac g4R^4.\n\\]\n\nDefine\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\lambda_+(k)=\nAk^4-Dk^3+Tk^2+M.\n}\n\\]\n\nThus\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\frac EL=\n\\frac12\\lambda_+(k)R^2+\n\\frac g4R^4.\n}\n\\]\n\nFor the opposite handedness,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\lambda_-(k)=\nAk^4+Dk^3+Tk^2+M.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe handed coupling distinguishes the two geometries.\n\n---\n\n# 6. First analytical result: the straight tube is stable without a destabilizing mechanism\n\nSet\n\n\\[\nD=0.\n\\]\n\nAssume\n\n\\[\nA,T,M,g>0.\n\\]\n\nThen\n\n\\[\nE[\\mathbf q]\\ge0\n\\]\n\nfor every admissible periodic configuration.\n\nEquality occurs only for\n\n\\[\n\\mathbf q=0.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nD=0,\\quad A,T,M,g>0\n\\Longrightarrow\n\\text{straight tube is the unique minimum}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis is a useful construction constraint.\n\nOrdinary positive bending resistance and positive tension do not spontaneously produce a coil in this model.\n\nSomething in the inherited SAT/H(s)H geometry must supply a destabilizing contribution if spontaneous coiling is to occur.\n\nThis is a conditional mathematical result, not a claim that the actual worldtube energy has these coefficients.\n\n---\n\n# 7. Derive the coiling threshold\n\nA nonzero helical mode becomes energetically favorable when\n\n\\[\n\\lambda_+(k)<0.\n\\]\n\nThat requires\n\n\\[\nAk^4-Dk^3+Tk^2+M<0.\n\\]\n\nFor \\(k>0\\), divide by \\(k^3\\):\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nD>\nAk+\\frac Tk+\\frac M{k^3}.\n}\n\\]\n\nDefine\n\n\\[\nD_{\\mathrm{crit}}=\n\\min_{k>0}\n\\left(\nAk+\\frac Tk+\\frac M{k^3}\n\\right).\n\\]\n\nDifferentiate:\n\n\\[\nA-\\frac T{k^2}-\\frac{3M}{k^4}=0.\n\\]\n\nMultiply by \\(k^4\\):\n\n\\[\nAk^4-Tk^2-3M=0.\n\\]\n\nSet\n\n\\[\ny=k^2.\n\\]\n\nThen\n\n\\[\nAy^2-Ty-3M=0.\n\\]\n\nThe positive root is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nk_{\\mathrm{crit}}^2=\n\\frac{T+\\sqrt{T^2+12AM}}{2A}.\n}\n\\]\n\nConsequently,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nD_{\\mathrm{crit}}=\nAk_{\\mathrm{crit}}\n+\\frac T{k_{\\mathrm{crit}}}\n+\\frac M{k_{\\mathrm{crit}}^3}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis is the exact continuum instability threshold for the declared functional.\n\n---\n\n# 8. Second calculation: a complete-history unwinding construction\n\nNow construct a deformation that keeps the two worldtubes separated.\n\nUse\n\n\\[\nR=0.30\\ \\mathrm m,\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\rho=0.10\\ \\mathrm m,\n\\]\n\n\\[\nk=1.492231229732\\ \\mathrm m^{-1}.\n\\]\n\nChoose fourteen turns:\n\n\\[\nN=14.\n\\]\n\nThe history interval is\n\n\\[\nL=\\frac{2\\pi N}{k}.\n\\]\n\nNumerically,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nL=58.948367081362\\ \\mathrm m.\n}\n\\]\n\nDefine\n\n\\[\nt=kw\n\\]\n\nand a deformation parameter\n\n\\[\ns\\in[0,1].\n\\]\n\nLet\n\n\\[\nb=s(1-s).\n\\]\n\nConstruct the transverse vector\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nV_s(t)=\n\\begin{pmatrix}\ns+(1-s)\\cos t\\\\\n(1-s)\\sin t\\\\\n4b\\sin^2(t/2)\n\\end{pmatrix}.\n}\n\\]\n\nNormalize it:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nn_s(t)=\\frac{V_s(t)}{|V_s(t)|}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThen define the two worldtubes:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nX_\\pm(w;s)=\n\\left(\nw,\\,\n\\pm\\frac R2n_s(kw)\n\\right).\n}\n\\]\n\nThis is a family of complete four-dimensional geometries.\n\nIt is not a claim that the physical worldtubes dynamically pass through these configurations.\n\n### Initial geometry\n\nAt\n\n\\[\ns=0,\n\\]\n\nwe obtain\n\n\\[\nn_0(t)=\n(\\cos t,\\sin t,0).\n\\]\n\nAcross the history interval,\n\n\\[\nt:0\\rightarrow28\\pi.\n\\]\n\nThe relative displacement completes fourteen revolutions.\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{B_{\\mathrm{initial}}=14}.\n\\]\n\n### Ending geometry\n\nAt\n\n\\[\ns=1,\n\\]\n\nwe obtain\n\n\\[\nn_1(t)=(1,0,0).\n\\]\n\nThere is no winding.\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{B_{\\mathrm{ending}}=0}.\n\\]\n\n### Endpoint preservation\n\nAt both endpoints,\n\n\\[\nt=0,\\qquad t=28\\pi,\n\\]\n\nthe vector is\n\n\\[\nn_s=(1,0,0)\n\\]\n\nfor every \\(s\\).\n\nThus the complete-history endpoints remain fixed.\n\nThe deformation does not require an external winding carrier.\n\n---\n\n# 6. Prove the deformation is nonsingular\n\nThe normalization would fail if\n\n\\[\nV_s(t)=0.\n\\]\n\nWe can exclude that analytically.\n\nLet\n\n\\[\nq=b\\sin^2(t/2).\n\\]\n\nBecause\n\n\\[\n0\\le b\\le\\frac14,\n\\]\n\nwe have\n\n\\[\n0\\le q\\le\\frac14.\n\\]\n\nDirect expansion gives\n\n\\[\n|V_s|^2=\n1-4q+16q^2.\n\\]\n\nComplete the square:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n|V_s|^2=\n16\\left(q-\\frac18\\right)^2+\\frac34.\n}\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n|V_s|^2\\ge\\frac34.\n}\n\\]\n\nIn particular,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n|V_s|>0\n}\n\\]\n\neverywhere.\n\nThe deformation is smooth and nonsingular.\n\nBut that alone is not enough.\n\nWe must check separation between points at **different** values of \\(w\\).\n\n---\n\n# 7. Prove complete four-dimensional nonintersection\n\nDifferentiate the unnormalized vector with respect to \\(t\\).\n\nIts derivative obeys\n\n\\[\n\\left|\\frac{\\partial V_s}{\\partial t}\\right|\n\\le\\frac{\\sqrt5}{2}.\n\\]\n\nBecause\n\n\\[\n|V_s|\\ge\\frac{\\sqrt3}{2},\n\\]\n\nthe normalized vector obeys\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\left|\\frac{\\partial n_s}{\\partial t}\\right|\n\\le\\sqrt{\\frac53}.\n}\n\\]\n\nConvert to the \\(w\\) coordinate:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\left|\\frac{\\partial n_s}{\\partial w}\\right|\n\\le K\n=\nk\\sqrt{\\frac53}.\n}\n\\]\n\nNumerically,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nK=1.926462233814\\ \\mathrm m^{-1}.\n}\n\\]\n\nNow compare arbitrary points \\(X_+(w;s)\\) and \\(X_-(v;s)\\).\n\nTheir squared distance is\n\n\\[\nd^2=\n(w-v)^2+\n\\frac{R^2}{4}\n|n_s(kw)+n_s(kv)|^2.\n\\]\n\nSince both \\(n_s\\) vectors have unit length,\n\n\\[\n|n_1+n_2|^2=\n4-|n_1-n_2|^2.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\nd^2=\nR^2+(w-v)^2\n-\\frac{R^2}{4}|n_s(kw)-n_s(kv)|^2.\n\\]\n\nThe derivative bound gives\n\n\\[\n|n_s(kw)-n_s(kv)|\n\\le K|w-v|.\n\\]\n\nHence\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nd^2\\ge\nR^2+\n\\left[\n1-\\left(\\frac{RK}{2}\\right)^2\n\\right](w-v)^2.\n}\n\\]\n\nIf\n\n\\[\nRK<2,\n\\]\n\nthe second term is nonnegative.\n\nConsequently,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nd^2\\ge R^2.\n}\n\\]\n\nEquality occurs at\n\n\\[\nw=v.\n\\]\n\nThus the global minimum centerline separation is exactly\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nd_{\\min}=R.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis holds throughout the entire deformation, including cross-temporal comparisons.\n\n### Numerical result\n\nFor our fixture,\n\n\\[\nRK=\n0.577938670144.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\nRK<2.\n\\]\n\nThe minimum centerline separation is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nd_{\\min}=0.30\\ \\mathrm m.\n}\n\\]\n\nEach tube has radius\n\n\\[\n\\rho=0.10\\ \\mathrm m.\n\\]\n\nThe minimum separation between the complete tubular neighborhoods is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nd_{\\min}-2\\rho=0.10\\ \\mathrm m.\n}\n\\]\n\n**The fourteen-turn geometry can be deformed continuously into an unwound geometry while preserving a positive complete-four-dimensional core clearance.**\n\nThis is an analytical result. The numerical checks independently confirmed it.\n\n---\n\n# 8. What this means for BR-006\n\nThe result establishes a precise distinction.\n\n**Unwrapped winding history is not automatically a topological invariant of two nonintersecting worldtubes embedded in four-dimensional Euclidean space.**\n\nThe third transverse direction permits continuous deformation of the relative direction.\n\nHowever, BR-006 asserts more than nonintersection.\n\nIt asserts that the interbraided geometry is mechanically constraining, that the complete history matters, and that accumulated braiding cannot silently disappear.\n\nThose premises are not disproved by exhibiting a homotopy between different complete histories.\n\nThe deformation changes the entire four-dimensional configuration. Principal result\n\n## Changing planar winding requires a transverse escape event\n\nFor two worldtubes embedded in native Euclidean four-dimensional geometry, a continuous deformation can change their planar winding without allowing their finite cores to intersect.\n\nHowever, that change requires the relative displacement vector to leave its original winding plane.\n\nMore precisely:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\text{Changing planar winding requires the planar relative vector to vanish somewhere.}\n}\n\\]\n\nFor a relative unit vector in three transverse dimensions, this means reaching a direction perpendicular to the winding plane.\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{|n_z|=1}\n\\]\n\nThis provides a geometrically exact discriminator.\n\nIf the inherited SAT/H(s)H mechanics imposes a strict bound\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{|n_z|<1}\n\\]\n\nthroughout every admissible deformation, planar winding is conserved.\n\nIf transverse escape is permitted, nonintersection alone cannot guarantee winding conservation.\n\n**That is the central result of this relay.**\n\nThe calculation does not establish that H(s)H actually imposes the required bound.\n\n---\n\n# 3. Native four-dimensional construction\n\nUse coordinates\n\n\\[\nX=(w,x,y,z)\n\\]\n\nwith\n\n\\[\nds^2=dw^2+dx^2+dy^2+dz^2.\n\\]\n\nNo primitive Lorentzian null condition is introduced.\n\nRepresent two complete worldtube centerlines by\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nX_\\pm(w;s)=\n\\left(\nw,\\pm\\frac R2 n_s(kw)\n\\right).\n}\n\\]\n\nHere \\(n_s\\) is a unit vector in the three-dimensional transverse space.\n\nThe parameter\n\n\\[\ns\\in[0,1]\n\\]\n\nindexes different complete geometries.\n\nIt is not physical time.\n\nDefine\n\n\\[\nt=kw\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\nb=s(1-s).\n\\]\n\nConstruct\n\n\\[\nV_s(t)=\n\\begin{pmatrix}\ns+(1-s)\\cos t\\\\\n(1-s)\\sin t\\\\\n4b\\sin^2(t/2)\n\\end{pmatrix}.\n\\]\n\nNormalize:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nn_s(t)=\\frac{V_s(t)}{|V_s(t)|}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis is the explicit deformation introduced in the preceding Tern calculation.\n\nRavel's task is to identify its exact winding transition and quantify the geometric cost.\n\n---\n\n# 4. Initial and ending configurations\n\nAt\n\n\\[\ns=0,\n\\]\n\nwe have\n\n\\[\nn_0(t)=\n\\begin{pmatrix}\n\\cos t\\\\\n\\sin t\\\\\n0\n\\end{pmatrix}.\n\\]\n\nChoose fourteen revolutions:\n\n\\[\nN=14.\n\\]\n\nThe history interval is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nL=\\frac{2\\pi N}{k}.\n}\n\\]\n\nAt the other endpoint,\n\n\\[\ns=1,\n\\]\n\nwe obtain\n\n\\[\nn_1(t)=\n\\begin{pmatrix}\n1\\\\\n0\\\\\n0\n\\end{pmatrix}.\n\\]\n\nThus the initial relative displacement has fourteen planar revolutions, while the ending configuration has none.\n\nAt both ends of the history interval, the relative direction is fixed:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nn_s(0)=n_s(2\\pi N)=(1,0,0).\n}\n\\]\n\nThe construction preserves these endpoints throughout.\n\n---\n\n# 5. Exact planar winding calculation\n\nThe planar part of the unnormalized relative vector is\n\n\\[\nz_s(t)=s+(1-s)e^{it}.\n\\]\n\nFor fixed \\(s\\), this describes a circle in the complex plane.\n\nIts center is\n\n\\[\ns\n\\]\n\nand its radius is\n\n\\[\n1-s.\n\\]\n\nThe circle encloses the origin precisely when\n\n\\[\n1-s>s.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{s<\\frac12}.\n\\]\n\nFor those configurations, the planar winding number is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{W(s)=14}.\n\\]\n\nWhen\n\n\\[\ns>\\frac12,\n\\]\n\nthe circle does not enclose the origin.\n\nThus\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{W(s)=0}.\n\\]\n\nAt\n\n\\[\ns=\\frac12,\n\\]\n\nthe circle passes through the origin.\n\nThe planar winding number is undefined at that configuration.\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nW(s)=\n\\begin{cases}\n14,&s<1/2,\\\\\n\\text{undefined},&s=1/2,\\\\\n0,&s>1/2.\n\\end{cases}\n}\n\\]\n\nThis is an exact result.\n\n---\n\n# 6. Where does the winding disappear?\n\nAt\n\n\\[\ns=\\frac12,\n\\]\n\nconsider\n\n\\[\nt=(2j+1)\\pi.\n\\]\n\nThen\n\n\\[\n\\cos t=-1,\\qquad \\sin t=0.\n\\]\n\nThe first two components vanish:\n\n\\[\nV_x=0,\n\\]\n\n\\[\nV_y=0.\n\\]\n\nThe third component is\n\n\\[\nV_z=\n4\\left(\\frac14\\right)\n\\sin^2\\left(\\frac{(2j+1)\\pi}{2}\\right)\n=1.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nn_{1/2}((2j+1)\\pi)=(0,0,1).\n}\n\\]\n\nThe relative displacement has not vanished.\n\nIt has rotated completely out of the original winding plane.\n\nThe two worldtube centerlines remain separated.\n\n**The planar winding changes because the relative direction passes through the transverse pole, not because the two cores collide.**\n\nThis distinction is important for BR-006.\n\n---\n\n# 7. Exact nonintersection proof\n\nFirst establish that the normalization is nonsingular.\n\nDefine\n\n\\[\nq=b\\sin^2(t/2).\n\\]\n\nThen\n\n\\[\n0\\le q\\le\\frac14.\n\\]\n\nDirect expansion gives\n\n\\[\n|V_s|^2=1-4q+16q^2.\n\\]\n\nComplete the square:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n|V_s|^2=\n16\\left(q-\\frac18\\right)^2+\\frac34.\n}\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n|V_s|^2\\ge\\frac34.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe normalized vector exists everywhere.\n\nNext, differentiate:\n\n\\[\nV_t=\n\\begin{pmatrix}\n-(1-s)\\sin t\\\\\n(1-s)\\cos t\\\\\n2b\\sin t\n\\end{pmatrix}.\n\\]\n\nIts norm satisfies\n\n\\[\n|V_t|^2\n=\n(1-s)^2+4b^2\\sin^2t.\n\\]\n\nSince\n\n\\[\nb\\le\\frac14,\n\\]\n\nwe have\n\n\\[\n|V_t|^2\\le\\frac54.\n\\]\n\nHence\n\n\\[\n|V_t|\\le\\frac{\\sqrt5}{2}.\n\\]\n\nFor the normalized vector,\n\n\\[\n\\left|\\frac{dn_s}{dt}\\right|\n\\le\\frac{|V_t|}{|V_s|}.\n\\]\n\nThus\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\left|\\frac{dn_s}{dt}\\right|\n\\le\\sqrt{\\frac53}.\n}\n\\]\n\nConverting to \\(w\\),\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\left|\\frac{dn_s}{dw}\\right|\n\\le k\\sqrt{\\frac53}.\n}\n\\]\n\nDefine\n\n\\[\nK_{\\mathrm{geom}}=\nk\\sqrt{\\frac53}.\n\\]\n\nFor arbitrary points on opposite centerlines,\n\n\\[\nd^2=\n(w-v)^2+\n\\frac{R^2}{4}|n_s(kw)+n_s(kv)|^2.\n\\]\n\nUsing\n\n\\[\n|n_1+n_2|^2=4-|n_1-n_2|^2,\n\\]\n\nwe obtain\n\n\\[\nd^2=\nR^2+(w-v)^2\n-\\frac{R^2}{4}|n_s(kw)-n_s(kv)|^2.\n\\]\n\nThe derivative bound gives\n\n\\[\n|n_s(kw)-n_s(kv)|\n\\le K_{\\mathrm{geom}}|w-v|.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nd^2\\ge\nR^2+\n\\left[\n1-\\frac{R^2K_{\\mathrm{geom}}^2}{4}\n\\right](w-v)^2.\n}\n\\]\n\nWhenever\n\n\\[\nRK_{\\mathrm{geom}}<2,\n\\]\n\nthe second term is nonnegative.\n\nConsequently,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nd_{\\min}=R.\n}\n\\]\n\nEquality is attained when \\(w=v\\).\n\nThis is a complete four-dimensional separation result, not merely an equal-time calculation.\n\n---\n\n# 8. Numerical fixture\n\nThe executed calculations used\n\n\\[\nR=0.30\\ \\mathrm m,\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\rho=0.10\\ \\mathrm m,\n\\]\n\n\\[\nk=1.492231229732\\ \\mathrm m^{-1},\n\\]\n\n\\[\nN=14.\n\\]\n\nThe history length is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nL=58.948367081362\\ \\mathrm m.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe geometric derivative bound is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nK_{\\mathrm{geom}}\n=\n1.926462233814\\ \\mathrm m^{-1}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThus\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nRK_{\\mathrm{geom}}\n=\n0.577938670144.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe coefficient in the separation inequality is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n1-\\frac{R^2K_{\\mathrm{geom}}^2}{4}\n=\n0.916496723388.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis is positive.\n\nThe complete-history minimum centerline separation is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{0.30\\ \\mathrm m}.\n\\]\n\nThe finite-core clearance is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nR-2\\rho=0.10\\ \\mathrm m.\n}\n\\]\n\n**The cores remain separated throughout the winding transition.**\n\n---\n\n# 9. A physical distinction: topology versus admissibility\n\nThe mathematics now identifies two different questions.\n\nOne concerns whether a continuous deformation exists in the ambient geometry.\n\nThe other concerns whether that deformation is physically permitted.\n\nFor a relative direction confined to a plane, winding is integer-valued and conserved under continuous deformations that preserve nonzero separation.\n\nFor a relative direction free to explore all three transverse dimensions, the same winding can be contracted through an out-of-plane excursion.\n\nThis is the distinction between planar winding and the topology of a sphere of possible relative directions.\n\nIt is closely related to the fact that\n\n\\[\n\\pi_1(S^1)=\\mathbb Z\n\\]\n\nwhereas\n\n\\[\n\\pi_1(S^2)=0.\n\\]\n\nHowever, this mathematical comparison is not an imported H(s)H ontology.\n\nIt identifies the missing admissibility condition.\n\nA candidate physical constraint might prevent the relative direction from reaching the transverse pole.\n\nBut **that constraint must come from the inherited filament/timesheet/interbraid geometry**, rather than being inserted merely to preserve a desired conclusion.\n\n---\n\n# 10. Exact small-deformation analysis\n\nWe can go further than numerical integration.\n\nExpand the normalized vector around\n\n\\[\ns=0.\n\\]\n\nWrite\n\n\\[\nn_s=n_0+s\\,a+s^2b+O(s^3).\n\\]\n\nThe first-order correction is\n\n\\[\na=\n\\begin{pmatrix}\n\\sin^2t\\\\\n-\\sin t\\cos t\\\\\n2(1-\\cos t)\n\\end{pmatrix}.\n\\]\n\nThe quadratic contribution to\n\n\\[\n\\left|\\frac{dn}{dt}\\right|^2\n\\]\n\nsimplifies to\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n-3\\cos^2t+6\\cos t-2.\n}\n\\]\n\nIts average over a complete revolution is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{-\\frac72}.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nE_t(s)=\nE_0\\left[\n1-\\frac72s^2+O(s^3)\n\\right].\n}\n\\]\n\nMeanwhile,\n\n\\[\nn_z=\n2s(1-\\cos t)+O(s^2).\n\\]\n\nHence\n\n\\[\nn_z^2=\n4s^2(1-\\cos t)^2+O(s^3).\n\\]\n\nThe average of\n\n\\[\n4(1-\\cos t)^2\n\\]\n\nis exactly\n\n\\[\n6.\n\\]\n\nThus\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nE_z(s)=3\\mu Ls^2+O(s^3).\n}\n\\]\n\nCombining,\n\n\\[\nE(s)=\nE_0+\n\\left(\n-\\frac72E_0+3\\mu L\n\\right)s^2\n+O(s^3).\n\\]\n\nThe local quadratic coefficient changes sign when\n\n\\[\n3\\mu L=\\frac72E_0.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\mu_{\\mathrm{local}}=\n\\frac{7E_0}{6L}.\n}\n\\]\n\nSubstitute\n\n\\[\nE_0=\\frac{KR^2k^2L}{4}.\n\\]\n\nWe obtain\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\mu_{\\mathrm{local}}\n=\n\\frac{7KR^2k^2}{24}.\n}\n\\]\n\nFor the numerical fixture,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\mu_{\\mathrm{local}}\n=\n0.058452293628\\ U/\\mathrm m.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis is an exact local threshold for the declared deformation and trial energy.\n\nIt is not a universal H(s)H constant.\n\n---\n\n# 13. General lower bound on transverse-excursion cost\n\nThere is another useful analytical result.\n\nDefine\n\n\\[\nK_{\\mathrm{eff}}=\\frac{KR^2}{2}.\n\\]\n\nThen\n\n\\[\nE_t=\n\\frac{K_{\\mathrm{eff}}}{2}\n\\int|n'|^2dw.\n\\]\n\nLet\n\n\\[\n\\alpha=\\arcsin|n_z|.\n\\]\n\nFor a deformation that starts in the winding plane, reaches the transverse pole, and returns to the plane, \\(\\alpha\\) must travel\n\n\\[\n0\\rightarrow\\frac\\pi2\\rightarrow0.\n\\]\n\nThe energy satisfies\n\n\\[\nE_t+E_z\n\\ge\n\\int\n\\left[\n\\frac{K_{\\mathrm{eff}}}{2}\\alpha'^2+\n\\frac\\mu2\\sin^2\\alpha\n\\right]dw.\n\\]\n\nUsing the arithmetic-geometric mean inequality,\n\n\\[\n\\frac{K_{\\mathrm{eff}}}{2}\\alpha'^2+\n\\frac\\mu2\\sin^2\\alpha\n\\ge\n\\sqrt{K_{\\mathrm{eff}}\\mu}\n|\\alpha'|\\sin\\alpha.\n\\]\n\nIntegrate:\n\n\\[\nE_t+E_z\n\\ge\n\\sqrt{K_{\\mathrm{eff}}\\mu}\n\\int|\\alpha'|\\sin\\alpha\\,dw.\n\\]\n\nThe excursion to the pole and back gives\n\n\\[\n\\int|\\alpha'|\\sin\\alpha\\,dw\\ge2.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nE_t+E_z\n\\ge\n2\\sqrt{K_{\\mathrm{eff}}\\mu}.\n}\n\\]\n\nEquivalently,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nE_t+E_z\n\\ge\nR\\sqrt{2K\\mu}.\n}\n\\]\n\nFor the declared fixture,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nE_t+E_z\\ge0.30\\ U.\n}\n\\]\n\nThis is a lower bound on the positive tilt-and-penalty energy for a pole excursion. It is **not** a lower bound on the net energy barrier relative to the original coiled configuration.\n\nThe distinction matters because the deformation can simultaneously release stored winding tension.\n\n---\n\n# 15. Principal result\n\n## A continuous geometric-history quantity survives the loss of planar winding\n\nConsider the fourteen-turn worldtube configuration constructed by Tern and subsequently analyzed by Ravel.\n\nThe previous calculations established that its planar winding can change from\n\n\\[\nW=14\n\\]\n\nto\n\n\\[\nW=0\n\\]\n\nwithout allowing the finite cores to intersect.\n\nThe integer winding changes discontinuously as a coordinate-dependent index.\n\nBut the complete geometry changes continuously.\n\n**Can we construct a continuous geometric quantity that records this deformation?**\n\nYes.\n\nAriadne constructed an oriented solid-angle functional over the relative direction of the two worldtubes.\n\nIt has three useful properties:\n\n1. Native four-dimensional geometry\n\nUse\n\n\\[\n\\mathbb R^4\n\\]\n\nwith Euclidean metric\n\n\\[\nds^2=dw^2+dx^2+dy^2+dz^2.\n\\]\n\nDefine two worldtube centerlines:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nX_\\pm(w;s)=\n\\left(\nw,\\pm\\frac R2n_s(kw)\n\\right).\n}\n\\]\n\nHere \\(s\\) indexes possible complete geometries.\n\nIt is not physical time.\n\nLet\n\n\\[\nt=kw,\n\\qquad\nb=s(1-s).\n\\]\n\nConstruct\n\n\\[\nV_s(t)=\n\\begin{pmatrix}\ns+(1-s)\\cos t\\\\\n(1-s)\\sin t\\\\\n2b(1-\\cos t)\n\\end{pmatrix}.\n\\]\n\nNormalize:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nn_s(t)=\\frac{V_s(t)}{|V_s(t)|}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe numerical parameters are\n\n\\[\nR=0.30\\ \\mathrm m,\n\\]\n\n\\[\n\\rho=0.10\\ \\mathrm m,\n\\]\n\n\\[\nk=1.492231229732\\ \\mathrm m^{-1},\n\\]\n\n\\[\nN=14.\n\\]\n\nThe history interval is\n\n\\[\nL=\\frac{2\\pi N}{k}.\n\\]\n\nNumerically,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nL=58.948367081362\\ \\mathrm m.\n}\n\\]\n\n---\n\n# 4. Complete-history nonintersection\n\nDefine\n\n\\[\nq=b\\sin^2(t/2).\n\\]\n\nThe unnormalized vector satisfies\n\n\\[\n|V_s|^2=1-4q+16q^2.\n\\]\n\nCompleting the square,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n|V_s|^2=\n16\\left(q-\\frac18\\right)^2+\\frac34.\n}\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n|V_s|^2\\ge\\frac34.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe normalization is nonsingular.\n\nThe derivative bound established for this construction is\n\n\\[\n\\left|\\frac{dn_s}{dt}\\right|\n\\le\\sqrt{\\frac53}.\n\\]\n\nFor arbitrary points on opposite centerlines,\n\n\\[\n\\begin{aligned}\nd_4^2\n&=(w-v)^2\\\\\n&\\quad+\n\\frac{R^2}{4}\n|n_s(kw)+n_s(kv)|^2.\n\\end{aligned}\n\\]\n\nUsing the unit-vector identity\n\n\\[\n|n_1+n_2|^2=4-|n_1-n_2|^2,\n\\]\n\nand the derivative bound,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nd_4^2\\ge\nR^2+\n\\left[\n1-\\frac{R^2k^2}{4}\\frac53\n\\right](w-v)^2.\n}\n\\]\n\nFor the selected parameters,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nRk\\sqrt{\\frac53}\n=\n0.577938670144<2.\n}\n\\]\n\nConsequently,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nd_{\\min}=R=0.30\\ \\mathrm m.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe complete finite-core clearance is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nd_{\\min}-2\\rho=0.10\\ \\mathrm m.\n}\n\\]\n\nThus the cores remain separated throughout the deformation, including comparisons between different values of \\(w\\).\n\n---\n\n# 5. Planar winding\n\nThe planar relative vector can be represented as\n\n\\[\nz_s(t)=s+(1-s)e^{it}.\n\\]\n\nFor fixed \\(s\\), this is a circle in the complex plane.\n\nIts center is \\(s\\), and its radius is \\(1-s\\).\n\nThe origin lies inside the circle when\n\n\\[\ns<\\frac12.\n\\]\n\nTherefore, over fourteen complete revolutions,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nW(s)=\n\\begin{cases}\n14,&s<1/2,\\\\\n\\text{undefined},&s=1/2,\\\\\n0,&s>1/2.\n\\end{cases}\n}\n\\]\n\nAt the transition,\n\n\\[\ns=\\frac12,\n\\]\n\nand at\n\n\\[\nt=(2j+1)\\pi,\n\\]\n\nthe normalized relative direction becomes\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nn=(0,0,1).\n}\n\\]\n\nThe planar projection vanishes, but the full three-dimensional relative direction does not.\n\nThis is the precise transverse escape event.\n\n---\n\n# 6. Model definition\n\nLet the unobserved binary state be\n\n\\[\nT\\sim\\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p).\n\\]\n\nThe observed binary value is\n\n\\[\nY=T\\oplus F,\n\\]\n\nwhere\n\n\\[\nF\\sim\\operatorname{Bernoulli}(e)\n\\]\n\nrepresents classification error.\n\nAssume the main observations are independent, with fixed error probability \\(e\\).\n\nThen\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\theta=P(Y=1)=e+(1-2e)p.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe inference target is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\np=\\frac{\\theta-e}{1-2e}.\n}\n\\]\n\nWe restrict the physically meaningful classification branch to\n\n\\[\n0\\le e<\\frac12.\n\\]\n\nThe declared numerical parameters are\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\np=0.7,\\qquad e=0.1,\\qquad\\theta=0.66.\n}\n\\]\n\nFor \\(n\\) independent main observations,\n\n\\[\nX\\sim\\operatorname{Binomial}(n,\\theta).\n\\]\n\nThe calibration sample contains\n\n\\[\nm=24\n\\]\n\nknown-state observations.\n\nUnlike the main sample, calibration observations may share a session-specific latent error rate.\n\n---\n\n# 4. Clustered calibration\n\nDivide the calibration observations into\n\n\\[\nG=\\frac ms\n\\]\n\nindependent sessions of size \\(s\\).\n\nFor each session, draw\n\n\\[\nU_g\\sim\\operatorname{Beta}(a,b).\n\\]\n\nConditional on \\(U_g\\), its \\(s\\) error indicators are independent Bernoulli variables with probability \\(U_g\\).\n\nUse\n\n\\[\na=0.4,\\qquad b=3.6.\n\\]\n\nConsequently,\n\n\\[\nE[U_g]=\\frac{a}{a+b}=0.1.\n\\]\n\nThe intraclass correlation between two error indicators from the same session is\n\n\\[\n\\rho=\\frac1{a+b+1}.\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\\rho=0.2}.\n\\]\n\nThe number of errors in session \\(g\\) follows a beta-binomial distribution:\n\n\\[\nK_g\\sim\\operatorname{BetaBinomial}(s,0.4,3.6).\n\\]\n\nThe total calibration-error count is\n\n\\[\nK=\\sum_{g=1}^{G}K_g.\n\\]\n\nThe probability-generating function is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nP_K(z)=\n\\left[\n\\sum_{j=0}^{s}\n\\binom sj\n\\frac{B(j+a,s-j+b)}{B(a,b)}\nz^j\n\\right]^{m/s}.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe coefficient of \\(z^k\\) gives the exact finite-sample probability of observing \\(K=k\\).\n\nThis distribution was calculated by repeated discrete convolution.\n\n---\n\n# 5. Derive the calibration variance\n\nFor a single error indicator,\n\n\\[\n\\operatorname{Var}(F)=e(1-e).\n\\]\n\nFor two distinct indicators in the same session,\n\n\\[\n\\operatorname{Cov}(F_i,F_j)=\\rho e(1-e).\n\\]\n\nTherefore,\n\n\\[\n\\begin{aligned}\n\\operatorname{Var}(K_g)\n&=\ns e(1-e)+s(s-1)\\rho e(1-e)\\\\\n&=\ns e(1-e)[1+(s-1)\\rho].\n\\end{aligned}\n\\]\n\nBecause sessions are independent,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\operatorname{Var}(K)\n=\nm e(1-e)[1+(s-1)\\rho].\n}\n\\]\n\nThis is an exact population result under the stipulated model.\n\n### Executed moment checks\n\n| Session size \\(s\\) | Sessions | \\(E[K]\\) | \\(\\operatorname{Var}(K)\\) |\n|---:|---:|---:|---:|\n| 1 | 24 | 2.4 | 2.160 |\n| 2 | 12 | 2.4 | 2.592 |\n| 3 | 8 | 2.4 | 3.024 |\n| 4 | 6 | 2.4 | 3.456 |\n| 6 | 4 | 2.4 | 4.320 |\n| 8 | 3 | 2.4 | 5.184 |\n| 12 | 2 | 2.4 | 6.912 |\n| 24 | 1 | 2.4 | 12.096 |\n\nEvery calculated mean and variance agreed with its analytical expression to the asserted numerical tolerance.\n\nFor the globally shared calibration latent, \\(s=24\\),\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\frac{\\operatorname{Var}(K)_{\\mathrm{global}}}\n{\\operatorname{Var}(K)_{\\mathrm{iid}}}\n=5.6.\n}\n\\]\n\nThe usual variance-equivalent effective sample size is\n\n\\[\nm_{\\mathrm{eff}}=\n\\frac{m}{1+(s-1)\\rho}.\n\\]\n\nThus\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nm_{\\mathrm{eff}}=\\frac{24}{5.6}\n=4.2857142857.\n}\n\\]\n\nTwenty-four calibration observations contain only about 4.29 independent-observation equivalents for estimating their common marginal error rate under this variance criterion.\n\nThat is a substantial information loss.\n\n---\n\n# 6. Confidence-interval construction\n\nTwo independent datasets are used: the main observations and the calibration observations.\n\nConstruct a 97.5% Clopper-Pearson interval for \\(\\theta\\):\n\n\\[\nI_\\theta(X).\n\\]\n\nConstruct a separate 97.5% interval for \\(e\\):\n\n\\[\nI_e(K).\n\\]\n\nFor a binomial count \\(k\\) from \\(n\\) observations, the Clopper-Pearson endpoints are\n\n\\[\nL=\n\\begin{cases}\n0,&k=0,\\\\\nB^{-1}(\\alpha/2;k,n-k+1),&k>0,\n\\end{cases}\n\\]\n\nand\n\n\\[\nU=\n\\begin{cases}\n1,&k=n,\\\\\nB^{-1}(1-\\alpha/2;k+1,n-k),&k<n.\n\\end{cases}\n\\]\n\nHere\n\n\\[\n\\alpha=0.025.\n\\]\n\nFor clustered calibration, the interval is instead constructed by inverting the appropriate beta-binomial tail probabilities.\n\nThe lower endpoint satisfies\n\n\\[\nP_e(K\\ge k)=\\alpha/2,\n\\]\n\nand the upper endpoint satisfies\n\n\\[\nP_e(K\\le k)=\\alpha/2,\n\\]\n\nwith the usual endpoint conventions.\n\nThe beta family is parameterized by\n\n\\[\na=e\\kappa,\\qquad b=(1-e)\\kappa,\n\\]\n\nwhere\n\n\\[\n\\kappa=\\frac{1-\\rho}{\\rho}=4.\n\\]\n\nThis holds the intraclass correlation fixed while varying the hypothesized error probability.\n\n### Transforming the intervals\n\nConstruct the identified interval for \\(p\\) from\n\n\\[\np=\\frac{\\theta-e}{1-2e}\n\\]\n\nover\n\n\\[\n(\\theta,e)\\in I_\\theta\\times I_e,\n\\]\n\nsubject to\n\n\\[\n0\\le p\\le1,\\qquad 0\\le e<\\frac12.\n\\]\n\nThe distinction at \\(e=1/2\\) is essential.\n\nWhen the calibration interval crosses \\(1/2\\), it does **not** automatically follow that the entire interval \\(p\\in[0,1]\\) is admissible. The observed \\(\\theta\\) can still constrain \\(p\\).\n\nThe implemented calculation respects this restriction.\n\nUnder correctly specified sampling models, the union bound guarantees at least\n\n\\[\n1-\\alpha_\\theta-\\alpha_e=0.95\n\\]\n\ncoverage for the joint confidence rectangle.\n\nThe transformed interval inherits that lower guarantee.\n\n---\n\n# 7. Exact finite-sample coverage\n\nLet \\(I_p(x,k)\\) be the interval obtained from observed main count \\(x\\) and calibration count \\(k\\).\n\nThe exact coverage is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nC_p=\n\\sum_{k=0}^{m}\n\\sum_{x=0}^{n}\nP(K=k)\nP(X=x)\n\\mathbf1[p\\in I_p(x,k)].\n}\n\\]\n\nThe calibration probability \\(P(K=k)\\) is computed under the **true** session model.\n\nThe interval \\(I_p\\) is constructed under the **assumed** calibration model.\n\nThis separation permits a direct test of model misspecification.\n\nThe calculation evaluates every possible pair \\((x,k)\\).\n\nNo sampling approximation is required, although numerical probabilities are evaluated in floating-point arithmetic.\n\n---\n\n# 8. Executed results at \\(n=40\\)\n\nThe main dataset contains forty independent observations.\n\nThe calibration dataset contains twenty-four observations.\n\n| True \\(s\\) | Assumed \\(s\\) | Calibration coverage | \\(p\\) coverage | Mean \\(p\\)-interval width |\n|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|\n| 1 | 1 | 0.992544 | 0.997307 | 0.609997 |\n| 3 | 1 | 0.978342 | 0.996984 | 0.609903 |\n| 3 | 3 | 0.992098 | 0.997345 | 0.643941 |\n| 6 | 1 | 0.954569 | 0.996448 | 0.608420 |\n| 6 | 3 | 0.977403 | 0.996955 | 0.640894 |\n| 6 | 6 | 0.989338 | 0.997622 | 0.681023 |\n| 24 | 1 | **0.879146** | 0.987899 | 0.586439 |\n| 24 | 3 | 0.905159 | 0.990654 | 0.615983 |\n| 24 | 24 | 0.991093 | 0.997722 | 0.782104 |\n\nThe striking result is the difference between calibration coverage and underlying-parameter coverage.\n\nFor globally shared calibration errors, the incorrectly assumed iid calibration interval covers the true \\(e\\) only\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{87.9146\\%}\n\\]\n\nof the time.\n\nYet the resulting interval for \\(p\\) covers its true value\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{98.7899\\%}\n\\]\n\nof the time.\n\nThe second figure looks excellent.\n\nBut the apparent success is partly caused by the broad uncertainty in the forty-observation main dataset.\n\nIt does not establish that the calibration model is adequate.\n\n---\n\n# 9. Increasing the main sample size\n\nThe next execution varied \\(n\\) while keeping the calibration dataset fixed at twenty-four observations.\n\nThe true calibration process was globally shared:\n\n\\[\ns_{\\mathrm{true}}=24.\n\\]\n\nThree inference models were compared.\n\n| Main \\(n\\) | Assume iid \\(s=1\\) | Assume \\(s=3\\) | Correct \\(s=24\\) |\n|---:|---:|---:|---:|\n| 40 | 0.987899 | 0.990654 | 0.997722 |\n| 100 | 0.981103 | 0.986442 | 0.998591 |\n| 400 | 0.958687 | 0.969412 | 0.998086 |\n| 1,600 | **0.932216** | **0.947943** | 0.996063 |\n| 6,400 | **0.911545** | **0.930955** | 0.993799 |\n| 12,000 | **0.904820** | Not evaluated | 0.992949 |\n| 24,000 | **0.900570** | Not evaluated | 0.991998 |\n| 48,000 | **0.895912** | Not evaluated | 0.991230 |\n\nThe values below 0.95 are genuine undercoverage under the declared synthetic data-generating process.\n\nThe correctly specified model retains coverage above its nominal lower bound.\n\n### Interpretation\n\nAs \\(n\\) grows, uncertainty in\n\n\\[\n\\theta\n\\]\n\nshrinks.\n\nBut the uncertainty in\n\n\\[\ne\n\\]\n\ndoes not shrink, because the calibration dataset remains fixed.\n\nThe inferred parameter\n\n\\[\np=\\frac{\\theta-e}{1-2e}\n\\]\n\ntherefore becomes increasingly sensitive to whether the calibration interval correctly represents the remaining uncertainty.\n\nThe larger main sample exposes the defect.\n\nIt does not repair it.\n\n---\n\n# 10. z=np.convolve(z,block)\n    z=np.maximum(z,0.)\n    return z/z.sum()\n\ndef cluster_ci(k,s,alpha=ALPHA_E):\n    # Exact inversion of two-sided test tails,\n    # with beta family and ICC fixed.\n (t-e)/(1-2*e)\n        for t in (tl,tu)\n        for e in (el,eu)\n    ]\n\n    pl=max(0.,min(vals))\n    pu=min(1.,max(vals))\n\n    return (pl,pu) if pl<=pu else (1.,0.)\n\ndef degenerate=0.\n\n    for k in range(M+1):\n        for x in range(N+1):\n            pl,pu=p_interval(tci[x],eci[k])\n            mass=probs[k]*xp[x]\n\n            cover+=mass*(pl<=P<=pu)\n            width+=mass*max(0.,pu-pl)\n            degenerate+=mass*(pl==0 and pu==1)\n\n    return calcov,cover,width,degenerate\n\ndef main():\n    print(\n        'HALE S4 EXACT INTERVAL COVERAGE | (np.arange(M+1)-mean)**2,z\n            )\n        )\n\n        expected=(\n            M*E*(1-E)*(1+(s-1)*RHO)\n        )\n\n        assert abs(mean-M*E)<2e-11\n        assert Interpretation and limitations\n\nThis result is relevant to the research program's measurement discipline.\n\nA large dataset does not necessarily compensate for an incorrectly specified observation process.\n\nIn particular, a highly precise measurement of a transformed quantity can become misleading if the transformation depends on a poorly calibrated nuisance parameter.\n\nThe calculation also shows why a conservative interval should not automatically be taken as evidence that its underlying statistical model is correct.\n\nThere are important limitations.\n\nThe main observations were stipulated to be independent, while calibration observations alone were clustered.
